memory-and-knowledge-of-the-past.title: Memory and Knowledge of the Past
memory-and-knowledge-of-the-past.aka: the epistemology of memory; memory as a source of knowledge
memory-and-knowledge-of-the-past.note: Locke's annexed pastness, Russell's acquaintance with the past, Reid's original principle
memory-and-knowledge-of-the-past.question: Everything you know about the past — that you ate breakfast, that there was a yesterday at all — you know, in the end, by memory. But memory is a present state: an image, a feeling of familiarity, a judgement made now. How can a present state amount to knowledge of something that no longer exists? If memory merely stores and revives old perceptions, what marks a revival as a *memory* rather than an imagining — and what secures it against the plain fact that memory is, as Russell concedes, "notoriously fallacious"? The problem is foundational in an unusually literal way: take memory away and there is no past to reason about, no testimony to check (witnesses must remember), no induction (its premises are remembered observations), and no persisting self to do the reasoning.
memory-and-knowledge-of-the-past.ninety: *No Carneades lecture in the corpus is devoted to memory, so this version is distilled from the textbook presentation — Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. XI — and is marked as such.* Suppose an insistent questioner drives your beliefs back, reason by reason, to what needs no further reason. For the past, the regress ends at judgements of memory: you simply remember that the house next door was struck by lightning half a minute ago, and demanding a further ground misses what memory is. But memory will not stay uniformly solid. Run back over your day and certainty thins by degrees: you are quite certain of breakfast, less certain of the conversation at it, doubtful of some of it, blank on the rest — and there exist firm, confident memories that are wholly false. Russell's proposal is that the gradation is itself the guide: memory has *degrees of self-evidence*, and these correspond to its degrees of trustworthiness, reaching a limit of perfect self-evidence in the recent and vivid. Whether that correspondence can be trusted is the problem the three positions below divide over.

positions.name: Locke: memory is a power of revival, not a storehouse

blocks.text: Locke's *retention* (Essay, Book II, ch. x) is the mind's keeping of the simple ideas it has received, in two modes: contemplation, keeping an idea actually in view, and memory. Memory is usually pictured as a repository — "the storehouse of our ideas" — but Locke immediately corrects the picture. Our ideas "are nothing but actual perceptions in the mind, which cease to be anything when there is no perception of them"; so laying ideas up in memory "signifies no more but this — that the mind has a power in many cases to revive perceptions which it has once had, **with this additional perception annexed to them, that it has had them before**."

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Locke, *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding*, Book II, ch. x, §§1–6 — a formalization

steps.text: Ideas exist only while perceived; therefore nothing is literally warehoused in the mind between perceptions.

What we call memory is the power to revive a past perception, with an annexed perception of pastness — of *having had it before*. It is that annex, not the revived content, that makes the state a memory rather than a fresh imagining.

Revival is imperfect and perishable: attention, repetition, pleasure and pain fix ideas; without renewal they fade "like pictures drawn in fading colours," some minds retaining characters "like marble," others "little better than sand"; a fever can in days "calcine all those images to dust and confusion," and children blinded young lose their very ideas of colours.

Knowledge of the past, so far as it rests on retention, is the exercise of a fallible reproductive power whose credential is a present feeling of pastness — Locke gives no further guarantee, and the decay he catalogues is the price of the storehouse metaphor's correction.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Russell's (next position): if what is before the mind is only a present image plus a feeling, we could never *compare* the image with the remembered object and know how far it is accurate — yet we manifestly do, "within somewhat wide limits." A revived image whose pastness is a present annex seems to leave the past itself out of the transaction.

positions.name: Russell: acquaintance with the past, and self-evidence in degrees

blocks.text: Russell classifies memory twice, and the two classifications do different work. In ch. V, memory is a form of *acquaintance*: "we are still immediately aware of what we remember, in spite of the fact that it appears as past"; and this "immediate knowledge by memory is the source of all our knowledge concerning the past: without it, there could be no knowledge of the past by inference, since we should never know that there was anything past to be inferred." In ch. XI he analyses the corresponding *judgements* of memory as intuitive — not inferred from anything more evident — and faces the fallibility Locke catalogued.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. XI, "On Intuitive Knowledge" — a formalization

steps.text: The essence of memory is not an image. The image is present; what is remembered is known to be past. And we can compare our image with the object remembered and judge its accuracy — impossible unless the object, as opposed to the image, is "in some way before the mind."

Hence there must be intuitive judgements of memory: the past object itself immediately before the mind, recognized as past. "But for the fact of memory in this sense, we should not know that there ever was a past at all, nor should we be able to understand the word 'past'."

Fallibility is real but graded: memory "is trustworthy in proportion to the vividness of the experience and to its nearness in time," and degrees of self-evidence correspond to degrees of trustworthiness, up to the limit case (lightning half a minute ago) where doubt would be preposterous.

Memory is a basic, non-inferential source of knowledge of the past whose deliverances are self-evident *in degrees*; its fallibility qualifies its certainty case by case rather than disqualifying the faculty.

blocks.label: Russell's diagnosis of the counterexamples
blocks.text: the apparently fatal cases, of very firm belief in a wholly false memory, are argued to be not memory at all in the strict sense. George IV "is said to have at last believed that he was at the battle of Waterloo, because he had so often said that he was": what he immediately remembered was his repeated assertion; the further belief was produced by association with what was remembered, and association is not memory. "It would seem that cases of fallacious memory can probably all be dealt with in this way" — note the *probably*: Russell advances the diagnosis as a programme, not a proof.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the difficulty Russell himself states and does not claim to dissolve: fallacious memory "throws doubt on the trustworthiness of intuitive judgements in general." His own late-chapter suggestion (end of ch. XI) is that "self-evidence" combines two notions — one, corresponding to the highest degree, an infallible guarantee of truth; the other a mere presumption — and that he cannot yet develop the distinction. The degrees-reply also leans on a correlation (vividness/recency with accuracy) that is itself known, if at all, through memory.

positions.name: Reid: memory is an original principle of belief — asking for its reason is a category error

blocks.text: Reid's *Inquiry* (ch. II, §3, "Sensation and remembrance, natural principles of belief") draws the parallel Russell's account half-suggests. "There is a smell," is the immediate testimony of sense; "There was a smell," is the immediate testimony of memory — and neither admits a further reason. "If you ask me why I believe that the smell exists, I can give no other reason… than that I smell it. If you ask why I believe that it existed yesterday, I can give no other reason but that I remember it."

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Reid, *Inquiry into the Human Mind*, ch. II, §3 — a formalization; the corpus copy is a noisy OCR scan, and the passage used is among its legible ones

steps.text: Sensation compels my belief in the present existence of its object; memory compels my belief in its past existence; the compulsion in both cases is immediate, not the conclusion of an argument.

Sensation and memory are "simple, original, and perfectly distinct operations of the mind," and both are original *principles of belief* — starting points of the constitution, not inferences from more basic data (imagination, by contrast, compels no belief at all).

Memory's authority is constitutional and underived. To demand a justification of memory from outside memory is to demand of a first principle what first principles, by their nature, cannot have — the same demand Reid shows being made, with sceptical results, of sensation itself.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: from within this corpus, the standing difficulty is fallibility again: a principle that "compels belief" compels it also in cases like George IV's. Reid's framework can distinguish genuine remembrance from associated belief only by the felt character of the operation, which is what the false-memory cases put in doubt; the *Inquiry*'s text as we have it does not address that case directly, and this entry does not pretend otherwise.

thought.name: George IV at Waterloo
thought.text: (Russell, ch. XI). The king, having so often said he was at the battle, came at last to believe he had been there. Meant to test theories of memory against confident falsehood. Russell's use is diagnostic: the case must be reclassified (remembered assertion + associated belief) if memory proper is to remain a knowledge-source — a reclassification whose availability in *every* case is asserted only as probable. Pressures acquaintance and constitutional accounts hardest; Locke's revival-with-annex model accommodates the case more cheaply, since the annexed pastness can attach to the wrong content.

thought.name: Half a minute ago, and breakfast
thought.text: (Russell, ch. XI). Lightning struck the house next door half a minute ago: doubt is preposterous. Breakfast this morning: certain. The conversation at breakfast: partly recallable, partly doubtful, partly gone. Meant to exhibit self-evidence as a continuous magnitude tied to vividness and recency. Pressures any theory on which memory is simply reliable or simply not — and supplies the data the degrees-doctrine is built to fit.

thought.name: The blinded child's colours
thought.text: (Locke, Book II, ch. x, §5). Children who lose their sight young find, years later, that their ideas of colours have worn out entirely, "no more notion nor memory of colours left in their minds, than in those of people born blind." Meant to show ideas unrevised by the senses decay to nothing. Pressures the storehouse picture from inside (warehouses do not selectively evaporate) and any acquaintance account on which remembered data persist as objects of awareness: on Locke's showing, the past they give access to is itself shrinking.

thought.name: "There is a smell / There was a smell"
thought.text: (Reid, *Inquiry*, ch. II, §3). The minimal pair, offered as a complete epistemology of memory in two sentences: the second judgement has exactly the immediacy, and exactly the absence of supporting argument, as the first. Meant to shift the burden: memory needs no more vindication than perception does. Pressures the assumption — shared by Locke's revival model and by Russell's worry — that memory is perception's poorer relation.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: no lecture treats this problem; begin with Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. XI (judgements of memory; degrees of self-evidence; the George IV case) — also this entry's 90-second source.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Russell, ch. V (memory as acquaintance, and why all knowledge of the past rests on it).

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: Locke, *Essay*, Book II, ch. x, "Of Retention" (book 007, ch07 — full text); Reid, *Inquiry*, ch. II, §3 (book 007, ch11 — OCR-noisy but legible in the passages used).

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: book 007 stages no dedicated memory reading; the classical treatments are the *Essay* and *Inquiry* chapters above, with Plato's *Meno* recollection material (ch01) belonging to the different doctrine of anamnesis rather than to this problem.

memory-and-knowledge-of-the-past.verdict: The three sources agree on the load-bearing negative point: knowledge of the past is not inferred from present data by an argument that could be supplied on demand — each, in his own vocabulary (revival with annexed pastness; acquaintance with the past object; an original principle of belief), makes memory a basic source. They disagree about its anatomy and its credential. Locke's model explains fallibility and decay most naturally but leaves the pastness-annex doing unexplained work, and Russell's comparison objection — we can check an image against the remembered object — is directed at exactly that gap. Russell's model explains directness but must manage fallibility with the degrees doctrine and the not-really-memory diagnosis, both of which he presents with visible hedges ("probably," "it would seem," "only a suggestion"). Reid declines the management problem: compulsion by constitution is the end of justification, here as for perception. Nothing in the corpus adjudicates between them, and the corpus's contemporary epistemology (book 007, Parts II) contains no memory reading at all — the debate, as this corpus can state it, is a three-way classical stand-off over the faculty on which all the other entries' historical premises depend.

connections.text: [The Problem of Induction](problem-of-induction.md) — induction's data are remembered observations; if memory's gradations of self-evidence are not trustworthy, the inductive principle never gets its premises.

perception-and-sense-data.title: Perception and Sense-Data
perception-and-sense-data.aka: the problem of perception; appearance and reality
perception-and-sense-data.note: Locke's qualities, Berkeley's collapse, Russell's sense-data, Reid's sign-reading
perception-and-sense-data.question: When you look at a table, what are you actually aware of? The colour you see changes with the light, the point of view, and the state of your eyes; the shape you see changes as you move; a microscope replaces the smooth surface with hills and valleys. If what you immediately perceive is never quite the object as it is in itself, then perception does not hand you the world directly — it hands you appearances, which depend as much on you as on the object. What, then, do we perceive: the objects themselves, private data caused by them, or nothing but our own ideas? And which of the qualities we perceive — colour, warmth, shape, size — belong to the objects at all?
perception-and-sense-data.ninety: *No Carneades lecture in the corpus is devoted to this problem, so this version is distilled from the textbook presentation — Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. I — and is marked as such.* Concentrate on a table. To the eye it is oblong, brown, and shiny; to the touch, smooth, cool, and hard. But try to be precise and the troubles begin. No one colour is pre-eminently the table's colour: parts reflecting the light look brighter, the colour changes under artificial light, for a colour-blind observer, and through blue spectacles, and in the dark there is no colour at all, though touch and hearing find the table unchanged. The shape fares no better: a rectangular table looks, from almost every viewpoint, as if it had two acute and two obtuse angles, and its parallel sides look as if they converged. What we see is constantly changing as we move; the "real" shape is not seen but inferred. Russell's conclusion is terminological and substantive at once: call the things immediately known in sensation — colours, sounds, hardnesses, roughnesses — *sense-data*, and the experience of being aware of them *sensation*. The real table, if there is one, is not the sense-data and is not immediately known at all; it must be inferred from them. Everything else in this entry is a fight over what that inference delivers, and whether it is needed.

positions.name: Locke: primary qualities resemble, secondary qualities are powers

blocks.text: Bodies produce ideas in us, but the ideas divide. *Primary* qualities — solidity, extension, figure, motion or rest, number — are inseparable from body in every state and are found by sense in every perceptible particle of matter. *Secondary* qualities — colours, sounds, tastes, smells — are nothing in the objects themselves but powers, arising from the bulk, figure, texture, and motion of their insensible parts, to produce sensations in us.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Locke, *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding*, Book II, ch. viii, §§9–21 — a formalization

steps.text: Primary qualities survive every division and alteration: divide a grain of wheat as far as you like, each part still has solidity, extension, figure, and mobility.

Secondary-quality ideas fail the parallel tests. Porphyry's red and white vanish in the dark and return with the light, though no real alteration is made in the stone; pounding an almond changes its colour and taste by changing only its texture; the same water feels cold to one hand and warm to the other, which it could not do if heat and cold were both really in it — and nobody thinks the pain or sickness manna causes is *in* the manna, though it is produced by the same kind of operation as its sweetness and whiteness.

"The ideas of primary qualities of bodies are resemblances of them, and their patterns do really exist in the bodies themselves; but the ideas produced in us by these secondary qualities have no resemblance of them at all" (§15).

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Berkeley (below): the two classes cannot be prised apart, since extension and figure cannot be conceived without some secondary quality, and the primary qualities are just as relative to the perceiver as the secondary ones.

positions.name: Berkeley: there is no material substratum behind the ideas

blocks.text: Berkeley accepts Locke's starting point — what we perceive are ideas — and denies the step beyond them. In the *Treatise* (§§3–4) he argues that the very meaning of *exist*, applied to sensible things, is to be perceived: "Their *esse* is *percipi*, nor is it possible they should have any existence out of the minds or thinking things which perceive them." The table exists when nobody is in the study because some other spirit perceives it, or because it would be perceived by anyone suitably placed — permanence is supplied by God's perception, not by an unthinking substance.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Berkeley, *A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge*, Part I, §§3–4, 9–11 — a formalization

steps.text: The objects of perception are the things we perceive by sense; and what we perceive besides our own ideas or sensations, Berkeley challenges us to name.
It is repugnant that any idea, or combination of ideas, should exist unperceived, since an idea can be like nothing but another idea, and its whole being is to be before a mind.

The escape route — Locke's distinction — fails: figure, motion, and the rest of the primary qualities are inseparably united with the secondary qualities and cannot even in thought be abstracted from them (§10); and great/small, swift/slow are relative to the perceiver's frame and organs, so mind-free extension would be neither great nor small — nothing at all (§11).

The notion of matter — an inert, senseless substance in which extension, figure, and motion actually subsist unperceived — involves a contradiction. Sensible things are ideas, and ideas exist only in minds.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. IV: the argument trades on confusing the *act* of apprehension, which is mental, with the *object* apprehended, which need not be. "When a man says that some business he had to arrange went clean out of his mind, he does not mean to imply that the business itself was ever in his mind": being *before* the mind is not being *in* the mind in the sense that would make the tree mental. Russell adds that Berkeley's arguments of detail — that sense-data depend on us — are "almost certainly valid," but they prove dependence on the perceiver's organs and standpoint, not mentality.

positions.name: Russell: sense-data are signs; of the physical object we know structure, not intrinsic nature

blocks.text: Granting (ch. II, and the skepticism entry) that physical objects exist independently, Russell asks what perception tells us about them — and answers: their relations, not their qualities. Physical space is public and one; our spaces of sight and touch are private and many. The two must correspond in arrangement — the house that looks nearer is reached sooner, is nearer on the map, and looks nearer to everyone — but correspondence of arrangement is all we get.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. III, "The Nature of Matter" — a formalization

steps.text: Sense-data are in private spaces (the space of sight, the space of touch), which differ from person to person and sense to sense; the physical object is in one public, physical space — as the sun we see is the sun of eight minutes ago shows, sense-data and object are not even straightforwardly simultaneous.

If sense-data are to be evidence for physical objects, the relative positions of objects in physical space must more or less correspond to the relative positions of sense-data in private spaces; order (before/after, left/right in a marching regiment) is preserved across viewpoints while shape is not.

We can know only what the correspondence requires: that one physical distance is greater than another, or collinear with it — as a man born blind can know everything about the space of sight that other people can tell him, except what sight is like.

"Although the relations of physical objects have all sorts of knowable properties, derived from their correspondence with the relations of sense-data, the physical objects themselves remain unknown in their intrinsic nature, so far at least as can be discovered by means of the senses."

blocks.label: A resemblance Russell refuses
blocks.text: the tempting compromise, that physical objects really have colours and we sometimes see them as they are, is "not capable of being definitely refuted, but it can be shown to be groundless": the colour seen depends only on the light-waves reaching the eye, modified by the intervening medium and the manner of reflection, so the same colour would be seen whether the object had any colour or not. What holds for colours "is closely similar to what holds for other sense-data."

positions.name: Reid: perception is the constitution reading natural signs — no inference, no resemblance required

blocks.text: Reid rejects the shared premise of Locke, Berkeley, and (as he would see it) Russell: that the mind's immediate objects are ideas or data from which the world must be recovered. In the *Inquiry* a sensation is a *natural sign*: nature has established a connexion between sign and thing signified, and has also taught us the interpretation, so that "previous to experience, the sign suggests the thing signified, and creates the belief of it." By one original principle of our constitution a certain sensation signifies hardness in the body handled; by another, motion. Perception therefore involves, from the start, a conception of the external quality and an irresistible belief in its present existence — not a conclusion drawn from a private datum.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Reid, *Inquiry into the Human Mind*, ch. V, "Of Touch," and ch. VI, "Of Seeing" — a formalization; the corpus copy is a noisy OCR scan of a 19th-century edition, and the reconstruction keeps only to passages legible in it

steps.text: There are three ways the mind passes from a natural sign to the conception and belief of the thing signified: by original principles of our constitution, by custom, and by reasoning. Our *original* perceptions come by the first way; *acquired* perceptions by the second.

The conception of hardness — one of our most common and distinct notions — resembles no sensation and is derived from neither sensation nor reflection considered as a copy; it is "suggested by our constitution," together with belief.

Perception is not the inspection of an inner object plus an inference outward. The theory that makes ideas the immediate objects of perception is the innovation to be justified — and, Reid argues in ch. I, it is the shared system of Descartes, Malebranche, and Locke that, consistently developed by Berkeley and Hume, ends in scepticism.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Russell's variation arguments (ch. I) are the standing pressure: if perception delivered the quality itself, why does the delivered colour vary with light, organ, and viewpoint while the object does not? Reid's framework has a reply available in his own terms — the sensation varies because it is a sign, and signs need not resemble what they signify — but it comes at the cost of making the connexion between this sensation and that quality a brute fact of our constitution, which is exactly where Reid is content to stop and his opponents are not.

thought.name: The table
thought.text: (Russell, ch. I). Setup as in the 90-second version: colour, texture, and shape all vary with viewpoint, light, and instrument. Meant to show that no appearance can simply be identified with the object. Pressures any direct identification of what is perceived with the physical object; it is the seed of the sense-data vocabulary.

thought.name: Porphyry in the dark
thought.text: (Locke, II.viii §19). Hinder light from striking the red-and-white stone and its colours vanish; restore the light and they return — with no real alteration in the stone. Meant to show that colour is a power grounded in texture, not a quality resident in the stone as perceived. Pressures naive realism about colour specifically; Berkeley extends the same treatment to the primary qualities Locke exempts.

thought.name: Manna: sweetness and sickness
thought.text: (Locke, II.viii §18). Everyone agrees the sickness and griping manna causes are not *in* the manna. But sweetness and whiteness are produced by the same sort of operation of the same parts. Meant to show the asymmetry between primary and secondary qualities cannot be the familiar one between "really in it" and "merely caused in us." Pressures the common-sense placement of tastes and colours in objects.

thought.name: The same water, two hands
thought.text: (Locke, II.viii §21). Water feels cold to one hand and warm to the other at the same time. If both ideas were resemblances of qualities in the water, the water would be both hot and cold at once. Meant to show heat/cold ideas are effects of relative motion in the perceiver's parts. Pressures resemblance theories for the felt qualities.

thought.name: The circular coin and the blind man
thought.text: (Russell, ch. III). A coin judged circular looks oval from almost every angle; its real shape belongs to physical space, which nobody's private space reproduces. And what we can know of physical space is exactly what a man born blind could be told about visual space — every structural fact, nothing of what it is like. Meant to fix the ceiling on perceptual knowledge: structure without intrinsic nature. Pressures both Locke (resemblance survives, at best, for structure) and any view promising direct acquaintance with physical qualities.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: no lecture covers this problem directly; begin with Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. I (the table), which is also this entry's 90-second source.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Russell, ch. III (the nature of matter: private vs physical space, structure) and ch. IV (idealism and the act/object reply).

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: Locke, *Essay*, Book II, ch. viii (qualities, §§7–22); Berkeley, *Treatise*, Part I, §§1–12 (book 007, ch09 — full text in the corpus); Reid, *Inquiry*, chs. V–VI (book 007, ch11 — full but OCR-noisy).

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: the classical sequence as book 007 stages it — Locke (ch07) → Berkeley (ch09) → Reid (ch11) — read against Russell's chs. I, III, IV in book 006.

perception-and-sense-data.verdict: Nothing here is settled, and the four positions in this corpus disagree at different joints. Locke and Berkeley agree that colours as perceived are not in objects as perceived; they split on whether figure and extension fare better — Berkeley's inseparability argument is aimed exactly at that exemption, and Russell judges Berkeley's detail arguments largely valid while rejecting his conclusion on act/object grounds. Russell and Locke agree there is a mind-independent object; they split on resemblance — Russell keeps only structural correspondence and calls fuller resemblance groundless. Reid rejects the common starting point of the other three: if sensations are signs interpreted by constitution, the demand to recover the object from a datum never arises — but his stopping point (original principles of our constitution) is one the others treat as the thing to be explained. The corpus's later anthology material that would develop the debate (C. I. Lewis on the given, book 007 ch16; Ayer, ch15) is present only as citation stubs, so no further side can be stated from the corpus yet.

connections.title: External-World Skepticism
connections.text: [External-World Skepticism](external-world-skepticism.md) — the prior question: whether anything exists beyond the sense-data at all. This entry assumes Russell's ch. II answer (something does) and asks what perception then tells us about it.

connections.title: Knowledge by Acquaintance and by Description
connections.text: [Knowledge by Acquaintance and by Description](knowledge-by-acquaintance-and-description.md) — the machinery that names the two sides of the perceptual relation: sense-data are the paradigm of acquaintance; the physical object, known only as "the object which causes such-and-such sense-data," is the paradigm of description.

connections.title: Memory and Knowledge of the Past
connections.text: [Memory and Knowledge of the Past](memory-and-knowledge-of-the-past.md) — Reid pairs the two throughout: "There is a smell" is the testimony of sense, "There was a smell" the equally immediate testimony of memory.

sources: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy* (book 006): ch. I, "Appearance and Reality" (extraction files ch05–ch06); ch. III, "The Nature of Matter" (files ch09–ch10); ch. IV, "Idealism" (files ch11–ch12) — all read in full.
Locke, *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (book 007, ch07 — the file is the complete *Essay*): Book II, ch. viii, §§7–22, read in full.
Berkeley, *A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge* (book 007, ch09): Introduction §§1–6 and Part I, §§1–12, read in full.

Reid, *Inquiry into the Human Mind* (book 007, ch11): contents; ch. I (the "ideal system" and its sceptical issue); ch. II, §3 (sensation and remembrance as principles of belief); ch. V (the conception and belief of hardness suggested by constitution); ch. VI (original and acquired perception; natural signs) — read in the scanned edition; OCR noise (long-s misreadings, some interleaved pages) noted where it affects a passage.

Lectures: the youtube corpus was searched by title and by transcript for a perception / sense-data lecture ("sense data," "primary qualities"); none exists. The only transcript hits were incidental mentions in "A Priori and A Posteriori Distinction" and "Who Was John Locke," neither of which treats this problem.

problem-of-induction.title: The Problem of Induction
problem-of-induction.aka: Hume's problem; the justification of induction; (Goodman's version) the new riddle of induction
problem-of-induction.note: Hume's circle, Russell's a priori principle, Goodman's new riddle
problem-of-induction.question: Nearly everything we expect — that the sun will rise tomorrow, that bread will nourish rather than poison, that dropped stones fall — rests on induction: inferring from observed cases to unobserved ones, from "every A so far has been B" to "the next A will be B" or "all A's are B." The inference is not deductively valid: no contradiction follows from supposing the pattern breaks tomorrow. And the obvious bridging principle — nature is uniform, the future will resemble the past — seems to be supportable only by pointing to its past success, which is the very kind of inference in question. Can induction be justified at all, and if not, what are we doing when we rely on it?
problem-of-induction.ninety: Draw black balls from an urn, one after another — black, black, black. The *strong* conclusion, that the next ball must be black, does not follow: to get from past to future you need a bridge premise, "the future will resemble the past," and the only support for that premise is that the future has resembled the past *so far* — a claim about what has already happened, offered in support of a claim about what will happen, by assuming the bridge itself. That is begging the question. The sunrise is the same argument at larger scale. So the lecture counsels suspending judgment about any claim that science delivers certainty — and even the *weak* conclusion, that the next ball will *probably* be black, gets attacked in the follow-up: Nelson Goodman's new riddle asks which predicates induction is allowed to project. All observed emeralds are green; but define "grue" — green if examined before some future time *t*, blue thereafter — and every observation so far confirms "all emeralds are grue" just as well, with the opposite prediction after *t*. Goodman's own answer, that "green" wins only by *entrenchment* (our habit of projecting it), makes the choice look conventional rather than justified. (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [The Problem of Induction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sd8cxXfPJU4), [The New Riddle of Induction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kGE2Ig2dvaE).)

positions.name: Hume's sceptical argument: no reasoning supports the step

blocks.text: Hume's *Enquiry* §IV first narrows all factual reasoning to cause and effect, and causal knowledge to experience: "the knowledge of this relation is not, in any instance, attained by reasonings *a priori*; but arises entirely from experience, when we find that any particular objects are constantly conjoined with each other." Adam, with perfect rational faculties, "could not have inferred from the fluidity and transparency of water that it would suffocate him." An effect "is a distinct event from its cause" and can never be discovered by scrutinizing the cause. Then Part II presses the remaining question: what founds our conclusions *from* experience?

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Hume, *Enquiry*, §IV, ¶¶28–32 — the negative argument

steps.text: All our experimental conclusions "proceed upon the supposition that the future will be conformable to the past."

This supposition cannot be established demonstratively: its contrary implies no contradiction — "May I not clearly and distinctly conceive that a body, falling from the clouds, and which, in all other respects, resembles snow, has yet the taste of salt or feeling of fire?"

It cannot be established by probable (experimental) argument either: all such arguments are themselves founded on the relation of cause and effect as learned from experience, and so "must be evidently going in a circle, and taking that for granted, which is the very point in question."
Even after we have experience of constant conjunction, "our conclusions from that experience are *not* founded on reasoning, or any process of the understanding."

blocks.text: Two supporting tests in the text. The missing medium: "These two propositions are far from being the same, *I have found that such an object has always been attended with such an effect*, and *I foresee, that other objects, which are, in appearance, similar, will be attended with similar effects*" — whoever claims a chain of reasoning joins them is asked to produce it. And the infant test: if the inference were made by reason, it "would be as perfect at first, and upon one instance, as after ever so long a course of experience" — yet nothing so like as eggs still requires long experience before we trust the taste; children and even animals learn from experience, so the operative process cannot be an argument too abstruse for them (¶¶31, 33).

positions.name: Hume's sceptical solution: custom or habit

blocks.text: Hume's answer to his own argument is not a justification but a diagnosis of what actually moves us.

steps.text: After the constant conjunction of two objects, "we are determined by custom alone to expect the one from the appearance of the other." Custom — repetition producing a propensity to renew the inference "without being impelled by any reasoning or process of the understanding" — is "the ultimate principle, which we can assign, of all our conclusions from experience."

This principle operates as instinct: nature has "implanted in us an instinct, which carries forward the thought in a correspondent course to that which she has established among external objects," and it "will preserve its influence as long as human nature remains the same" regardless of our sceptical conclusions.

Inductive inference is natural, unavoidable, and indispensable — but its foundation is a propensity of human nature, not a justification by reason. Hume calls this the *sceptical solution* of the doubts of §IV, in contrast to a refutation he does not offer.

positions.name: Russell: the inductive principle, accepted a priori

blocks.text: Russell takes up exactly Hume's question — "Do any number of cases of a law being fulfilled in the past afford evidence that it will be fulfilled in the future?" — and states the principle on which all such inference tacitly relies. (The chicken is his: the man who fed the chicken every day of its life "at last wrings its neck instead, showing that more refined views as to the uniformity of nature would have been useful to the chicken.")

blocks.label: The principle of induction
blocks.source: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. VI
blocks.text: , for particular cases and, repeated, for general laws:

items: (a) When a thing of sort A has been found associated with a thing of sort B and never dissociated, "the greater the number of cases in which A and B have been associated, the greater is the probability that they will be associated in a fresh case."
(b) "Under the same circumstances, a sufficient number of cases of association will make the probability of a fresh association nearly a certainty, and will make it approach certainty without limit."

blocks.label: Russell's argument for accepting it
blocks.source: *Problems*, chs. VI–VII

steps.text: The principle "is equally incapable of being proved by an appeal to experience": experience could confirm it only for cases already examined, while its whole use concerns the unexamined — "we can never use experience to prove the inductive principle without begging the question."

Nor can experience disprove it: probability is always relative to data, and failures (the black swan against "all swans are white") show only that other data can alter a probability, not that the original estimate was wrong.

Some principles are known otherwise than by experiential proof: the self-evident logical principles ("whatever follows from a true proposition is true"; the traditional laws of thought) cannot be proved by experience because all proof presupposes them, yet are known — experience *elicits* such knowledge without *proving* it; this knowledge is a priori.

The inductive principle belongs with these principles of inference, except that where the logical ones yield certainty it yields only probability; in ch. VII Russell calls it "perhaps the most important example" of the principles that let us infer "a greater or less probability that something is true."
"We must either accept the inductive principle on the ground of its intrinsic evidence, or forgo all justification of our expectations about the future."

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the standing objection is Hume's circle itself (above), which Russell does not dispute: his move is to relocate the principle outside experience rather than to answer the circularity charge on its own ground. Whether "intrinsic evidence" names a genuine kind of justification, or merely labels the place where justification runs out, is a question Russell's text leaves the reader to judge; in his ch. VII he is careful that all a priori knowledge concerning *existence* is only hypothetical — connexions between universals, not guarantees about what will happen.

positions.name: Goodman's new riddle: which predicates may we project?

blocks.text: Goodman grants, for argument, what Hume and Russell debate, and finds a second problem underneath: induction does not work for generalizations as such, but only for *law-like* ones, and we have no non-circular way to say which are law-like. ("The last three men to board this bus wore glasses" is not confirmed by its instances the way "all icicles are cold" is.)

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades lecture, "The New Riddle of Induction," presenting Goodman, "The New Riddle of Induction," 1954 — formalized; Goodman's paper is not in this corpus

steps.text: A generalization is confirmed by its instances, in a way that supports prediction, only if its predicates are law-like (projectible); coincidental generalizations are not.

Define *grue*: an object is grue if it is examined before time *t* and green, or not examined before *t* and blue. Every emerald examined so far is grue as well as green, so the same evidence confirms "all emeralds are grue" — which predicts that emeralds first examined after *t* will be blue.

The only difference Goodman finds between "green" and "grue" is *entrenchment*: we are accustomed to projecting "green." In a language that had entrenched "grue" and "bleen" instead, "green" would be definable only disjunctively ("grue before *t*, bleen after") and would look like the artificial predicate.

We cannot determine, from the evidence and the logic of confirmation alone, which predicates form law-like generalizations — and so cannot tell, by that route, when induction is working and when it is not.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the corpus's lecture series stages two. The *disjunctive objection* (grue is disjunctive, green is not) is answered, per the lecture's report of Goodman, by the symmetry of P3: relative to a grue/bleen language, green is the disjunctive predicate. *Swinburne's objection* (source: Carneades, [Swinburne's Objection](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ye9qprxFP28)) draws a different line: *qualitative* predicates (like green) can be applied without knowing the time or place, while *locational* predicates (like grue) cannot — around *t*, the grue-speakers "would have to look at their watches in order to talk about colors." So, when two predicates fit equally, prefer the qualitative: grue is superfluous. The lecture closes by announcing a further video giving Goodman's possible response — so within the corpus's own staging, the exchange is left open.

thought.name: The urn
thought.text: ([The Problem of Induction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sd8cxXfPJU4)). Black ball after black ball from an unseen urn; the case is built to separate the strong conclusion (the next *will* be black) from the weak one (it *probably* will), and to show the strong one needs the question-begging bridge.

thought.name: The sunrise
thought.text: (the lecture; Russell, ch. VI). "We are all convinced that the sun will rise to-morrow" — Russell's point is that appealing to the laws of motion only relocates the doubt, since our reason for trusting those laws tomorrow is again that they have held so far.

thought.name: The chicken
thought.text: (Russell, ch. VI). Fed daily by the same hand throughout its life; the hand wrings its neck. Crude expectations of uniformity are "liable to be misleading" even after a lifetime of confirmations — the case pressures naive confidence without touching the principle's probabilistic core.

thought.name: Bread
thought.text: (Hume, §IV ¶29; Russell, ch. VI). Bread's sensible qualities tell us nothing of its "secret powers" of nourishment; that past bread nourished does not, without the contested step, show the next loaf will not poison.

thought.name: Grue emeralds
thought.text: (Goodman, via the lecture). The time-indexed predicate; see the argument above. What it is meant to show: confirmation is predicate-relative, and evidence alone does not choose between rival projections.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: [The Problem of Induction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sd8cxXfPJU4) → [The New Riddle of Induction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kGE2Ig2dvaE) → [Swinburne's Objection](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ye9qprxFP28).

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. VI ("On Induction") and ch. VII ("On Our Knowledge of General Principles").

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: Hume, *Enquiry*, §IV ("Sceptical Doubts concerning the Operations of the Understanding") and §V ("Sceptical Solution of these Doubts") — book 007, ch10, full text in the corpus.

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: Goodman's "The New Riddle of Induction" itself (not in this corpus; the lectures are the corpus's access point), and book 007's Kant (ch12, *Prolegomena* — full text) for the most famous attempt to relocate the problem.

problem-of-induction.verdict: Within these sources, the negative core is common ground: no justification of induction from experience alone can avoid circularity — Hume proves it, Russell concedes it, and the lecture's strong-claim verdict ("suspend judgment") restates it. The disagreement is over the remainder. Hume stops at psychology: custom does the work, and no foundation in reason is to be had. Russell insists a foundation exists but is a priori and merely probabilistic — acceptance "on the ground of its intrinsic evidence." Goodman's riddle (as the lectures present it) undercuts a lazy version of the probabilistic remainder by asking which generalizations probability is even allowed to attach to, and in this corpus its exchange with Swinburne is unfinished — a response on Goodman's behalf is promised, not delivered. No source here claims induction yields certainty; the most anyone claims is probability approaching it.

connections.title: External-World Skepticism
connections.text: [External-World Skepticism](external-world-skepticism.md) — the twin problem by the same author: in both, experience cannot non-circularly certify a step beyond itself (to external objects; to unobserved cases), and Russell deploys the same toolkit (instinctive belief, a priori principles) on both.

connections.title: Gettier and the Analysis of Knowledge
connections.text: [Gettier and the Analysis of Knowledge](gettier-and-the-analysis-of-knowledge.md) — whether an inductively formed true belief counts as knowledge depends on the analysandum there; Russell's *derivative knowledge* is defined so as to route through intuitively known premises and a priori principles, induction included.
A priori knowledge (Russell, chs. VII–VIII; Kant in book 007, ch12) — the proposed home of the inductive principle, and the next problem in the subfield's spine.

sources: Hume, *Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding* (book 007, file ch10): §IV, Parts I–II, and §V, Parts I–II — read in full; §XII read in full for the cross-connection to skepticism.
Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy* (book 006): ch. VI, "On Induction" (extraction files ch15–ch16); ch. VII, "On Our Knowledge of General Principles" (files ch17–ch18) — read in full.
Lectures (Carneades.org): "The Problem of Induction"; "The New Riddle of Induction"; "Swinburne's Objection (To The New Riddle of Induction)".

truth-and-falsehood.title: Truth and Falsehood
truth-and-falsehood.aka: the theory of truth; correspondence vs coherence
truth-and-falsehood.note: Russell's requisites, coherence as criterion, the multiple-relation theory
truth-and-falsehood.question: Beliefs and statements can be true or false; tables and colours cannot. What does the difference consist in? "Charles I died on the scaffold" is true and "Charles I died in his bed" is false, and nothing about the beliefs themselves — their vividness, their coherence with what else the believer holds, the care taken in arriving at them — settles which is which: an event of two and a half centuries ago does. So truth seems to be a relation between a belief and something outside it. But saying exactly what the relation is, and to what, without either smuggling truth back into the definition or positing queer entities for false beliefs to relate to, is the problem of truth. Note what the problem is not: it is not "which of our beliefs are true?" — Russell insists the questions be kept entirely separate, on pain of answering neither.
truth-and-falsehood.ninety: Take a homely case: is today a holiday — really? Say "today is New Year's Day." What would make that true? On the *correspondence* theory, something in the world: but a holiday is not a physical object like a cup or a piano, and if the term corresponded to the objects people celebrate with, the holiday would cease to exist when the fireworks stopped, and different celebrations in different places would splinter one holiday into many. On the *coherence* theory, a statement is true if it is consistent with, and fits into, a set of other beliefs: "today is Halloween" is true because it coheres with the beliefs of your culture. But then whose set decides, when Europeans, Ethiopians, Chinese, and Muslims keep different New Years? The lecture's suggestion is that holiday-truths sit between the objective and the subjective — culturally relative — while noting that both theories carry further problems of their own. The homely case is a probe: whatever truth is, it must handle statements whose truth-makers are not obviously sitting in the physical world. (Distilled from the Carneades lecture: [Are Holidays Real? (Theories of Truth)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ei_bbIO8L1Y).)

positions.name: Preliminary: truth belongs to propositions, not to ideas (Locke)

blocks.text: Locke opens his chapter "Of True and False Ideas" by withdrawing the terms from ideas altogether. Truth and falsehood belong, in propriety of speech, only to propositions — to affirmations and negations. An idea, a bare appearance in the mind, can no more be false than a single name can: the idea of a centaur has no more falsehood in it than the word "centaur" pronounced aloud. Ideas get *called* true or false only when the mind tacitly refers them to something outside them — to other men's ideas under the same name, to real existence, or to a thing's real essence — thereby making a secret proposition about their conformity, which proposition is what is actually true or false. Russell begins from the same boundary (below, requisite (2)): truth and falsehood are properties of beliefs and statements, and a world of mere matter would contain facts but no truths.

positions.name: Russell's three requisites, and the rejection of coherence as a definition

blocks.text: Russell (ch. XII) sets three conditions any theory of truth must meet: (1) it must admit an opposite, falsehood — a theory under which all our thinking ought to have been true has failed before it starts; (2) truth and falsehood are properties of beliefs and statements — no beliefs, no truth, in the sense correlative to falsehood; (3) the truth of a belief depends on something outside the belief itself, as the Charles I example shows. Requisite (3) pushes toward correspondence; but before following it, Russell examines the most important theory that tries to do without an outside relatum.

blocks.label: The coherence theory, as Russell states it
blocks.text: the mark of falsehood is failure to cohere in the body of our beliefs, and the essence of a truth is to form part of the completely rounded system which is The Truth.

blocks.label: Canonical argument against it
blocks.source: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. XII — a formalization

steps.text: If coherence defined truth, there could be at most one coherent body of beliefs. But there is no reason to suppose only one is possible: a novelist might invent a past for the world that fits everything we know and differs entirely from the real past, and in science two or more hypotheses routinely account for all the known facts.

Coherence itself presupposes truth: two propositions are coherent when both *may be true*, incoherent when one at least *must be false*; whether "this tree is a beech" and "this tree is not a beech" can both be true is known only via the law of contradiction — and if that law were itself subjected to the coherence test, nothing would be incoherent with anything. The laws of logic supply the framework within which the test applies and cannot be established by it.
"Coherence cannot be accepted as giving the meaning of truth, though it is often a most important test of truth after a certain amount of truth has become known."

positions.name: Correspondence, defined: the multiple-relation theory (Russell)

blocks.text: The obstacle to a correspondence definition is falsehood. If belief were a two-term relation between a mind and a single object — what is believed — then Othello's false belief that Desdemona loves Cassio would require an object, "Desdemona's love for Cassio," which does not exist; and positing objective falsehoods as subsistent entities is a theory "to be avoided if possible." Russell's solution: believing is a *multiple* relation, knitting the subject and the several objects into one complex in a definite order (the "sense" or direction of the relation does the ordering: Desdemona–loving–Cassio is a different judgement from Cassio–loving–Desdemona with the same constituents).

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. XII — a formalization of the chapter's constructive argument

steps.text: In every judgement there is a subject (the mind) and objects (the terms judged about, one of which is a relation — here, *loving* — occurring in the belief as a brick in the structure, not as the cement; the cement is the relation *believing*).

When the belief is true, there is a second complex unity composed exclusively of the objects, in the same order, with the object-relation now doing the uniting: "Desdemona's love for Cassio." When the belief is false, there is no such complex.

A belief is true when there is a corresponding *fact* — such a complex unity of its object-terms united by its object-relation — and false when there is no corresponding fact. Hence truth depends on minds for the existence of beliefs, but not for their truth: "minds do not create truth or falsehood. They create beliefs… What makes a belief true is a fact," and the fact (catching-trains-type exceptions aside) does not involve the believer's mind at all.

blocks.label: Where Russell takes it next
blocks.text: ch. XIII demotes the defeated rival to an instrument: coherence, rejected as the *definition* of truth, returns as a *criterion* among probable opinions. A body of individually probable beliefs that are mutually coherent become more probable than any alone; it is the coherence test that "condemns the dreams and confirms the waking life." But the test "never gives absolute certainty, unless there is certainty already at some point in the coherent system" — organization of probable opinion cannot by itself manufacture indubitable knowledge.

thought.name: Charles I: scaffold or bed
thought.text: (Russell, ch. XII). Two beliefs, alike in every intrinsic respect a believer could inspect; one true, one false, in virtue of an event two and a half centuries old. Meant to isolate requisite (3): truth is extrinsic to the belief. Pressures every internalist definition — vividness, felt certainty, and (the chapter argues next) coherence among the believer's other beliefs.

thought.name: Othello's belief
thought.text: (Russell, ch. XII). Othello falsely believes Desdemona loves Cassio. There is no such thing as Desdemona's love for Cassio for his belief to be *of*. Meant to show belief cannot be a relation to a single object, on pain of objective falsehoods. Pressures simple correspondence pictures ("a belief pictures a fact") into Russell's multiple-relation refinement.

thought.name: The novelist's alternative past
thought.text: (Russell, ch. XII). A sufficiently imaginative novelist invents a past that fits everything we know and is wholly different from the real one; the resulting system coheres as well as ours does. Meant to show coherence cannot be the *meaning* of truth. Pressures coherence theories to explain what singles out one coherent system — and connects this entry to the skepticism entry's dream hypothesis, which Russell gives as the philosophical case of the same construction.

thought.name: New Year's Day, in four calendars
thought.text: (the Theories of Truth lecture). Europeans, Ethiopians, Chinese, and Muslims celebrate different New Years; "today is New Year's Day" coheres with each community's beliefs on different days. Meant to press the coherence theory's unanswered question — whose belief-set is the standard? — and correspondence's mirror-image question, what worldly item makes any of them true. Pressures both theories at once, which is the lecture's point: holiday statements are where each theory's bookkeeping gets hard.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: [Are Holidays Real? (Theories of Truth)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ei_bbIO8L1Y) — correspondence and coherence tested on statements with elusive truth-makers.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy*, ch. XII ("Truth and Falsehood") — the requisites, the coherence objections, the multiple-relation definition — with ch. XIII for coherence's second career as a criterion.

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: Russell ch. XII is itself the primary text in this corpus; Locke, *Essay*, Book II, ch. xxxii (book 007, ch07) for the prior boundary question — what truth and falsehood can even be properties *of*.

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: book 007 contains no dedicated truth anthology section; its nearest neighbours are Aquinas on truth (ch05 — in this corpus only the *Summa*'s prologue and tables of contents, no usable text on truth itself) and James (ch13 — the file is the *Will to Believe* essay collection, which does not contain James's later pragmatist theory of truth). The contemporary truth debate is therefore not yet statable from this corpus.

truth-and-falsehood.verdict: In these sources, correspondence wins the definitional contest by elimination and construction: coherence fails Russell's two tests (possible rival systems; presupposition of logical truth), and his multiple-relation account is offered as satisfying all three requisites at once. But the victory is carefully bounded. Russell does not claim the definition tells us which beliefs are true — that harder question is deferred to ch. XIII and answered there only with degrees of self-evidence and probability. The lecture's holiday case marks a class of statements where correspondence's truth-makers are genuinely obscure and coherence's standard-set is genuinely ambiguous, and it leaves the case — and with it the contest between the theories — open, gesturing at a cultural-relativity middle position it does not develop. Locke's contribution stands apart from the contest: whichever theory wins, its subject matter is propositions and beliefs, not ideas or things. Unsettled: whether Russell's "fact" (a complex unity of the belief's objects) can be specified without circularity for all belief-types, and what to say about domains, like holidays, where the putative facts are themselves partly constituted by belief.

connections.title: Gettier and the Analysis of Knowledge
connections.text: [Gettier and the Analysis of Knowledge](gettier-and-the-analysis-of-knowledge.md) — the "T" in justified true belief presupposes this entry's problem; Russell's ch. XIII (this entry's criterion discussion) is also where the corpus's earliest Gettier-style cases live.

connections.title: Knowledge by Acquaintance and by Description
connections.text: [Knowledge by Acquaintance and by Description](knowledge-by-acquaintance-and-description.md) — acquaintance admits no opposite: there is no erroneous acquaintance, only erroneous judgement. The dualism of truth and falsehood begins exactly where acquaintance ends and judgement begins.

connections.title: A Priori Knowledge
connections.text: [A Priori Knowledge](a-priori-knowledge.md) — the laws of logic do double duty: paradigms of a priori knowledge there; here, the framework that the coherence definition of truth must presuppose.

connections.title: External-World Skepticism
connections.text: [External-World Skepticism](external-world-skepticism.md) — the dream hypothesis reappears in ch. XIII as the test case coherence-as-criterion is asked to adjudicate (it condemns the dreams), an adjudication the skepticism entry reports as probabilistic, not demonstrative.

sources: Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy* (book 006): ch. XII, "Truth and Falsehood" (extraction files ch27–ch28); ch. XIII, "Knowledge, Error, and Probable Opinion" (files ch29–ch30) — read in full.

are-moral-considerations-overriding.title: Are Moral Considerations Overriding?
are-moral-considerations-overriding.aka: the overridingness (authority) of morality; the demands of impartiality vs personal projects
are-moral-considerations-overriding.question: Suppose morality speaks: it tells you what you must do. How much authority should its voice have against everything else you care about — your family, your friendships, your projects, your life's work, your own flourishing? The **overridingness** thesis says moral considerations always trump: when morality and personal concern conflict, morality wins, and wins by its nature as morality. The textbook's final section of ch. 2 doubts this — not by denying morality's importance, but by asking whether two great modern systems (Kantian impartiality and act-utilitarianism) have *built in* an overridingness that distorts moral life itself: making the agent a stranger to her own attachments, and demanding a saintliness that would extinguish most of what makes a life worth living. The problem is not whether morality matters, but whether "mattering most, always" is a coherent or attractive thing for morality to claim.
are-moral-considerations-overriding.ninety: *No Carneades lecture is devoted to this problem; the following is distilled from the textbook (Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 2, final section) and is marked accordingly, per the build rules.* Bernard Williams's charge against both Kantianism and utilitarianism is that they demand an **impartiality** no recognisable human life can contain. The utilitarian agent, in Williams's phrase, is a mere "representative of the satisfaction system": when his own child's need competes with a marginally greater aggregate good elsewhere, the theory instructs him to compute, not to love — his attachments count only as one utility-source among millions, and his integrity, the projects that make him *him*, have no standing of their own. Kantian impartiality is gentler in form but similar in effect: universalizability tests maxims from a standpoint stripped of exactly the particular relations — parent, friend, compatriot — that Hume and Smith took to be morality's own root (our "private connexions" are not moral failures but the school and substance of the moral sentiments). Susan Wolf completes the pincer: imagine someone who maximises overridingness perfectly — the **moral saint**, whose every waking act is as morally good as possible. Such a person would have no time, and no permission, for the non-moral excellences — art, wit, sport, cuisine, love of learning for its own sake — except as means to moral ends; those goods enter his life only as "happy accidents." A morality whose perfect embodiment is an unattractive, diminished life has, Wolf argues, misdescribed its own place among the values.

positions.name: The overridingness thesis (the target)

blocks.text: Moral considerations are, by their nature, overriding: if an act is morally required, the moral reason for doing it defeats all competing reasons — self-interested, personal, aesthetic — and an agent who lets a non-moral consideration win has acted wrongly *for that reason*. The thesis is rarely stated baldly; Jacobs's procedure is to exhibit it as the operating assumption of the two dominant modern systems and to ask what it costs. Its attraction is real: it is what gives morality its unconditional ring (compare Kant in [Moral Motivation](moral-motivation.md)) and what distinguishes moral requirements from counsels of taste.

positions.name: Williams: impartiality against integrity

blocks.text: Both Kantian universalizability and utilitarian aggregation require the agent, at the point of decision, to deliberate from *outside* his own attachments: one's own projects and relations enter the calculus, if at all, only as data. Williams's objection is that a person *is* his ground projects and attachments; a morality that systematically requires him to treat them as dispensable does not elevate his agency but alienates him from it — the famous demand that he have, in the moment of rescuing his wife, "one thought too many" is the shape of the complaint (the textbook presents the general argument — the agent as representative of the satisfaction system, equal status misconstrued as blanket impartiality — rather than that later slogan). Equal moral status of persons does not entail that each agent must deliberate with blanket impartiality: that everyone counts for one is a fact about *worth*, from which nothing follows about how a parent may weigh his own child's claim on *him*.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 2, presenting Williams's critiques of Kantianism and utilitarianism — a formalization

steps.text: A moral theory that requires agents to deliberate in a way that abstracts from their ground projects and constitutive attachments requires them, at the point of action, to surrender the standpoint from which their lives have meaning and their actions are *theirs*.

Both act-utilitarianism (agent as "representative of the satisfaction system," attachments counting only as satisfiable preferences among others) and impartialist Kantianism (maxims tested from a standpoint purged of particular relations) impose exactly that requirement.

Both theories misdescribe morality's authority: whatever morality's claims are, they cannot coherently claim overridingness *of this impartialist form* — the form destroys the agent whose morality it was supposed to be.

blocks.label: Replies available in the corpus
blocks.text: the chapter notes the systems' defences without endorsing them: the utilitarian can reply that a *rule*-level or disposition-level impartiality (cultivate the attachments; they maximise good) recovers personal life at the level of practice while keeping impartiality at the level of justification — at the price of a two-level structure whose stability Williams's side questions. The Kantian can insist that universalizability constrains maxims, not loves: nothing in the test forbids saving one's wife; it forbids maxims one could not will universal. Whether these replies answer the charge or concede its substance is the live dispute.

positions.name: Hume and Smith: partiality as morality's root, not its rival

blocks.text: The older tradition inverts the modern assumption. Our moral sentiments *begin* in "private connexions" — family, friends, neighbours — and generalise outward through sympathy and the impartial spectator's corrections; the partial attachments are not pre-moral material morality must override but the very substance from which moral concern is extended. A theory that treats special relations as biases to be corrected *away* has mistaken the scaffolding for an obstacle. On this view the question "are moral considerations overriding?" partly dissolves: the considerations generated *by* one's relations are themselves moral considerations, and morality rightly understood does not standardly pit itself against them.

positions.name: Wolf: the moral saint as reductio

blocks.text: Susan Wolf's contribution isolates the ideal rather than the decision-procedure. The moral saint — Loving Saint or Rational Saint — is the person whose life maximally realises overridingness: every action as morally good as it can be. Such a life, Wolf argues, cannot contain, *as intrinsic goods*, the non-moral excellences we admire and want: artistic creation, humour, athletic grace, gourmet pleasure, intellectual curiosity pursued for itself. The saint may possess them only instrumentally or by accident. But a conception of the ideally good life that excludes most of what makes lives good — and a morality whose perfect follower we would not want to be, or to have as a friend, parent, or colleague — has overclaimed: morality is *a* value, perhaps the weightiest in conflict, but not a value whose maximal pursuit is identical with human flourishing.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 2, presenting Wolf, "Moral Saints" — a formalization

steps.text: If moral considerations were overriding in the strong sense, the morally perfect person — the moral saint, who acts as morally well as possible at every point — would be the ideal of a human life.

The moral saint's life necessarily subordinates or excludes non-moral excellences except as instruments or accidents; it is, by our own settled judgments about good lives, an unattractive and diminished ideal.
Moral considerations are not overriding in the strong sense: morality's authority, however great, is one authority among the values that constitute a good life.

thought.name: The moral saint
thought.text: (Wolf, via Jacobs). Not a puzzle-case but an ideal-case: construct the person who perfectly embodies a thesis and inspect the life. If the construction repels, the thesis — not our taste — is the suspect. The device pressures overridingness specifically, since weaker claims for morality (weighty, usually decisive) generate no saint.

thought.name: The satisfaction-system agent
thought.text: (Williams, via Jacobs). A parent at a disaster site who can save either his own child or two strangers' children, and who — faithfully representing the aggregate — pauses to compute. The case is not that the computation's *answer* is wrong; it is that a morality requiring the pause has already lost something it should have protected.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: no lecture covers this problem — begin with the Survey.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 2, "Are Moral Considerations Overriding?" (the chapter's final section).

ladder.label: Primary (as presented in Jacobs)
ladder.text: Williams, "Persons, Character and Morality" and related essays; Wolf, "Moral Saints"; Hume and Smith on sympathy and private connexions (see also ch. 1).

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: ch. 2 whole, then ch. 3 — the impartiality of the utilitarian and Kantian *forms* is stated in their own terms there.

are-moral-considerations-overriding.verdict: The chapter ends the section — and, nearly, the chapter — with the challenge standing rather than answered. Jacobs's presentation gives Williams and Wolf the last words; the replies sketched above (two-level utilitarianism, Kantian constraint-not-content readings) are the standard defences a reader will meet elsewhere but are *not* developed as rebuttals in this text, and the entry has marked them accordingly. The residual question the text leaves sharp: if morality is *not* overriding, what is its authority *instead* — supreme in some domains, defeasible in others, one voice in a plurality (compare Nagel's pluralism in [Moral Objectivity and Realism](moral-objectivity-and-realism.md))? The book does not say, and the KB should not pretend it does.

connections.title: Forms of Moral Theory
connections.text: [Forms of Moral Theory](forms-of-moral-theory.md) — the targets here are two of the five forms (consequentialism, Kantian) in their decision-guiding dress; the virtue-centred form is partly *motivated* by this critique, since it begins from character and attachment rather than from impartial rules.

connections.title: Moral Motivation
connections.text: [Moral Motivation](moral-motivation.md) — overridingness presupposes an answer there: a consideration can override only if it can motivate; Hume's impotence thesis thus limits overridingness twice over.

connections.title: Moral Luck
connections.text: [Moral Luck](moral-luck.md) — Williams is the connecting figure: the same philosopher who exposes Kantianism's luck-immunity as consolation exposes its impartiality as alienation.

connections.title: Self-interest and Egoism
connections.text: [Self-interest and Egoism](self-interest-and-egoism.md) — Wolf's saint is the mirror image of the egoist: a life organised around a single consideration, shown unattractive from the opposite pole.

sources: Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory* (book 028), ch. 2: "Are Moral Considerations Overriding?" — read in full (extraction file ch03), with the chapter's earlier sections for context.
