bullshit-vs-lying.title: Bullshit vs Lying
bullshit-vs-lying.aka: Frankfurt on bullshit; bullshit as a category distinct from lying and from nonsense
bullshit-vs-lying.sub_display: Ethics & Metaethics (philosophy of language / epistemology of discourse)
bullshit-vs-lying.note: Frankfurt as presented by book 005's essayists (his own text is not in the corpus)
bullshit-vs-lying.question: What is bullshit, and how does it differ from lying? The liar and the bullshitter both produce discourse we distrust, but Harry Frankfurt's celebrated analysis — the occasion for the anthology that is this entry's source — claims they are doing *fundamentally different things*: the liar is engaged with the truth (he must know or believe it, in order to conceal it), while the bullshitter is **indifferent** to whether what he says is true or false; his eye is on the impression he makes, not on the facts. If that is right, bullshit is not failed truth-telling but a different enterprise altogether — and, Frankfurt concluded, "a greater enemy of the truth than lies are." The anthology's contributors then fight over the definition: whether indifference is the essence or merely the usual tactic; whether some bullshit is identifiable in the *product* rather than the producer; whether the real wrong is semantic or pragmatic; whether bullshitting can be blameless — or even, in the case of politeness, part of what manners *are*. **Source declaration**: Frankfurt's own *On Bullshit* is *not* in this corpus. Everything attributed to Frankfurt below is as presented and quoted within the anthology *Bullshit and Philosophy* (book 005), and is labelled as such.
bullshit-vs-lying.ninety: *No Carneades lecture treats bullshit (a filename search of the full lecture corpus found no bullshit or sincerity lecture); the following is distilled from the textbook (book 005) and is marked accordingly, per the build rules.* Frankfurt's puzzle, with which the anthology opens: why do we tolerate bullshit so much more readily than lying? The liar at least honours the truth by hiding from it; the bullshitter does not care whether his statements are true or false, so long as they serve his purpose — typically, making an impression or getting something past an audience. Two ingredients, on the anthology's best survey: **indifference to truth** in the content, and **pretence** about the enterprise — the bullshitter misrepresents what he is *doing* (he represents himself as engaged in truth-telling inquiry while being engaged in something else). Hence the slogan: bullshit is a greater enemy of the truth than lies are, because the liar remains in the truth's orbit — he needs it, tracks it, and can be caught by it — while the bullshitter has left the orbit entirely. The volume then complicates its hero: maybe pretence is not essential (the openly indifferent politician bullshits without pretending); maybe some bullshit is blameless or even socially necessary — the polite formula, the faked apology, the pleasantry nobody believes and nobody is deceived by — so that, in one contributor's phrase, bullshit constitutes the greater part of civility; and maybe there is a third kind Frankfurt missed, the pseudoscientific, which is neither insincere nor obscure but simply *insensitive to evidence*.

positions.name: Frankfurt's account: truth-indifference plus pretence (as presented in the volume)

blocks.text: Bullshit is discourse produced with indifference to its truth-value, where the speaker represents himself as engaged in a truth-aimed enterprise. The bullshitter is not (typically) trying to get a falsehood believed — that is the liar's game, and the fraud's; he is trying to get *himself* believed in: as knowledgeable, as sincere, as the sort of person who holds forth on this. That is why detection so often fails: the sentences may be true, and checking them misses the point.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Hardcastle & Reisch (eds.
blocks.text: , *Bullshit and Philosophy*, Introduction and ch. 11 (Maes & Schaubroeck), presenting Frankfurt, *On Bullshit* — a formalization):

steps.text: The liar intends to deceive about the facts: he believes (or takes) the truth to be one thing and asserts another; his enterprise is defined by its relation — opposition — to the truth.

The bullshitter's assertions are unconstrained by belief about the facts either way: he "does not care whether the things he says describe reality correctly"; he selects them to suit his purpose, while representing his enterprise as the truth-telling one the liar honestly opposes.

Bullshit is not a species of lying but a distinct and, in one respect, graver offence against discourse: lying respects the authority of truth enough to hide from it; bullshit disregards that authority altogether — "bullshit is a greater enemy of the truth than lies are."

blocks.text: **Internal exclusions** (Frankfurt, as reported by Maes & Schaubroeck) — mere bull *sessions* (men talking loosely, not pretending to precision) are not bullshit proper, since the pretence ingredient fails; the volume's critics contest whether that line can be held (below).

positions.name: Cohen: bullshit as product — unclarifiable unclarity

blocks.text: G. A. Cohen argues Frankfurt located the phenomenon in the wrong place: in the producer's process rather than the product. There is a kind of discourse identifiable as bullshit *on its face* — discourse that is **unclarifiably unclear**: it resists every attempt to state clearly what it says, and its obscurity is not the fertile obscurity of poetry (which rewards interpretation with suggestion) but a dead obscurity that persists when suggestiveness is subtracted. The test is a kind of negation: take the discourse, remove what can be clarified, and ask whether anything remains that could be true or false — Cohen's bullshit leaves nothing standing. Producers of such discourse may be perfectly sincere (seminar-room bullshit often is), which Frankfurt's process account cannot capture.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: *Bullshit and Philosophy*, ch. 8, Cohen, "Deeper into Bullshit" — a formalization

steps.text: Some discourse is recognisably bullshit independently of anything known about its producer's intentions or sincerity: its sentences cannot be clarified into any determinate claim — every paraphrase either changes the subject or exposes a banality the original's obscurity was concealing.
A process-based (intention-based) definition classifies discourse by its producer's attitudes and so must call such discourse non-bullshit whenever the producer is sincere — the wrong result.

Bullshit exists as a *product*-category — unclarifiable unclarity — alongside whatever intention-based category Frankfurt identified; a complete theory needs both senses (which the OED, Cohen notes, already distinguishes).

blocks.label: Objections in the volume
blocks.text: Cohen's own caution: the "essence" formulation he himself reaches for risks the same overreach he charges Frankfurt with; and the tactic/goal distinction (Pavel's Minsk/Pinsk joke: the peasant who names the wrong station *tactically*, to misdirect, vs *strategically*) shows intention-analyses also fragment. Maes & Schaubroeck's survey lets both definitions stand as marking different, overlapping phenomena.

positions.name: Bernal: the target — bullshit as obscuring something specific

blocks.text: Against Frankfurt's indifference, Bernal argues the bullshitter is usually *connected* to the truth through a **target**: something specific he needs hidden. Two modes: (a) *indirect implication* — saying something literally true in a way engineered to implicate a falsehood (a resort advertised as "alive with pleasure"); (b) *distraction* — flooding attention elsewhere so the target goes unexamined (the anthology's example: the Niger yellowcake story's role in fixing attention during the Iraq WMD case). Consciousness of the target is a spectrum: split-brain confabulation shows the mind producing confident, false, self-serving narrative with no conscious deceiving self behind it — bullshitting without a bullshitter fully in charge — which is why Bernal links the phenomenon to personality and habit: unconscious bullshitting, lacking conscience's sting, is the easier habit to fall into.

positions.name: Reisch: bullshit as pragmatic cloaking

blocks.text: The editor's own rival definition relocates the essence from semantics to **pragmatics**: bullshit cloaks one kind of speech-engagement inside another — advocacy dressed as inquiry, salesmanship dressed as scholarship. The test case is Intelligent Design: its advocates are *not* truth-indifferent (they care intensely about a specific conclusion), so Frankfurt's definition fails them; what they conceal is not a fact but an *agenda* — the engagement is evangelism conducted in the costume of science. This also dissolves Frankfurt's puzzle about tolerance: the liar sins against semantics (against the statement's relation to fact, which we police), the bullshitter against pragmatics (against the terms of the engagement, which we police less, and differently). A corollary Reisch calls **purism**: properly defined, there is much less real bullshit than casual usage supposes — most of what gets called bullshit is error, disagreement, or ordinary persuasion.

positions.name: Maes & Schaubroeck: two revisions and a third kind

blocks.text: The volume's most systematic revision. **Revision 1 — pretence is not essential**: Pascal's self-description (he is like "a dog that has been run over" for philosophy — Wittgenstein's borrowed line) and the openly indifferent politician show bullshit without any misrepresentation of enterprise; Frankfurt's exclusion of bull sessions on pretence-grounds is, they argue, artificial. **Revision 2 — bullshit is not always bad**: banter, Wildean paradox, and the polite formulae of social life (Thomas Nagel's "How nice to see you" said to someone one is not pleased to see) are bullshit by the definition and *good* — the lubricant of civility, deception-free because nobody is meant to be deceived. **A third kind — pseudoscience**: sincere, often crystal-clear, so neither Frankfurt's nor Cohen's category fits; its marks are insensitivity to evidence and fallacious reasoning — bullshit by epistemic conduct rather than by indifference or obscurity.

positions.name: Kimbrough: why we let it slide — bullshit, politeness, and manners

blocks.text: The volume's opening chapter takes up Frankfurt's puzzle (our tolerance) functionally. We tolerate bullshit when its *ends* are served cheaply and its costs low: entertainment (the bull session as play), **politeness** — via Jennifer Miller's *Faking It*, the argument that insincere-seeming performances (the faked apology, the performed enthusiasm) are not failures of civility but its mechanism, so that "bullshit constitutes the greater part of civility" — and evasion where directness would cost more than the truth is worth there. Tolerance ends where bullshit becomes a method: Kimbrough's positive proposal is to see bullshit as **lame methods of justification** — discourse that licenses dismissal of what should have been answered — whose social function, for its producers, is exactly that licence. Some bullshit is blameless (Newton's alchemy: sincere, methodical, wrong — the false content carried by honest enterprise); what we should restrict is not the category but its use as an excuse for not giving reasons. (This chapter, with Maes & Schaubroeck on polite formulae, is where this corpus's *manners* material actually lives — see the declaration under "Sources read.")

blocks.label: Supporting voices in the volume
blocks.text: Preti (ch. 2): the missing third element is the *audience's* compliance — bullshit is partly our fault; Moore's "What exactly do you mean?" is the model resistance. Aberdein (ch. 10): Frankfurt's category is better named **semantic negligence** — and Frankfurt's own definition is a *persuasive definition*, though (Aberdein argues) a diligent rather than negligent one. De Waal (ch. 7): the literature divides into *intentionalist* and *structuralist* schools; bullshitting as *fake inquiry* violates an "epistemic imperative" — with permissible cases (politeness, play) conceded. Fuller (ch. 16) dissents from the whole detector stance: the bullshit-hunt moralises epistemics, and the category slides toward sophistry/hypocrisy charges against whoever one dislikes.

thought.name: The polite formula
thought.text: (Nagel, via Maes & Schaubroeck). "How nice to see you," said without pleasure to someone one would rather avoid. Indifferent to truth, conventionally produced, nobody deceived, socially valuable. If it is bullshit, bullshit is not always a vice; if it is not, the definition owes an account of why not that does not collapse into "bullshit we approve of." The case is the volume's pressure-point between Frankfurt and the revisionists.

thought.name: The faked apology
thought.text: (Miller, via Kimbrough). An apology performed without felt contrition, which nonetheless repairs the relationship — both parties may know the feeling is absent. Civility running on performed sincerity: the "bullshit" *is* the manner. Readers arriving at this entry from the manners question should start here.

thought.name: Pavel's stations
thought.text: (the Minsk/Pinsk joke, via Cohen). Pavel says he is going to Minsk — actually Pinsk — so that when you conclude he lies, you will think Pinsk… The joke's analytic use in ch. 8: it separates *tactical* deception (the local false move) from *strategic* aim, showing that intention-based analyses of discourse must specify which level of intention they mean — a complication for every position above.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: no lecture exists for this problem — begin with the Survey.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Hardcastle & Reisch (eds.), *Bullshit and Philosophy* — Introduction ("On Bullshitmania"); ch. 11 (Maes & Schaubroeck) as the volume's own map of the debate; ch. 1 (Kimbrough) for the tolerance puzzle.

ladder.label: Primary within the volume
ladder.text: ch. 8 (Cohen), ch. 3 (Reisch), ch. 5 (Bernal); Frankfurt's *On Bullshit* itself is **not in this corpus** — consult it directly for the primary text.

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: the volume whole, including its sceptics (Fuller, ch. 16) and its applications (chapters on politics, science, religion, and rhetoric).

bullshit-vs-lying.verdict: The volume is an anthology, not a treatise, and its honest state is a contested definition with converging diagnostics. Agreement: bullshit is not lying, and is not mere falsehood or error; something about the speaker's *relation to truth* (or the discourse's relation to clarifiability, or the engagement's honesty) is the differentia. Disagreement: whether the essence is indifference (Frankfurt), target-obscuring engagement with truth (Bernal), pragmatic cloaking (Reisch), unclarifiable unclarity in the product (Cohen), evidence-insensitivity (Maes & Schaubroeck's third kind), or negligent speech (Aberdein) — and whether the category is a vice-term at all (Kimbrough and the politeness cases say: not always). The entry takes no side; the KB's rule against settling what sources leave open applies with special force to a book whose chapters argue with each other.

connections.title: Emotivism and Expressivism
connections.text: [Emotivism and Expressivism](emotivism-and-expressivism.md) — the shared moral: surface grammar misleads about function. Moral sentences look fact-stating; bullshit looks truth-aimed; both analyses proceed by asking what the speaker is *doing*.

connections.title: Moral Objectivity and Realism
connections.text: [Moral Objectivity and Realism](moral-objectivity-and-realism.md) — Hume's bonfire ("commit it to the flames," quoted in the volume's Introduction) stands behind both projects: Ayer's emotivism and Frankfurt's taxonomy are descendants of the same anti-metaphysical suspicion of discourse that floats free of fact.

The manners connection: the candidate entry "etiquette and the moral status of manners" could **not** be built — book 004, catalogued as "On Manners," contains no such work (see the declaration below and the book map). What survives of the topic in this corpus is the politeness material in book 005 (Kimbrough ch. 1; Maes & Schaubroeck ch. 11), and it is treated in this entry, under Kimbrough's position, where it belongs.

sources: Hardcastle & Reisch (eds.), *Bullshit and Philosophy* (book 005): Introduction, read in full; ch. 1 (Kimbrough), ch. 3 (Reisch), ch. 5 (Bernal), ch. 8 (Cohen), ch. 11 (Maes & Schaubroeck) — read in full; chs. 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 — openings, all section headings, and conclusions read (supporting voices only). Frankfurt's *On Bullshit* is not in the corpus; Frankfurt attributions are the volume's presentations, as declared at the head of this entry.

**Book 004 declaration**: the folder catalogued "004 - On Manners" was inspected in full (51 files, ~72,000 words). It does not contain a work on manners or etiquette: it contains Melissa Manners, *The Pannell Witch* (2022), a self-published historical novel about a seventeenth-century witch trial. It contains no philosophy of etiquette (the word "philosophy" occurs three times, incidentally). No entry could be sourced from it; the full finding is in its [book map](../../book-maps/004-on-manners.md).
No lecture is used as a source for this entry (none exists on this topic in the corpus); the 90-second version is textbook-distilled and is marked as such in place.

emotivism-and-expressivism.title: Emotivism and Expressivism
emotivism-and-expressivism.aka: non-cognitivism; the "boo–hurrah" theory (of emotivism); universal prescriptivism (Hare's variant)
emotivism-and-expressivism.question: What are we *doing* when we say "murder is wrong" or "charity is good"? The sentence looks like a statement of fact, fit to be true or false. Emotivism says the resemblance is superficial: a moral judgment does not state anything — it *expresses* an attitude, approval or disapproval, and typically tries to influence others' attitudes too. If that is right, moral judgments are not true or false at all, moral properties are not among the things that exist, and a whole set of questions — what makes moral judgments true? where in the world is value? — dissolve rather than get answered. The problem is whether this account can explain the features of moral discourse that make it *look* factual: that we argue, give reasons, demand consistency, and correct ourselves.
emotivism-and-expressivism.ninety: Emotivism is a metaethical theory: not a theory about which actions are good or bad, but about what "good" and "bad" mean. The emotivist answer is that statements about good and evil merely express the speaker's approval or disapproval. "Charity is good" amounts to "I approve of charity" — or simply "Hurray, charity!"; "Stealing is wrong" amounts to "I condemn stealing," or "Boo to theft!" — which is why the view is nicknamed the boo–yay (boo–hurrah) theory. Emotivists are non-cognitivists: moral statements do not express propositions that can be true or false, any more than "Hurray!" does. The lecture works through a refinement — thick terms like "brave": to call Kiki brave is at once to describe her (she is fearless) and to express approval of fearlessness; pick a differently-loaded word for the same trait ("brazen," if you disapprove of fearlessness) and the description stays while the expression flips. The standing objection the lecture ends on: when we say murder is wrong we seem to mean something more than "I don't like murder" — we seem to say *you must not* — and since emotivist statements report no facts, the emotivist seems to have no way of giving a reason to stop a murder that she lacks for stopping someone painting a living room bright green, beyond "eh, I don't like it." (Distilled from the Carneades lecture: [What is Emotivism? The Boo-Yay Theory](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=39uOXZVVHoA).)

videos.title: What is Emotivism? The Boo-Yay Theory

positions.name: Emotivism (Ayer)

blocks.text: Moral language is not fact-stating. Ayer's version, as Jacobs presents it, is driven by a translation test: can statements of ethical value be translated into statements of empirical fact? No — but not, as Moore thought, because ethical concepts are genuine yet unanalysable. For Ayer "they are mere pseudo-concepts. The presence of an ethical symbol in a proposition adds nothing to its factual content." In making ethical statements "we are merely expressing certain moral sentiments" — and, a point the simple "boo–hurrah" label hides, we are also concerned that others should share and be moved by them.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 4, presenting Ayer, *Language, Truth and Logic* — a formalization

steps.text: A sentence states a fact only if its content can be cashed out in factual, truth-evaluable terms; an ethical symbol in a proposition "adds nothing to its factual content" — "Murder is wrong" and "Murder is a killing" do not differ by any further fact the first reports.
What the ethical symbol does contribute is expressive: it expresses the speaker's sentiment of approval or disapproval and is apt to arouse similar sentiment in others.

Moral judgments are not true or false and do not refer to moral properties; their meaning is expressive, not cognitive. (Ch. 1's statement of the same view: if a sentence "makes no statement at all, there is obviously no sense in asking whether what it says is true or false.")

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: (i) The lecture's objection: moral condemnation presents itself as more than dislike — it claims authority over others, and bare expression supplies no reasons. (ii) Foot's objection (below): the descriptive and evaluative components cannot be prised apart in the way the theory requires. (iii) The standing worry from ch. 1: can *any* expressivism, however sophisticated, be "more than 'thinly' expressivist" — can it recover the genuineness of moral argument rather than merely its outward forms?

positions.name: Prescriptivism (Hare): emotivism plus universalizability

blocks.text: Hare accepts the non-cognitivist core — moral judgments do not report facts, and "what is wrong with naturalist theories is that they leave out the prescriptive or commendatory element in value-judgements, by seeking to make them derivable from statements of fact" — but adds the formal feature that distinguishes moral from merely expressive judgments: moral judgments are **prescriptions the speaker universalizes**. To judge that deceitful promising is wrong is to prescribe that deceitful promises are not to be made — by anyone, in relevantly identical circumstances, including oneself.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 4, presenting Hare, *The Language of Morals* and *Freedom and Reason* — a formalization

steps.text: Moral judgments are distinguished within the class of prescriptive judgments "by being universalizable": in making one, I commit myself to the same judgment for every exactly similar case.

This commitment is a matter of the judgment's prescriptive form, not of any fact it reports — contrast "this stuff is awful" (taste) or "you ought to get a calculus tutor" (conditional, person-specific), which carry no general prescriptive significance.

Moral judgment is action-guiding and reason-structured (consistency across cases is built in) without being fact-stating: the universal imperative force of moral judgments is grounded in their prescriptivity, not — as Kant held — in requirements of pure practical reason.

positions.name: Expressivism sophisticated: consistency and subjective supervenience (Hare, Blackburn)

blocks.text: The developed expressivism of ch. 4 concedes that moral judgments are tightly constrained by facts, and builds the constraint in. **Consistency**: "it is not possible to hold an attitude to a thing because of its possessing certain properties and, at the same time, not hold that attitude to another thing that is believed to have the same properties" (Blackburn). Hare's version: of two pictures exactly alike in every respect, one cannot say "P is a good picture and Q not" — the challenge "But how can one be good and the other not, if they are exactly alike?" has no expressivist answer except retreat. Jacobs calls the resulting relation **subjective supervenience**: moral responses depend regularly on non-moral properties, but the dependence runs through *us* — as being *uncomfortably loud* depends on facts about sound waves *and* facts about our thresholds, and is a property of our response, not of the sound. Blackburn's defence of the whole approach: the expressivist, in saying there are real obligations, "affirms *all that could ever properly be meant* by saying that there are real obligations."

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the critics' question (Jacobs): is consistency *enough*? On expressivist terms, responses must be uniform across like cases — but can the theory *disallow* the response itself? "Is that sufficient to disallow the possibility that on their terms, cruelty cannot be morally permissible?" If a consistent, fully informed agent prescribed cruelty universally, the formal machinery registers no defect; the defect the rest of us register seems to be a cognitive one — a failure to understand something.

positions.name: The fact–value challenge (Foot, McDowell): the reply from within this corpus

blocks.text: Philippa Foot, an early and important critic of both emotivism and prescriptivism, argues the descriptive/evaluative split is untenable: "there is no describing the evaluative meaning of 'good'… without fixing the object to which they are supposed to be attached." Can a person understand what fairness, benevolence, or honesty *is* without understanding that each is morally good? If not, evaluation is not a laminate applied to a neutral description; the concepts themselves carry their significance, and moral judgment is "a rational response to the normative significance of factual considerations" — cognitive in the way ordinary concept-use is cognitive, with sensibility playing a role *within* cognition rather than projecting quality onto a neutral world. (The full development — McDowell's secondary-quality analogy and "no-priority" view — is in [Naturalism, Non-naturalism, and the Open Question](naturalism-and-the-open-question.md).)

thought.name: The gallery pictures
thought.text: (Hare, via Jacobs ch. 4). P and Q are replicas, painted by the same artist at about the same time; you do not know which is the original. You cannot say "P is a good picture and Q not" — there must be some further difference to ground the difference in verdict. Meant to show: even pure expression is hostage to consistency across identical cases; it is the expressivist's own route to a supervenience-like structure. It pressures purely "thin" emotivism, which has no resources to explain why the challenge is unanswerable.

thought.name: The bright-green living room
thought.text: (lecture). If "murder is wrong" expresses only disapproval, the emotivist's ground for stopping a murder is the same kind as her ground for objecting to a neighbour's paint colour: "I don't like it." Meant to show the authority gap — moral language presents itself as giving *others* reasons, not as reporting the speaker's tastes.

ladder.text: Ayer, *Language, Truth and Logic*; Hare, *The Language of Morals*; Blackburn, *Essays in Quasi-realism*; Foot, "Moral Beliefs."

emotivism-and-expressivism.verdict: In this corpus the trajectory runs: Ayer's austere version (moral sentences say nothing) → Hare's repair (add universalizable prescription, recovering formal rationality) → Blackburn's further repair (consistency and quasi-realist truth-talk from inside the moral point of view) → the Foot/McDowell counter-attack (the fact/value split the whole family presupposes may itself be the mistake). Jacobs leaves the contest open, with the critics' question standing: expressivism can insist that stances respond to facts and must be consistent — "But is that sufficient?" The lecture's simpler version of the same pressure (the authority/reasons objection) is likewise posed, not answered. Note also the family agreement that survives every repair: emotivists, prescriptivists, and Moore all reject *naturalism* — the dispute is only over what follows from that rejection (see the naturalism entry).

connections.title: Moral Relativism and Subjectivism
connections.text: [Moral Relativism and Subjectivism](moral-relativism-and-subjectivism.md) — expressivism is one species of subjectivism; Hume's and Smith's sentiment theories are its ancestors but, on Jacobs's reading, richer than Ayer's limiting case.

connections.title: Naturalism, Non-naturalism, and the Open Question
connections.text: [Naturalism, Non-naturalism, and the Open Question](naturalism-and-the-open-question.md) — emotivism and prescriptivism both begin by *accepting* Moore's critique of naturalism while rejecting his non-natural realism; the shared fork is mapped there.

connections.title: Moral Motivation
connections.text: [Moral Motivation](moral-motivation.md) — expressivism's advertised explanatory advantage: if judgments express attitudes, it is no mystery why they move us — the Humean engine of the whole family.

connections.text: [Bullshit vs Lying](bullshit-vs-lying.md) — a different philosophy-of-language problem with the same moral: surface grammar misleads. "Murder is wrong" looks fact-stating but (the emotivist says) isn't; the bullshitter's sentences look truth-aimed but (Frankfurt says) aren't.

forms-of-moral-theory.title: Forms of Moral Theory
forms-of-moral-theory.aka: the locus-of-value question — consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics, intuitionism, contractarianism
forms-of-moral-theory.note: the five forms as positions; the trolley (lecture-only, labelled)
forms-of-moral-theory.question: Moral theories disagree about many things, but the deepest disagreement is architectural: **where is moral value located?** In the *consequences* an act produces? In the act's conformity to *duty or principle*? In the *character* of the agent? In a plurality of self-evident *duties* we simply recognise? Or in what free and equal persons could *agree* to? Each answer makes a different item **basic** — the thing in terms of which everything else (acts, rules, traits, obligations) is assessed — and each generates a different theory of what it is to deliberate, to be justified, and to go wrong. The textbook chapter surveys five forms; the Carneades lecture series approaches the same map from a different direction, asking of each theory what it takes as **primary** — outcomes, rules, or virtue — and what objection (too permissive, too restrictive) it characteristically invites.
forms-of-moral-theory.ninety: The lecture series organises normative ethics by a single question: *what is primary?* **Consequentialists** make outcomes primary: the morally right act is the one with the best consequences, full stop — and the standing objection is that this is *too permissive*, licensing horrors (kill one patient to distribute his organs to five) whenever the arithmetic favours them. **Deontologists** make rules primary: some act-types are required or forbidden regardless of outcome — the mirror objection is that this is *too restrictive*, commanding us to let terrible consequences happen rather than break a rule; divine command theory counts as a deontology here, its rules being God's. **Virtue ethicists** make character primary: right action is *built on top of* virtue — act as the practically wise, excellent person would — and the objection pressed is consistency and guidance: virtues are plural and can conflict, and "do what the virtuous person would do" underdetermines hard cases. A framing lecture sharpens the taxonomy into **deontic** theories (act/duty primary) versus **aretaic** theories (virtue primary), and further lectures split virtue ethics by structure: **target-centred** versions define the virtues by the target each aims at, in a way that leans consequentialist; **agent-centred** versions split again into motivation theories (right act = act from virtuous motives) and paragon theories (right act = what the virtuous exemplar would do). Utilitarianism gets its own lecture as consequentialism's most specified member — analysed as actual, hedonistic, act (direct), universal, evaluative, equal-consideration, and maximising — where each adjective is a choice the wider consequentialist family leaves open. (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [What is Consequentialism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aFEfoGLLWx0), [What is Deontology?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qMCeaXyrl7k), [What is Virtue Ethics?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JPV2KsWMRfc), [What is Utilitarianism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cbQx-Cmtqt0), [Deontic vs Aretaic Ethical Theories](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uqPIWhe2WVQ), [What is Target Centered Virtue Ethics?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DJYNu2mQO2c), [What is Agent Centered Virtue Ethics?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g1hSqpOISxg), and [Agent Centered Deontology](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FyEV-izx4K0).)

What is Agent Centered Virtue Ethics?

positions.name: Consequentialism: value located in outcomes

blocks.text: The rightness of an act is wholly a function of the value of its consequences; no act-type is intrinsically right or wrong. Mill's version makes **utility** the criterion — acts are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse — with *secondary principles* (the inherited rules of common morality) doing the everyday deliberative work, themselves justified by the criterion. Moore's variant keeps the consequentialist structure but pluralises the good (see [Moral Objectivity and Realism](moral-objectivity-and-realism.md)). The textbook's test case is **assisted suicide**: where a competent patient in irremediable suffering requests help to die, the consequentialist assessment turns entirely on outcomes — suffering ended, precedent effects, effects on trust in medicine — with no residue of intrinsic prohibition to weigh. The lecture series adds the family's internal variables: *which* consequences count (actual vs expected), and over what scope (the act/utilitarianism lecture: universal, equal-weighted, maximising).

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 3, presenting Mill, *Utilitarianism* — a formalization

steps.text: The sole fundamental criterion of right action is the value of what the action brings about: "actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness; wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness."

No feature of an act other than its consequences — its type, its motive, its conformity to rule — has intrinsic bearing on its rightness; rules and prohibitions derive their authority entirely from the outcomes of observing them (secondary principles).

Rightness is consequential through and through: in any case, including the hard ones, the right act is the one whose consequences are best, and apparent exceptions are either miscalculations or secondary principles doing their work.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the lecture's "too permissive": the organ-distribution case, in which the arithmetic licenses killing one to save five, tests whether "no intrinsic act-rightness" is a discovery or a reductio. From the textbook side: Williams's impartiality critique (the agent as representative of the satisfaction system — see [Are Moral Considerations Overriding?](are-moral-considerations-overriding.md)) and the standing worry about whether outcome-value can be specified without smuggling in the deontic notions it claims to replace. (The trolley problem, below, is the lecture family's preferred arena for this fight.)

positions.name: Kantian non-consequentialism (deontology): value located in duty and the will

blocks.text: "Moral worth does not lie in the effect" expected from an action, nor in any principle of action that borrows its motive from that effect. Rightness is conformity to the **categorical imperative** — act only on maxims you can will as universal law, and treat humanity, in yourself and others, always also as an end, never merely as a means. Persons have **unconditional worth** — a dignity that is not a price and cannot enter trade-offs — which is the deep ground of the theory's non-consequentialism: some things may not be done to a person *however good* the outcome, because the person is not a vessel of value but a source of claims. The lecture's agent-centred deontology lecture adds a structural refinement this textbook does not develop: duties can be **agent-relative** (my promises bind *me*, my children are *my* special charge) rather than agent-neutral, which softens the Williams impartiality charge from within the deontological family.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 3, presenting Kant — a formalization

steps.text: Moral worth and rightness cannot rest on effects: effects are contingent, luck-exposed, and common to good and bad actions alike; a principle whose motive is borrowed from an expected effect is heteronomous, not moral.
Rational agents possess unconditional worth as ends in themselves; a maxim is permissible only if it can be willed universally and treats every person it touches as such an end.

Right action is determined by the form of the agent's maxim against the categorical imperative — one principle, exceptionlessly — and consequences are morally relevant only as they bear on what maxims are in play.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the lecture's "too restrictive": rules held exceptionlessly command us to watch preventable catastrophes rather than lie, break, or kill our way out. From within this corpus: the overridingness critique (previous entry) and the question whether the single imperative can generate the *content* of duty without quietly importing the teleology Kant excluded.

positions.name: Intuitionism: value located in a plurality of self-evident duties (Ross)

blocks.text: Ross's middle way: there is no single criterion and no consequentialist reduction, but a plurality of **prima facie duties** — fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, non-maleficence — each **self-evident** to mature reflection, known by reason (not by a special moral sense or occult faculty), and each genuinely binding *unless* overridden in the circumstances by a weightier one. Crucially, one's **actual duty** in a concrete situation is *not* self-evident: it is a matter of judgment weighing the prima facie duties in play, and reasonable judges can differ.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 3, presenting Ross, *The Right and the Good* — a formalization

steps.text: Certain duties present themselves to reflection as self-evidently binding in their own right (a promise creates a claim; an injury, a debt of reparation) and none is reducible to another or to a single master-value.
These duties can conflict in concrete cases, and no further principle mechanically resolves the conflict.
Moral knowledge is real but plural and non-systematic: we know the prima facie duties directly, and we *judge* — fallibly — what our actual duty is.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Rawls's, recorded in the chapter: a plurality of principles with no priority rule is an "unconnected heap" — a list, not a theory; it describes our convictions without ordering them. The intuitionist's available reply (in the text's spirit): that the heap is what the moral phenomena actually look like, and tidiness purchased by reduction (to utility, or to one imperative) is tidiness at the phenomena's expense; compare pluralism in [Moral Objectivity and Realism](moral-objectivity-and-realism.md).

positions.name: Virtue-centred theory: value located in character (Aristotle)

blocks.text: The oldest form and, in the chapter's architecture, the standing alternative to the whole duty-and-criterion project. Aristotle seeks **no criterion** of right action: ethics is not that kind of inquiry. The standard is a *person* — the **phronimos**, the man of practical wisdom, is "standard and measure" of what is fine and pleasant — and the theory's basic notions are virtues: stable states of character in which reason and desire are aligned (see [Moral Motivation](moral-motivation.md)), each a **mean** between excess and deficiency (courage between cowardice and rashness — the doctrine the lecture on Aristotle's mean presents). "What ought I to do?" is answered by perception of the situation as the practically wise person perceives it, not by applying a decision procedure. The lecture family's subdivisions map onto this: agent-centred versions (motivation and paragon theories) are the textbook's Aristotle formalised; target-centred versions rebuild virtue from the ends each virtue aims at.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 3, presenting Aristotle — a formalization

steps.text: Practical matters are irreducibly particular: what courage, justice, or generosity require varies with circumstances in ways no finite rule-set captures in advance.
The practically wise person reliably perceives and does what the situation requires, because his desires and judgments have been formed, by habituation, to track the genuinely good.

The locus of moral value and knowledge is character, not criteria: right action is what the virtuous agent would do, and moral education (formation of character) replaces decision-procedure as ethics' central practical concern.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Hursthouse's, in the chapter: "what ought I to do?" still needs an answer *tonight*, in the hard case, and "what the phronimos would do" can seem to defer rather than answer — the virtue ethicist's reply (premises about what virtues require *do* generate action-guidance: "do what is honest, do not do what is dishonest") is recorded alongside. Williams's distinct worry: that virtue ethics, pressed to justify its virtues, collapses into a teleology (flourishing as the outcome to be produced) and becomes a disguised consequentialism — the target-centred lecture's consequentialist lean illustrates the pressure. And the chapter's caveat: Aristotle's *essentialist perfectionism* (a fixed human nature that virtue perfects) is detachable from the virtue-centred structure, and most modern versions detach it (see the naturalism discussion in [Naturalism](naturalism-and-the-open-question.md)).

positions.name: Contractarianism: value located in agreement

blocks.text: Moral norms are justified as the terms of an **agreement** — actual or hypothetical — among parties who must live together. Everything depends on how the parties and their situation are described, and the family's members are best distinguished by their descriptions. **Hobbes**: parties in a state of nature, roughly equal in vulnerability, self-interested; morality is the covenant that insecurity rationally compels. **Locke**: a state of nature already under natural law; agreement adds enforcement, not the norms themselves. **Rawls**: parties behind a **veil of ignorance**, ignorant of their place, talents, and conception of the good, choose principles of justice in an **original position** designed to be fair — the veil does the moral work (contrast the intuitionism objection above: Rawls's construction is meant to *order* our convictions, in reflective equilibrium, not merely list them). **Gauthier**: no veil — bargaining among fully informed, self-interested parties; morality as mutual advantage. **Scanlon**: no bargain at all — an act is wrong if it would be disallowed by principles no one could *reasonably reject*; agreement as a test of justifiability to each person.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 3, presenting the contractarian strategy via Rawls — a formalization

steps.text: A moral principle is justified if it would be chosen (or could not reasonably be rejected) by free and equal parties under conditions that model fairness — in Rawls's construction, ignorance of one's own position, so that no one can rig the principles to his advantage.
Principles so chosen bind not because they track an independent moral order but because no one situated as the parties are situated could object to them.

The authority of morality is the authority of fair agreement: the locus of value is relocated from the world, the will, or character to the *procedure* of mutual justification. (Jacobs's caution: since everything turns on the description of the parties, disputes *within* contractarianism — veil or no veil, bargain or rejectability — are disputes about what fairness itself requires, and the form's neutrality is only apparent.)

positions.name: The chapter's closing observations

blocks.text: Two remarks end Jacobs's survey and belong in this entry as its own meta-lesson. (1) **All five forms speak the idiom of duty**: even the virtue-centred theory, whose basic notion is character, articulates its demands as oughts — the idiom is harder to escape than any particular theory. (2) **Purity is not required**: the forms interpenetrate in practice — Mill "domesticates" virtue and justice inside utilitarianism (virtues as the dispositions utility commends; justice as utility's most stringent region) — and a theory's classification is a claim about what it makes *basic*, not a ban on its using the other forms' materials.

thought.name: The assisted-suicide case
thought.text: (Jacobs, ch. 3). A competent patient, suffering irremediably, requests assistance in dying. The chapter uses the case to *differentiate* the forms: the consequentialist weighs outcomes only; the Kantian asks after maxims, autonomy, and the humanity formula; the virtue theorist asks what compassion and practical wisdom perceive here; the contractarian, what terms no one could reasonably reject. Same case, five different questions — the cleanest exhibit of the locus thesis.

thought.name: The trolley problem
thought.text: (lecture-only; the textbook never mentions it). A runaway trolley heads for five workers; you may pull a switch diverting it to a track where it will kill one. The lecture presents the standing result — most judge diverting permissible, some even required — and frames it as the deontologist's hard case ("let five die rather than kill one") against the utilitarian's easy one ("kill one, save five"), with intuition siding with the utilitarians. It is included here, following the pilot's precedent of admitting series-neighbour cases, explicitly as lecture material: it pressures exactly the permissiveness/restrictiveness axis of the 90-second version. Its many variants in the series (Fat Man, Loop, Organ Donor, and others) are catalogued in the lectures index; they are not individually claimed by this entry.

forms-of-moral-theory.verdict: No adjudication is offered by either source, and the two sources' maps differ instructively. The textbook's five-form map (with intuitionism and contractarianism as full members) is finer than the lectures' three-way primary-question map (outcomes/rules/virtue), under which intuitionism distributes awkwardly (deontic in act-focus, but its epistemology is sui generis) and contractarianism does not appear at all. Where the sources agree: the classification question — *what is basic?* — is the right first question to ask of any moral theory, and the characteristic objections are structural (permissiveness for outcome-theories, restrictiveness for rule-theories, guidance for character-theories, heap-ness for pluralism, description-dependence for agreement-theories), recurring wherever the forms are rebuilt. This entry's reconstructions are the textbook's; the lecture refinements (agent-relative deontology, target- vs agent-centred virtue) are marked as lecture material where they appear.

god-and-morality.title: God and Morality
god-and-morality.aka: divine command theory and the Euthyphro problem; the authority problem for morality
god-and-morality.note: the Euthyphro as 028 and the lectures stage it
god-and-morality.question: Does morality need God — as its author, its ground, its guarantor, or its teacher? The standing suggestion is the **divine command theory**: an act is right because God wills it. The suggestion promises a great deal: a single source of unconditional obligation, a cosmic order in which justice is completed, an answer to "why be moral?" Against it stands a dilemma first posed in Plato's *Euthyphro* and never since retired. In our corpus the question is examined from both ends: the textbook asks what religious belief adds to (and subtracts from) morality, and two Carneades lectures press the dilemma and then test the most famous modern reply to it.
god-and-morality.ninety: The Euthyphro dilemma is a fork. Either God commands an act *because it is right* — but then rightness is independent of God, God is merely a transcriber of moral facts that exist without him, and he is not really the author of morality at all; or an act is right *because God commands it* — but then morality is arbitrary: had God commanded, say, the yearly murder of a hundred children, that would by definition be good, a conclusion no believer can accept; and praise of God's own goodness goes empty, since "God is good" would mean only "God does what God does." The lecture's verdict is that the dilemma is a serious problem for divine command theory and that we should be skeptical of the view, perhaps suspending judgment on it. The second lecture presents William Lane Craig's escape: the dilemma is a *false* dilemma, because goodness is not something God *wills* nor something *outside* God — God simply *is* the Good; his nature is the standard. The lecture then weighs a counter-dilemma: if God has no control over his nature, is he not again powerless, a transcriber of logic? The charitable reply available to the theist is that having no control over one's nature does not imply impotence — God has no control over logic either, yet omnipotence was never thought to require doing the illogical — but grounding goodness in God's nature as a matter of *logic* is, the lecture concludes, a "tall order." (Distilled from two Carneades lectures: [The Euthyphro Dilemma](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hMOD7ofD9Ck) and [God is the Good: William Lane Craig and the Euthyphro Dilemma](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aV-GpEcv554).)

videos.title: God is the Good: William Lane Craig and the Euthyphro Dilemma

positions.name: Divine command theory (as presented in the textbook)

blocks.text: On the theistic view Jacobs presents, "right action is action in accord with God's will": God is the ultimate authority to which morality answers, and this adds "an element of authority or of unconditional obligation" to morality that secular accounts struggle to supply. Jacobs is careful about what the theory is not: it is not the promise that good people will be rewarded and bad people punished (a prudential, desire-driven consideration), and it does not make God a moralist with cosmic police powers. What it claims is that on this view God is *necessarily* associated with morality — he is perfect goodness and his will accords with it.

blocks.label: Canonical argument — the Euthyphro dilemma against divine command
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 4, presenting Plato's *Euthyphro* — matching the lecture's fork

steps.text: Either acts are right because God commands them, or God commands them because they are right.

If the first: rightness is arbitrary (any command, however horrific, would constitute rightness), and God's own goodness becomes vacuous — he could not be praised for commanding what is right rather than what is not.

If the second: morality stands independent of God, divine authority is redundant to moral truth, and Kant's caution applies — "even the Holy One of the Gospel must first be compared with our ideal of moral perfection before we can recognize him as such."
Divine command cannot be the fundamental ground of moral rightness: it either makes rightness arbitrary or makes God unnecessary to it.

blocks.text: **The theist's reply** (as Jacobs reconstructs it) — God's commands are not unintelligible: "God's commands are intelligible and acceptable to reflective people because they make sense in terms of largely shared values." Commands cannot turn "morality on its head," because a *perfect being* cannot command just anything — the very idea of a cruel, wasteful, or mendacious ultimate authority is at odds with the perfection in question. Concede, though, that our understanding of why some things are commands may exceed our grasp; the authority rests on perfection, not on our ability to audit every rationale. Whether this reply answers the dilemma or restates the second horn with confidence (the perfections doing the work are recognisably *ours* — see Kant's comparison test) is left, in the text, to the reader.

positions.name: Craig's identity reply: God *is* the Good

blocks.text: The third option the fork omits: goodness is neither external to God (first horn) nor a product of his arbitrary will (second) — it is identical with God's nature. God does not *decide* what is good, and goodness does not *constrain* him from outside; his own character is the standard, and his commands express it. (As presented in the lecture; Craig's own text is not in this corpus.)

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: lecture presentation of Craig — a reconstruction from the lecture's exposition

steps.text: The Euthyphro fork assumes goodness is either willed by God or independent of God; a third possibility is that goodness is identical with God's nature.
If God is the Good, then his commands are good neither arbitrarily (they flow from a nature that *is* goodness) nor redundantly (there is no standard apart from God to which they answer).
The dilemma is a false dilemma, and divine command theory survives in modified form: rightness is grounded in God's commands *as expressions of* his necessarily good nature.

blocks.label: The lecture's counter-pressure
blocks.text: if God's nature is not up to him, he lacks control over the moral standard in the same way the first horn's transcriber does; and the defence (no control over logic, either; omnipotence never required the illogical) works only if goodness follows from God's nature with something like logical necessity — "a tall order."

positions.name: The epistemic and motivational questions (the textbook's wider frame)

blocks.text: Jacobs separates three claims that are easily run together. (1) *Moral knowledge without God?* Even Aquinas's natural-law theism allows that human reason perceives important moral truths without reference to revelation — someone who does not believe in God "can have moral knowledge," though the rest of his worldview will be very different. (2) *Moral motivation without God?* If lack of belief disables someone from being appropriately motivated, that "would be a psychological fact about that person," not a metaethical result. (3) *What religion adds*: not a new foundation so much as dimensions naturalism lacks scope for — grace, cosmic justice, faith, redemption, the struggle with sin: "there is more to life than we see or than science can disclose," and religions present a *meaningful order* that the naturalist, even the objectivist naturalist, does not claim to find. And a clarifying caution: a faith-based ethics is not a relativism — believers "do not think that their view is just one among many perspectives"; each believes his or her view true.

positions.name: Can theists be moral? (the reverse question)

blocks.text: A third lecture turns the usual question around and tests five arguments *against* the morality of theists. Its structure matters for this entry: each argument overreaches. **Clifford's ethics of belief**: it is wrong to believe on insufficient evidence (the shipowner who convinced himself his rotten ship was seaworthy, and drowned others, is guilty even when the ship happens to survive) — so theists qua believers violate an epistemic duty; the argument turns on a contested epistemology and would convict much ordinary belief besides. **Discrimination**: many religions discriminate in who can be saved or achieve nirvana — but that is *exclusivism*, arguably bad, not discrimination in the pejorative sense of arbitrary exclusion, and it is not true of every religion. **Complicity**: theists support organised religions that commit atrocities — but "theist" extends far beyond members of any atrocity-committing body; the argument fails against *all* theists. **The evil God**: an omnipotent, omniscient God who knowingly permits horrors might himself be evil, and then his followers immoral — but this targets one specific (Abrahamic, traditional-attribute) conception, and concludes at most that *that* God's followers might be immoral. The lecture's general lesson mirrors the textbook's caution against overreach: morality is not a binary possession — partial moral failure in one respect is not total immorality — and arguments that purport to settle "the theist question" wholesale prove, at most, something about some theists. (Distilled from the Carneades lecture: [Can Theists Be Moral? (5 Arguments)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Pd5GWAE_Z4) — the file's title promises five arguments; the lecture works through four before generalising.)

thought.name: The yearly command
thought.text: (lecture). Suppose God commanded that a hundred children be murdered each year. On the "right because commanded" horn, that would be *good* — and no theist will say it. The case is the arbitrariness horn made vivid; the theist's textbook reply (a perfect being could not command it) applies here directly, and the debate then turns on what "could not" means.

thought.name: Clifford's shipowner
thought.text: (lecture, from W. K. Clifford). A shipowner, knowing his vessel is old and suspect, talks himself into sincere belief that she is seaworthy; she sinks. Guilty of the deaths, says Clifford — and guilty *even if* she had completed the voyage, because he had no right to believe on such evidence. The case is the engine of the "ethics of belief" argument against theists; it also stands on its own as a claim about epistemic duty, usable far beyond this debate.

god-and-morality.verdict: The Euthyphro fork remains the organising pressure, and neither source in this corpus declares it dissolved. The lecture recommends skepticism about (or suspension of judgment on) simple divine command theory, and treats Craig's nature-identity move as the live option whose cost — goodness grounded in God's nature with near-logical necessity — is still to be paid. The textbook is more ecumenical and less verdictive: it presents the dilemma, the theist's three-part reply, and then relocates much of the interest to epistemology (natural law: moral knowledge without revelation) and to what religion adds *around* morality rather than under it (grace, cosmic justice, redemption). Both sources agree on two negative points: that divine command is not best understood as a reward-and-punishment scheme, and that a faith-held morality is not thereby a relativism.

moral-luck.title: Moral Luck
moral-luck.aka: the problem of luck in moral assessment
moral-luck.note: 028's own cases: the careless pair, the failed rescue, unacted intentions
moral-luck.question: How much of what we are morally judged for is up to us? Two drivers take the same icy road at the same careless speed; a child runs out in front of one of them. We blame the second driver vastly more than the first — yet the difference between them is pure luck: nothing in their choices, characters, or efforts differed. A would-be rescuer dives and misses; another dives and saves; the dives were identical. If moral assessment tracks what lies within the agent's control, outcome luck should make no difference to judgment. If it shouldn't matter but irresistibly *does* — in blame, in punishment, in the agent's own remorse — then either our practices are systematically unjust, or the control condition on moral judgment is false. The same problem recurs for *character*: nobody chooses the upbringing that formed their dispositions — "constitutive" luck — yet we judge people for the characters they have.
moral-luck.ninety: *No Carneades lecture is devoted to moral luck; the following is distilled from the textbook (Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 2, "What about Luck?") and is marked accordingly, per the build rules.* Kant saw the problem and built his theory to be immune to it: moral worth resides in rational volition alone — in the will's determination by duty — and the will is the one thing fortune cannot touch; a good will frustrated by every accident remains good, like a jewel shining by its own light. Bernard Williams, quoted in the chapter, names the attraction exactly: Kantianism promises "an ultimate form of justice" — assessment purified of luck — as "solace to a sense of the world's unfairness." Mill refuses the immunity: for him the *motive* bears on the worth of the agent and the *intention* on the morality of the act, and both are exposed to luck — what an agent manages to intend and effect depends, as Nagel puts it, on "what one did often depends on outcome." Aristotle sits uncomfortably between: upbringing is "all-important" for virtue, which no one chooses; yet virtuous activity, once formed, is something like up to us, and flourishing still needs external goods fortune can withhold. The chapter's question is whether Kant's immunity is purchased at too high a price — a moral worth so sealed off from outcomes, character, and circumstance that it stops resembling the judgments we actually make.

positions.name: Kantian immunity: worth in the will alone

blocks.text: Moral worth is located in rational volition — the quality of the agent's willing — and volition is the one item wholly within the agent's control. Outcomes, talents, temperament, and upbringing may affect what an agent *achieves* but not what the agent is *worth*, morally. Luck is thereby excluded from moral assessment by design.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 2, presenting Kant — a formalization

steps.text: It is unjust to assess an agent for what was not up to the agent; genuine moral assessment must track only what lies within the agent's control.
The quality of an agent's volition — whether the will is determined by duty — is within the agent's control in a way that outcomes, native temperament, and formative circumstances are not.
Moral worth resides in volition alone, and is therefore immune to luck: the frustrated good will and the successful one have equal worth.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: (i) The cost objection: our actual judgments do track outcomes (the two drivers), intentions realised and unrealised, and formed character; a theory declaring all of that morally irrelevant may be consistent but describes a practice recognisably not ours. (ii) The depth objection: is volition itself really luck-free? The capacity and disposition to will well are themselves shaped by constitution and upbringing — the immunity may only push luck one level down. The chapter airs both worries without resolving them; Williams's "solace" remark cuts both ways — a consolation can be a motive for believing, not a reason.

positions.name: Mill: motive and intention, both luck-exposed

blocks.text: Mill splits the assessment Kant unifies. The *motive* — what the agent acted from — determines the worth of the *agent*; the *intention* — what the agent meant to bring about — determines the morality of the *act*. Neither is sealed against fortune: which intentions an agent forms and carries through depends on capacities, opportunities, and outcomes, and motives are themselves products of temperament and education. Moral assessment, on this view, honestly registers luck rather than legislating it away — and the divergence between "objective rightness" (what in fact produced the best outcome) and "subjective rightness" (what the agent could reasonably have aimed at) becomes a permanent feature of moral judgment, not a defect.

positions.name: Nagel: the control condition collides with practice

blocks.text: Nagel's formulation in the chapter is diagnostic rather than constructive: we cannot give up the control condition (it seems constitutive of fairness in judgment), and we cannot give up our luck-tracking judgments either (attempted and completed crimes, the two careless drivers). "What one did often depends on outcome" — and as the sphere of the genuinely controlled shrinks under scrutiny (outcomes, circumstances, constitution, character), the area of agency threatens to contract to a vanishing point. Jacobs presents this as the problem in its sharpest form: not a puzzle with a known solution but a tension between two commitments neither of which we will surrender.

positions.name: Aristotle: character luck admitted, activity defended

blocks.text: Aristotle concedes the deepest luck of all: virtue requires a good upbringing, which is "all-important" and wholly unchosen — the badly raised may be permanently disabled from excellence. Three mitigations structure his position in the chapter. (i) Once formed, virtue is *activity*, and activity is the agent's own: the virtuous person does not merely have dispositions but exercises them. (ii) Flourishing (as distinct from virtue) admittedly needs external goods — friends, resources, a city — so fortune retains real power over the *life*, though less over the *character*. (iii) The result is a two-level view: moral assessment proper tracks the formed character and its exercise (partly luck's gift, then the agent's), while the assessment of a whole life remains frankly luck-exposed. Whether this is a resolution or a relabelling of Nagel's tension is left open.

positions.name: A supporting lecture note: motivation-based virtue ethics and luck

blocks.text: One Carneades lecture in the forms cluster observes, in passing, that *motivation-based* (agent-centred) virtue theories have a structural advantage exactly here: by locating moral assessment in the agent's motives rather than in outcomes, they insulate evaluation from bad outcome luck — a Kantian benefit reached by an Aristotelian route. The remark is brief and the lecture's main business is elsewhere; it is recorded here because it is the only luck-specific observation in the lecture corpus for this slice. (Distilled from: [What is Agent Centered Virtue Ethics?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g1hSqpOISxg).)

thought.name: The equally careless pair
thought.text: (Jacobs, ch. 2). Two drivers, identically careless on the same icy road; a child runs out before one. Our blame differs enormously; nothing about the agents does. The case isolates *outcome luck* in its purest form.

thought.name: The failed rescue
thought.text: (Jacobs, ch. 2). A rescuer dives, misses, and the swimmer drowns; a second rescuer, identically brave and identically skilled, succeeds. If worth is in the willing, the two are equals; if outcomes matter, they are not. The case is the Kant–Mill fork as a story.

thought.name: Unacted evil intentions
thought.text: (Jacobs, ch. 2). An agent fully intends a wrong, is prevented by sheer accident from ever attempting it, and is discovered. We judge him — but for what? An intention that luck kept causally inert. The case tests whether intention alone, with no outcome and no attempt, can bear the full weight of blame — and whether Kant's volition-centred view handles it *better* than its rivals, as it should if immunity is its virtue.

moral-luck.verdict: Open, in the strong sense: the chapter presents the tension (control condition vs luck-tracking practice) and four historically great managements of it — Kant's exclusion, Mill's admission, Nagel's sharpening, Aristotle's partial concession — and endorses none. Two scope notes for this KB. First, the literature's familiar taxonomy of luck (resultant, circumstantial, constitutive, causal) is Nagel's, but the *textbook* does not lay it out under those labels; this entry has used the cases (outcome, character/upbringing) without importing the labels as if they were the book's. Second, the textbook's own discussion questions are left as questions — including whether there is *subjective* vs *objective* rightness — and the entry preserves them as such rather than reporting a resolution the text does not contain.

moral-motivation.title: Moral Motivation
moral-motivation.aka: internalism vs externalism about motivation (the textbook does not use these labels; see "Where the debate stands")
moral-motivation.question: Can knowing what is right *by itself* move someone to act? Or is motivation always separate — supplied by desire, feeling, or interest — so that a person could fully accept a moral judgment and remain utterly unmoved? The question matters twice over. It is a question in moral psychology: what actually moves moral agents? And it is a lever in metaethics: if moral judgments were bare reports of fact, their apparent power to move us would be mysterious — the inertness charge Mackie pressed against objectivism. Our textbook chapter opens it with a deliberately ordinary case and three great rival answers: Kant's, Hume's, and Aristotle's.
moral-motivation.ninety: *No Carneades lecture is devoted to this problem; the following is distilled from the textbook (Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 2) and is marked accordingly, per the build rules.* A motorist is stranded by the roadside, his arm in a cast, unable to lift the hood of his car. A passer-by could stop and help. Why might he? The textbook lists ten distinguishable motives: because helping is the right thing to do; because he hopes for a reward; because he knows what helplessness feels like and would want help himself; sheer sympathy; because his father taught him never to pass someone in trouble; because he wants to feel good about himself; because he thinks it will please God; and more. Most motives are *sentiments or desires*, not recognitions of duty. Kant and Hume then fight over the special case: the motive "because it is right." For Kant, the moral motive must be reason itself — an act has moral worth when done *because* it is right, and reason alone, without the cooperation of inclination, can determine the will. For Hume this is impossible: "reason of itself is utterly impotent in this particular; it cannot either prevent volition or oppose the preference of any passion or emotion." A bare cognition that an act is right moves nothing; something must already *care*. Aristotle offers a third picture in which the fight dissolves: in the virtuous person, reason and desire are *aligned* — trained together from childhood — so that doing right is also what one enjoys; the question "which moved him, reason or desire?" has, for such a person, no sharp answer.

positions.name: Kant: reason alone can motivate, and only the rational motive has moral worth

blocks.text: Moral requirements bind rational agents as such; correspondingly, the will can be determined by reason's own recognition of duty, independently of desire. An action done from sympathy, or hope of reward, or habit, may *conform* to duty, but it lacks moral worth: worth requires that the agent act *because the act is right* — the rightness itself, apprehended by reason, is the motive. Jacobs notes the purifying consequence the theory intends: moral worth is thereby insulated from the accidents of temperament and fortune (see [Moral Luck](moral-luck.md)).

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 2, presenting Kant — a formalization

steps.text: A motive grounded in the agent's desires or inclinations binds only conditionally: it moves the agent only while the inclination lasts, and its authority is that of the inclination, not of morality.
Moral requirements have unconditional authority for rational agents — they bind the agent *as* a rational agent, whatever his inclinations.
The distinctively moral motive must be reason itself: the recognition that the act is required. Only action from that motive — duty done because it is duty — has full moral worth.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Hume's impotence charge (below) is the direct denial of the conclusion's psychology. A second pressure, from within the chapter: the plurality of the motorist's motives suggests that recognising duty is rarely how human beings are actually moved, and a theory of moral worth that discounts all ten motives but one risks describing an agent nobody is. Kant's framework can reply that moral worth is a standard, not a census — but the chapter leaves the exchange open.

positions.name: Hume: reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions

blocks.text: Reason's office is to discover truth — relations of ideas and matters of fact. But "where the truths which they discover are indifferent, and beget no desire or aversion, they can have no influence on conduct and behaviour." Motivation requires a passion; reason can inform a passion (correct its factual beliefs, find means to its end) but cannot originate one, and cannot oppose one except by another. Applied to morality: the judgment that cruelty is wrong moves us only because a sentiment — sympathy, the moral sense — is already engaged; the judgment's motivating force is borrowed from feeling, never from cognition alone.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 2, presenting Hume's *Treatise* and *Enquiry* — a formalization

steps.text: Cognition alone is motivationally inert: a state that merely represents how things are cannot, by itself, produce volition or oppose a passion.
Moral judgments do motivate — reliably, across agents who sincerely make them.

Moral judgment must involve more than cognition: it essentially engages sentiment. (This is the engine of [subjectivism](moral-relativism-and-subjectivism.md) and of [expressivism](emotivism-and-expressivism.md): if judgments move us, and bare facts cannot, judgments must express the feelings that move us.)

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Kant's position is the standing counter-thesis (reason's self-determination). Jacobs also records Korsgaard's more recent Kantian development: rational agents act under a **practical identity** — a conception of themselves (as parent, friend, professional, moral agent) — and motivation flows from the need to act in ways one can reflectively endorse as consistent with that identity; to act against it is to lose one's integrity as that kind of agent. This gives reason a motivational office without making it a rival passion — though whether "reflective endorsement" is reason moving us or a desire to be a certain sort of person is precisely the Kant–Hume dispute restated.

positions.name: Aristotle: in the virtuous agent, reason and desire are trained into alignment

blocks.text: Not a compromise between Kant and Hume but a different shape of answer. The virtuous person does not first apprehend a duty and then struggle to want it, nor act on raw feeling unguided by reason: upbringing and habituation have formed the desires so that they *track* what reason discerns as good. The virtuous enjoy acting well — pleasure in right action is a *sign* of achieved virtue, not a contaminant of it (contra Kant) — and their reason is genuinely practical, not a spectator of their passions (contra Hume). Moral motivation, on this view, is a *developmental achievement*, which is why Aristotle makes upbringing "all-important" — and why the theory inherits the luck problems of [Moral Luck](moral-luck.md).

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 2, presenting Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* — a formalization

steps.text: In excellent practical agency, what reason asserts is what desire pursues: the practically wise person's judgments and appetites have been formed together, by habituation, so that the objects reason discerns as worthy are the objects desire finds attractive.

Neither element explains the achievement alone: untrained desire is blind to worth; unhabituated reason knows the good without reliably wanting it (the incontinent agent is the standing case of the second failure).
Moral motivation is neither reason's solo act (Kant) nor passion's (Hume), but the condition of a character in which the two have been educated into one orientation toward the good.

positions.name: Mackie's rider: opting out is not irrational

blocks.text: Even granting morality its psychological machinery, a deflationary point survives. Mackie held that someone who simply declined to be moved by moral considerations — who opted out of the moral point of view — would not thereby be *irrational*: reason, on the Humean showing, cannot convict him of an error, since it cannot supply the missing sentiment. The textbook presents this as the sceptical residue of the debate: morality's authority over motivation is real for those inside it, but its grip on the amoralist cannot be demonstrated from reason alone. (Compare the egoist's role in [Self-interest and Egoism](self-interest-and-egoism.md).)

thought.name: The stranded motorist
thought.text: (Jacobs, ch. 2). The arm in a cast, the hood too heavy, the passer-by who might stop — and ten motives for stopping that are genuinely different from one another. The case's work is taxonomic: it forces the question of *which* motive, if any, is the moral one, and whether "the moral one" is even a single thing. Any theory of moral motivation must sort the ten without merely defining the answer in.

thought.name: The incontinent agent
thought.text: (Aristotle, via ch. 2). He judges, correctly, that he should not; he wants, anyway; he does. He is the standing refutation of simple intellectualism (knowing the good is not sufficient) and the datum the Aristotelian alignment view is built to explain: what he lacks is not information but formation.

moral-motivation.verdict: Unsettled, and the textbook is explicit that the three-way structure (Kant / Hume / Aristotle) is a standing menu, not a historical sequence with a winner. Two clarifications for the KB. First, terminology: the contemporary labels *internalism* and *externalism* about moral motivation are not used in this text; the debate is present in substance (must sincere moral judgment motivate? Kant and Hume divide over the mechanism) but readers should not import the modern taxonomy's finer subdivisions and expect to find them here. Second, the debate's metaethical leverage: Hume's P1 is the same premise as Mackie's inertness objection to objectivism — whoever wins here constrains the objectivity debate — and Jacobs's own leaning is visible only in the architecture: the Aristotelian third view is presented last in its section and at greatest sympathy, without a verdict.
