moral-objectivity-and-realism.title: Moral Objectivity and Realism
moral-objectivity-and-realism.aka: the objectivity of moral value; moral realism vs anti-realism
moral-objectivity-and-realism.note: Jacobs's seven objectivities; Mackie's error theory
moral-objectivity-and-realism.question: When we say that cruelty is wrong, are we stating a truth about the world — something that would be so whether or not anyone felt, believed, or decided it — or are we doing something else: expressing a feeling, projecting an attitude, reporting a convention? And if moral value *is* objective, what kind of objectivity is it? The candidates on offer in our textbook do not agree with each other: value as a mind-independent reality, value as rational necessity, value constructed by rational procedure, value as objective reasons, value grounded in empirical facts about desire, value grounded in human nature. The problem is therefore double: *whether* moral judgments answer to anything independent of us, and *what* they could be answering to.
moral-objectivity-and-realism.ninety: *No Carneades lecture is devoted to this problem; the following is distilled from the textbook (Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 1) and is marked accordingly, per the build rules.* "Objective" can mean several different things, and moral objectivists have meant most of them. Plato and Moore held that good is a real feature of reality that we know rather than make — we can be wrong about it as we can be wrong about geometry. Kant relocated the objectivity: moral claims are objective not because they describe a value-realm but because they pass a formal test any rational agent can apply, the test of universalizability. Rawls's constructivism and Nagel's "normative realism" soften the metaphysics further — constructed moral facts, or simply true propositions about what we have reason to do. Mill went the other way and grounded value in a plain empirical fact, that pleasure is the one thing desired for its own sake; Aristotle grounded it in what a human being, given its nature, needs in order to flourish. Against all of these stands John Mackie's challenge: objective values, if they existed, would be entities "of a very strange sort, utterly different from anything else in the universe," detectable only by a special faculty — and, worse, a bare fact about the world could not by itself move anyone to act. Moral considerations are supposed to be action-guiding; objective facts, as such, are inert. That pair of charges — queerness, and inertness — is what every objectivist account in this entry has to answer.

positions.name: Platonic–Moorean realism: value as a reality we know

blocks.text: Good is an impersonal, objective reality, independent of desire, feeling, custom, and convention. For Plato it is a Form: particular good things are good by approximating it, and knowledge of it is the most important knowledge there is. Moore's version keeps the realism but drops the separate realm: good is a real, irreducible property — its presence depends on the presence of other things, as texture depends on a surface, but it is identical with none of them — and we are aware of it directly, by what Moore called intuition. On both versions, moral judgments are cognitive: literally true or false, made true by the value they answer to.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 1, presenting Plato's *Republic* and Moore's *Principia Ethica* — a formalization

steps.text: When we truly judge that a man, an action, and a social arrangement are each *good*, there is some one property they share in virtue of which each is good.

That property is not constituted by our desires, feelings, or conventions: we can be correct or incorrect in our judgments of it, as in geometry, and correctness is fixed by the property itself, not by our valuing.
Goodness is an objective constituent of reality — something to be known, not stipulated, chosen, or invented.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Mackie's queerness charge (below) is aimed first of all here: a non-natural property, apprehended by no sense and no ordinary faculty, is metaphysically and epistemologically exotic. Jacobs also notes the standing question whether realism *must* be committed to value as an item in the inventory of the world — the dispute that Nagel's version (below) is designed to avoid.

positions.name: Kantian objectivity: the objectivity of rational necessity

blocks.text: Moral claims are objective, but not because they refer to a mind-independent reality. Their objectivity is the "universally valid necessity" of principles that any rational agent can endorse: a maxim is morally permissible if it can be universalized — willed as a law for all rational agents — without being conditioned by the agent's particular desires, passions, or interests. Moral judgments are therefore objectively true or false (Kant is a cognitivist), but their truth-maker is the formal structure of practical reason, not a value-realm.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 1, presenting Kant's *Foundations of the Metaphysics of Morals* — a formalization

steps.text: A principle conditioned by an agent's desires or interests commands only hypothetically: it binds only those who happen to have that desire or interest.
Moral requirements bind categorically — they have authority for an agent simply as a rational agent, independently of what the agent happens to want.

The criterion of moral rightness must be a formal, desire-independent test — universalizability — and objectivity in morals is the objectivity of rational necessity, not of a normative realm "out there."

blocks.label: Development
blocks.text: Rawls's *constructivism*: the search for moral truth "fixed by a prior and independent order of objects and relations" is replaced by grounds "rooted in our conception of ourselves"; moral facts are *constructed* by principles of moral reasoning rather than discovered. Whether Kant's own view counts as *realism* is, Jacobs notes, arguable — it is objectivist without being committed to moral value as an object of reason.

positions.name: Nagel's normative realism: objective reasons without value-entities

blocks.text: Realism need not posit occult entities. What is real is that "propositions about what gives us reasons for action can be true or false independently of how things appear to us" — discoverable by adopting an objective standpoint and subjecting appearances to critical assessment. Korsgaard's gloss, quoted by Jacobs: "We need only believe that reasons themselves exist, or that there are truths about what we have reason to do."

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 1, presenting Nagel, *The View from Nowhere* — a formalization

steps.text: For there to be objective values, what is required is true normative propositions — truths about what anyone has reason to do and want — holding independently of our beliefs and inclinations.
Such truths do not require, in addition, a further item in the world (a Form, a non-natural property) in virtue of which they hold.

Moral realism can be true without commitment to curious metaphysical objects: "the view that values are real is not the view that they are real occult entities or properties, but that they are real values."

positions.name: Mill's naturalistic objectivity: value grounded in desire

blocks.text: Value is objective, and its objectivity is empirical. Pleasure is the one thing desired for its own sake and only for its own sake; that psychological fact is an objective basis for the normative conclusion that pleasure is good and to be promoted, and it is a further matter of fact which actions produce more of it. Moral judgments are thus factual judgments — a deliberate demystification of morality. (Moore's charge that this commits the naturalistic fallacy is taken up in [Naturalism, Non-naturalism, and the Open Question](naturalism-and-the-open-question.md).)

positions.name: Aristotelian objectivity: value grounded in human nature

blocks.text: Given the distinctive constitution of human nature, there are objective conditions of a flourishing life. Practical reason — perfected in the person of practical wisdom — grasps what is genuinely good for a human being; in the virtuous agent "what reason asserts is what desire pursues," so correct desire, not desire as such, is the standard. This is a naturalistic objectivity, but of a very different kind from Mill's: where Mill cites a general fact about what people *do* desire, Aristotle cites what a human being *is* — the proper function of its essential capacities.

positions.name: Mackie's attack: queerness, the unexplained "because," and inertness — the error theory

blocks.text: The anti-realist challenge in its strongest form in this corpus. Ordinary moral judgments *claim* objectivity — but the claim is false, because there are no objective values for them to report.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 1, presenting Mackie, *Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong* — a formalization of three converging arguments

items: P1 (queerness). If there were objective values, they would be "entities or qualities or relations of a very strange sort, utterly different from anything else in the universe," and awareness of them would require "some special faculty of moral perception or intuition, utterly different from our ordinary ways of knowing everything else."

P2 (the supervenience puzzle). Take the natural fact that an action is deliberate cruelty — causing pain just for fun — and the alleged moral fact that it is wrong. The wrongness is said to hold *because* of the cruelty; but the connection "cannot be an entailment, a logical or semantic necessity," and is not mere co-occurrence either. Just what in the world the "because" signifies is unexplained — whereas replacing the moral quality with a *subjective response*, causally related to detecting the natural features, would make the situation "much simpler and more comprehensible."

P3 (inertness). Moral considerations are action-guiding; but merely *knowing* that something is the case does not, by itself, motivate. Hume: conclusions of the understanding "discover truths: but where the truths which they discover are indifferent, and beget no desire or aversion, they can have no influence on conduct and behaviour."

∴ C. There are no objective values. Since ordinary moral judgments presuppose them, those judgments are systematically false — an **error theory**: cognitivist about what moral claims *mean*, nihilist about whether any of them is *true*.

blocks.label: Replies available in the corpus
blocks.text: the objectivist's counters are developed across the neighbouring entries: that the "because" can be constitution or identity rather than entailment ([Naturalism](naturalism-and-the-open-question.md)); that responses can be *merited* by objective properties, as colour judgments are (McDowell, same entry); that moral facts earn their keep by figuring in our best explanations (Sturgeon/Railton, same entry); and that motivation need not be external to judgment in the way P3 assumes ([Moral Motivation](moral-motivation.md)). Jacobs is careful to note what Mackie does *not* conclude: that morality is unimportant. Mackie held that we make moral judgments and that doing so "is of the first importance" — they are to be reinterpreted in subjectivist terms, not abandoned.

positions.name: Monism and pluralism (a cross-cutting division)

blocks.text: Objectivists divide again over how many values there are. *Monists* (Kant, Mill) posit one fundamental value and one criterion of right action. *Pluralists* hold that values are irreducibly many: Moore's several intrinsic goods (pre-eminently "the pleasures of human intercourse and the enjoyment of beautiful objects"); Nagel's distinct sources of value — utility or welfare, autonomy, perfectionist considerations, rights — which cannot be measured against a common standard, though they can sometimes be ordered (fairness before utility, one right before another). Pluralism's burden is to show how irreducibly different values can jointly figure in a single judgment without making judgment arbitrary; its motivation is that attempts to reduce all value to one dimension look forced against the reality of value.

moral-objectivity-and-realism.verdict: In this corpus, unsettled — and unsettled at two levels. First, whether moral value is objective at all: Mackie's three challenges are stated at full strength and are nowhere in ch. 1 *answered*; the answers come piecemeal, in ch. 4's naturalism debates and ch. 2's motivation debate, and Jacobs presents them as moves in a live dispute, not as a verdict. Second, among objectivists, *which* objectivity: Jacobs's own summary caution is that all objectivists agree moral judgments are literally true or false, and "disagree over what *makes* them true or false" — Plato, Moore, Kant, Rawls, Nagel, Mill, and Aristotle give seven different answers. A further question the chapter leaves open is whether objectivity requires any one of: truth-values, independence of beliefs, independence of desires and feelings, determination by natural properties, or distinctness from natural properties — different combinations yield different positions, and the merits are "in the details."

moral-relativism-and-subjectivism.title: Moral Relativism and Subjectivism
moral-relativism-and-subjectivism.aka: subjectivism about moral value; cultural relativism (for the relativist variant)
moral-relativism-and-subjectivism.question: Suppose moral value is not an objective feature of the world. Two different deflations are possible, and they are often confused. The truth of a moral judgment might depend on *whose* standards are in play — the norms of a culture, community, or person — so that the same act is right here and wrong there, with no neutral standpoint from which to adjudicate: that is **relativism**. Or moral judgments might be grounded in *mental states* — sentiment, feeling, approval — rather than in facts about the world: that is **subjectivism**. Either could hold without the other, and the interesting subjectivisms in our textbook (Hume's, Smith's) are explicitly *not* relativist: they ground morality in a sentiment common to all mankind. The problem is to say what, if anything, secures the authority and correctness of moral judgment once objectivity is given up — or whether nothing needs to.
moral-relativism-and-subjectivism.ninety: Relativism and subjectivism are independent positions that are often held together and therefore confused. Relativism says the morality of an action differs from person to person or culture to culture; it is opposed to *universalism*, the claim that ethical statements apply the same to everyone. Subjectivism says the morality of actions depends on the content of someone's mental states — beliefs, desires, feelings — rather than on objective facts about the world; it is opposed to *objectivism*. You can be a relativist without being a subjectivist: someone who holds that you must do whatever *your* holy text (or your country's laws) prescribe is a relativist, because different texts and laws give different rules, but an objectivist, because what the text says is an objective fact, not a mental state. And you can be a subjectivist without being a relativist: a divine-command theorist who holds that right is whatever the one God wills is a universalist — the same rule binds everyone — but a subjectivist, because rightness depends on a mental state, namely God's. The lecture also distinguishes *descriptive* relativism (the empirical observation that people do disagree about morality) from *metaethical* relativism (the claim that the truth of a moral statement depends on who utters it), and voices a skeptic's worry about arguing from the first to the second: that we cannot prove which moral claim is correct does not seem to imply that all of them are correct, each for different people. (Distilled from the Carneades lecture: [Moral Relativism vs Moral Subjectivism (Meta-Ethics)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0UQdlu_spyk).)

positions.name: Sentiment subjectivism (Hume and Smith): subjective ground, universal reach

blocks.text: Moral distinctions are grounded in sentiment, not detected by reason — but the sentiment in question is not private taste. Hume: "The notion of morals implies some sentiment common to all mankind, which recommends the same object to general approbation"; the affection of humanity, "being common to all men, can alone be the foundation of morals, or of any general system of blame or praise." To judge morally one must "depart from his private and particular situation, and must choose a point of view, common to him with others." Smith's version disciplines sentiment through the **impartial spectator** — "only by consulting this judge within… can we ever see what relates to ourselves in its proper shape and dimensions" — so sentiments can be proper or improper, felt in due measure or not.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 1, presenting Hume's *Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals* and Smith's *Theory of Moral Sentiments* — a formalization

steps.text: Moral judgment has its basis in sentiment: first perceptions of right and wrong are felt, not derived from reason — reason instructs us in the tendencies of actions, but a sentiment must "display itself" to give the useful the preference over the pernicious.

The relevant sentiments, suitably corrected (the common point of view; the impartial spectator), are common to mankind rather than idiosyncratic: within that corrected standpoint, someone who does not see that cruelty is wrong is *mistaken*, not merely possessed of a different taste.
Morality can be fully genuine — with argument, criticism, correction, and authority — on a subjectivist basis, without objective values and without relativity to groups or persons.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the objectivist's standing suspicion (Jacobs): is this having it both ways? If there are no moral facts, in what sense are moral statements "true"? The subjectivist's answer in the text: truth-talk within morality needs no realm of objective values behind it — we accept certain statements as true, argue for them, and argue against their contradictories, and Hume's universal sentiments supply "an adequate basis for morality." The objectivist counters with the *games* analogy: within cricket's rules we can say a move was well played, but we cannot say cricket is a *better game* than baseball — evaluation inside a practice is not evaluation of the practice, and the subjectivist (the charge runs) mistakes the first for the second. Jacobs presents this dispute through an analogy with compatibilism about free will: subjectivism about moral truth, like compatibilism, claims we can make all the distinctions that matter (correct/incorrect, sound/unsound views) without the contested metaphysics; critics of both reply that the distinctions are unstable without it.

positions.name: Ayer's expressivism: subjectivism without truth at all

blocks.text: The uncompromising version. A moral sentence "makes no statement at all": "sentences which simply express moral judgements do not say anything. They are pure expressions of feeling and as such do not come under the category of truth and falsehood." Note the precision Jacobs insists on: Ayer does *not* say moral judgments are reports *about* the speaker's feelings (those would be true or false); "That's wrong" expresses feeling, the way an exclamation does, where "I strongly disapprove of that" reports it. This position is developed as [Emotivism and Expressivism](emotivism-and-expressivism.md); it appears here as the limiting case of subjectivism — the version Blackburn's quasi-realism then tries to soften (truth *internal* to the moral point of view: "the existence of the truth depends on nothing (externally), and on those features that make it wrong (internally)").

positions.name: Relativism: correctness relative to norms

blocks.text: The correctness of moral judgments is relative to the norms of different times, places, and communities. Within a set of norms, judgments can be true or false; but there is no objective or neutral standpoint from which the norms themselves can be assessed, and no universal basis for morality. A universally shared morality is not ruled out — but if it existed it would be "a historical, contingent matter," everyone's happening to agree, not their agreeing on something objective.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 1, presenting the relativist case including Mackie's argument from relativity — a formalization

steps.text: Moral codes vary persistently across cultures and across the history of single cultures, and the disagreements do not resolve the way disagreements about (say) the causes of illness do.

The variations are better explained without objective values: in Mackie's words, "the actual variations in moral codes are more readily explained by the hypothesis that they reflect ways of life than by the hypothesis that they express perceptions, most of them seriously inadequate and badly distorted, of objective values." Commonalities (e.g. prohibitions on murder) are likewise explicable by needs and interests almost any community has.
Claims to have ascertained objective values are always made from *inside* one or another culture, whose norms shape the alleged ascertainment.
There are no objectively true or false moral claims; correctness is always correctness relative to customs, practices, and ideals.

blocks.text: **Objections** (the objectivist replies, as Jacobs presents them) — (1) Difference, even persistent difference, does not show there is no fact of the matter: a society that denied prime numbers would prompt questions about its mathematics, not doubts about primes; "objective" does not mean obvious, and disagreements may be resolvable in principle. (2) Explanations of diversity are *consistent with* objective values existing; that a society's morality has sociological causes does not show its judgments answer to nothing. (3) The aspiration objection: if slavery or causing pain for sport is wrong, it seems wrong "because of what *they* are, not just because of who *we* are" — "it's wrong for us, but not wrong for them" drains the judgment of the content we meant it to have. (4) **The group-specification problem**: relative to *which* group? If the whole of humanity, the view collapses into Humean subjectivism; if a smaller group — which, given that each of us belongs to many overlapping communities? Were Southern abolitionists in the early 1800s *wrong*, diverging from the prevailing system? Can a minority be one person — is an act "wrong for P" only if P accepts norms condemning it? Jacobs's verdict on the dialectic: the relativist's arguments against objectivity do not by themselves establish relativism, which "must have merits of its own."

blocks.label: A caution the relativist must accept
blocks.text: relativism is a thesis about the *status* of values, not a first-order value: it does not entail tolerance. Tolerance, if affirmed, is affirmed from inside some value system; relativism "is consistent with the most lethal dogmatism and closed-mindedness, as well as being consistent with valuing diversity." Arguing that relativism *objectively* supports tolerance would be inconsistent.

positions.name: The independence of the two positions

blocks.text: The lecture's logical map matches the textbook's taxonomy. Subjectivism need not be relativist (Hume, Smith: universal sentiment; the lecture: divine command, subjectivist about God's mental states, universalist in scope). Relativism need not be subjectivist (the lecture: personal holy texts and national laws — different rules for different people, but the rules themselves objective facts). Textbook and lecture also agree on the common case: the familiar view that a moral statement is true iff it matches the beliefs of one's culture is *both* — relativist (varies by culture) and subjectivist (depends on mental states) — which is why the two are so often conflated. One textbook refinement the lecture lacks: on some uses, "subjectivism" names the narrower report-view (to say "X is bad" is to state that I believe X is bad) or is used loosely for emotivism; Jacobs's Hume/Smith subjectivism is neither — sentiment is the *basis* of judgment, not its reported content, and not mere expression either ("not 'blind' expressivism by any means").

thought.name: The abolitionist test
thought.text: (Jacobs, ch. 1). Were Southern abolitionists in the early 1800s morally *mistaken*, because they diverged from the prevailing system to which rightness is relative? And are critics of mutilation punishments mistaken where tradition sanctions those punishments? The case pressures relativism's group-specification and its ability to make sense of moral reformers — people a culture's own norms condemn but whom we want to call right.

thought.name: The holy-text relativist
thought.text: (lecture). A person who holds that everyone must do what *their own* holy text says: relativist (contradictory rules for different readers) yet objectivist (the text's content is a physical fact). Constructed to prove the two distinctions cross-cut.

moral-relativism-and-subjectivism.verdict: Unsettled at every joint, in these sources. Against relativism, the objectivist objections (especially group-specification and the reformer's case) are presented as serious but not fatal — "it needs to be addressed in a careful manner." For subjectivism, the live question is whether the Hume/Smith/Blackburn strategy — full-strength morality on a subjective basis, with truth internal to the moral point of view — is a stable position or, as the objectivist suspects, an unstable halfway house that must either find a stronger ground or admit the genuineness it claims to preserve is only apparent. The lecture ends one step further back, with the skeptic's procedural doubt: even granting irresolvable disagreement, it does not follow that each side is right for its own people — ignorance of which claim is correct is not evidence that all are.

naturalism-and-the-open-question.title: Naturalism, Non-naturalism, and the Open Question
naturalism-and-the-open-question.aka: the fact–value problem; moral naturalism vs non-naturalism (the is/ought gap is the popular name for the divide this entry examines — see the note in "Where the debate stands")
naturalism-and-the-open-question.note: Moore, reconstructed naturalism, Harman vs Sturgeon/Railton
naturalism-and-the-open-question.question: An action is cruel: it was a deliberate wounding of another person, done for the sake of harming him, and the attacker took pleasure in it. All of that is factual description — the sort of thing observation and the sciences can identify. The action is also *wrong, because* it is cruel. Is the wrongness one more descriptive property of the action? How is moral value related to the natural, non-moral facts and properties of the world — defined by them, constituted by them, dependent on them, identical with them, wholly independent of them, or not a feature of the world at all, but something our judgments *express*? This is the question "Where (if anywhere) in the world is moral value?", and every answer reorganises the rest of metaethics.
naturalism-and-the-open-question.ninety: Moore's open question argument begins from a contrast. Some questions are *closed*: "Are bachelors unmarried?" is answered by knowing the language — a "yes" costs nothing because it is true by definition, a barren tautology that gives no reason to act. The argument tests proposed definitions of good the same way. Suppose good just *means* pleasure (or happiness, or God's will). Then "Is pleasure good?" should be as closed as the bachelor question. It is not: competent speakers who know exactly what every word means can still genuinely ask it — it stays **open**. So no candidate X is synonymous with good; good cannot be defined. The lecture then draws a further, more skeptical moral than Moore drew: if goodness is not the property picked out by any predicate, perhaps goodness is not a property at all — "just a strange concept we invented." Hold that last step at arm's length: in the textbook's presentation, Moore himself was a *realist* about good — indefinable, but real — and the lecture's conclusion (that good does not exist) is the skeptical spin the channel puts on the argument, not Moore's. (Distilled from the Carneades lecture: [Moore's Open Question](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_GI1KsjBQYs).)

positions.name: Moore's non-naturalism: good is simple, indefinable, and real

blocks.text: "If I am asked 'What is good?' my answer is that good is good, and that is the end of the matter." Any attempt to define good in other terms — naturalistic terms above all — commits the **naturalistic fallacy**: it confuses good with some *other* property that good things also have, as yellowness is confused with the vibrations yellow things produce. Good things may all be pleasant, or desired, but pleasantness is not what *good* is.

blocks.label: Canonical argument — the open question argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 4, presenting Moore, *Principia Ethica* — a formalization; the lecture's version is structurally the same

steps.text: If "good" were definable as D (pleasure, happiness, what is desired, or any other candidate), then "Is what is D good?" would not be a genuine, open question — it would collapse into "Is what is D D?", settled by the meanings of the words.
For every candidate D, "Is what is D good?" remains an open question: "it may be always asked, with significance, of the complex so defined, whether it is itself good."

Good is not definable in terms of anything else. It is a simple, *sui generis* property — real and objective, dependent for its presence on non-moral properties (a thing is good *in virtue of* its good-making properties), but reducible to none of them.

blocks.label: The stakes Moore saw
blocks.text: if good *could* be defined in non-moral terms, the definition would show that what we called a fundamental moral value "is really, ultimately, something non-moral": defining the moral away eliminates it. Jacobs's caution for the naturalist side: Moore's alternatives (simple and indefinable; a complex awaiting correct analysis; meaningless — "there is no such subject as Ethics") were driven by a *semantic* test, as though definition were the only way to establish a necessary connection between properties. The reconstructed naturalists attack exactly that assumption.

positions.name: Reconstructed naturalism: constitution and identity without definition

blocks.text: Keep cognitivism and the reality of moral value; drop the definitional route. Moral properties **supervene** on natural properties *because they are constituted by them* (Brink) — as wetness is constituted by the properties of H₂O: a real property, non-accidentally dependent on a base unlike itself, connected by discoverable (empirical, law-like) relations rather than by meanings. The stronger variant is an **identity thesis**: moral value is *identical with* certain natural properties, as water is identical with H₂O — a necessary truth, but one discovered by inquiry and theory, not by analysing words; people used "water" correctly before chemistry existed.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 4 — a formalization of the reconstructed-naturalist strategy

steps.text: A necessary connection between moral and natural properties need not be semantic: constitution (wetness/H₂O) and theoretical identity (water = H₂O) are necessary relations ascertainable only by substantive inquiry.

If moral properties are constituted by, or identical with, natural properties in either of those ways, then "Is what is D good?" can remain an open *question* for speakers — openness reflects our epistemic position, not a metaphysical gap.
The open question argument does not refute naturalism; it refutes only the claim that good is *definable* in natural terms, which the reconstructed naturalist also denies.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Moore himself held dependence without constitution: good is *sui generis*, and (Jacobs judges) he would have balked at its being *literally constituted* by anything non-moral; his focus on definition missed the H₂O model partly because that model was not his target. Whether identity claims for value can actually be *established* the way chemical identities were is left, in this text, as the naturalist's promissory note.

positions.name: Humean ("skeptical") naturalism and expressivism

blocks.text: A second way to be a naturalist: deny that values are natural *properties* at all, while insisting that nothing non-natural is needed to explain moral valuing. Moral judgments express sentiments, propensities, and concerns that are themselves natural facts about human beings; the relation to non-moral properties is *subjective* supervenience. This is [Emotivism and Expressivism](emotivism-and-expressivism.md) in its ch. 4 dress: naturalism about what morality *is made of* (human nature), anti-realism about what moral judgments *say*. Jacobs's contrast is exact: realist naturalism tries "to save moral objectivity without non-naturalism"; Humean naturalism "also avoids non-naturalism but without treating moral values as objective… skeptical naturalism, in contrast to realist naturalism."

positions.name: Reconnecting fact and value (Foot, McDowell): the dichotomy itself is the mistake

blocks.text: Both camps above assume descriptive meaning and evaluative meaning can be cleanly separated. Foot denies it: you cannot extract an "evaluative meaning" of *good* specifiable independently of its objects — can one understand what fairness or cruelty *is* and then face a further, open question of stance toward it? McDowell's analogy: redness is "a property the ascription of which to an object is not adequately understood except as true, if it is true, in virtue of the object's disposition to present a certain sort of perceptual appearance" — the tomato *is* red, though our access to its redness runs through our sensibility. Moral properties are relevantly similar: judgments about them are **merited** by their objects (the moral difference from perception is that the relation is merit, not causation). In McDowell's later "no-priority" view, neither world nor response comes first: as with the funny — our laughing doesn't make things funny, unfunny things get laughed at, funny things go unlaughed at — the response is *apt or not* in light of its object. Corollaries Jacobs lists: no fact/value distinction of the classic kind; sensibility's role does not undermine objectivity; moral judgments are literally true or false; and none of this works by theoretically reducing moral to natural properties.

positions.name: Aristotle's naturalism

blocks.text: Value grounded in natures: for each natural kind there is a condition of successful actualisation, and for humans — who pursue their good deliberately, through reason and choice — the virtues are the states in which feeling and cognition are aligned toward the genuinely good ("virtue makes the goal correct, and intelligence makes what promotes the goal [correct]"). Moral significance is found *in* the facts, acts, and situations of the natural world, without identity or supervenience machinery. The standing objection: the view rides on a teleological conception of nature that modern science has abandoned — "there are no norms or values 'built into' nature." The modern retrieval (Foot, McDowell) attempts to keep the moral psychology and epistemology — character, the reason–desire alignment, good and bad pleasures — while dropping the cosmic teleology; whether the elements survive the extraction is, Jacobs says, an open question the theorists themselves are pursuing.

positions.name: Do moral facts explain anything? (Harman vs Sturgeon and Railton)

blocks.text: A second front, independent of definition: entities earn their place by explanatory work — we posit genes because inheritance needs them, not demons, because schizophrenia doesn't. **Harman**: a moral observation is not evidence for a moral theory the way a physical observation is evidence for a physical theory, because "the truth or falsity of the moral observation seems to be completely irrelevant to any reasonable explanation of why that observation was made" — your moral sensibility plus the non-moral facts explain your judgment that the cruel act is wrong, whether or not it *is* wrong. Moral facts are "an explanatorily idle accessory." **Sturgeon** replies that the idleness claim overreaches: it is not just judgments but *behaviour* that moral facts explain — Hitler's being depraved is part of the best explanation of what he did; had everything non-moral been the same but not constituted depravity, would he really have done exactly the same? Moral facts also explain why the virtuous are trusted with office and why just arrangements are stable. **Railton**: ought-facts are "facts of a special kind about the way things are" — supervening, hence metaphysically unsuspect — and we can ask empirically whether our judgment-forming processes are *reliable* routes to them (the near-universal rejection of trial by ordeal has factual grounds of exactly this kind).

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 4, presenting Harman, *The Nature of Morality* — a formalization

steps.text: We are justified in positing a kind of fact only if it is needed in the best explanation of some range of phenomena (genes: yes; demons: no).

Every moral judgment and observation is fully explained by two kinds of fact — facts about the psychology (sensibility, principles) of the judge, and non-moral facts about the world — without supposing the judgment true.
There is no explanatory need to posit moral facts; commitment to them is unsupported by the method that supports our other factual commitments.

blocks.text: Sturgeon's rebuttal targets P2's scope (behaviour, not just judgment) and its counterfactual (same psychology, no depravity, same actions?); the text presents the exchange without a winner.

thought.name: Water and wetness
thought.text: (Jacobs, ch. 4). Wetness supervenes on H₂O without being definable in terms of hydrogen and oxygen; water *is* H₂O without "water" meaning H₂O. The double analogy is the reconstructed naturalist's whole case in miniature: it exhibits necessary moral–natural connections that Moore's semantic test cannot see. It pressures non-naturalism by demanding to know why value could not stand to its base as wetness stands to its base.

thought.name: The run-over dog belongs to the bullshit entry
thought.text: ; this entry's perceptual case is **the ripe tomato**: its red as experienced is not an exact copy of the physical structures causing the experience — which tempts the projection model of value (value as "colouring" we add) — until McDowell's dispositional reading restores the red to the tomato.

naturalism-and-the-open-question.verdict: Jacobs's map offers seven possible moral–natural relations — definition, constitution, dependence, identity-without-definability, full independence, expressive understanding, supernatural grounding — and no verdict among them; "all of the debates that we identified remain very much alive." Two honest notes for this KB. First, terminology: the textbook never uses the label "is/ought gap." What it examines is the same divide under other descriptions — Hume's insistence that reason discovers truths but cannot, without sentiment, produce blame or approbation; Mackie's question about the "because" linking natural fact to wrongness; Moore's open question; the twentieth century's fact/value distinction. Readers arriving with the "is/ought" label should map it onto those discussions rather than expect the slogan. Second, the lecture's closing move — from "good is indefinable" to "goodness is not a property / does not exist" — is a step *beyond* both Moore and Jacobs's presentation of him, in which indefinability is combined with full-blooded realism about good; the entry has kept the two apart deliberately.

self-interest-and-egoism.title: Self-interest and Egoism
self-interest-and-egoism.aka: psychological egoism; the egoistic challenge to morality
self-interest-and-egoism.note: the egoism equivocation; Hobbes to Plato's reversal
self-interest-and-egoism.question: Is every human action, at bottom, self-interested? The rescuer, the martyr, the anonymous donor: does each act, however it appears, from a desire for the agent's *own* good — pleasure, relief, reputation, a quiet conscience — so that genuinely other-regarding motivation is an illusion? **Psychological egoism** is the descriptive thesis that this is so, universally. It is not a moral theory (it recommends nothing) but a claim about human motivation, and if it were true it would reshape moral psychology: benevolence would need re-describing, and morality's demands would have to work through self-interest or not at all — the route Hobbes took. Our textbook's question is the prior one: is the thesis even *true*, and what would count as showing it?
self-interest-and-egoism.ninety: *No Carneades lecture is devoted to this problem; the following is distilled from the textbook (Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 2) and is marked accordingly, per the build rules.* The egoist's favourite evidence is a verbal slide. The donor is *pleased* by the recipient's relief; the rescuer *wanted* to help; so — the egoist concludes — each acted for his own pleasure, his own want: self-interest everywhere. The textbook presses the slide. That an action satisfies the agent's desire does not make its *object* the agent: I desire *that she be relieved*, and my pleasure is the by-product of getting what I wanted, which was her relief, not my pleasure. "It pleases me" is not the same as "it is in my interest," and a desire for another's good is not made selfish by being *mine* — every desire is someone's. Against the egoist's suspicion that benevolence is always disguised, the chapter sets Hume, Smith, and Mill: human beings have real social feelings — sympathy is a basic feature of our constitution, not a costume self-interest wears. Hobbes is the interesting middle case: he built morality *out of* self-interest (covenants kept because insecurity is worse) without needing the strong psychological thesis to be a definition. And Plato and Aristotle reverse the egoist's direction entirely: justice is not a tax on the soul's good but a constituent of it — the just person profits *in his soul* — so the opposition between morality and self-interest is itself the mistake.

positions.name: Psychological egoism: all motivation is self-interested

blocks.text: The thesis: every voluntary action is motivated, ultimately, by the agent's own interest or pleasure. In its crude form it trades on the slide diagnosed above; in careful forms it claims that apparent benevolence always has a self-regarding payoff (relief of one's own sympathetic distress, anticipated reciprocity, self-image) that is the real object of desire.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Jacobs, ch. 2 — a formalization of the egoist case as the chapter presents it

steps.text: In every apparently benevolent action, the agent acts on his own desire, and its satisfaction gives him pleasure or relieves his discomfort.
Acting to satisfy one's own desire, for the pleasure or relief its satisfaction brings, is acting self-interestedly.
Every action is self-interested; benevolence is self-interest under a description that hides it.

blocks.text: **Objections** (the chapter's replies) — P2 is where the argument lives or dies, and it equivocates. (i) *Ownership vs object*: that the desire is the agent's does not make the agent its object. A desire *that the stranded motorist be helped* is satisfied by his being helped, whether or not the helper ever learns of it or feels anything; a desire for one's own pleasure is satisfied only by one's pleasure. The two have different objects and different satisfaction-conditions, and collapsing them is a verbal trick, not a discovery. (ii) *Pleasure as by-product*: the pleasure of benevolence *presupposes* the benevolent desire — you cannot take pleasure in her relief unless you first wanted her relieved for her sake; so pleasure cannot be the desire's original object without circularity. (iii) *Unfalsifiability*: if every counterexample is re-described as hidden self-interest, the thesis stops being an empirical discovery and becomes a definition in disguise — and as a definition it proves nothing about how people actually are. Jacobs's verdict on method (via the scepticism analogy below): the *possibility* of an egoistic redescription is not evidence of its truth.

positions.name: Hobbes: morality constructed from self-interest

blocks.text: Hobbes accepts something like the egoist's psychology but draws the opposite moral from the debunkers: precisely *because* agents pursue their own preservation and good, they have reason to covenant — to lay down the right to all things in exchange for security — and to keep covenants, since the war of all against all is the worst outcome for each. Morality and political obligation are *artifacts of* self-interest rationally pursued, not illusions exposed by it. The textbook's point in placing Hobbes here: egoistic premises do not by themselves settle anything against morality; everything depends on what is built on them.

positions.name: The social-feelings reply (Hume, Smith, Mill)

blocks.text: Benevolence is real and basic. Hume: the affection of humanity is "common to all men" and is the foundation of morals; Smith's impartial spectator (see [Moral Relativism and Subjectivism](moral-relativism-and-subjectivism.md)) works *because* sympathy is a genuine other-directed capacity; Mill treats the social feelings of mankind as a natural sentiment, "one of the principal ingredients" of moral motivation, needing cultivation rather than unmasking. On this view the egoist has the explanatory direction backwards: self-interest is the special case that sometimes needs explaining, not the universal solvent.

positions.name: Plato and Aristotle: justice as the soul's profit

blocks.text: The reversal. The question "why be just, if justice costs me?" assumes justice and the agent's good are rivals. Plato's *Republic* argues the just soul is the *ordered* soul — each part doing its work under reason's rule — and that injustice is a kind of psychic disorder, bad for its possessor as disease is bad for the body, whether or not it is detected. Aristotle likewise makes the excellent life *constitutively* the pleasant and flourishing one for the person whose desires are rightly formed. On this family of views, morality is not self-interest's competitor but its correct specification: the egoist and the moralist are both wrong to accept the dichotomy (compare the alignment thesis in [Moral Motivation](moral-motivation.md)).

positions.name: The egoist as global sceptic (the chapter's methodological moral)

blocks.text: Jacobs closes the section with an analogy this KB should preserve. The egoist's procedure — for every apparently benevolent act, produce a possible self-interested reinterpretation — mirrors the global sceptic's procedure in epistemology (for every belief, a possible deception scenario), and the replies mirror too: as Reid, Moore, Wittgenstein, and Chisholm argued in their different ways against scepticism, the bare *possibility* of a systematic reinterpretation does not dislodge the straightforward reading of the phenomena. Egoism, like scepticism, wins only if its reinterpretations are *better explanations*, and the chapter's burden is that — once the ownership/object equivocation is removed — they are not.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: no lecture covers this problem — begin with the Survey.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Jacobs, *Dimensions of Moral Theory*, ch. 2, "Self-interest."

ladder.label: Primary (as presented in Jacobs)
ladder.text: Hobbes, *Leviathan*; Hume, *Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals*; Smith, *The Theory of Moral Sentiments*; Mill, *Utilitarianism* ch. 3; Plato, *Republic*; Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics*.

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: ch. 2 whole, with the motivation debate that frames it.

self-interest-and-egoism.verdict: The textbook's stance is unusually definite for this book, and the entry reports it as the textbook's stance, not as settled philosophy: crude psychological egoism rests on an equivocation, and the sophisticated version purchases immunity at the price of unfalsifiability; benevolence, on the Hume–Smith–Mill line, is a datum to be built on, not an appearance to be explained away. What remains genuinely open in the chapter: how *much* of actual motivation is other-regarding (an empirical question the text does not pretend to settle), and the normative question Hobbes and Plato answer in opposite directions — whether morality should be *founded on* self-interest (contract) or *identified with* the agent's deepest good (the soul's order) — which reappears in [Forms of Moral Theory](forms-of-moral-theory.md) as the contractarian and virtue-centred options.

connections.title: Moral Motivation
connections.text: [Moral Motivation](moral-motivation.md) — the parent problem: egoism is the claim that one item on the motorist's list of ten motives is secretly the whole list.

connections.title: Forms of Moral Theory
connections.text: [Forms of Moral Theory](forms-of-moral-theory.md) — Hobbes's construction becomes the contractarian form; the Plato/Aristotle reversal becomes the virtue-centred form.

connections.title: Moral Relativism and Subjectivism
connections.text: [Moral Relativism and Subjectivism](moral-relativism-and-subjectivism.md) — Hume's and Smith's social feelings do double duty: they ground morality's content there and its motivational reality here.

Epistemology's [External-World Skepticism](../epistemology/external-world-skepticism.md) — the methodological analogy is explicit in the text: egoism stands to moral psychology as global scepticism stands to epistemology, and the anti-sceptical replies transfer.

existence-precedes-essence.title: Existence Precedes Essence: Sartre on Freedom and Self-Deception
existence-precedes-essence.aka: Sartrean existentialism; "condemned to be free"; bad faith (in this corpus, "self-deception")
existence-precedes-essence.question: Is a human being a thing with a nature fixed in advance — by God, by biology, by temperament, by upbringing — which then explains, and excuses, what the person does? Or does a person exist first, with no nature given, and become whatever their choices make them — so that nothing, not even a strong feeling or a hard past, can be produced as an excuse? Sartre's 1946 lecture *Existentialism is a Humanism* is the corpus's fullest staging of the second answer, and the *Being and Nothingness* chapter anthologized beside it poses the problem that answer creates: if I am transparent to myself and radically free, how can I possibly lie to myself?
existence-precedes-essence.ninety: *No Carneades lecture in the corpus treats Sartre or existentialism, so this version is distilled from the textbook texts themselves (Sartre's lecture, book 018, ch. NINE §4) and is marked accordingly.* A paper-knife is made to a conception: its essence — what it is for, how it is made — precedes its existence. Religious doctrine treated man the same way, as an article in the mind of a divine artisan; eighteenth-century atheism dropped the artisan but kept the conception, as "human nature." Sartre's atheistic existentialism drops both: "man first of all exists, encounters himself, surges up in the world — and defines himself afterwards." There is no human nature because there is no God to conceive it, and so no determinism and no excuse: "man is condemned to be free" — condemned because he did not create himself, free because, once thrown into the world, "he is responsible for everything he does." Choosing is unavoidable and never private: in choosing myself I fashion an image of man for all. The feelings that accompany this are anguish (total responsibility, with no sign to certify a choice), abandonment (no values written in an intelligible heaven), and despair (relying only on what is within our wills). And the standing temptation is to flee all of it into *self-deception* — playing at being a thing with a fixed nature, as the café waiter plays at being a waiter.

positions.name: Atheistic existentialism: existence precedes essence (Sartre)

blocks.text: Man "is nothing else but that which he makes of himself. That is the first principle of existentialism." What is true of manufactured things and of the God-made man of doctrine — essence first — is false of us.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Sartre, "Existentialism is a Humanism," book 018, ch. NINE §4

steps.text: For an article of manufacture (Sartre's example is the paper-knife), essence precedes existence: the artisan's conception and technique define the thing before it is produced. The traditional doctrine of God as creator, and even godless doctrines of a universal "human nature," treat man on this same model.
If God does not exist, that model loses its ground for man: "there is no human nature, because there is no God to have a conception of it."
For man, existence precedes essence: he first exists and encounters himself, and defines himself afterwards — "he will be what he makes of himself."

blocks.text: **Canonical argument — freedom and the absence of excuses** (same source):

steps.text: If existence precedes essence, "one will never be able to explain one's action by reference to a given and specific human nature; in other words, there is no determinism — man is free, man is freedom."

Nor, if God does not exist, are there a priori values or commands "inscribed in an intelligible heaven" that could justify or excuse a choice: "It is nowhere written that 'the good' exists, that one must be honest or must not lie."

"We are left alone, without excuse… man is condemned to be free" — he did not create himself, yet "from the moment that he is thrown into this world he is responsible for everything he does," passion included: "man is responsible for his passion."

blocks.text: **Choosing for all men** (same source) — the move that is meant to answer the charge of mere subjectivism: "when we say that man chooses himself, we do mean that every one of us must choose himself; but by that we also mean that in choosing for himself he chooses for all men," since every act fashions "an image of man such as he believes he ought to be." Anguish is the felt form of this: Kierkegaard's "anguish of Abraham," who must decide, with no possible proof, that the voice is an angel's and that he is Abraham.

positions.name: Self-deception (*mauvaise foi*): the flight from freedom (Sartre)

blocks.text: The same volume's *Being and Nothingness* selection (in this corpus's translation: "self-deception," where most editions print "bad faith" — see the Sources note) asks how lying to oneself is even possible, and answers by locating its patterns.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Sartre, "Self-Deception," book 018, ch. NINE §2 — a formalization of the chapter's opening puzzle

steps.text: An ordinary lie requires a deceiver who possesses the truth and a deceived who does not; in self-deception "the one to whom the lie is told and the one who lies are one and the same person," so "I must know in my capacity as deceiver the truth which is hidden from me in my capacity as the one deceived" — and consciousness is wholly translucent, so a deliberately cynical lie to oneself "fails completely… the lie falls back and collapses under my regard."

The Freudian rescue — splitting the psyche into id and ego behind a censor — restores the duality only by making part of me a thing to be interpreted from outside, which relocates rather than solves the problem.

Self-deception must be an "evanescent," "metastable" project of consciousness itself: a pattern in which a person flees what they are (free, self-making) by playing at being a fixed thing — and it "can even be the normal aspect of life for a very great number of people."

blocks.text: The patterns (§2, Part II): a woman on a first date who knows the man's intentions perfectly well but "does not want to realize the urgency," attending only to what is respectful in his conduct; and the café waiter whose movements are "a little too precise, a little too rapid," who is *playing* at being a waiter — "I can be he only in the neutralized mode, as the actor is Hamlet… What I attempt to realize is a being-in-itself of the café waiter," as if his duties were not his free choice to confer value upon.

positions.name: The editor's caution: the slogan obstructs the movement (Kaufmann)

blocks.text: The anthology's editor refuses to let this entry's title stand for the whole anthology. "Existentialism is not a philosophy but a label for several widely different revolts against traditional philosophy"; Jaspers, Heidegger, and Sartre "are not in agreement on essentials," and the alleged precursors include a dedicated Christian (Kierkegaard) and "an impassioned anti-Christian" (Nietzsche). On the slogan itself: "it has become a commonplace that existentialism is the doctrine that existence precedes essence, and this phrase obstructs the understanding of this complex movement as well as of Sartre's philosophy" — Heidegger's *Letter on Humanism*, prompted by Sartre's lecture, is quoted making the reversal point: Plato's metaphysics already says *essentia* precedes *existentia*, and "Sartre reverses this sentence" rather than leaving metaphysics behind.

blocks.label: Objections Sartre stages and answers in the lecture
blocks.text: (i) *Quietism of despair* (the Communist reproach): the doctrine "declares that there is no reality except in action" and that "man is nothing else but what he purposes"; despair means only acting without hope beyond one's will, as Descartes' "conquer yourself rather than the world" meant. (ii) *Cowardice as temperament*: "there is no such thing as a cowardly temperament… he has made himself into a coward by his actions"; likewise "there is no genius other than that which is expressed in works of art" — the genius of Proust is the totality of Proust's works. (iii) *Which adviser, which sign?*: the pupil torn between staying with his mother and joining the Free French can get no a priori answer from Christian doctrine or Kant's ethic (each horn treats someone as a means); even choosing an adviser "is nevertheless to commit oneself by that choice." "You are free, therefore choose — that is to say, invent."

thought.name: The paper-knife
thought.text: (Sartre, lecture). An artifact whose essence precedes its existence, because a maker conceived it first. Sets up the contrast the whole position turns on: everything made is like this; the question is whether man is made.

thought.name: The pupil's choice
thought.text: (Sartre, lecture). A student must choose between his widowed mother, who lives only for him, and a possibly futile journey to join the Free French. Every offered guide fails in turn — doctrine, Kant, feeling (a feeling's strength is known only by the act that ratifies it, so consulting it is circular), and advice (choosing the adviser chooses the advice). Meant to show abandonment concretely: no sign is vouchsafed, and interpreting any sign is itself the chooser's responsibility.

thought.name: The café waiter
thought.text: (Sartre, *Being and Nothingness* ch., §2). A waiter performing waiterness a fraction too eagerly, balancing his tray "with the recklessness of a tight-rope-walker." Meant to make self-deception visible as *play*: treating a freely sustained role as a thing's nature. Pressures anyone who says "that's just my job / my character / how I am."

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: Sartre's lecture itself — it was written for a general audience and is the clearest statement in the corpus.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Kaufmann's introduction (book 018, ch. ONE) — the map of the movement and the warning against reducing it to the slogan; the history surveys (books 001 ch. 32, 026 "Modern Era"/"Post-Modern Era") for orientation only.

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: the "Self-Deception" chapter of *Being and Nothingness* (book 018, ch. NINE §2) for the mechanism; "Portrait of the Anti-Semite" (§3) for self-deception at social scale.

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: the whole Sartre chapter (book 018, ch. NINE), including "The Wall," read against Jaspers (ch. SEVEN) and Heidegger (ch. EIGHT) in the same volume.

existence-precedes-essence.verdict: Inside this corpus, the position is stated at full strength and answered only against the objections Sartre himself selects (quietism, subjectivism, the denial of values). The deepest pressure in the volume comes from its own editor and from Heidegger, and it is taxonomic rather than refuting: the slogan may be a reversal inside the metaphysics it claims to escape, and the movement it names may not exist as one doctrine at all. Whether a fixed human nature can be reinstated on other grounds (biology, psychoanalysis) is a fight the corpus stages only in Sartre's dismissal of the Freudian censor; the texts here leave it open.

connections.title: The Absurd and Sisyphus
connections.text: [The Absurd and Sisyphus](the-absurd-and-sisyphus.md) — Camus, anthologized as this volume's finale, starts from the same godless world and refuses Sartre's move: no self-created meaning dissolves the absurd, which must be kept alive by lucidity and scorn.

connections.text: [Master Morality, Slave Morality, and the Problem of Morality Itself](master-and-slave-morality.md) — the anthology's other route out of given values: Nietzsche (book 018, ch. FOUR; book 019) treats values as created too, but by types and ages, not by each individual's choice — and Kaufmann's introduction presents existentialism as one facet of Nietzsche's impact.

connections.text: [Postmodernism and Its Applied Turn](postmodernism-and-its-applied-turn.md) — a later French inheritance: book 003 presents Foucault, Derrida, and Lyotard as dissolving the very subject Sartre made sovereign.

Sartre, "Self-Deception" (book 018, ch. NINE §2, file ch14) — §I and the §II patterns (the woman, the waiter) read in full.

master-and-slave-morality.title: Master Morality, Slave Morality, and the Problem of Morality Itself
master-and-slave-morality.aka: Nietzsche's critique of morality; the natural history of morals
master-and-slave-morality.note: *Beyond Good and Evil* §§186–262, with Nietzsche's own mixture caveat
master-and-slave-morality.question: Where do moral values come from — and what is a morality *for*? Philosophers, Nietzsche charges, have always taken their own morality as simply given and looked for a rational foundation underneath it; nobody had treated morality itself as a problem. What happens when you do — when you compare many moralities across peoples and ages and ask what type of human being each one expresses and serves? *Beyond Good and Evil* (1886), the corpus's Nietzsche primary text, answers with a typology: two basic ways of valuing, born from two opposite social positions, whose mixture is still the moral air Europe breathes.
master-and-slave-morality.ninety: Nietzsche is the philosopher of "God is dead" — not a corpse in heaven, the lecture explains, but the collapse of the Christian worldview under secular and scientific pressure, and with it the standing morality. That collapse opens an era of *nihilism*: if the old values lose their ground, morality and meaning can look unjustifiable altogether — a result Nietzsche predicted and opposed, arguing we should pass *through* nihilism, tearing down the old structures, to create new values rather than stay in the wreckage; his Übermensch is that value-creator, closer (the lecture insists, against the Nazi misuse arranged by his sister's doctored posthumous editions) to an Aristotelian figure of excellence than to a master race. The nihilism lecture adds the spectrum this creates: anti-nihilists who say morality needs God, atheist moral cognitivists who keep morality on other grounds, non-cognitivists, and only at the far end actual nihilists. Nietzsche's own move in *Beyond Good and Evil* is diagnostic before it is creative: first find out what moralities there have been and what they are symptoms *of*. (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [Who Was Friedrich Nietzsche?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ugkxY1ntDu8), [What is Nihilism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B9aMLkwpf0U).)

positions.name: The problem of morality itself (Nietzsche, Part Five)

blocks.text: Before any typology: the discipline that should have produced one never saw its object. "In all 'science of morals' so far one thing was *lacking*, strange as it may sound: the problem of morality itself; what was lacking was any suspicion that there was something problematic here."

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Nietzsche, *Beyond Good and Evil*, Part Five, §186

steps.text: Moral philosophers "knew the facts of morality only very approximately in arbitrary extracts or in accidental epitomes — for example, as the morality of their environment, their class, their church, the spirit of their time, their climate and part of the world."

What they called supplying "a rational foundation for morality" was therefore "merely a scholarly variation of the common *faith* in the prevalent morality… in the last analysis a kind of denial that this morality might ever be considered problematic."

The real problems of morality "emerge only when we compare *many* moralities"; the justified task so far is descriptive — "to collect material, to conceptualize and arrange a vast realm of subtle feelings of value" — to prepare a *typology* of morals, since "moralities are also merely a sign language of the affects" (§187).

positions.name: Master morality (Nietzsche, Part Nine, §260)

blocks.text: Valuation originates with a ruling group conscious, with delight, of its difference from the ruled. "The noble human being separates from himself those in whom the opposite of such exalted, proud states finds expression: he despises them."

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Nietzsche, *Beyond Good and Evil*, Part Nine, §260 — a formalization of the section's typology

steps.text: Moral designations were "everywhere first applied to *human beings* and only later, derivatively, to actions," and the noble type "experiences *itself* as determining values; it does not need approval; it judges, 'what is harmful to me is harmful in itself'… it is *value-creating*."

Its governing opposition is therefore "good" and *bad* — "approximately the same as 'noble' and 'contemptible'" (the opposition of "good" and "evil" "has a different origin") — and what it honours is itself: fullness of power, pride, severity toward oneself; it helps the unfortunate "not, or almost not, from pity, but prompted more by an urge begotten by excess of power."

Master morality is "self-glorification": faith in oneself and hostility to "selflessness" belong to it "just as definitely… as does a slight disdain and caution regarding compassionate feelings and a 'warm heart.'"

positions.name: Slave morality (Nietzsche, Part Nine, §260)

blocks.text: "Suppose the violated, oppressed, suffering, unfree, who are uncertain of themselves and weary, moralize: what will their moral valuations have in common?"

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Nietzsche, *Beyond Good and Evil*, Part Nine, §260 — a formalization of the same section

steps.text: The slave's eye "is not favorable to the virtues of the powerful: he is skeptical and suspicious, *subtly* suspicious, of all the 'good' that is honored there — he would like to persuade himself that even their happiness is not genuine."

What gets honoured instead are "those qualities… which serve to ease existence for those who suffer: here pity, the complaisant and obliging hand, the warm heart, patience, industry, humility, and friendliness are honored — for here these are the most useful qualities."

"Slave morality is essentially a morality of utility," and its governing opposition is "good" and *evil*: "into evil one's feelings project power and dangerousness, a certain terribleness, subtlety, and strength that does not permit contempt to develop" — while its own "good" human being must be *undangerous*: "good-natured, easy to deceive, a little stupid perhaps, *un bonhomme*."

blocks.text: Nietzsche's own caveats, stated in the same section, are part of the position and are not to be trimmed off: in higher, mixed cultures the two types mediate, interpenetrate, and misunderstand each other, "and at times they occur directly alongside each other — even in the same human being, within a *single* soul." And §262 adds the historical sequel: moralities fix a type under constant unfavourable conditions, and when conditions relax, variation erupts and "the 'individual' appears, obliged to give himself laws."

positions.name: The will to truth, questioned (Nietzsche, Part One, §§1–4)

blocks.text: The critique of morality is one instance of the book's opening move: turning on philosophy's own ruling value. "We asked about the *value* of this will. Suppose we want truth: *why not rather* untruth? and uncertainty? even ignorance?" (§1). §2 names the metaphysicians' "faith in opposite values" — that the highest things cannot grow from their opposites — and §4 re-prices judgement itself:

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Nietzsche, *Beyond Good and Evil*, Part One, §4

steps.text: "The falseness of a judgment is for us not necessarily an objection to a judgment… The question is to what extent it is life-promoting, life-preserving, species-preserving, perhaps even species-cultivating."
The falsest judgements (the synthetic a priori among them) are "the most indispensable for us": without "a constant falsification of the world by means of numbers, man could not live."

"To recognize untruth as a condition of life — that certainly means resisting accustomed value feelings in a dangerous way; and a philosophy that risks this would by that token alone place itself beyond good and evil."

blocks.label: Objections and standing pressures, as the corpus presents them
blocks.text: Kaufmann's anthology introduction (book 018) records the catastrophic misreading: the Nazis "had no use at all for any of his books as a whole" yet "brazenly used him, too"; the Nietzsche lecture makes the same defence against the Übermensch-as-master-race reading. Kaufmann also anthologizes Nietzsche inside *existentialism* (book 018, ch. FOUR, "Live Dangerously") — selections on self-overcoming — which is a different Nietzsche emphasis than Book 019's moral typology, and the two should not be conflated. The corpus contains no systematic rebuttal of the typology itself (no defence of pity-morality from within its own texts, apart from the positions Nietzsche is describing); the entry therefore reports the typology as Nietzsche's claim, historically bold and empirically underargued in these pages — he offers it, by his own §186 standard, as the beginning of a descriptive science, not its completion.

thought.name: The two origins
thought.text: (§260). One act of valuation, staged twice: from the ruling group's delight in itself, and from the suffering group's need to endure. Same words ("good"), different opposites (bad vs. evil), different virtues. Meant to show that a morality's content is legible from the position of whoever made it — which pressures any morality that presents itself as positionless.

thought.name: The barbarian beginning
thought.text: (§257). Every higher culture "has *begun*" with "men of prey… more *whole* human beings" hurling themselves on weaker races — Nietzsche explicitly warns against "humanitarian illusions about the origins of an aristocratic society." A deliberately hard case for any progress story about morality's origins.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: the Carneades lectures *Who Was Friedrich Nietzsche?* and *What is Nihilism?* — biography, the death of God, and the nihilism spectrum, in plain language.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Harwood (book 026, "The Modern Era"), the Nietzsche entry; *Sophie's World* has no Nietzsche chapter (its 19th-century coverage runs Kierkegaard–Marx–Darwin–Freud) — a coverage hole worth noticing.

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: *Beyond Good and Evil* itself (book 019): Preface, Part One §§1–4, Part Five §§186–188, Part Nine §§257–262.

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: the whole of book 019 read with Kaufmann's commentary footnotes; Kaufmann's *Portable Nietzsche* selections in book 018, ch. FOUR for the self-overcoming emphasis.

master-and-slave-morality.verdict: The corpus stages Nietzsche's critique at full strength and surrounds it with defences against the political misreading, but it does not stage the scholarly counter-arguments (historical challenges to the typology; defences of compassion-based morality on independent grounds), and Nietzsche's own text concedes the descriptive work is preliminary. Two things the texts do settle between themselves: the typology is two ideal types, not two peoples — mixture "within a single soul" is built into §260 — and the critique of the will to truth (§§1–4) applies to the typology too: by §4's standard its worth is the question of what it promotes, not a correspondence it demonstrates.

connections.text: [Existence Precedes Essence: Sartre on Freedom and Self-Deception](existence-precedes-essence.md) — Sartre inherits the godless world and the death of given values; Kaufmann's introduction treats existentialism as one facet of Nietzsche's impact, and his Nietzsche chapter (book 018) is the bridge.

connections.title: The Absurd and Sisyphus
connections.text: [The Absurd and Sisyphus](the-absurd-and-sisyphus.md) — nihilism answered by lucidity rather than by new values.

connections.title: Postmodernism and Its Applied Turn
connections.text: [Postmodernism and Its Applied Turn](postmodernism-and-its-applied-turn.md) — book 003 and book 026 both treat Nietzsche as a precursor of postmodernism; book 003's authors enlist the liberal tradition against the descendants, a use of Nietzsche's legacy he would not obviously have signed.

sources: Nietzsche, *Beyond Good and Evil* (book 019, Kaufmann translation): Preface (file ch09); Part One §§1–5 (file ch12); Part Five §186 and §§187–188 openings (file ch20); Part Nine §§257–262 (file ch28) — all read in full.
