semantic-analysis-and-clarity-of-meaning.title: Semantic Analysis and the Clarity of Meaning
semantic-analysis-and-clarity-of-meaning.aka: 語理分析 (linguistic–conceptual analysis); the critique of linguistic harms; "What does it mean?"
semantic-analysis-and-clarity-of-meaning.note: Li's 語理分析 programme, vagueness vs ambiguity, the heap
semantic-analysis-and-clarity-of-meaning.question: A large share of disputes never reach disagreement about facts: the parties are using the same words in different senses, or words with no settled sense at all, and so argue past each other indefinitely — sometimes lethally. What should a thinker do *before* asking whether a claim is true? Li Tianming's answer is a discipline of its own: first establish what the claim means — or whether it means anything. No Carneades lecture is devoted to semantic analysis itself; the front door below pairs the closest lecture (on the kinds of unclarity) with Li's own procedure, and is marked accordingly.
semantic-analysis-and-clarity-of-meaning.ninety: Unclarity comes in kinds, and the kinds matter. A term is **ambiguous** when it has several distinct definitions in play ("bank": riverside or financial institution). A term is **vague** when it has absolute borderline cases no inquiry can settle — how many grains make a heap, how sparse hair must be to count as bald; vague terms generate the sorites paradox, in which one grain never makes a heap yet heaps somehow form. A term is **general** when its meaning is clear but ranges over many things ("prime number" — no borderline cases, hence not vague). Li's programme starts where the lecture stops: most consequential confusion is not innocent vagueness but *undetected* unclarity — words taken as clear because they are familiar, or taken as profound because they are obscure. His method, semantic analysis, is simply the disciplined habit of asking "What does it mean?" about the key terms of a problem before debating its answer: clarify "democracy" first, and the question "Is Vietnam a democracy?" splits into a meaning-question (settleable by analysis) and a fact-question (settleable by investigation). A statement that survives no clarification at all is worse than false — it is *not even false*, since a claim must have a meaning before truth or falsity can apply to it. (Lecture part distilled from [Vagueness vs Ambiguity vs Generality](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8SGizqyt8EM) and [The Paradox of the Heap](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b2yC-kQK_1o); the programme part distilled from Li's textbook chapters, there being no lecture on semantic analysis in the series.)

positions.name: Semantic analysis as the first link of methodology (Li)

blocks.text: Thinking methodology has four departments — semantic analysis, logical method, scientific method, fallacy analysis — and semantic analysis is the first link, because "when we think about a problem, in principle our first step must be to know what the problem asks." It is also one half of the key habit of critical thinking: the two questions "What does it mean?" and "What are the grounds for it?", meaning first, grounds second — with the rider that both questions must be asked *aptly*: where meaning is already clear enough, asking again is nitpicking, and Li is explicit that semantic analysis "is absolutely not nitpicking over words; it is the sharp instrument that specialises in breaking word tricks."

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Li, *Methods of Thinking and Independent Thinking*, book 002 ch09, Part I §I — a formalization of the chapter's methodological argument; read in my English translation

steps.text: A question can be answered — and a statement assessed as true or false — only once it is known what the question asks and what the statement means. ("When we can recognise a statement as true or as false, we already know what it means.")
Many disputes and statements fail exactly here: their key terms are ambiguous, floating without fixed standards, or such that no meaning can be extracted at all.

Clarifying meaning is methodologically prior to seeking answers and appraising truth: it settles the meaningful questions into parts that investigation can then decide, and dissolves the meaningless ones at the root ("not even false").

positions.name: The two illusions of clarity (Li)

blocks.text: Two standing errors protect unclear speech (source: ch09, Part I §II):

items: **Taking obscurity for profundity.** Obscure speech is admired as deep; the more muddled the speaker, "the more the listener admires him" (Li quoting Thouless). Li's counter-maxim: "Muddled speech does not reflect profound thought; muddled speech reflects only a muddled brain." A test with teeth: clear statements expose their own defects, whereas obscure ones hide whether they have any others — including fallacies.

**Taking familiarity for clarity.** Grammatical, familiar formulas — "from the viewpoint of history…," "with a Chinese heart," "do heroes make the times or the times make heroes?," "which matters more, money or friends?" — pass as meaningful because they are heard daily. Clarification of the last example shows the method in miniature: "friends" ranges from death-oath intimates to nodding acquaintances and "money" from coins to fortunes, and the answer flips with the clarification; before it, the question has no discussion-basis at all.

positions.name: Pseudo-semantic projection (Li)

blocks.text: A third ill, named in ch09 §II(C): assuming a compound expression must have a meaning because its parts do. "Half a catty" and "music" mean something; "half-a-catty music" need not. The chapter's worked target is theological God-talk — "omnipresent but not in space and time, without emotions yet wrathful" — and the two standard defences, demolished in sequence:

blocks.label: The defence, as Li reconstructs it
blocks.source: ch09 §II(C

items: P1 (defence). Such statements exceed human understanding — they are inconceivable and unspeakable.
P2 (defence). They are, instead, metaphorical and symbolic speech about God.

blocks.text: **Li's refutation** (same source):

items: Against P1: what is too deep to understand (recursion theory, the proof of Gödel's theorem, for most people) is still *meaningful*; a meaningless string is not beyond understanding but beneath its application. Appending "inconceivable and unspeakable" to "Yoh-zi-oh-xi ▲● Geba-ge" does not give it meaning either — and saying at length that God is unspeakable is itself a performance of self-contradiction ("slapping one's own face").

Against P2: if x is inconceivable, no one can know what resembles or symbolises x; and metaphorical *speaking* is still speaking. The defence therefore re-commits the contradiction it was meant to escape.

positions.name: The taxonomy of linguistic harms (Li)

blocks.text: *Thinking and the Mind-Demons* (book 002 ch10) organises the failure modes into three categories — the "mind-demons" of the title — each exhibited, not merely defined:

1. **Semantic ambiguity** （語意曖昧）: words like "mission" and "fate" (usable of any outcome whatever), the dialectical use of "negation" (under which one cannot say whether the negation of knowing is not-knowing); **terminological camouflage** — jargon and symbols as smokescreen (statistics without base numbers; pseudo-formulas in aesthetics); **semantic floating** （虛浮）: words without fixed standards, where Li insists on degree — "young" has approximate bounds (18 yes, 80 no) where "counter-revolutionary" has none; **semantic incoherence** （錯亂）: word-salad that no sympathetic reading can rescue.
2. **Empty verbiage** （言辭空廢）: statements with meaning but no information content are taken up in *Closed Systems and Pseudo-Explanation*; the bridge is Category III:

3. **Conceptual slippage** （概念滑轉）: sliding between senses mid-argument — **conceptual confusion** between two licit senses ("same" as identical vs similar, which makes "no two people can communicate, since no two have the same experiences" either empty or false), and **conceptual distortion** into senses usage does not licence (criticism of religion relabelled "infringing religious freedom"; "another kind of freedom," "real equality" — **calling a deer a horse**). Voltaire's Holy Roman Empire — neither holy, Roman, nor an empire — is Li's emblem for the cure: check the substance a stirring name refers to.

positions.name: The boundary cases: vagueness and the heap (the lectures)

blocks.text: The lecture taxonomy insists on one point Li's framework needs and does not supply in the same form: some unclarity is *in the predicate*, not in the speaker. "Bald," "heap," "short" have absolute borderline cases; no amount of counting hairs or grains settles them, and the sorites argument (one grain is not a heap; one grain never turns a non-heap into a heap; so there are no heaps) shows vagueness generating paradox, not mere muddle. The lecture ends in questions rather than a verdict: are vague terms sloppiness to be engineered away, or does language lose something real if every predicate is given a cut-off? It also notes the recursive sting — "vague" itself has borderline cases — against the view (attributed to "Fraga" in the captions, presumably Frege) that vague predicates are simply meaningless.

blocks.label: Objections to Li's harder line
blocks.text: from within Li's own text: his notes concede that whether speech counts as *floating* is context-dependent (a phrase with legal articles or precedents behind it may be clear enough), that elastic words are often indispensable, and that demanding logical precision in everyday talk is itself a student error he corrects. The calculus he actually applies is proportionality: clarification is owed where the dispute turns on the term, not everywhere.

thought.name: The nursemaid's application
thought.text: (Li, ch10 introduction). "I eat anything, and I am most fond of children": fond as in *dotes on*, or fond as in *likes to eat*? The hiring decision cannot even begin before the clarification — Li's domestic proof that "don't sign before you've seen clearly" applies to sentences as to contracts.

thought.name: The three birds
thought.text: (Li, ch10 §III(B)). "Three birds on a tree; one is shot dead; how many are left?" As arithmetic, 2; as an empirical question, 0–3 (and "more than 3" is arguable) depending on deaf, silly, stunned, and branch-caught birds. The school's single mandated answer is, for Li, conceptual confusion institutionalised.

thought.name: "Half a wife"
thought.text: (Li, ch09 §II(C)). Lover? fiancée? concubine? the half rescued from cannibals? The parts mean; the compound's meaning is exactly what is in question — the pseudo-semantic projection test case.

thought.name: The heap
thought.text: (lecture). Add grains one by one: the paradox is that every step is innocent and the destination undeniable — vagueness with a proof-shaped shadow.

semantic-analysis-and-clarity-of-meaning.verdict: Within these sources the programme is argued, not merely announced: Li's ch09 answers the two standing objections — that analysis is pedantry (the "don't scratch where it doesn't itch" rule; target the problem's core) and that language itself is the prison ("shackles thesis" — refuted, in his view, by the performative fact that its advocates must use language, at length, to urge escaping it, and by the chaos that its formula "non-x is x" licenses). The sources disagree more quietly at one seam: Li's paradigm harms are *curable* unclarities — senses unsettled because nobody has done the work — while the vagueness lecture's borderline cases are presented as incurable in principle (no inquiry settles the last grain), and it leaves open whether that is a defect of language or a feature thought cannot do without. Li's degree doctrine for floating terms ("young" has approximate bounds) sits between the two, and nothing in the corpus forces a choice. Book 025's title-level pairs (Profundity/Obscurity; Discussion/Argument) gesture at the same territory, but its text is absent from the corpus and can settle nothing.

causal-necessity-and-humes-dictum.title: Causal Necessity and Hume's Dictum
causal-necessity-and-humes-dictum.aka: Humeanism vs non-Humeanism; constitutional vs causal necessity
causal-necessity-and-humes-dictum.question: Humeans and non-Humeans agree on a surprising amount: there can be necessary connections between things that are not wholly distinct — a set and its members, a whole and its parts, a kind and the intrinsic properties essential to its members. They divide over one line: Hume's Dictum, that there are *no* necessary connections between wholly distinct entities — in particular, no necessary *causal* connections, so that a cause, even with all background conditions in place, could always have failed to produce its effect. Jessica Wilson's chapter in book 013 argues the Humean's line is unprincipled: accept the constitutional necessities, and you should accept certain causal necessities too.
causal-necessity-and-humes-dictum.ninety: *No lecture in the corpus covers this problem; this version is distilled from the textbook (Wilson, book 013, ch. 11) and marked as such.* Everyone in the debate accepts some necessities: water's identity with H₂O, sets being constituted by their members, fusions by their parts. These are *constitutional* necessities — the connected entities partly constitute each other, so they are not wholly distinct. Hume's Dictum permits exactly those, while forbidding necessary connections between wholly distinct things — paradigmatically causes and their separate effects. Wilson's move is a conditional: *if* you accept certain constitutional necessities, *then* consistency requires accepting certain causal necessities. Her lever is the *warrant*: the proof that identities are necessary is a special, compelling, broadly logical proof, but no such proof exists for the other constitutional necessities Humeans happily accept — sets, fusions, determinates and determinables. Those beliefs rest on the same softer warrants (systematization of beliefs, contemplation of hypothetical scenarios, inference to the best explanation) that are available in the causal case. So the Humean can keep the Dictum only at, in Wilson's phrase, costs of "implausibility and ad hocery" — and the non-Humean framework, which feels no tension here, comes out ahead.

positions.name: Humeanism under Hume's Dictum

blocks.label: Canonical statement
blocks.source: Wilson, "From Constitutional Necessities to Causal Necessities", book 013 ch. 11, opening

steps.text: There may be necessary connections between entities that are identical (Hesperus/Phosphorus, water/H₂O) or merely partly distinct — sets and their members, fusions and their parts, determinates and determinables, members of certain natural kinds and certain of their intrinsic properties, and (for physicalists) certain physical and mental states.

(Hume's Dictum) There are no necessary connections between entities that are *wholly* distinct — in particular no necessary causal connections, even when the background conditions requisite for causation are in place.

The differential treatment is principled: commonly accepted necessary connections involve constitutional relations (existential ontological dependence), whereas causes and effects do not constitute each other.

blocks.text: Wilson's chapter is the argument that P2's principled appearance is "not genuine".

positions.name: Schaffer's principled basis — and its limit

blocks.text: Jonathan Schaffer (as Wilson presents him) tries to ground the differential treatment epistemically: intuitions of causal contingency ("like charges might have attracted") should be trusted, unlike intuitions that identities are contingent, because for identity there is an *independent reason* — a compelling, broadly logical proof of the necessity of identity — to think our contingency intuitions misdescribe the case (Shoemaker's Kripkean redescription strategy for causation is thereby rejected: the law that strychnine is fatal may be *imagined* to fail only because we imagine something passing the tests for strychnine, or for a human being, rather than the real thing surviving).

blocks.label: Wilson's objection
blocks.source: Wilson, book 013 ch. 11, §1.1

steps.text: Schaffer's compelling-proof criterion warrants accepting necessities of *identity* while rejecting causal necessities.

But Humeans and non-Humeans alike also accept constitutional necessities between non-identical entities — set membership, parthood, the determinable/determinate relation, essential instantiation, realization — and for none of these is there any compelling proof: set theory is silent on the modal individuation of sets, mereology's axioms do not yield that fusions are necessarily constituted by their parts, and for several such relations there are not even candidate axioms.

The criterion "fails to warrant acceptance of many constitutional necessities that Humeans and non-Humeans alike commonly and reasonably accept" — so it cannot be what entitles the Humean to the differential treatment.

positions.name: Wilson's conditional: Constitutional → Causal

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Wilson, book 013 ch. 11, introduction and §§1–3

steps.text: The warrants actually supporting the accepted constitutional necessities are broadly non-logical: "systematization of relevant beliefs, contemplation of hypothetical scenarios, transcendental arguments, or… inference to the best explanation" of experiential, semantic, scientific, and philosophical facts — convincing, often, but not the sort to *compel* assent as a logical proof does.
Warrants of exactly those kinds are available for certain causal necessities; there is no difference in the *type or strength of warrant* that maps onto the constitutional/causal line.

*Constitutional → Causal*: if one accepts certain constitutional necessities, one should accept certain causal necessities. The Humean can resist only at attendant costs of implausibility and ad hocery; the non-Humean framework faces no such tension and "in this respect comes out ahead".

blocks.text: **Scope note (the author's own)**: the argument is presented as leverage for assessing "the two main frameworks in the metaphysics of science" precisely because direct criticism of either framework has tended to presuppose a stance on the Dictum and so talk past the other side; Wilson's arguments instead rest on "general and independent considerations about which facts in the world might plausibly warrant our beliefs in constitutional necessities". The conclusion is conditional and comparative — it does not, by itself, assert any particular causal necessity.

thought.name: Like charges attracting.
thought.text: Hume and Schaffer intuit that actual causes might have had different effects — that it is possible for like charges to attract, even with the background conditions for repulsion in place. The contingency intuition is the Humean's datum.

thought.name: Strychnine survived
thought.text: (Shoemaker). Imagine ingesting vast amounts of what passes every test for strychnine and surviving: Shoemaker says you have imagined test-passing stuff, not strychnine — the same redescription Kripke licenses for "water might not have been H₂O". Whether the redescription is legitimate *here* is exactly what is disputed: Schaffer says no independent reason compels it; Wilson's reply is that the compulsion standard, applied evenly, would also dissolve most constitutional necessities.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: no Carneades lecture covers Hume's Dictum or causal necessity — begin with the textbook.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Wilson's chapter is self-contained; Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary's Introduction (book 013, ch. 1) supplies the surrounding natural-kinds context.

ladder.label: Primary / full treatment
ladder.text: Wilson, "From Constitutional Necessities to Causal Necessities" (book 013, ch. 11) — the corpus's only chapter on the problem. (Hume's own texts in the corpus, in book 007, treat causation in the epistemology of induction; they were not used here, since Wilson's argument is about the modal, not the epistemic, claim.)

causal-necessity-and-humes-dictum.verdict: Wilson's verdict is explicit but bounded: on the warrant question, the non-Humean framework "comes out ahead", and the Humean's remaining options carry costs of implausibility and ad hocery — costs she argues for, in the chapter, rather than merely naming. Hume's Dictum itself is not refuted: the conclusion is a conditional about consistency of commitments, addressed to theorists who already accept the constitutional necessities. The volume contains no Humean reply chapter.

connections.text: [The Necessary A Posteriori](the-necessary-a-posteriori.md) — necessities of identity (water = H₂O) are the agreed starting data on both sides here; Ellis's essentialism is one route from them to necessary laws, Wilson's parity argument another.

connections.text: [Natural Kinds](natural-kinds.md) — "members of certain natural kinds and certain of their intrinsic properties" is one of Wilson's agreed constitutional necessities; the metaphysics of science frameworks she is assessing are the same ones Boyd's chapter (ch. 12) inhabits from the realist side.

classification-and-the-hierarchy-thesis.title: Classification and the Hierarchy Thesis
classification-and-the-hierarchy-thesis.question: The Linnaean picture is seductively tidy: species nest in genera, genera in families, and so on up to kingdoms, so that whenever two kinds overlap, one contains the other. The hierarchy thesis says real natural kinds must form such a single nested hierarchy. But actual scientific classification, in biology *and* in chemistry, is full of kinds that overlap without nesting — *crosscutting* kinds. Does that refute realism about natural kinds, show the classifications are merely conventional, or only show that the hierarchy requirement should be dropped?
classification-and-the-hierarchy-thesis.ninety: *No lecture in the corpus covers this problem; this version is distilled from the textbook (Tobin, book 013, ch. 10) and marked as such.* Kinds crosscut when they overlap but neither contains the other. Humans and dogs are both mammals; dogs and crocodiles are both quadrupeds; but humans and crocodiles share neither kind — so "quadrupeds" and "mammals" overlap in dogs without nesting. Chemistry, the paradigm home of natural kinds, does it too: albumin and renin are both proteins; renin and the hairpin ribozyme are both enzymes; but albumin and the hairpin ribozyme are neither both proteins nor both enzymes — enzymes are not a subkind of proteins, nor proteins of enzymes. The hierarchy thesis therefore fails as a description of scientific taxonomy. Tobin's question is what follows: Khalidi and Dupré say, reject the thesis; Hacking says, further, that kind distinctions are merely conventional; Ellis-style realists say crosscutting categories cannot be real kinds at all. Tobin defends the first answer against the second and third: crosscutting refutes the hierarchy thesis, not realism.

positions.name: The hierarchy thesis (Ellis, Kuhn — as Tobin presents them)

blocks.text: Natural kinds form a nested hierarchy: if any two kinds overlap, one is subsumed under the other as a subkind. Ellis builds this into his criteria for natural kindhood (criterion 5 in the editors' list — see [Natural Kinds](natural-kinds.md)); Kuhn's version is the *no-overlap principle*, motivated semantically: real kind terms in a taxonomy must not overlap except as genus to species — "there is no gold that is also silver, and that is what makes the terms 'silver' and 'gold' kind terms" — and scientific revolutions are marked precisely by taxonomies that cross-classify the same things.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Tobin, "Crosscutting Natural Kinds and the Hierarchy Thesis", book 013 ch. 10, §§1–2 — the thesis in Tobin's statement; labelled formalization

steps.text: A taxonomy of real natural kinds carves nature at its joints; a joint-carving classification cannot leave two legitimate kinds partially overlapping, since neither would mark the single natural division.

Paradigm taxonomies take the hierarchical form: Linnaean ranks (species → genus → family → order → class → phylum → kingdom), and in chemistry the periodic system, where sodium nests under alkali metals under metals.
Where apparent kinds crosscut, at least one of them is not a genuine natural kind.

positions.name: Reject the thesis, keep the kinds (Tobin, with Khalidi and Dupré)

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Tobin, book 013 ch. 10

steps.text: Crosscutting categories are not marginal or disreputable: the protein/enzyme case occurs in chemistry itself, the essentialist's paradigm science, and the classifications involved "would appear to be more than merely conventional".

If crosscutting entailed conventionalism, these well-confirmed chemical classifications would have to be dismissed as mere convention — the Hacking inference Tobin rejects (*pace* Hacking 2007, rejecting the hierarchy thesis "does not entail conventionalism about natural kinds").

"Crosscutting categories in science entail the rejection of the hierarchy thesis" — and metaphysical accounts of natural kinds must be rebuilt to *allow* crosscutting categories, not to explain them away.

positions.name: Pluralism and the species-as-individuals response (Kitcher, Dupré, Ereshefsky — as Tobin reports them)

blocks.text: Crosscutting in biological taxonomy is often taken as evidence that species should be construed as *individuals* rather than kinds, and more generally as support for pluralism: different, equally legitimate classifications answer to different interests and branches of inquiry, with no single taxonomy privileged. Tobin groups this with her own conclusion on the hierarchy thesis while keeping the question of what crosscutting shows about realism separate.

**Objections — the realist's dilemma (as Tobin states the consensus she is answering)**. Before her chapter, the shared assumption across otherwise opposed views was that "cases of crosscutting seriously jeopardize the view that natural kinds can be construed realistically": realists (Ellis) protect realism by denying crosscutting categories are kinds; conventionalists (Hacking) protect the classifications by denying realism. Tobin's chapter is precisely the refusal of that shared assumption.

thought.name: Mammals and quadrupeds
thought.text: (biology). Dogs belong to both; humans only to the first; crocodiles only to the second. On the hierarchy thesis, "quadrupeds" must be rejected as a legitimate kind category (Khalidi, as Tobin cites him).

thought.name: Proteins and enzymes
thought.text: (chemistry). Albumin is a protein but not an enzyme; the hairpin ribozyme is an enzyme but not a protein; renin is both. Because this crosscut occurs among molecular kinds individuated by structure and function, it cannot be waved away as biological untidiness — it strikes the paradigm case for the hierarchy thesis (Ellis's criterion 5 fails even for chemistry).

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: no Carneades lecture covers this problem — begin with the textbook.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary, Introduction (book 013, ch. 1), §1 (Ellis's criteria, with Tobin's protein/enzyme counterexample flagged).

ladder.label: Primary / full treatment
ladder.text: Tobin, "Crosscutting Natural Kinds and the Hierarchy Thesis" (book 013, ch. 10) — the corpus's only chapter on the problem.

classification-and-the-hierarchy-thesis.verdict: Tobin reports a consensus that crosscutting is a serious problem for *realism construed hierarchically*, and her chapter argues the consensus mislocates the damage: what falls is the hierarchy thesis (and with it Ellis's criterion 5 and Kuhn's no-overlap principle as a constraint on real kinds), not the reality of the kinds themselves. The volume offers no reply chapter; Boyd's discipline-relative, cluster-based account (see Connections) is the one position in the book that accommodates crosscutting without strain, since HPC kinds were never required to nest.

essences-and-theoretical-identities.title: Essences and Theoretical Identities
essences-and-theoretical-identities.aka: natural kind essentialism; discovered vs stipulated identities
essences-and-theoretical-identities.question: "Water is H₂O"; "gold is the element with atomic number 79". The Kripke–Putnam tradition says such theoretical identity statements report *discoveries*: scientists find the essences kinds had all along, and the terms meant those kinds from the start. Or is the truth less tidy — do scientists, faced with disrupted concepts, *decide* how the old terms will be used, so that the identities become true by stipulative precisification rather than being found true? Three chapters of book 013 stage this as a direct dispute: LaPorte against the tradition, Bird against LaPorte, Hendry testing both against the actual history of chemistry.
essences-and-theoretical-identities.ninety: Putnam's Twin Earth makes the essentialist intuition vivid. Imagine, before anyone knew water's chemistry, a planet exactly like Earth except that its watery liquid is not H₂O but a different compound, XYZ — while looking, tasting, and behaving just like water. Oscar on Earth and his molecule-for-molecule twin on Twin Earth have identical brains and use the word "water" identically, yet Oscar refers to H₂O and Twin Oscar to XYZ, because Oscar has only ever encountered H₂O and Twin Oscar only XYZ. So meaning "just ain't in the head": what a kind term refers to is fixed partly by the world, and — the essentialist adds — by the underlying nature of the samples speakers originally encountered. Whether science then *discovers* essences, or *decides* them, is what the positions below fight over. (Distilled from the Carneades lecture: [Twin Earth](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KE8NL9G_Fq8).)

positions.name: The Kripke–Putnam tradition (as LaPorte states it, in order to answer it)

blocks.text: "So-called 'natural kind terms' that were coined before much science was known, like 'oak', 'water', and 'mammal', refer to kinds with theoretically interesting essences"; scientists learn those essences empirically and state them in theoretical identities, the paradigm being "water = H₂O"; and these are "discoveries, not stipulations" — "scientific discoveries of species essence do not constitute a 'change of meaning'; the possibility of such discoveries was part of the original enterprise" (Kripke, as quoted by LaPorte).

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: LaPorte, "Theoretical Identity Statements, Their Truth, and Their Discovery", book 013 ch. 6, §1 — the tradition in LaPorte's own summary; labelled formalization

steps.text: A kind term's reference is fixed by the samples its speakers originally encountered, not by the descriptions they associated with it.
Those samples have an underlying nature (an essence) which empirical science can subsequently uncover.
A theoretical identity such as "water = H₂O" states what the term referred to all along: it is discovered to be true, not made true.

positions.name: LaPorte: true, perhaps — but not discovered

blocks.text: LaPorte's verdict is deliberately mixed: usual theoretical identity statements "(i) are not *discovered* to be true, but, at least sometimes, (ii) they *are* true". Essences are not the problem — on cladistic systematics, *Mammalia* is the clade consisting of the nearest common ancestor of horses and echidnas ("M") plus all and only M's descendants, in every possible world, and *Chordata* likewise. The problem is the discovery claim.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: LaPorte, book 013 ch. 6, §1

steps.text: Kind terms have *open texture*: vernacular use leaves boundary cases undetermined, so more than one precisification is consistent with everything earlier speakers meant.

When science disrupts a concept, different responses are each acceptable and none is required by prescientific use: we kept "whales are not fish" but reversed "birds are not dinosaurs" on relevantly similar evidence; scientists also disagree among themselves about what delimits a taxon (interbreeding vs common descent), and even given one agreed characterization, the *scope* of a kind (a stem population and its descendants, or something broader/narrower) must still be fixed by stipulation.
Scientists change the meanings of kind terms by stipulatively deciding how to use them in response to conceptual disruption; essence-stating identities are not discovered to have been true all along.

positions.name: Bird: discovery defended

blocks.text: Bird accepts LaPorte's framework — precisification divides a concept's undetermined boundary region — and denies his cases meet its conditions.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Bird, "Discovering the Essences of Natural Kinds", book 013 ch. 7

steps.text: A precisification may divide the boundary of the old concept anywhere; but some of LaPorte's cases are not precisifications at all, because the old concept itself already determined the disputed cases. In particular, by the division of linguistic labour it is *chemists'* facts that determine the identity of substances; chemical facts class D₂O (heavy water) with the other isotopic variants of H₂O — same structure, same reactions, differing only quantitatively (reaction rates) — so "water" already included D₂O, and excluding it would have been a conceptual *shift*, not a permitted precisification.

Many essential truths are not identities at all, and LaPorte's stipulation story does not account for them; and there are identities between two *scientific* terms, neither vernacular nor highly vague — elements named in the nineteenth century before atomic structure was understood — where the later identity plainly extends knowledge rather than recording a decision.

"There remains considerable scope for essentialists to maintain that many essentialist truths, both those asserting essentially necessary conditions and those asserting identities, are not stipulated but are discovered *a posteriori*."

positions.name: Hendry: the chemist's caution

blocks.text: Hendry tests the dispute on the elements, the essentialist's best case, and splits the difference in a specific place: the *inference* from necessity to essence.

blocks.label: Position
blocks.source: Hendry, "The Elements and Conceptual Change", book 013 ch. 8, §5
blocks.text: it is a fallacy to *deduce* essence from metaphysical necessity — Fine's singleton set necessarily contains its member and the member necessarily belongs to the set, yet the set's identity depends on the member's, not vice versa, so necessity alone establishes no priority. But necessity can be *evidence* within an explanatory argument. Chemical practice itself holds water's composition fixed in counternomic explanation (why water's boiling point is "unexpectedly high": hydrogen bonding, assessed against what would happen were it absent, with nuclear charges and electron counts kept fixed); and nuclear charge is the kind of property that can ground essence — causally important across contexts, and explaining why the elements are countable rather than a continuum. Lavoisier, on Hendry's account, could refer to populations of atoms of nuclear charge eight without knowing it, because element names were grounded in the actual samples chemists studied.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Hendry also records the standing worries about the whole project: that essentialism is "smuggled in" to allegedly purely semantic premises about rigidity (Salmon's objection), and that Twin Earth elicits divergent intuitions — some judge XYZ is not water because it is not H₂O, others, just as surely, that it *is* water because it is colourless, tasteless, and boils at 100 °C.

thought.name: Twin Earth
thought.text: (Putnam 1973/1975; lecture above; used by every party). Earth Oscar / Twin Oscar, H₂O / XYZ, pre-chemistry. Meant by Putnam to show reference is world-involving; used by the tradition to support essences; used by LaPorte (rerun with D₂O) to argue the concept leaves the verdict open; answered by Bird via the division of linguistic labour. Pressures descriptivism and internalism about meaning.

thought.name: Whales, fish, and birds that are dinosaurs
thought.text: (LaPorte, ch. 6). Two reversals handled oppositely on similar evidence. Meant to show no unique response to conceptual disruption is dictated by earlier use. Pressures the discovery picture specifically.

thought.name: Fool's water
thought.text: (Kripke, via Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary, ch. 9). "Just as there is a fool's gold there could be a fool's water": a substance with a completely different atomic structure that resembles water in feel, appearance, and taste. Kripke's judgement: not water. This intuition is the load-bearing premise for the necessity of "water is H₂O" — see [The Necessary A Posteriori](the-necessary-a-posteriori.md).

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: [Twin Earth](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KE8NL9G_Fq8) (Carneades).

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary, Introduction (book 013, ch. 1), §3.

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: LaPorte (ch. 6) → Bird (ch. 7) → Hendry (ch. 8) of book 013, in that order — a dispute and its two replies.

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: LaPorte, *Natural Kinds and Conceptual Change* (2004) — present in this corpus only as summarized and answered in chs. 6–7.

essences-and-theoretical-identities.verdict: The volume leaves the dispute exactly where its three chapters leave it. All three parties accept that some theoretical identities are true and that kinds such as clades can be given essence-like specifications. They divide on the *epistemology of the identity statements*: stipulative precisification of open-textured concepts (LaPorte), discovery constrained by the division of linguistic labour and by non-identity essential truths (Bird), or — for chemistry — discovery of reference across conceptual change, with essence following from explanatory practice rather than from necessity alone (Hendry). No chapter claims the others are refuted; Bird's conclusion is explicitly a claim about "considerable scope" for essentialism, not a demonstration of it.

connections.text: [The Necessary A Posteriori](the-necessary-a-posteriori.md) — if identities are stipulated rather than discovered, their alleged necessity and a posteriority both need re-examination; Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary's chapter takes up exactly that thread.

natural-kinds.title: Natural Kinds
natural-kinds.aka: natural kinds and classification; carving nature at its joints
natural-kinds.note: Ellis's criteria, Boyd's HPC kinds, Quine on similarity
natural-kinds.question: Some groupings seem to be found in nature and others merely made by us. "Gold", "water", "tiger" and "electron" appear to pick out categories that would be there whether or not we classified anything; "object bigger than a car" does not. What, if anything, makes a kind *natural* — a real structure in the world that science discovers, rather than a convenient way of talking? And if naturalness is real, what form does it take: an essence every member shares, a cluster of properties that hang together, or something discipline-relative?
natural-kinds.ninety: Natural kinds are groups of things that occur naturally in the world, independently of our choice to classify them: elements such as hydrogen, compounds such as water or carbon dioxide, and — more controversially — species such as *Homo sapiens*. Scientific realism is vindicated, on this picture, if science's classifications map onto those naturally occurring types. The questions then split three ways. Metaphysical: do kinds exist, and what are they — irreducible entities, universals, or clusters of properties? Semantic: how do kind terms refer? And from the philosophy of science: does the metaphysics actually match what each science does? Chemistry is the strongest case: elements fall into their categories by number of protons, not by anything we stipulated — a view called microstructuralism. Biology is harder: species can be delineated by interbreeding or by common descent, the two delineations cross, and that pushes some toward saying species are conventions, and others toward a "promiscuous realism" on which many overlapping delineations are all natural and we simply pick out some of them. Positions run from naturalism/realism (kinds are real and discovered), through cluster-kind realism (kinds are co-occurring clusters of properties used for induction), to conventionalism (kinds are only ways scientists classify). (Distilled from the Carneades lecture: [What are Natural Kinds?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dXgnn8u5Hho).)

positions.name: Metaphysical essentialism (Brian Ellis, as the volume presents and tests him)

blocks.text: A kind is natural only if it meets strict, a priori statable conditions. Ellis's six criteria, as the editors summarize them, require a natural kind to (1) be objective (mind-independent), (2) be categorically distinct, with no ontologically vague boundaries, (3) be demarcated from all other kinds by its intrinsic properties, (4) allow species variation (isotopes share an element-kind by essence — atomic number — while differing in atomic mass), (5) form a species-to-genus hierarchy where a particular belongs to two or more kinds, and (6) have an intrinsic essence both necessary and sufficient for membership.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary, Introduction, book 013 ch. 1 — a formalization of the editors' presentation of Ellis

steps.text: Predictive and explanatory success comes in degrees, with no cut-off anywhere in the spectrum from physics through chemistry and biology to common sense; so success cannot *define* a metaphysically distinctive category of kinds.

A metaphysically distinctive category therefore needs a priori criteria of the Ellis type — objectivity, categorical distinctness, intrinsic demarcation, hierarchy, and a necessary-and-sufficient intrinsic essence.
Kinds failing the criteria — biological species, whose boundaries evolution makes vague, among them — are not genuine natural kinds.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the editors: the criteria rule out by stipulation what the sciences treat as paradigms. Species are excluded for violating categorical distinctness; "protein" and "enzyme" — which on Tobin's showing "indicate real ontological differences in kind" — violate the hierarchy criterion (see [Classification and the Hierarchy Thesis](classification-and-the-hierarchy-thesis.md)). If natural kindhood is instead fixed by the explanatory and predictive role of kind concepts in scientific theorizing, nothing requires kinds to be hierarchically arranged or sharply bounded.

positions.name: Homeostatic property cluster kinds and accommodation (Richard Boyd)

blocks.text: Boyd's is the volume's fully developed alternative. On his accommodation theory, classificatory practices are epistemically reliable insofar as they are *accommodated* to the causal structures of their subject matter — and some kinds are defined not by an essence but by a "naturally occurring clustering of properties", with the consequences that (1) the kind lacks precisely defined membership conditions and sometimes (2) the properties in the defining cluster vary over time and space.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Boyd, "Realism, Natural Kinds, and Philosophical Methods", book 013 ch. 12

steps.text: Biological species are paradigmatic natural kinds, yet evolutionary theory entails that they will ordinarily lack completely determinate boundaries; any precisified definition would misrepresent biological reality and undermine accommodation.
The vagueness of an HPC kind term's extension therefore reflects not imprecision but a *precise accommodation* of classification to causal phenomena.

A kind can be natural without an essence or sharp boundaries; and naturalness is discipline-relative — there are no kinds natural *simpliciter*, only kinds natural with respect to the inferential architecture of a particular discipline.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: from the essentialist side (as the Introduction frames the dispute): if naturalness is discipline-relative and degree-like, the metaphysically distinctive category the essentialist wanted has been given up, not explained. Boyd accepts the consequence and draws the metaphilosophical moral instead: epistemology and the theory of kinds are themselves empirical, anti-foundationalist inquiries. His §4.1 adds the deliberately provocative corollary that "natural kinds are social constructions" — Locke's "workmanship of men" — while insisting (§4.2) that this is compatible with their reality and mind-independence, since the workmanship succeeds only when accommodated to causal structure.

positions.name: Similarity and projectibility (Quine, as the Introduction presents him)

blocks.text: Quine claimed that kindhood and similarity are "variations or adaptations of a single notion", but that *theoretical* standards of similarity lend themselves to better inductions: "by primitive standards the marsupial mouse is more similar to the ordinary mouse than to the kangaroo; by theoretical standards the reverse is true", and cosmically "colours would not qualify as kinds".

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary, Introduction, book 013 ch. 1, presenting Quine 1969 — labelled formalization

steps.text: A kind term earns its keep by supporting inductions: from something's being a member, much besides membership should be inferable (the invented kind "narg" — objects bigger than a car — supports almost nothing).
Which similarities count is fixed not by our innate quality space but by mature theory.
Natural kinds are those groupings that align with theoretical standards of similarity and so deliver superior inductive and explanatory success.

blocks.label: Replies / limits
blocks.text: this is explicitly *not* Quine's own resting point: he held that maturity in a science is marked by its no longer needing "an irreducible notion of similarity and kind" at all. And the editors note the pressure this account puts on the essentialist (success comes in degrees), which is precisely what drives Ellis to his a priori criteria above.

thought.name: "Nargs"
thought.text: (Introduction, ch. 1). Coin a simple word for *objects bigger than a car* — buses, elephants, office blocks. The term is semantically simple, yet the grouping supports no inductions beyond a size bound. Meant to show: naturalness is not semantic simplicity, and a real kind must underwrite inference and explanation. Pressures purely linguistic criteria of kindhood.

thought.name: The marsupial mouse
thought.text: (Quine, via Introduction, ch. 1). By surface similarity the marsupial mouse belongs with mice; by theoretical (evolutionary) standards it belongs with kangaroos. Meant to show that the similarity natural kinds track is theory-mediated. Pressures common-sense classification.

natural-kinds.verdict: Nothing in this volume is settled, and the volume is built to display that. The editors' own framing leaves three live options standing: essentialism with a priori criteria (which buys metaphysical distinctiveness at the price of excluding species and crosscutting chemical kinds), Boyd's accommodationist HPC account (which keeps species and vagueness at the price of discipline-relativity), and the semantic route — settle what natural kind *terms* are first — which the next entry shows collapsing into disagreement of its own. Tobin's chapter (see Connections) removes one apparently safe assumption shared by several parties: that genuine kinds must nest in a single hierarchy.

rigidity-and-natural-kind-terms.title: Rigidity and Natural Kind Terms
rigidity-and-natural-kind-terms.aka: natural kind semantics; general terms as designators
rigidity-and-natural-kind-terms.question: Proper names, Kripke argued, are rigid designators: they pick out the same individual in every possible world in which that individual exists, and they do so directly, not via a description. Are natural kind terms — "water", "gold", "tiger" — a parallel, semantically distinctive class of *general* terms? Four consecutive chapters of book 013 give four different answers, and the disagreement is not over details: it is over whether there is a nontrivial phenomenon here at all.
rigidity-and-natural-kind-terms.ninety: A rigid designator refers to the same object in all possible worlds where that object exists. "Saul Kripke" refers to Kripke whether he is a philosopher in this world, a wizard in another, or a lawyer in a third; by contrast "the 44th President of the United States" picks out different people in different worlds and is non-rigid — although some descriptions, like "the predecessor of 3", rigidly designate (the number 2) in every world. The distinction was introduced for singular terms such as names. Everything in this entry is about whether it survives the move to general terms. (Distilled from the Carneades lecture: [What is a Rigid Designator?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h0GNeCRdx9s).)

positions.name: De jure obstinate rigidity (Corine Besson)

blocks.text: The starting problem is *trivialization*: extended to general terms, Kripke's definition makes natural kind terms rigid — but so does it make all other general terms, including descriptive ones, rigid. Besson's remedy relocates the distinction from semantics to metasemantics.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Besson, "Rigidity, Natural Kind Terms, and Metasemantics", book 013 ch. 2

steps.text: (Kripke Rigidity) A rigid designator designates the same object in every possible world in which that object exists, and nothing in worlds where it does not exist; on this definition, applied to general terms, natural kind terms and descriptive general terms alike come out rigid — the distinction trivializes.

Natural kind terms are introduced by "dubbing" — name-acquiring transactions subject to clearly defined metasemantic conditions that descriptive general terms cannot satisfy — and their rigidity is therefore obstinacy *de jure* (by stipulation in the dubbing), not merely *de facto*.

Natural kind terms are de jure obstinately rigid designators, and other general terms are not: the asymmetry between the classes is real, but grounded in how the terms are introduced, not in their truth-conditional behaviour alone.

positions.name: The View defended — and the bullet bitten (Genoveva Martí & José Martínez-Fernández)

blocks.text: "The View" holds that general terms designate universals — kinds, colours, species — as singular terms designate individuals. Against it stand the trivialization problem, the overgeneralization problem, and the charge that it cannot explain the necessity of theoretical identifications.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Martí & Martínez-Fernández, "General Terms as Designators", book 013 ch. 3 — as summarized in the editors' Introduction and stated in the chapter

steps.text: The trivialization problem alleges no difference in truth conditions between rigid and non-rigid readings of a general term used as a predicate; but there are cases where the contribution to truth conditions does differ between the readings.

The overgeneralization problem alleges that if "water" rigidly designates the water-kind, "fridge" equally designates the refrigerator-kind; the correct response is to accept the symmetry — "there is just no interesting semantic distinction" between simple general terms such as "philosopher" and "tungsten".

Theoretical identities are claims about *kinds*, not universally quantified biconditionals about the objects falling under kind predicates; distinguishing a term's denoting (kind) use from its predicative (exemplifier) use explains why true theoretical identities are necessary.
The View survives all three objections — but at the cost, cheerfully paid, of denying that natural kind terms are semantically set apart from other simple general terms.

blocks.text: **Note the tension**: Besson and Martí & Martínez-Fernández both claim to save rigidity for general terms, but Besson saves it by making natural kind terms special (metasemantically) and Martí & Martínez-Fernández save it by making them *not* special (semantically uniform with the rest). The volume does not adjudicate between them.

positions.name: Natural kind terms are not special (Åsa Wikforss)

blocks.text: Wikforss rejects the Kripke–Putnam account in favour of a version of descriptivism, on grounds that begin one step earlier than the others: we cannot even identify the alleged class without doing empirical science.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Wikforss, "Are Natural Kind Terms Special?", book 013 ch. 4

steps.text: A semantic category should not depend for its membership on sophisticated empirical theory; yet identifying natural kind terms — on the microstructural conception, whether a term picks out a kind with a unifying microstructural essence — does: witness the failures, "jade", "sugar", "air", "sand", and many plant, animal, and disease terms, where no such property exists.

Neither of the two leading semantic marks works: rigidity does not single the terms out, and neither does non-descriptionality; nor does externalism about how meaning is determined rescue a special *semantic* content.
Natural kind terms have no distinctive semantics or metasemantics. "Any special significance they have is a product of the role they play in scientific explanation" (the editors' summary).

positions.name: A Fregean reconciliation (Harold Noonan)

blocks.text: Noonan, unconvinced by Kripke's arguments against Frege–Russell, asks how the commonalities between names and kind terms can be explained *within* a Fregean account: via (Fregean) rigid designation, deferential intentions in propositional attitudes, and a Fregean reading of Twin Earth.

blocks.label: Position in brief
blocks.source: Noonan, "The Commonalities between Proper Names and Natural Kind Terms", book 013 ch. 5
blocks.text: the modal argument does not force Millian direct reference; the phenomena Kripke collects can be accommodated with sense as well as reference. Noonan also dismisses the necessary a posteriori for kind terms — on his view it rests on conflating an essential property with an a posteriori but contingently true thought (developed in [The Necessary A Posteriori](the-necessary-a-posteriori.md)).

thought.name: The rigidified description
thought.text: (Besson, ch. 2). "The *actual* pupil of Plato and teacher of Alexander" designates Aristotle in every world — a description can be made rigid by "actual", and descriptions of necessary existents ("the smallest prime") are rigid outright. Meant to show: bare rigidity is too cheap to mark off names, let alone kind terms; the interesting question is always *why* a term is rigid. Pressures every purely semantic criterion in this entry.

thought.name: Twin Earth
thought.text: (Putnam; Noonan ch. 5, §3). See [Essences and Theoretical Identities](essences-and-theoretical-identities.md), where it does its main work; Noonan's chapter is the volume's attempt to show a Fregean can absorb it.

rigidity-and-natural-kind-terms.verdict: Unresolved, four ways. All parties grant the trivialization problem is real for a naive extension of Kripke's definition. They divide on the remedy: metasemantic specialness (Besson), semantic uniformity (Martí & Martínez-Fernández), descriptivism and no special category (Wikforss), or Fregean sense (Noonan). The editors' own closing questions for the section stand as the honest summary: is there a nontrivial phenomenon of rigidity for kind terms at all — and if so, does it apply to the terms denoting the metaphysician's genuine natural kinds?

the-necessary-a-posteriori.title: The Necessary A Posteriori
the-necessary-a-posteriori.aka: a posteriori necessity; Kripke's necessary a posteriori statements
the-necessary-a-posteriori.note: Kripke's category and the Ellis "abuse" verdict
the-necessary-a-posteriori.question: Before Kripke, the map of modal and epistemic categories was assumed to align: necessary truths are knowable a priori, contingent truths a posteriori. Kripke split the categories: some truths — "Hesperus is Phosphorus", "water is H₂O" — are necessary (true in every possible world) yet knowable only through experience. Is the category real? And — the question book 013's own editors press — how far does it extend beyond Kripke's original cases before its use becomes, in their word, abuse?
the-necessary-a-posteriori.ninety: Take two rigid designators that in fact pick out the same object. Since each picks out that object in every possible world, a true identity between them is true in every possible world — it is necessary. Hesperus and Phosphorus were ancient names for the evening and morning appearances of Venus; astronomers *discovered* empirically that they are one body. So "Hesperus is Phosphorus" is necessary, yet only experience could reveal it: a necessary a posteriori truth. Lois Lane needs empirical evidence to learn that Superman is Clark Kent, although — both names being rigid — the identity, if true, is necessarily true. Kripke argues the mirror category also exists: contingent a priori statements (the standard metre stick, stipulated to define the metre, is known without measurement to be one metre long, although it could have been a different length). Together the two categories break the assumed alignment of the necessary with the a priori. (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [Kripke's Necessary, A Posteriori Statements](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CisaX71OD9s), [Necessary and Contingent Distinction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vt4h7uvvcXc), [Kripke's Contingent, A Priori Statements](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=enIsXrWAqvc).)

positions.name: Kripke's category (as the volume presents it)

blocks.text: For theoretical identities, the editors' favoured reading of Kripke runs as follows. In "water is H₂O" and "gold is the element with atomic number 79": the left-hand term is analogous to a proper name — (i) non-descriptive, (ii) rigid, (iii) introduced by baptism; the right-hand side is a definite description, used attributively, which is (i) *de facto* rigid and (ii) gives the *essence* of the kind, discovered and described by science. The identity is then necessary (nothing lacking that atomic structure could be water — "just as there is a fool's gold there could be a fool's water") and knowable only a posteriori.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary, "On the Abuse of the Necessary *A Posteriori*", book 013 ch. 9, §2 — the editors' reconstruction of Kripke; labelled formalization

steps.text: "Water" is rigid and non-descriptive, like a name; "H₂O" / "the element with atomic number 79" states the underlying nature of the kind the name picks out.
Twin Earth–style judgement: a substance with a completely different atomic structure that merely resembled water in feel, appearance, and taste would not be water.
Water's underlying nature is its essence; "water is H₂O" is metaphysically necessary — and, since the nature was found empirically, a posteriori.

positions.name: Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary: the category is real but its extension must be argued, case by case

blocks.text: The editors do not attack the category; they attack its unargued extension. "Even if we accept that Kripke's story holds for proper names and natural kind terms, it can by no means be taken for granted that the story extends to cover other cases."

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary, book 013 ch. 9, §§1–2

steps.text: A claim that some truth is necessary a posteriori requires a *Necessity* component: an argument that the underlying nature in question is the kind's *essence* — which, for kind terms, means running the Twin Earth–style test, since "water" might instead have meant something like "whatever potable liquid is typically to be found in rivers and lakes and falls from the sky", in which case "water is H₂O" would be contingent.

It also requires an *A Posteriority* component: the term must not have been introduced by stipulative definition (as "bachelor" is defined as an unmarried man), or the truth would be a priori after all.

Brian Ellis's scientific essentialism claims, for a vastly extended range of kinds — substance kinds and process kinds well beyond molecular constitution and species — that the laws of nature are metaphysically necessary but knowable only a posteriori; but clear cases among Ellis's "natural kinds" fail to fit Kripke's model, and no argument of the P1–P2 form is supplied for them.

Ellis's extension is an *abuse* of the necessary a posteriori; and the failure of the alleged a posteriori necessities undermines his own account of de re necessity — his scientific essentialism loses the modal foundation it claimed.

positions.name: Noonan: the category, for kind terms, is a conflation

blocks.text: Harold Noonan's Fregean chapter reaches the more radical verdict that the necessary a posteriori *in the case of natural kinds* "stems from the conflation of the notion of an essential property, and an a posteriori but only contingently true thought" (editors' summary of book 013 ch. 5). Where the editors demand more argument, Noonan denies the phenomenon: what is genuinely a posteriori in the theoretical-identity cases is, on his view, contingent, and Kripkean metaphysical necessity of the kind-term sort belongs, in the editors' phrase for his conclusion, "on Hume's bonfire".

blocks.label: Objections (to Noonan, from the volume's other chapters)
blocks.text: Bird's and Hendry's chapters supply the material for a reply without addressing Noonan directly: essential truths that are not identities at all, and identities between scientific terms introduced before the relevant discoveries, look a posteriori in a way that does not obviously trade on any conflation; and chemical explanatory practice holds composition fixed across counternomic scenarios whether or not one endorses Noonan's Fregean semantics. The volume states no verdict between ch. 5 and chs. 7–9.

thought.name: Hesperus and Phosphorus
thought.text: (Kripke; lecture). Two rigid names, one planet, an astronomical discovery. Meant to show necessity and a posteriority can coincide. Pressures the pre-Kripke alignment of modal and epistemic categories.

thought.name: Fool's water
thought.text: (Kripke, via ch. 9). A substance resembling water in every observable respect but with a completely different atomic structure. The judgement "not water" is what converts "water has structure H₂O" into "H₂O is water's essence" — and the editors' point is that this judgement must actually be elicited and defended for each new alleged case, not assumed.

thought.name: The standard metre
thought.text: (Kripke; lecture on the contingent a priori). The stick that defines the metre is known a priori to be a metre long at the moment of stipulation, though its length is contingent. The mirror-image case; it matters here because Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary's A Posteriority component excludes exactly this route — a term introduced by stipulative definition cannot generate a necessary *a posteriori* truth.

the-necessary-a-posteriori.verdict: Within this volume: the existence of *some* necessary a posteriori truths (identity statements between rigid designators; the paradigmatic theoretical identities) is treated by the editors as Kripke's achievement, "relatively uncontroversial" as an interpretation of his view of names. Everything beyond the paradigms is contested. The editors' methodological rule — no extension without a Necessity argument and an A Posteriority argument — is the volume's own contribution, and their worked verdict is negative for Ellis's scientific essentialism. Noonan's stronger rejection stands in the same volume unanswered by name. LaPorte's stipulation argument (see Connections) is a further internal pressure: if identities are partly *decided*, their epistemic status needs redescription case by case.
