communicative-competence-and-pragmatic-f.title: Communicative Competence and Pragmatic Failure
communicative-competence-and-pragmatic-f.aka: knowing how to use a language; interlanguage pragmatics
communicative-competence-and-pragmatic-f.note: Thomas on pragmatic failure; speech-act lectures as front door
communicative-competence-and-pragmatic-f.question: What does someone know when they know a language? The narrow answer — the grammar: the rules that make sentences well-formed — leaves out something every language learner discovers painfully: you can produce a flawless sentence and still fail. You can curse correctly and have the curse fall flat because you smiled; you can answer a question accurately and give offence because the form was wrong for the relationship; you can pass the grammar test and have nothing to say. The wider answer developed in applied linguistics is *communicative competence*: grammatical knowledge plus knowledge of how to do things with words, appropriately, in context. This entry states the rival answers as the corpus gives them — the narrow one, the accuracy-first policy built on it, the expanded competence that replaced it, and the fine-grained account of how utterances succeed and fail pragmatically — and uses the speech-act lectures as its front door, because the expanded answer is unintelligible without the distinction those lectures draw between what words literally say, what a speaker is doing in saying them, and what actually happens as a result.
communicative-competence-and-pragmatic-f.ninety: Every utterance works on three levels at once. The *locution* is the literal meaning of the words: "The library closes in 15 minutes" states a fact about closing time. The *illocution* is what the speaker is doing in saying it — the force invested in it: the librarian is asking everyone to pack up and leave, just as "That tiger looks angry" can be a warning, and "It's getting hot in here" can be a request, a warning or a peace offering depending on context. The *perlocution* is the actual effect: the patrons gather their books and go. Illocution can be made explicit — add "so please leave" and no competent hearer can miss it — but perlocution cannot be guaranteed by any wording: you can understand perfectly that you are being asked to be quiet and still not quieten down, and effects can misfire entirely, landing as irritation where persuasion was intended. Knowing a language, on the view this entry tracks, is knowing all three levels — and pragmatic failure is what happens when the grammar is right and one of the other levels goes wrong. (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [What is Locution?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MEFgY0LHM5w), [What is Illocution?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ciRkQU2WHsM), [What is Perlocution?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5dvyRtiP-N4).)

positions.name: The narrow target: grammatical competence (and competence vs performance)

blocks.text: On the view Nattinger sets up as his foil, the subject matter of language teaching is the abstract system — the competence of an idealized speaker-hearer — and success is formal correctness within it.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Nattinger, *Second Language Acquisition / Foreign Language Learning*, ch. 13 — a formalization of his opening case against competence-based grammars

steps.text: The goal of language teaching is that students comprehend and produce language successfully and meaningfully.

Conventional grammars offer only definitions and structure lists, social prescriptions of "correct" form, or descriptions of the abstract competence system; and "the precise relationship between the theoretical competence of an idealized speaker-hearer and the actual language performance of a specific human being is a highly tenuous matter."
Limiting teaching to the underlying system is no guarantee of the goal; teachers should look to theories of language *use* — performance grammars — instead.

positions.name: Accuracy first: the fossilization warning (Higgs & Clifford, as Savignon presents and contests them)

blocks.text: The policy form of the narrow view: postpone free communication, correct errors early and intensely, or learners' inaccuracies harden permanently — "fossilization," the "terminal 2" profile.

blocks.label: The claim as presented
blocks.source: Savignon, ch. 12, presenting Higgs & Clifford 1982
blocks.text: communicative competence has been misread as "communication in spite of language, rather than communication through language"; grammatical precision has been downplayed; and the terminal profiles are explained by proactive interference plus fossilized development, found in learners whose programmes either lacked grammatically masterful instructors or chose, "for philosophical, methodological, or personal reasons," not to correct mistakes.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Savignon's chapter is largely a demolition of the claim's evidential base: "there is no research evidence to support the purported link between teacher correction practice and formal features of learner language," and the seminar audit she reports sorts Higgs & Clifford's support into "anecdotal opinion and hearsay, citation and quotation, and formal data" — finding the first two doing the work ("'evidence suggests', and 'evidence abounds'"). The same chapter makes the parallel objection to the ACTFL Proficiency Guidelines (1986): a hierarchy of performance levels promoted as "not based on a particular linguistic theory or pedagogical method" cannot be theory-free while prescribing methods, and its view of interaction is, in Kramsch's quoted verdict, neo-behaviouristic — behavioural functions over notional development, static content, "accuracy to the detriment of discourse aptitude." **Status:** the corpus contains this position only through its critic; it is recorded here as presented-and-contested, not as established.

positions.name: Expanded communicative competence (Savignon; Kramsch)

blocks.text: Competence is plural: knowing a language is knowing several distinguishable things, of which grammar is only one.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Savignon, ch. 12, reporting the framework of Lapkin & Swain 1984; and Kramsch, ch. 3

steps.text: Learner ability in immersion and classroom settings is intelligible only in a broad frame: not only "sentence-level morphosyntactic features, i.e. grammatical competence, but … sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic competence" besides.

The components come apart empirically and pedagogically: the same programme is a "linguistic failure" judged by non-native morphosyntax (Hammerly) and "highly successful" judged by academic achievement *cum* functional competence (Stern) — so the verdict on learning depends on which competence is measured; and Savignon's 1971 Illinois study found adults given the opportunity to *use* French for communication from the very beginning developed communicative ability that repetition-bound learners did not.

(Kramsch) A research programme adequate to classrooms must treat language whole — not split into separate skills — as "quintessentially indeterminate and culturally relative," communication being "the negotiation of meanings intended and interpreted within an interactional context."
What it is to know a language, and therefore what teaching and testing should target, is communicative competence in the expanded sense, not grammatical competence alone.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: from inside the volume: the expanded notion is exactly what the accuracy-first camp (above) charges with vagueness and with licensing error; and Savignon herself notes the measurement problem on the other side — there is "lack of agreement on what constitutes learning 'success'," and programme-fair evaluation can be gamed by the choice of test (Beretta's Bangalore quandary: a conventional grammar test on communicatively taught beginners "would be perverse"). The expansion solves the narrowness problem at the price of a standing dispute about what counts as evidence for the wider competence.

positions.name: Pragmatic competence and its failures (Wildner-Bassett; Thomas as she presents him)

blocks.text: The finest-grained position in the book: using a language means managing conversation under sociocultural conventions, and there are two different ways to get it wrong.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Wildner-Bassett, ch. 9, using Thomas 1983/1984 as presented there

steps.text: A learner faces conventions for managing conversation in the target culture that may conflict with the conventions of their own; failures divide into *sociopragmatic* failure (misjudging the social conditions — what this situation, relationship or setting calls for) and *pragmalinguistic* failure (mapping the intended force onto the wrong linguistic form).

What an utterance is doing is fixed not by the sentence alone but by the *discourse world* dominantly operant — a discourse world being the set of elements (intended recipient, shared presuppositions, intended speaker meaning or *illocutionary value*, interactional function) within which a unit of talk acquires its negotiated communicative value — and several worlds (role-play, real life, native-speaker–learner, teacher–student) coexist in a single exchange, with different situational frames (participants and their power relations, setting, purpose, restrictions, even facial expression).

No interpretation of a learner's pragmatic performance from a single world or frame is valid; pragmatic competence is the developing ability to operate across coexisting worlds, and it must be taught — routine formulas explicitly, and metapragmatic awareness of the worlds themselves.

positions.name: The classroom as a communicative world of its own (Brooks; Green & Weade as he presents them)

blocks.text: Zoom in further: the place where competence is supposedly built is itself a rule-governed communicative environment whose rules are learned tacitly, and can hijack the lesson.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Brooks, ch. 10, and its Appendix 10.1 propositions

steps.text: Classrooms are communicative environments in which meaning is context-specific, participation rules are implicit and constructed over time, and "communicative competence is reflected in appropriate behaviour" — so students simultaneously learn the academic content and how to conduct themselves as members of this classroom.

In the observed lesson, two students assigned a communicative simulation instead reproduced the teacher's patterns — repeat-the-word correction and *muy bien* evaluation/topic-shift signals, the initiation–response–feedback rhythm — converting communication practice into grammar-quiz preparation, having acquired the patterns by imitation and inference rather than instruction (the stronger student had not noticed doing so until he watched himself on video).

What learners practise in a classroom is never only the target language's pragmatics; it is also the classroom's — and an account of competence that ignores the learning environment's own discourse world will misread both.

positions.name: Knowing as chunks first: prefabricated speech (Nattinger)

blocks.text: A developmental correction to every position above: whatever competence finally consists in, learners do not start from rules.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Nattinger, ch. 13

steps.text: Children — and, on the adult evidence available, adults — begin with prefabricated chunks: unvarying *routines* and *patterns* with a movable slot, stored and retrieved whole to express functions they cannot yet construct from rules (Wong-Fillmore: the strategy of acquiring formulaic speech is "central to the learning of language").

Chunks are then segmented — compared across contexts, split into pieces (Brown's *korewa* audibly "cracking" into *kore* + *wa* once *kore o* is heard) — and the pieces become the raw material from which the creative rule system is built; item-learning precedes system-learning at every level.

Creative, rule-governed competence grows *out of* unanalysed wholes rather than preceding them, so a curriculum should run routines → patterns with widening variation → creative use, grouped by function (Social Interactions, Necessary Topics, Discourse Devices).

positions.name: Translation competence is communicative competence (Kiraly)

blocks.text: The same dispute replayed in translator training, where the narrow view has a name and a canonical statement.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Kiraly, ch. 14

steps.text: The traditional paradigm defines translation as Catford (1965) does — "the replacement of textual material in one language by equivalent material in another language" — and trains accordingly: learn the equivalents, produce them spontaneously, be corrected against the instructor's definitive solutions. Its lived result is Röhl's silent day: a great deal of "learning" and virtually no use of the language for self-expression or communication.

On Firth's theory, linguistic behaviour is "a network of relations between people, things, and events," and every utterance belongs to a context of situation (participants, verbal and non-verbal action, relevant objects and events, effects of the verbal action); Krashen's distinction then separates the *learner*, who consciously identifies elements and equivalence relations inside subsystems, from the *acquirer*, who uses language inside real contexts of situation.

Since the translator is receiver of the source text and co-creator of the target text across two contexts of situation, translation competence is a special type of communicative competence — trainees must acquire as well as learn, and whether translators should "translate texts or words, messages or linguistic signs" is decided by which model of competence their training presupposes.

thought.name: "This bloody England" — and the smile
thought.text: (Wildner-Bassett, ch. 9, Extract 3). In role-play, a learner answers a native speaker's parody tirade with a correctly formed, forceful curse. Lexically and grammatically it succeeds; it still fails, because he smiles as he says it — the concomitant activity belongs to the real-life co-worker world, not the hostile role-play world, and it redefines the utterance toward humour, cancelling its pragmatic force. Wildner-Bassett pairs it with Harder's **reduced personality**: a foreigner "is not permitted to go beyond a certain limited repertoire; if he starts swearing fluently … he is unlikely to achieve the conventional communicative effect," and this learner seems to know it — he cannot take his own utterance seriously. The case isolates exactly what grammatical competence leaves out.

thought.name: The pig's cold
thought.text: (Wildner-Bassett, ch. 9, Extract 4). A learner responds to "I have a little cold" with *Schweine kalt* — reaching for the colloquial routine *Saukalt* ("sow-cold," a comment on bitter weather) and producing a remark about the other person's health. A pure pragmalinguistic failure: the social judgement was fine, the form-to-force mapping was wrong, the native speaker saved the exchange by changing the topic, and there is no evidence the learner noticed anything had happened.

thought.name: The cat for 24 hours
thought.text: (Bacon, ch. 11). In oral interviews, the highest-rated speakers chose unstructured topics and circumlocuted around missing vocabulary to keep developing them (the would-be cat who loves eating from the table), while the weakest clung to structured topics and abandoned them at the first missing word ("darn! Next card"). Bacon's gloss: the able treated the interview as communication, the weak as a test — evidence, against the ACTFL presumption, that measured proficiency is not context-free, because what is being measured includes the willingness and ability to *do* things with incomplete language.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: the Carneades speech-act lectures — Locution, Illocution, Perlocution.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Savignon, ch. 12 (the expanded-competence framework and its policy fights); Kramsch, ch. 3 (the concept of language underneath it).

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: Wildner-Bassett, ch. 9 (pragmatic failure and discourse worlds); Brooks, ch. 10 (classroom discourse worlds in the wild); Kiraly, ch. 14 (Catford vs Firth on translation).

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: the cluster as a whole in book 031 — Nattinger, ch. 13 (the developmental route), Bacon, ch. 11 (the assessment consequence), plus the editors' verdict (ch. 17) that the SLA/FLL distinction matters precisely here, for psychosocial processes and language *use*.

communicative-competence-and-pragmatic-f.verdict: The expansion won the book's argument but not a settled metric. Every chapter in this cluster presupposes that grammatical competence is not the whole of knowing a language, and the volume's editors ratify the point by making language use the one domain where context distinctions genuinely matter. What remains open in these texts is threefold. First, evidence: the accuracy-first objection survives in weakened form — Savignon shows its flagship claim (uncorrected communication fossilizes) is undocumented, but the positive construct validity of communicative testing is itself contested in her own chapter. Second, analysis: Wildner-Bassett's discourse-worlds machinery shows single-frame interpretations are invalid, without supplying a replacement decision procedure — interpretation must be multi-level, and that is a discipline, not an algorithm. Third, the locution problem the lecture series itself raises: the speech-act front door assumes a literal level (locution) can be isolated from force and context, and the Locution lecture ends by doubting exactly that — even literal meaning may need speaker intention and context to fix it, which would blur the triad the 90-second version relies on. The corpus leaves that doubt standing.

connections.title: Second or Foreign? The Classification of Language-Learning Contexts
connections.text: [Second or Foreign? The Classification of Language-Learning Contexts](second-or-foreign-language-contexts.md) — the sibling problem: contexts matter most, on the editors' synthesis, exactly where this entry lives — in the psychosocial processes of use.

connections.title: Names, Descriptions and Reference
connections.text: [Names, Descriptions and Reference](names-descriptions-and-reference.md) — the locutionary level is sense and reference; Edmondson's definition of a discourse world builds "intended speaker meaning (or illocutionary value)" into the unit of analysis, which is where the two problems meet.

connections.title: Language as a Resource: Conservation and Policy
connections.text: [Language as a Resource: Conservation and Policy](language-as-a-resource-conservation-and-policy.md) — competence judgements are never socially neutral: Kramsch (ch. 3) quotes Bourdieu that the competence sufficient to be understood "may be totally insufficient to produce sentences likely to be listened to," and Wildner-Bassett's target-culture learners risk negative *personal* judgements from sociopragmatic failure.

sources: VanPatten & Lee (eds.), *Second Language Acquisition / Foreign Language Learning* (book 031): ch. 3, Kramsch (pp. 27–33); ch. 9, Wildner-Bassett, "Coexisting Discourse Worlds…" (pp. 140–152); ch. 10, Brooks, "Foreign Language Learning: A Social Interaction Perspective" (pp. 153–169, including Appendix 10.1); ch. 11, Bacon, "On Topic Choice in Oral Proficiency Assessment" (pp. 170–180); ch. 12, Savignon, "Nothing is More Practical than a Good Theory" (pp. 185–197); ch. 13, Nattinger, "Prefabricated Speech for Language Learning" (pp. 198–206); ch. 14, Kiraly, "A Role for Communicative Competence…" (pp. 207–215); ch. 17 (pp. 240–245, for the editors' use/process verdict) — all read in full.
Lectures (Carneades.org): "What is Locution? (Phonetic, Phatic, and Rhetic Acts)"; "What is Illocution? (Philosophy of Language)"; "What is Perlocution? (Philosophy of Language)" — all read in full.

language-as-a-resource-conservation-and-.title: Language as a Resource: Conservation and Policy
language-as-a-resource-conservation-and-.aka: language conservation; additive vs subtractive bilingualism
language-as-a-resource-conservation-and-.note: Campbell & Lindholm against the subtractive default
language-as-a-resource-conservation-and-.question: A five-year-old arrives at school already fluent in Korean, Spanish or another home language — years of acquisition, completed free of charge, to a level adult students rarely reach after thousands of classroom hours. What should the school system do with that competence? One answer treats the home language as an obstacle: schooling replaces it with the majority language, and the child's first language withers as the price of membership. The other treats it as a *resource* — in the ecological sense of the word: something valuable, already produced, that a foolish policy can squander and a wise one can conserve and develop. The question is therefore not only pedagogical but normative and political: is a minority language a private inheritance to be traded away, or a collective asset — the child's, the family's and the nation's — that policy should protect? Book 031 contains the corpus's one sustained treatment, Campbell & Lindholm's "Conservation of Language Resources," and it is deliberately one-sided: it argues the resource case against a subtractive default it describes but no chapter in the volume defends. This entry keeps that asymmetry visible.
language-as-a-resource-conservation-and-.ninety: *[Textbook-distilled — no Carneades lecture covers this problem; distilled from Campbell & Lindholm, ch. 16, of book 031.]* Picture a Korean-American five-year-old starting kindergarten in Los Angeles. She already speaks Korean the way native five-year-olds do: the sound system complete, nearly all the grammar for building sentences and holding conversations, and the social rules too — different vocabulary, honorifics and even body language for different listeners. On the US Government's proficiency scale she would rate, allowing for a child's vocabulary and illiteracy, around 3+ or 4. An adult at the Defense Language Institute needs some 1,400 hours of intensive instruction to reach a 2 or 2+ — routine social demands and limited work requirements. So the child walks in holding, at no public cost, what the state elsewhere pays thousands of hours to produce — and the system's normal response is to let it disappear, requiring her to give up the ancestral language as dues for joining the monolingual majority. The conservation proposal is simply to reverse the default: teach *through* both languages, so the home language keeps developing toward adult, literate proficiency while English is added — bilingualism as addition rather than replacement. Early results from programmes built that way show children gaining in both languages at once, which is exactly what the subtractive picture says should not happen.

positions.name: The subtractive default (as Campbell & Lindholm characterize it)

blocks.text: The position under attack, stated in the form its critics give it — no chapter in book 031 argues it in its own voice.

blocks.label: The default as characterized
blocks.source: Campbell & Lindholm, ch. 16
blocks.text: despite periodic official alarm about national foreign-language deficits, actual practice amounts to "an unspoken national policy to do whatever is necessary to deny opportunities for the conservation of the competence held by these linguistic minority students"; the policy "is basically 'subtractive' in nature: we seem to insist that linguistic minority children give up their ancestral languages as dues if they wish to become members of the generally monolingual English-speaking majority club." Most bilingual education for minority children, the authors add, "seldom provide[s] for the development and maturation of adult-level linguistic competence in the children's L1."

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the characterization is the objection's target as much as its statement: a reader should note that "unspoken policy" is an inference from outcomes (programmes that do not develop L1), not a documented intent, and the volume offers no defence of assimilationist schooling against which to test it. The entry therefore treats the subtractive picture as the foil the chapter constructs, and the conservation argument below as an argument against that foil.

positions.name: The conservation argument: the resource, its magnitude, and its waste

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Campbell & Lindholm, ch. 16 — a formalization of the chapter's opening case

steps.text: Linguistic-minority children enter school with substantial, already-acquired competence in a home language: by age five, complete phonology, nearly all morphology and syntax for sentence formation and discourse, and sociolinguistic rule-governed variation by interlocutor — rated, with the stated limits of child semantic networks and literacy, at 3+/4 on the Interagency Language Round Table scale, against the 2/2+ that roughly 1,400 hours of Defense Language Institute instruction produces in adults.

This competence was acquired "without the expenditure of community resources," while reproducing it through foreign-language instruction would cost thousands of hours per learner "at huge financial costs to taxpayers" — if the instructional technology to reach it existed at all.

Subtractive schooling does not merely neglect the resource but destroys it, and — on the bilingual-education literature the authors invoke (Cummins; Skutnabb-Kangas; and others cited in the chapter) — works against the children's general education and their progress in English itself, as well as against the national interest in foreign-language capacity.
Policy should conserve and enhance the resource — priority to maintaining and developing the home language through schooling — rather than squander it.

positions.name: The additive models: bilingual immersion and its variants

blocks.text: Conservation is given institutional form: use both languages as media of instruction, with the home language developing alongside, not before, English.

blocks.label: The elementary model
blocks.source: Campbell & Lindholm, ch. 16
blocks.text: two-way bilingual immersion mixes native English speakers with native speakers of the partner language (roughly one-third / two-thirds), teaches mainly through the partner language in kindergarten–grade 2 (with a small daily English block), rising to 50% English by grades 4–6, never mixing languages within a period, and integrating content with language instruction. First-year evaluation (112 kindergarten and first-grade pupils in four California schools): all pupils gained in *both* languages (Spanish speakers' Spanish gains highly significant; English speakers gained English despite minimal English instruction), both groups scored average to above average on achievement tests, and content learned in Spanish was available when tested in English — the pattern the model's assumptions predict, and the reverse of the subtractive expectation that home-language instruction costs English or achievement.

**The secondary and university variants** (same source): at Mount Miguel High School, a bilingual partial-immersion programme streams heritage speakers (Spanish for Native Speakers) separately from second-language learners for a year, then teaches content jointly in Spanish; across two years, heritage speakers outscored the intensive second-language stream, which outscored traditional grammar-based Spanish classes, on listening, reading and writing — and heritage speakers' profile problem is the inverse of beginners': educated almost entirely in English, they hold more *academic* proficiency in English than in their native language. At UCLA, heritage Korean students with spoken competence take an intensive Seoul National University programme (30 hours a week for ten weeks, content courses in sheltered Korean, homestays) aimed at adult literacy; proficiency, self-esteem and ethnolinguistic loyalties were being monitored, with analysis incomplete when the chapter was written — the authors record optimism, not results.

**Objections — the authors' own** (same source): the three programmes "are in their infancy"; the heritage population has not been adequately studied by second-language researchers; "more information is needed about their process of Spanish language development"; and there is a "lack of tests that can adequately measure the Spanish language skills that these students possess." The positive findings are first-year and partly single-site; the university programme's case rests on design and expectation. The chapter argues conservation is the right priority for research and policy; it does not claim the programme science is finished.

thought.name: The Korean-American five-year-old
thought.text: (Campbell & Lindholm, ch. 16). The chapter's central device is a deliberate hypothetical: one child, described competence by competence — phonology, morphology and syntax, discourse, honorifics and interlocutor-sensitive variation — and then priced, twice: once against the Defense Language Institute's 1,400 hours to a lower rating, and once against a university student's 600 hours over four years, who "would be fortunate" to reach the same 2/2+ range. The device converts an abstract policy word ("resources") into a measurable asymmetry: the state pays enormously to build in adults a fraction of what it lets evaporate in children. Everything in the chapter's normative case depends on the reader granting that the child's competence really is the same kind of thing the proficiency scale measures in adults — the authors flag the disanalogies themselves (no literacy; semantic networks limited to a five-year-old's worlds).

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: Campbell & Lindholm, ch. 16 (the resource case and the three models) — there is no Carneades lecture for this problem.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Berns, ch. 1 (the status of English across Japan, West Germany and India — what makes a language count, institutionally, as worth teaching through), and the Part III introduction's framing question (pp. 181–183).

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: Campbell & Lindholm's programme evaluations inside ch. 16 (elementary immersion; Mount Miguel; UCLA–Seoul).

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: book 031 itself is the corpus's whole treatment; the neighbouring policy question — what political and societal forces govern language teaching regardless of research — is posed but not answered in Kramsch, ch. 3, Q8.

language-as-a-resource-conservation-and-.verdict: Within this corpus there is no debate to report, and the entry does not manufacture one: book 031 stages the conservation position at length and the subtractive default only as its foil. What the chapter itself leaves open is considerable. The causal chain from home-language maintenance to better English and achievement is asserted on cited literature, not demonstrated in the chapter's own data, which are first-year programme evaluations with comparison groups that are small (at elementary level, 39 non-immersion pupils on one test) or absent (the university programme). The normative step — from "the competence is valuable and costly to replace" to "schools ought to conserve it" — is taken briskly, via the national-interest frame ("resolution of our national foreign language resource deficits"); the child's and community's own claims on the language appear in the data instruments (ethnolinguistic loyalties, self-esteem, attitudes) rather than as argued premises. And the classification question from the sibling entry cuts both ways here: the heritage secondary students are simultaneously native speakers and, academically, second-language learners of their own language — a profile the foreign/second scheme has no box for, and which the authors flag as a research gap in its own right.

connections.title: Second or Foreign? The Classification of Language-Learning Contexts
connections.text: [Second or Foreign? The Classification of Language-Learning Contexts](second-or-foreign-language-contexts.md) — Berns's cline is a classification of *status*, and status is what policy acts on: India's English is conserved by institutions (courts, administration, universities) in a way Japan's is not, and Campbell & Lindholm's programmes are attempts to give US minority languages a fraction of that institutional footing.

connections.title: Communicative Competence and Pragmatic Failure
connections.text: [Communicative Competence and Pragmatic Failure](communicative-competence-and-pragmatic-failure.md) — what would be conserved is communicative, not merely grammatical, competence: the five-year-old's sociolinguistic rule-following (honorifics, register, body language by interlocutor) is precisely the expanded competence that entry describes, and it is the part classroom foreign-language teaching finds hardest to rebuild.

sources: VanPatten & Lee (eds.), *Second Language Acquisition / Foreign Language Learning* (book 031): ch. 16, Campbell & Lindholm, "Conservation of Language Resources" (pp. 226–239); ch. 1, Berns (pp. 3–11, for language status); ch. 3, Kramsch (pp. 27–33, for Q8 and the sociolinguistic frame); ch. 15, Schinke-Llano (pp. 216–225, for the majority-language immersion contrast — Schinke-Llano expressly excludes minority children and additive/subtractive bilingualism from her discussion); Part III introduction (pp. 181–183) — all read in full.

Lectures: none assigned. No Carneades lecture in the corpus addresses language policy, conservation or bilingual education; the 90-second version is therefore textbook-distilled and is marked as such. (The lecture searches run for this slice — language, meaning, reference, analyticity, words, naming, speech — returned no policy lecture.)

names-descriptions-and-reference.title: Names, Descriptions and Reference
names-descriptions-and-reference.note: **lecture-led** (Russell, Kripke, indexicals); the entry declares the book's non-support plainly
names-descriptions-and-reference.question: How does an expression latch onto an object? A name like "Saul Kripke" seems to point straight at a person. A description like "the 44th President of the United States" points by way of a condition — whoever satisfies it. An indexical like "I," "here" or "now" points only relative to who is speaking, where and when. These mechanisms look interchangeable in ordinary speech, and the classical puzzles of the philosophy of language arise exactly where they come apart: substitute one co-referring expression for another inside a belief report and a truth can turn false; ask what a description picks out in a world where things went differently and names and descriptions diverge; try to state the truth of "I am here now" without the context and the truth will not stay still. **A note on sources, before anything else:** this entry is lecture-led. The Carneades series covers reference richly; book 031 — an applied-linguistics volume — contains no theory of reference at all, and contributes only neighbouring material on how learners handle form–meaning relations, flagged as such where it appears. Nothing below presents book 031 as a semantics text.
names-descriptions-and-reference.ninety: Some expressions refer the same way in every situation; others borrow their reference from the situation. A definite description — "the tallest building in the world," "the largest two-digit prime number" — picks out whatever uniquely fits the condition, and Russell's proposal was that such phrases do not really name anything at all: "Yuri is the smartest" unpacks into the claim that for everyone, if they are the smartest, they are Yuri. Names behave differently. A rigid designator picks out the same object in every possible world where that object exists: "Saul Kripke" refers to Kripke whether he is a philosopher, a wizard or a lawyer in that world, while "the 44th President" is a *flaccid* designator, free to pick out someone else in a world where the election went otherwise. Indexicals split the difference by tying reference to the occasion: "I," "here," "now," "yesterday" refer to different people, places and times depending on who utters them and when, so the sentence "I am standing" has no truth value until a context supplies one. Three devices, three behaviours — and the puzzles begin when a theory built for one device is applied to another. (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [What is a Definite Description?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=btLfQX0PJ5k), [What is a Rigid Designator?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h0GNeCRdx9s), [What is a Flaccid Designator?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=txLEbIplCPQ), [What is an Indexical?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n-Mxfe6Yz6M).)

positions.name: Russell: definite descriptions are not names (as the lecture presents him)

blocks.text: Descriptions only *appear* to behave like names; their logical form is quantificational, which dissolves the puzzles they generate (the lecture instances the riddle of negative existentials and the bald king of France).

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, "What is a Definite Description?" — a formalization of the analysis the lecture states

steps.text: A sentence of the form "A is *the* X" is true just in case: there is something that is X, and for every object B, if B is X then B is identical to A (the lecture's example: for all people, if someone is the smartest, that someone is Yuri).
So understood, the description contributes a uniqueness-and-identity condition, not a referring constituent that must have a bearer for the sentence to be meaningful.
Definite descriptions have "a very different logical form" from names, despite surface appearances.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the lecture itself ends by putting the worry to the audience: is Russell's version "too revisionist"? The analysis trades a simple utterance for a much more complicated one, and whether the logical form "truly represent[s] what we mean" is left as an open question, not a verdict.

positions.name: Kripke: names are rigid, most descriptions are flaccid (as the lectures present him)

blocks.text: Reference across possible worlds separates the devices cleanly.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, "What is a Rigid Designator?" and "What is a Flaccid Designator?" — a formalization

steps.text: A rigid designator refers to the same object in all possible worlds in which that object exists; proper names (Saul Kripke, Barack Obama, Earth, China) are the paradigm — there is no world where China is not China, though plenty where China is not the most populous country.

Most definite descriptions are flaccid: "the most populous country on Earth in 2020," "the Queen of England," "the smallest star in the Milky Way" can pick out different objects in different worlds — even when they contain rigid parts (the Milky Way stays fixed while its smallest star varies). Descriptions go rigid only where logic or mathematics fixes the satisfier in every world ("the predecessor of 3" always picks out 2; "the sum of four and five" always picks out 9).
Names cannot be flaccid designators, and name–description equivalence in this world does not make the two devices the same device.

blocks.label: Payoff — necessary truths known only by experience
blocks.source: Carneades, "Kripke's Necessary, A Posteriori Statements" — a formalization

steps.text: If two rigid designators refer to the same object, they refer to it in every world where it exists, so the identity statement between them is true in all such worlds — necessary.

Hesperus and Phosphorus are both rigid designators (ancient names for the morning and evening appearances of Venus), yet that they co-refer was discovered by astronomers, not by reflection on the concepts — Lois Lane likewise needs empirical evidence that Superman is Clark Kent.

"Hesperus is Phosphorus" is necessary and a posteriori — a combination the traditional alignment of necessary with a priori said should not exist. (The companion lecture, "Kripke's Contingent, A Priori Statements," runs the separation the other way with the standard-metre stick; both lectures flag their own pressure points — whether "here" really rigidly designates, whether the metre case is genuinely knowable without measurement — and leave them open.)

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the Flaccid Designator lecture raises the border troubles itself: nickname-like names ("Al 'Scarface' Capone") seem partly descriptive and world-dependent; honorifics inside names ("Sir Terry Pratchett") are plainly contingent. Behind them sits the unanswered question of transworld identity — what makes the Obama who lost in one world the same person as the Obama who won in another, and what the criteria for successful cross-world identification by name even are. The lectures pose these; they do not resolve them.

positions.name: Indexicals: reference that will not leave the context behind

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, "What is an Indexical?" — a formalization

steps.text: Indexicals ("I," "here," "now," "you," "yesterday," "in an hour") take their reference from the context of utterance — who speaks, where, when, and for demonstratives ("this," "he" with a gesture) what the speaker is doing.

Their contribution cannot be eliminated by substituting a context-free equivalent: believing "the meeting is at 4:00 p.m." is compatible with not believing "the meeting is now," even when it is 4:00 p.m. — so "now" is not translatable away without loss.
Sentences containing indexicals have no truth value independent of context, and indexicals resist reduction within a purely extensional logical framework.

blocks.text: The lecture refines the class: *pure* indexicals ("I," "here," "now") need only the context's coordinates, while *demonstratives* ("this," "that," "he/she" on an occasion) need a demonstration besides. It also notes — without developing — that indexicals behave badly inside belief contexts, which is the bridge to the next position.

positions.name: The attitude-reports puzzle: substitution fails where belief begins

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, "The Puzzle of Propositional Attitude Reports" — the puzzle stated as the lecture states it

steps.text: The principle of identity substitution: if a = b and a satisfies F, then b satisfies F. In extensional contexts it validates obviously good inferences — from "Kikuchi is tall" and "Kikuchi is Mr. Khalichi" to "Mr. Khalichi is tall"; from "the Morning Star is a planet" and "the Morning Star is the Evening Star" to "the Evening Star is a planet."

Inside propositional attitude reports — reports of a subject's belief, hope, desire or claim toward a proposition — the same substitutions fail: Victor may think Mark Twain is a good writer while having no thought that Samuel Clemens is; Tommy may say he wants to be Batman without saying he wants to be Bruce Wayne; Sanji may believe 90/9 is the answer without believing 10 is; and the speaker who claims to like eating Soylent Green does not thereby claim to like eating people.

The principle holds in extensional contexts and breaks in *intensional* (attitude) contexts; what it is about those contexts that breaks it — a defect in the principle, or something about how attitudes individuate their objects — is the puzzle.

blocks.label: The de re / de dicto distinction
blocks.source: Carneades, "Semantically De Re and De Dicto"
blocks.text: one diagnostic tool the series offers is scope-like. "Ralph believes the man he is pointing at in the dark is a spy" is true *de dicto* only: substitute the co-referring "the mayor" (the man is Orchid, the mayor, though Ralph does not know it) and the belief report goes false. But "the mayor is such that Ralph believes of him that he is a spy" is true *de re* — true *of the man*, under any designation. The lecture presents the distinction as a way of marking where substitution is and is not licensed; it does not present it as a solution to the puzzle, and the series' promised Fregean and Russellian solutions are announced for later videos that are not part of what was read for this entry.

positions.name: What book 031 adds — neighbouring evidence, honestly labelled

blocks.text: Book 031 contains no position on reference. What it contains is three accounts of learners colliding with the fact that form–meaning links are not one-to-one — the developmental shadow of this entry's problem, included as anchoring context and nothing more. Kramsch (ch. 3) sets as the first question of the FLL research agenda how learners "acquire lexical meanings … and pass from one-to-one equivalence to multifunctionality within the L2 system of semantic relations" — a question posed, not answered. Andersen (ch. 5) gives the mechanism its names: learners begin under a **One-to-One Principle** (one intended meaning, one clear invariant surface form) and are driven by the **Multifunctionality Principle** toward forms that do many jobs at once — the learner's version of discovering that reference and meaning do not pair off neatly. Gass (ch. 4) adds the comprehension side: establishing the relations among a sentence's elements uses language-specific cues (English leans on word order — "The picture kisses the girl" can only be the picture kissing; Italian distributes the work across agreement, semantic and pragmatic factors), English learners of Italian differed sharply by environment on exactly this, and some such sensitivity may be unavailable from textbooks at all, only from ambient speech. None of this is a theory of reference; it is evidence that the devices this entry describes are not transparent to the people who must acquire them.

thought.name: Hesperus and Phosphorus
thought.text: (Kripke lectures). Two names, one planet, centuries of competent speakers who did not know it. If names referred *via* the descriptions speakers associate with them (the morning star / the evening star), the identity would be a confusion of two objects; because the names are rigid, it is instead a discovery about one. The case is the engine of the necessary-a-posteriori argument above.

thought.name: Ralph, Orchid and the man in the dark
thought.text: (De Re and De Dicto lecture). Ralph believes the man he points at in the dark is a spy; the man is Orchid, the mayor; Ralph also knows Orchid as the mayor and does not believe the mayor is a spy. One man, two designations, opposite belief verdicts — the cleanest exhibition in the read lectures of why attitude contexts are intensional, and of what the de re/de dicto distinction is for.

thought.name: Superman and Clark Kent
thought.text: (Necessary A Posteriori lecture; also the Attitude Reports lecture's Batman/Bruce Wayne case). The same co-reference does double duty in the series: as an identity between rigid designators it is necessary; as material inside Lois Lane's (or Tommy's) attitudes it is exactly what cannot be substituted. Holding both facts about one pair of names is the shortest statement of this entry's problem.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: the Carneades definition lectures — Definite Description; Rigid Designator; Flaccid Designator; Indexical.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: the Carneades puzzle and Kripke lectures — The Puzzle of Propositional Attitude Reports; Semantically De Re and De Dicto; Kripke's Necessary, A Posteriori Statements; Kripke's Contingent, A Priori Statements.

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: none available in this corpus — no primary text on reference (no Russell, Frege or Kripke paper) was read for this entry, and book 007's and book 006's Russell is the epistemologist of sense-data, not here conscripted as a theory of denoting.

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: none available in this corpus. Book 031's adjacent material (Kramsch ch. 3, Q1; Andersen ch. 5; Gass ch. 4) is catalogued above under its own honest heading.

names-descriptions-and-reference.verdict: As the read sources leave it: the distinctions are in good order and the puzzles are open. Russell's analysis of descriptions is presented with an explicit "too revisionist?" doubt attached; Kripke's rigidity is presented with its border cases (Scarface, honorifics, transworld identity) flagged by the lecturer himself; the attitude-reports puzzle is posed, the de re/de dicto distinction supplied as a diagnostic, and the Fregean and Russellian solutions explicitly deferred to videos outside this entry's reading. The corpus therefore supports the *statement* of the reference problem and its main devices, but no adjudication among theories of reference — and any entry claiming more would be writing from outside its sources. Book 031's contribution stands at the level of acquisition: speakers demonstrably begin by assuming one form per meaning and must learn their way out of it, which is a fact about us, not about reference itself.

connections.title: Communicative Competence and Pragmatic Failure
connections.text: [Communicative Competence and Pragmatic Failure](communicative-competence-and-pragmatic-failure.md) — the locutionary level of a speech act just is sense and reference at work; the two entries share the speech-act lectures' framework from opposite ends (what is said vs what is done in saying it).

Analyticity and synonymy — *cross-referenced, not rebuilt here.* Whether "bachelor" *means* unmarried man — and whether any statement is true by meaning alone — is the analyticity problem, whose home in this KB is the epistemology slice (the a priori thread in [The Problem of Induction](../epistemology/problem-of-induction.md); and book 007, ch. 18, Quine's "Two Dogmas of Empiricism," which the corpus holds only as a corrupted file — see the book map for 007). The two Carneades lectures on the topic were read for this slice — [Analytic and Synthetic Distinction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zX-nNQ2Opsc) (analytic: true by definition, predicate contained in subject — "bachelors are unmarried men"; synthetic: true by experience — "all bachelors are unhappy") and [Quine's Demonstration of the Circularity of Analyticity](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8U873MryWrU) (every attempted definition of analyticity via synonymy, definition, interchangeability *salva veritate* or necessity circles back to analyticity itself, so the positivist notion should be dropped). They are recorded here because synonymy is a meaning relation and belongs to this subfield's map; no position is reconstructed from them in this slice, and book 031 contributes nothing to the problem — Kramsch's passing phrase for language, "indeterminate and culturally relative" (ch. 3), is a sociolinguistic commitment, not a treatment of analyticity, and is not presented as one.

second-or-foreign-language-contexts.title: Second or Foreign? The Classification of Language-Learning Contexts
second-or-foreign-language-contexts.aka: the SLA/FLL distinction; the foreign–second dichotomy
second-or-foreign-language-contexts.note: Stern, Berns, Gass, Schinke-Llano, the editors' synthesis
second-or-foreign-language-contexts.question: When someone learns a language that is not their first, we sort the situation into kinds: the language is a *second* language if it is learned where it is spoken, a *foreign* language if it is learned in a classroom far from its speakers. The sorting looks like a mere labelling convenience, but a surprising amount turns on it — what counts as evidence for a theory of acquisition, what a curriculum should imitate, what outcome a learner can be promised. So: does the distinction carve language learning at a real joint, is it a smooth continuum misdescribed as a dichotomy, or does it dissolve once you ask *for what purpose* the classification is being made? The one book in this corpus that takes the question head-on — VanPatten & Lee's *Second Language Acquisition / Foreign Language Learning* (book 031, mislabelled in the corpus as "Language Matters") — is a whole volume organized around it, and its contributors do not agree.
second-or-foreign-language-contexts.ninety: *[Textbook-distilled — no Carneades lecture covers this problem; distilled from Berns, ch. 1, and VanPatten & Lee, ch. 17, of book 031.]* Start with the textbook definition: a language is "second" when it is learned with reference to a speech community inside your own country, "foreign" when the community is outside it. Now test it on real cases. English in Japan is learned almost entirely at school, for exams and cultivated status, with few chances to use it — clearly "foreign." English in India is a medium of instruction, law and administration, used daily between Indians — clearly "second." But English in West Germany, learned at school yet heard in the media, used on holiday and at work across Europe, sits in between: forcing it into either box loses exactly what is distinctive about it. The fix proposed in the book is to replace the two boxes with a line — a cline with "foreign" at one end and "second" at the other, Germany near the middle — and to add a third label, "international," for the common case of two non-native speakers using English with each other, which belongs to neither national community. The volume's editors end somewhere more radical still: whether the distinction matters depends on what you are studying — the social context, the mental processes, or the eventual product — and for the mental processes themselves, it may not matter at all.

positions.name: The dichotomy (Stern's definition, as Berns presents it)

blocks.text: Contexts come in two kinds, fixed by geography: where the reference speech community sits relative to the learner's national or territorial boundaries.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Berns, *Second Language Acquisition / Foreign Language Learning*, ch. 1, presenting Stern 1983 — a formalization of the definition Berns takes as her starting point

steps.text: A learned language is used with reference to some speech community whose norms the learner approximates.
That community is either inside or outside the national or territorial boundaries within which the learning takes place.
Every learning context is therefore either a second-language context (community inside) or a foreign-language context (community outside).

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Berns's own profiles are the objection: the definition classifies Japan and India cleanly but leaves West Germany oscillating between the boxes (see Thought experiments), and it has no slot at all for English used between non-native speakers across borders. A classification that cannot place one of its three parade cases, and cannot state one of the commonest uses, is not false so much as too coarse for the work asked of it.

positions.name: Berns: replace the dichotomy with a cline — and add "international"

blocks.text: The geography is real, but it comes in degrees, because what matters is the pattern of users, uses, motivations and attitudes in a *sociolinguistic profile*, and profiles shade into one another.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Berns, ch. 1

steps.text: The Japan, West Germany and India profiles differ continuously in opportunity for use, domains covered, and contact with users of English inside the country — not by a single inside/outside switch.

A two-box scheme forces the German case to be described as either strictly foreign (false to its in-country contact and interpersonal uses) or strictly second (false to its lack of institutional and literary roles).

One widespread use — English between non-native speakers for business, trade and commerce — belongs to an international speech community that is neither the learner's national community nor a foreign native one.
Contexts are better placed on a cline of language status (Japan near the "foreign" pole, India near the "second" pole, West Germany near the midpoint), supplemented by the category "international."

blocks.label: Replies and limits
blocks.text: Berns adds the learner's perspective as a corrective inside her own proposal: the terms are "meaningful and useful only to researchers and other 'outside' observers," while from the learner's side purposes vary individual by individual within a single community, so even a cline describes contexts, not learners. The editors' Introduction presses the point with Spanish in the United States, which reproduces all three of Berns's English profiles within one country (see Thought experiments).

positions.name: Gass: the same/different question dissolves — ask after extent and nature instead

blocks.text: Look inside the learner, and the processes are the same; look outside, at what information the environment supplies, and they differ — in degree, and only sometimes in kind.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Gass, ch. 4

steps.text: The psycholinguistic task is context-independent: all learners take in input, organize it within their current system, generalize and misgeneralize — classroom-induced errors (Stenson's *any*-examples) are the same generalizing process with different instantiations, and Krashen's learning/acquisition contrast itself occurs both in and out of classrooms.

What the context changes is the availability of relevant information: negative evidence (direct correction is a classroom staple, indirect cues the outside norm, and indirect cues may be unusable across cultures), the range and control of input, and some interpretation strategies that appear learnable only from ambient speech.

Even the apparent product difference — completeness — may be one of degree: on Coppieters' evidence, apparently native-like speakers' intuitions still diverge from natives', so "native-like competence is only possible in one language" may hold for second-language learners generally, not just classroom ones.

SLA and FLL show both quantitative and qualitative differences amid numerous similarities; the research agenda should not be whether they are the same or different — "the answer is 'yes'" — but the extent and nature of the similarities and differences.

positions.name: Schinke-Llano: define the pair by product, and test it on immersion

blocks.text: A different cut entirely: stop defining the terms by where learning happens and define them by what comes out.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Schinke-Llano, ch. 15 — the definition is stated as an operating definition, and the argument is a formalization of her immersion comparison

steps.text: Let "SLA" mean learning that results in native-like use of the target language, and "FLL" learning that does not (operating definitions).

Immersion schooling — target language as medium of instruction — supplies the facilitative conditions the SLA literature identifies (acquisition rather than formal learning, abundant comprehensible input, negotiated interaction, comprehensible output, a silent period, a low affective filter) far more fully than FLEX or FLES courses, and immersion pupils outperform their non-immersion peers.
Yet immersion pupils still do not reach native-like speaking and writing, needing six to seven years even for native-like listening and reading.

SLA-like environments can be approximated in a classroom, and the product moves toward SLA — but approximation is not identity, so on the product definition classroom learning remains FLL-like to a degree.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Genesee, quoted by Schinke-Llano herself: it is "unlikely that any student will attain totally native-like competence in a language if language learning and use are restricted to the school environment," because school offers only a limited range of the functions the speech community demands. Schinke-Llano accepts the fact and rejects the defeatism: the right response is not to declare the goal unattainable but to use classroom-interaction research to close the gap.

positions.name: The editors' synthesis: the distinction is purpose-relative (contexts / processes / products)

blocks.text: The volume's own conclusion refuses a single verdict and sorts the question instead.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: VanPatten & Lee, ch. 17

steps.text: For *context* — the social situations of use, which shape the quality and quantity of input and output — the SLA/FLL distinction is important.

For *processes*, it splits: psycholinguistic processes (how a grammatical system is built from input) do not change from environment to environment, so the distinction is irrelevant there; psychosocial processes (how speakers act in speech events) do change with discourse context, so the distinction matters there — VanPatten's Spanish-clitic comparison and Eubank's German-negation analysis find only *superficial* (output) differences over shared *deep* processes, while Wildner-Bassett's differences of "pragmatic impact" are genuinely important for use.
For *products* — eventual proficiency, and how present L1 influence is in the outcome — the distinction is useful, though the influence process itself does not change, only its degree in the product.
FLL is neither contained in SLA nor contains it; the two are overlapping circles, and whether the distinction should be drawn at all "is a function of one's own purpose."

thought.name: West Germany as the midpoint case
thought.text: (Berns, ch. 1). English there is a school subject (foreign-like) but also a media presence, a source of borrowings, and a working *lingua franca* with other Europeans at every social level (second-like) — while never becoming a medium of instruction, law or literature (unlike India). Any adequate classification must say *in-between* here without contradiction; the dichotomy cannot, the cline can. It is the case that does the argumentative work of the whole chapter.

thought.name: Spanish in the United States
thought.text: (VanPatten & Lee, Introduction). One language, one country, three profiles: Spanish in Alaska behaves like English in Japan, in Los Angeles and Dade County like English in India, in Chicago, New York and Dallas like English in West Germany. And the editors add the twist Berns's learner perspective predicts: a learner in a Spanish-rich community may never seek outside input, and a learner in Alaska may seek it avidly — so community-level classification and learner-level reality can come apart in both directions.

thought.name: Immersion as the limiting classroom
thought.text: (Schinke-Llano, ch. 15). Build the classroom that does everything the acquisition literature asks — years of content teaching through the target language from kindergarten — and measure the product against natives. The persistent gap in speaking and writing is the volume's best evidence that "classroom vs community" tracks something real about outcomes even where processes are shared.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: Berns, ch. 1 (the profiles and the cline) — there is no Carneades lecture for this problem.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Gass, ch. 4 (internal vs external variables; completeness), and the editors' synthesis, ch. 17.

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: VanPatten, ch. 2 (why the classification is also a fight about who produces theory); Schinke-Llano, ch. 15 (the product definition and the immersion evidence).

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: book 031 as a whole — the volume *is* the treatment; its Part introductions (pp. 13–16, 69–71, 181–183) stage the disagreement chapter by chapter.

second-or-foreign-language-contexts.verdict: Inside this corpus, unsettled — by the editors' own admission. Chapter 17 opens its terminology discussion with the verdict that on what "second language acquisition" and "foreign language learning" mean there is "quite simply" no consensus among the volume's contributors: some subsume FLL under SLA, some restrict SLA so it does not encompass FLL, some keep the distinction only for use, some ignore it. What the volume does establish is a shared negative point — a bare same/different verdict is the wrong output — and three candidate replacements that do not coincide: a continuum of contexts (Berns), an extent-and-nature research programme (Gass), and a purpose-relative sorting (the editors), with Schinke-Llano's product definition cutting across all three. Nothing in the corpus decides among them, and the corpus's one attempt at a neighbouring classification problem — Kramsch's (ch. 3) insistence that FLL research is neither SLA nor FL education — shows the same pattern one level up: the boundaries of the *fields* are as contested as the boundaries of the *contexts*.

connections.title: Communicative Competence and Pragmatic Failure
connections.text: [Communicative Competence and Pragmatic Failure](communicative-competence-and-pragmatic-failure.md) — the editors' reason for keeping the distinction for psychosocial processes is that pragmatic devices change with discourse context; what those devices are, and how they fail, is that entry's subject.

connections.title: Language as a Resource: Conservation and Policy
connections.text: [Language as a Resource: Conservation and Policy](language-as-a-resource-conservation-and-policy.md) — Berns's profiles are also status descriptions: which languages a society treats as resources, and for whom, is decided partly by the classifications this entry examines (the Part III introduction asks, of US bilingual pupils, "What, then, is a foreign language in the United States?").

Vagueness (Carneades, [Vagueness vs Ambiguity vs Generality](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8SGizqyt8EM)) — a structural cousin, not a source for this entry: the foreign/second pair behaves the way the lecture says vague predicates do, with absolute borderline cases (West Germany) that no further inquiry resolves into one box or the other. Berns's cline is, in effect, the refusal to stipulate a sharp boundary — compare the lecture's question whether stipulating one ("over 400 grains = a heap") would lose something real.

(pp. 27–33); ch. 4, Gass, "Second and Foreign Language Learning: Same, Different or None of the Above?" (pp. 34–44); ch. 15, Schinke-Llano, "Can Foreign Language Learning Be Like Second Language Acquisition?" (pp. 216–225); ch. 17, VanPatten & Lee, "Contexts, Processes, and Products…" (pp. 240–245); Part I introduction (pp. 13–16) and Part III introduction (pp. 181–183) — all read in full.

No Carneades lecture addresses second/foreign language contexts; the 90-second version is therefore textbook-distilled and is marked as such.

cosmological-argument.title: The Cosmological Argument
cosmological-argument.note: Aquinas, kalām, Russell/Hume/Kant objections, Bhāviveka's anti-creator arguments (020)
cosmological-argument.question: Everything we meet exists, but might not have: it was caused, made, set in motion by something else. Follow the chain back — causes of causes, movers of movers — and one of two things must be true: the chain goes back forever, or it stops at something that does not itself need a cause: a first cause, an unmoved mover, a necessary being. The cosmological argument is the family of arguments that says the chain must stop, and that what stops it is God. Its mirror image also belongs to this entry: a classical Buddhist argument, preserved in book 020, that the chain cannot stop at a *Lord* — because a creator who deals out pleasure and pain unevenly looks less like an explanation than like one more thing to explain.
cosmological-argument.ninety: Think of the most obnoxious question a child can ask: *why?* — and then ask it again about every answer. Why are the leaves green? Chlorophyll. Why chlorophyll? Energy. Why…? The cosmological argument is the refusal to let that conversation either run forever or end with "because I said so." Aquinas's version works with change: whatever changes is changed by something else, and a chain of changers where every member is itself being changed cannot regress infinitely — so there is a first mover that moves without being moved. The kalām version works with time: everything that *begins* to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist (a beginningless series would be an actual infinite, and an actual infinite is impossible); so the universe has a cause, and since no physical explanation can cover the origin of the physical itself, the cause must be a personal agent — God. The critics ask whether the chain really can't regress (Hume: explain every part and you've explained the whole; Russell: inferring a cause for the whole from causes of the parts is the fallacy of composition — "the universe just is"), and whether the "necessary being" at the end is the ontological argument in disguise (Kant). The lecture series closes by conceding the argument may not prove God — while insisting it leaves the denier with the child's question still unanswered: *why is there something rather than nothing?* (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [St. Thomas Aquinas's Cosmological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lX-2htH5wnM), [Kalam Cosmological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22ELxgVDwb4), [Final Thoughts on the Cosmological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_Apg8jbAa1Y).)

videos.title: Final Thoughts on the Cosmological Argument

positions.name: Aquinas's argument from contingency (the Thomistic cosmological argument)

blocks.text: Aquinas argues not from a temporal beginning but from dependence here and now: an *essentially ordered* regress — where each cause is simultaneously sustaining the next — cannot be infinite.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [St. Thomas Aquinas's Cosmological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lX-2htH5wnM
blocks.text: , following the Stanford Encyclopedia's outline of Aquinas — the lecture's own formulation):

steps.text: A contingent being — a being that might not have existed — exists. (Your computer: there are possible worlds with no computer, no you, no Earth.)
This contingent being has a cause of its existence. (It didn't just pop into existence from nowhere.)
The cause of this contingent being's existence is something other than the contingent being itself. (It didn't cause itself.)
What causes or explains a contingent being must either be solely other contingent beings, or include a necessary being.
Contingent beings alone cannot provide an adequate causal account of the existence of a contingent being.
The cause of a contingent being must include a necessary being — God exists.

positions.name: The First Way: the unmoved mover (Aquinas)

blocks.text: The first of the Five Ways (*Summa Theologica*) argues from *motion* in Aristotle's sense — change, the actualization of a potentiality (the hot stove actualizing the water's potential to be warm).

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [The Unmoved Mover (Aquinas's First Way
blocks.text: ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-YFtBC9lJmo) and [St. Thomas Aquinas's Five Ways (Proofs of God)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=unExjvKb7xU) — a formalization of the lectures' presentation, labelled as such):

steps.text: Some things are in motion (change from potentiality to actuality).

Whatever is moved is moved by another: a thing's actuality causes change in others, while its own potentiality is actualized by something already actual (nothing is simultaneously actual and potential in the same respect).
A regress of movers, each moved by another, cannot proceed to infinity in an essentially ordered series.

There is a first, unmoved mover — pure actuality — which Aquinas identifies with the God of the tradition (the lectures note Aristotle's beyond-physics cause of all motion was ready to hand for the identification, and that Aquinas's immediate goal is to prove *a* god, some god, exists — that it is the Christian God requires further argument).

blocks.text: The Five Ways as a set — first way (unmoved mover), second (first cause), third (necessity and contingency), fourth (degrees of perfection), fifth (teleology, from the directedness of things) — are mostly cosmological in character, the fifth excepted; the lecture series examines each with its objections in turn ([Objections to St Thomas Aquinas's First Way](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XJzCYqiLWt0) for the first).

positions.name: The kalām cosmological argument

blocks.text: The kalām family (presented in the lectures in William Lane Craig's formulation) turns on *temporal* regress: the universe cannot have existed forever, because a beginningless temporal series would be an actual infinite.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [Kalam Cosmological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22ELxgVDwb4
blocks.text: ; the lecture's own premises):

steps.text: Everything that begins to exist has a cause of its existence.
The universe began to exist. (Support: an actual infinite cannot exist; a beginningless temporal series of events is an actual infinite; therefore a beginningless temporal series cannot exist.)

No scientific explanation in terms of physical laws can provide a causal account of the origin of the universe; all explanations are either scientific or personal; so the cause's explanation must be personal.
The cause of the universe is a personal agent — God.

blocks.text: The series devotes a lecture each to the pressure points: the beginning of the universe ([Objections to the Beginning of the Universe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cmhADdYk9Sg)), the causal principle ([Objections to the Principle of Causality](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=53tcPgmmCK8)), and the personal-explanation step ([Objections to Personal Explanation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VGaMuuw6vyU)). This entry does not reproduce those objection lectures' contents in detail; the three canonical critics below are the ones the Aquinas series develops, and the kalām objections stand as the corpus's record that each kalām premise is independently contested.

positions.name: The classical objections (Russell, Hume, Kant — as the lecture series presents them)

blocks.text: **Russell: the fallacy of composition** ([Russell's Objection to the Cosmological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ppBxkTTGoRQ)). From "every part has a property" it does not follow that the whole has it: bricks can each be small while the wall is big. Just because everything *in* the universe has a cause, it does not follow that the *universe* has a cause; just because every part is contingent, the whole need not need an explanation. Russell's own verdict, per the lecture: "the universe just is." The lecturer reports finding this the most convincing of the three.

**Hume (i): explaining the parts is sufficient** ([Hume's Objections to the Cosmological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RF6GVgZgiWA)). Give me twenty balls of matter and explain each one, and I have explained the twenty — no further explanation of "the whole" is owed. Likewise the universe. The lecture's own pushback: explaining parts *in terms of each other* (chicken by egg, egg by chicken) is circular, and a satisfactory explanation seems to require stepping back to the whole system — so Hume's first objection is "a little worrisome" rather than decisive. **Hume (ii): the causal principle is dubious.** We can conceive of something without a cause; what is conceivable is possible; so "everything has a cause" is questionable. The lecture again notes the symmetry problem: arguments from conceivability are themselves questionable, since we can seem to conceive a necessary truth false merely by not fully understanding it.

**Kant: the argument leans on the ontological argument** ([Kant's Objection to the Cosmological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gqrRl-1UT70)). The cosmological argument concludes to a *necessary* being — but necessity in which sense? If logical necessity (contradiction inconceivable), note that we *can* imagine a world without God, unlike a four-sided triangle; and the claim that God is logically necessary anyway "seems to presuppose the truth of the ontological argument" — God as greatest possible being whose existence is built in. Modal necessity (existing in all possible worlds) falls into the same trap: it needs an argument for God's *possibility* of the ontological kind, and a being modally necessary but not logically necessary might exist in no world at all. Either way: "if the ontological argument was successful, then the cosmological argument would also be successful. But, if the ontological argument failed, the cosmological argument would not be able to stand on its own two feet."

**The lecturer's final thought** ([Final Thoughts](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_Apg8jbAa1Y)): after objecting "to almost every premise," the lecturer concedes the argument's residual force as a *question*. The denier "has not given a sufficient answer to the central question of the cosmological argument" — why is there something and not nothing, why is *this* possible world the real one? "Although the cosmological argument does not seem to prove the existence of God, it does pose a very good question for anyone who does not believe in God."

positions.name: The anti-creator argument: Bhāviveka against the Lord (book 020, ch. 13)

blocks.text: The corpus's primary text against a creator is not Western at all. In his commentary on Nāgārjuna's *Mūlamadhyamakakārikāḥ* 1.1, the sixth-century Buddhist philosopher Bhāviveka reads the verse's "no-cause" (*ahetu*) as an *implicative* negation — a "bad cause" (*kuhetu*), as a "no-wife" is a wife who exists but does not do what a wife does. Among such no-causes he lists the Hindu Lord (*īśvara*): the Lord may exist, but he does not *create* the world. Eckel's chapter (the source for this section) stresses that Bhāviveka grants the Lord's conventional existence throughout — what he attacks is only the Lord's capacity to function as the world's cause.

blocks.label: Canonical argument 1 — the uneven hand
blocks.source: Eckel, book 020, ch. 13, §13.3, reporting Bhāviveka's inference from conventional truth

steps.text: The Lord, on the opponent's own showing (the *Mahābhārata*'s Draupadī: humans "impelled by the Lord … may go to heaven or hell"), causes pleasure for some and pain for others — dealing them out like a cowherd, with the virtuous (Yudhiṣṭhira: "upright, gentle, bountiful, modest, and truthful") ruined at dice while the vicious prosper.
A cause whose effects show such capricious, cruel unevenness cannot be the cause of an orderly, just world.
"The Lord cannot be the cause of the arising of the world even conventionally."

blocks.text: Eckel is explicit that P1 is a theodicy argument: Draupadī "is raising what we would call the problem of theodicy" (see [The Evidential Argument from Evil](evidential-argument-from-evil.md)).

blocks.label: Canonical argument 2 — no single creator
blocks.source: same

steps.text: The world is an object of cognition (*prameya*).
The Lord himself is an object of cognition (*prameya*) — known, on the opponent's own texts, by meditating yogis.

The world shares the relevant property with the Lord: as the Lord was not created by the Lord, "the world certainly does not possess a single creator called the 'Lord.'" (Eckel presents this as the *beginning* of an argument — the opponent may reply that world and Lord differ in the relevant respect.)

blocks.label: The ultimate-level argument
