blocks.source: same
blocks.text: even granting the Lord as cause, the effect must be either the Lord himself, different from him, or both — and each option has already been refuted in Nāgārjuna's tetralemma analysis of arising (nothing arises from itself, from another, from both, or from no cause). "Therefore there ultimately is nothing that arises from the Lord."

**The alternative**: if "Lord" is to name the world's cause at all, let it name *karma* — "the cause of the multifaceted world of sentient beings along with their physical environment," which produces pleasure and pain, arising and destruction. Taken conventionally Bhāviveka accepts this; taken ultimately he does not (karma does not ultimately arise either). Eckel, citing Weber, notes why this answers the uneven-hand argument: karma makes the world "a completely connected and self-contained cosmos of ethical retribution," shifting the explanation of Yudhiṣṭhira's loss from a capricious agent to the agent's own prior action — "the most complete formal solution to the problem of theodicy."

thought.name: The obnoxious child
thought.text: (Aquinas's Cosmological Argument lecture). Every cosmological argument, the lecturer suggests, has the form of the child's endless *why?*: either the conversation goes on forever (infinite regress), or it terminates in something that cannot itself be explained further — and "the only thing that can't be explained is God." An oversimplification, the lecture admits, offered for the intuition: the argument is a theory of where the why-chain may legitimately end.

thought.name: The computer
thought.text: (same lecture). Your computer is the paradigm contingent being: easy to picture a world without it, without you, without computers, without Earth. It didn't pop into existence from nowhere and didn't cause itself. The mundane case carries P1–P3 of the Thomistic argument before the contested steps (P4–P5) begin.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: [St. Thomas Aquinas's Five Ways](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=unExjvKb7xU) and [The Unmoved Mover](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-YFtBC9lJmo); [Kalam Cosmological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22ELxgVDwb4). → Survey: the Aquinas argument lecture and its objection trilogy (Russell, Hume, Kant) + [Final Thoughts](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_Apg8jbAa1Y). → Primary (in this corpus): Bhāviveka via Eckel (book 020, ch. 13), a primary argument *against* a creator from the Buddhist side of the Indian creation debate. Aquinas's *Summa Theologica* itself is the lectures' recommended further reading but is not among the corpus's extracted books.

cosmological-argument.verdict: The lecture series ends where it ends deliberately: unconvinced by the argument as a proof, unwilling to say the underlying question is answered. Each load-bearing premise has a named, argued objection in the corpus — composition (Russell), sufficiency of parts and the causal principle (Hume), borrowed necessity (Kant), and premise-by-premise objection lectures for the kalām — and no corpus source stages a systematic theistic reply to the trilogy. Book 020 contributes the debate's non-Western mirror: Bhāviveka's conclusion is narrower than atheism (the Lord may exist; he does not create; ultimately nothing arises from anything), and the positive doctrine he defends — karma as the world's conventional cause — is a *dissolution* of the first-cause question rather than an answer of the argument's own shape. Two honest cautions: the teleological member of the family (Aquinas's fifth way, argument from design by analogy) cannot be treated from this corpus — its lecture has no transcript (see Sources) — and the "cause" the arguments conclude to is, even on their own lectures' telling, only *a* necessary being or personal agent: identifying it with the God of a particular religion is further work none of these sources does.

connections.title: The Ontological Argument
connections.text: [The Ontological Argument](ontological-argument.md) — Kant's objection makes the dependence explicit: the cosmological argument's necessary being needs the ontological argument's machinery, so the two families stand or fall partly together.

connections.title: The Evidential Argument from Evil
connections.text: [The Evidential Argument from Evil](evidential-argument-from-evil.md) — Bhāviveka's uneven-hand argument is the problem of evil operating inside a creation debate six centuries before Mackie; and a first cause that is also perfectly good inherits the evidential problem as its next question.

connections.title: The Logical Problem of Evil
connections.text: [The Logical Problem of Evil](logical-problem-of-evil.md) — Rowe's list of the theist's traditional grounds (book 027, ch. 1) includes the cosmological argument; these are the grounds whose strength the Moorean shift asks us to weigh.

sources: Eckel, "Who or What Created the World? Bhāviveka's Arguments Against the Hindu Concept of God" (book 020, ch. 13) — read in full.

Lectures (Carneades.org) — read in full: "St. Thomas Aquinas's Cosmological Argument"; "Kalam Cosmological Argument"; "St. Thomas Aquinas's Five Ways (Proofs of God)"; "The Unmoved Mover (Aquinas's First Way)"; "Russell's Objection to the Cosmological Argument"; "Hume's Objections to the Cosmological Argument"; "Kant's Objection to the Cosmological Argument"; "Final Thoughts on the Cosmological Argument".

Inspected but unusable: "Teleological Arguments From Analogy" — the file records "No English captions available for this video; no transcript text," so the teleological argument receives no treatment in this subfield's entries beyond Aquinas's fifth way being named in the Five Ways lecture.

evidential-argument-from-evil.title: The Evidential Argument from Evil
evidential-argument-from-evil.aka: the inductive / probabilistic / empirical argument from evil; the evidential problem of evil
evidential-argument-from-evil.note: Rowe, Draper, and the replies, from book 027's papers; left unsettled as the authors leave it
evidential-argument-from-evil.question: Suppose it is granted — as nearly every contributor to the modern debate grants — that the existence of evil does not *logically contradict* the existence of an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God. A harder question remains: does the evil we actually find — its amount, its kinds, and above all particular horrors that seem to serve no purpose at all — make it *unlikely*, or unreasonable to believe, that such a God exists? The evidential argument from evil says yes: not that theism is disproved, but that the evidence of suffering counts against it, rationally supports atheism, or gives us a prima facie reason to reject it. The theist's replies do not claim to explain the suffering; they claim we are in no position to draw the inference the argument needs.
evidential-argument-from-evil.ninety: Start with the horrors. Walk through a forest after a fire and picture a fawn, trapped and burned, lying in agony for days before it dies — suffering that, so far as anyone can see, serves no purpose whatsoever. The evidential argument begins there: if a perfectly good, all-powerful God existed, he would prevent suffering like that unless preventing it meant losing some greater good; we can see no such good; so, probably, there is no such good, and no such God. The other side answers with a warning about eyesight. Not seeing something is only evidence that it isn't there when you could reasonably expect to see it if it were — you can conclude there is no dog in the garage that way, but not that there is no flea. Between a creator's view of all the goods there could be and ours, the gap is so large that "we see no reason" may tell us about our limits rather than about God's. A second argument skips the horrors entirely: pain and pleasure are biological tools, shaped for survival, and that whole pattern is exactly what you'd expect if no benevolent or malevolent mind is in charge of sentient life — and much less what you'd expect if a perfectly good God were. (Distilled from the Carneades lecture [The Problem of Evil](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CYEg3SgfEDc), which presents the logical and evidential problems side by side; the argument itself is staged in book 027, *The Evidential Argument from Evil*.)

positions.name: Rowe's argument from apparently pointless suffering (William L. Rowe)

blocks.text: Rowe focuses on intense human and animal suffering — "in itself bad, an evil," even when it is sometimes justified as a means. His target is theism in the narrow sense: an omnipotent, omniscient, eternal, supremely good creator.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Rowe, "The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism," book 027, ch. 1

steps.text: There exist instances of intense suffering which an omnipotent, omniscient being could have prevented without thereby losing some greater good or permitting some evil equally bad or worse.

An omniscient, wholly good being would prevent the occurrence of any intense suffering it could, unless it could not do so without thereby losing some greater good or permitting some evil equally bad or worse.
There does not exist an omnipotent, omniscient, wholly good being.

blocks.text: P2, Rowe argues, states only a *necessary* condition on a good being's permitting suffering, and "accords with our basic moral principles, principles shared by both theists and nontheists." The fight is over P1, and Rowe is explicit about its epistemic status: the fawn's case "does not *prove* that (1) is true," and "we cannot know with certainty that instances of suffering of the sort described in 1 do occur in the world." His claim is weaker and, he thinks, enough: given the "enormous variety and profusion" of suffering, much of it apparently unrelated to any greater good and none of it plausibly *all* so related, "it is, nevertheless, altogether *reasonable* to believe that (1) is true."

In his later restatement (book 027, ch. 14), the argument is pinned to two cases — E1, the fawn ("Bambi"), and E2, the rape, beating, and murder of a five-year-old girl ("Sue") — and the support for P1 is made an explicit induction:

items: P. No good *we know of* justifies God in permitting E1 and E2.
∴ (inductively) Q. No good *at all* justifies God in permitting E1 and E2.
∴ (deductively) Not-G. There is no omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good being.

blocks.text: Rowe also develops a Bayesian version using argued-for probability assignments, and a further variant that argues from P toward the probable falsity of theism without passing through Q. In ch. 14 he concedes ground: the bare enumerative induction from P "increases the antecedent probability of Q" but does not, as it stands, make Q more likely than not.

blocks.label: The theist's best reply, on Rowe's own telling
blocks.text: not the *direct attack* (pointing to goods suffering serves: character development, free choice). That fails twice over, Rowe argues: suffering routinely exceeds what such goods require and much of it does not result from free choices; and the theist "does not know what greater goods might be served … by each instance" anyway — his own tradition says God's purposes in particular sufferings are not given to us. The best reply is the *indirect attack*, the **G. E. Moore shift**: construct the equally valid counter-argument from not-C and P2 to not-P1, and let the choice between the two arguments turn on which first premise it is more rational to believe — God's existence, or P1.

blocks.label: Rowe's verdict on the dialectic
blocks.text: he is himself persuaded by the argument, yet defends **friendly atheism**: some theists, including informed modern ones, are rationally justified in believing theism anyway, because rational justification does not require truth, and disputants' evidence and situations genuinely differ (his example: your friends are justified in believing your plane went down with no survivors while you, bobbing in a life vest, are justified in believing you are alive).

positions.name: Draper's argument from pain and pleasure (Paul Draper)

blocks.text: Draper's is, in Howard-Snyder's taxonomy, an *explanatory* evidential argument: it never claims any evil is pointless, and never needs a premise saying theism is incompatible with a fact about evil. Its force is comparative — following a question Hume asked and (Draper says) contemporary philosophers ignored: does some serious hypothesis inconsistent with theism explain facts about good and evil *much better* than theism does?

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Draper, "Pain and Pleasure: An Evidential Problem for Theists," book 027, ch. 2 — formalization labelled as such

steps.text: Let O report our observations and testimony about sentient beings experiencing pain and pleasure, and let HI (the Hypothesis of Indifference) be: neither the nature nor the condition of sentient beings on earth is the result of benevolent or malevolent actions performed by non-human persons.
Because of the biological role pain and pleasure play in goal-directed organisms, O is antecedently much more probable on HI than on theism: Pr(O/HI) >! Pr(O/theism) (claim C).
Theistic stories (theodicies) do not significantly raise Pr(O/theism) (defended in the chapter's §III, against free-will, moral-advancement, and "infinite intellect" theodicies).
We have a prima facie good epistemic reason to reject theism: theism is less probable than HI, hence less probable than not.

blocks.text: The probabilities throughout are *epistemic* — relative to a person's epistemic situation — and the conclusion is expressly *prima facie*: sufficient reason to reject theism "unless overridden by other reasons."

positions.name: Theodicy: the goods require the evils (Richard Swinburne; Eleonore Stump)

blocks.text: A theodicy, in Swinburne's definition, undertakes to show "that evils of the kind and quantity we find on Earth are neither incompatible with nor render improbable the existence of God." His own view is that this can be done without leaning on independent evidence for God to outweigh the counterevidence.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Swinburne, "Some Major Strands of Theodicy," book 027, ch. 3 — a compressed reconstruction of the chapter's stated strategy, labelled as such

steps.text: A perfectly good being may allow an evil only if he has the *right* to do so and there is some good brought about by allowing it which could not be brought about in any better way — for an omnipotent being, it must be logically impossible to obtain that good without the evil (or an equally bad one).

With a sufficiently wide conception of good — wider than pleasure and pain — many actual goods meet that condition: the satisfaction of *persisting* desire requires its temporary frustration; compassion and kindred involvements require suffering to respond to; significant free choice between doing great good and great evil requires knowledge of how to harm, which observation of natural evil supplies (a strand Swinburne names but sets aside as too long to prove here).
Evils of the kind (and, the chapter begins to argue, the quantity) we find serve greater goods in the way P1 requires.

blocks.text: Swinburne is candid about the limit: that the goods are *so good that it is worth* allowing the evils "I shall also begin to show but could not within the compass of a philosophical paper of normal length possibly show conclusively."

Stump's chapter (book 027, ch. 4) changes the question before answering it. Aquinas, reading Job, does not treat innocent suffering as a threat to God's existence but as a puzzle about *providence*: Job's friends assume providence pays out rewards and punishments in this life; Aquinas holds that what happens in this life "can be justified only by reference to [one's] state in the afterlife," suffering functioning as medicine for a condition that blocks eternal communion with God. Stump's conclusion is methodological: assessments of theodicy wait on settling what human happiness is and what the goal of human life is.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Gale (ch. 11) charges theodicies with epistemic laxness (accepting justifying stories on too little) and axiological laxness (miscounting the values at stake); Howard-Snyder's Introduction notes the recurring gap between goods that might justify God in permitting evil *in general* and the *particular* evils Rowe's argument cites.

positions.name: Skeptical theism: we are in no position to judge (Alston, Wykstra, van Inwagen, Plantinga)

blocks.text: The volume's most developed reply does not offer a theodicy. It attacks the inference from "no good *we know of* justifies God" to "probably *no good* justifies God" — what Howard-Snyder calls "the inference from inscrutable to pointless evil."

blocks.label: Alston's agnostic thesis
blocks.source: Alston, "The Inductive Argument from Evil and the Human Cognitive Condition," book 027, ch. 6

steps.text: To be justified in accepting Rowe's P1, we would have to justifiably judge, of some particular suffering, that God could have no sufficient reason to permit it.

Our grasp of the goods there are, of their value, and of the conditions under which they could be realized is radically insufficient for that judgment — the magnitude and complexity of the question outrun our powers and access to data.
We are not justified in accepting P1, and the inductive argument collapses. (Alston stresses this is *agnosticism* about P1, not a theodicy claiming P1 is false.)

blocks.label: Wykstra's CORNEA
blocks.source: Wykstra, "Rowe's Noseeum Arguments from Evil," book 027, ch. 7

steps.text: An inference from "we see no X" to "there is no X" is justified only if X has reasonable *seeability* in the situation — only if, were X present, we could reasonably expect to see it. (Seeing no dog in the garage licenses "no dog"; seeing no flea does not license "no flea.")
Given the disparity between a creator's vision and ours, God-purposed goods — if there are any — are not the sort of thing we could reasonably expect to see.
Rowe's "noseeum" inference (so named for the tiny biting flies you "no see 'um") fails the seeability condition; the move from "appears pointless" to "pointless" is not justified.

blocks.text: **Van Inwagen** (ch. 8) presses the parallel point against Draper-style arguments: we cannot judge what to expect on theism, so we cannot judge that a rival hypothesis explains the suffering better — a diagnosis he supports with two deliberately parallel, obviously faulty arguments (an "evidential argument from air" for an ancient atomist; an argument from God's silence), technicalized in ch. 12. **Plantinga** (chs. 5 and 13) adds two moves: the *total evidence* point (even a successful evidential argument shows at most that evil disconfirms theism relative to part of our evidence), and the claim that the real question is *nonpropositional* — the theist may have nonpropositional grounds for belief (of the sort classical theism itself predicts) better than the propositional grounds any argument from evil gives against it, so whether the argument renders her belief unreasonable depends on whether theism is true.

blocks.label: Objections to skeptical theism
blocks.text: the volume gives the other side the next word, three times over:

items: **Draper (ch. 9, "The Skeptical Theist")**: the skeptical thesis (ST1 — we cannot judge directly that God would be unlikely to have a sufficient reason) may be true, but it only touches arguments that *need* that judgment. His own ch. 2 argument does not: it compares Pr(O/HI) with Pr(O/theism) without claiming any evil is probably unjustified. Inferring the failure of *all* probabilistic arguments from ST1 is "a considerable leap of faith." Skeptical theists "have not yet solved the evidential problem of evil."

**Russell (ch. 10, "Defenseless")**: the unrepresentative-sample charge cuts only if there is reason to believe there *are* goods beyond our ken; merely possible hidden goods are like hypothetical crows that hide whenever anyone looks — they do not by themselves defeat the inference. (He concedes the limiting case: if we had no idea whether our sample was representative, suspension of judgment would be right.)

**Gale (ch. 11)**: defensive skepticism must also reckon with the judgments that if some good justified God we would very likely know of it, and that it is "improbable in the extreme" that there are goods outside our ken of the required kind.

**Howard-Snyder (ch. 15)** turns the specificity screw from the theist's side: the atheist's appeal to *particular* horrors presupposes that God must have a reason to permit *that* evil — that child, then and there, in that way — and a threshold thesis that exactly this much horrific evil, and no less, serves God's purposes. Both presuppositions, he argues, are questionable — so the argument must be run at the level of amounts and kinds, not individual cases. (His title distinction: *inscrutable* evil — we cannot grasp a reason — does not by itself justify belief in *pointless* evil.)

blocks.text: Alston's closing chapter (ch. 16) candidly re-works his own position: his ch. 6, he says, tried to do two things that "did not smoothly blend" — neutralize Rowe/Russell and mine theodicies for unexcludable possibilities. He drops the second project and rests on "the live possibility of divine reasons unenvisaged by us," which he believes sufficient to take up whatever slack the arguments leave.

thought.name: The fawn
thought.text: (Rowe, chs. 1 and 14). Lightning strikes a dead tree in a distant forest; a fawn is trapped, horribly burned, and lies in terrible agony for several days before death relieves it. No one sees it; nothing, so far as we can tell, comes of it. It is the argument's engine: an omnipotent being could trivially have prevented it, so if any suffering is pointless, this looks like it — and Rowe's whole case is that "apparently pointless," multiplied across the world's suffering, rationally supports "pointless." Pressures P1's critics to say why appearance should not be trusted here.

thought.name: Sue
thought.text: (Rowe, ch. 14, case E2). The rape, beating, and strangling murder of a five-year-old girl — paired with the fawn so the argument cannot be deflected as concerning only animal or only natural evil. Ivan Karamazov's tortured children (the boy thrown to the general's hounds; the girl beaten "until her body was one bruise") play the same role in Howard-Snyder's ch. 15, which is why his specificity challenge matters: must God's reason attach to *this* child, *this* way?

thought.name: The garage: dog and flea
thought.text: (Wykstra, ch. 7). Looking around my garage and seeing no dog entitles me to conclude none is present; seeing no flea does not. The difference is *seeability*. Meant to show that "we see no justifying good" is evidence only under a condition Rowe has not established for divine purposes.

thought.name: The zagaloops and the blue crows
thought.text: (Russell, ch. 10). Aliens show us a wholly new kind of animal: from none of the many seen being red, we may not infer none are red — we have no idea whether the sample is representative. But hypothetical crows that hide whenever observed do not defeat "there are no blue crows": unobserved possibilities matter only given reason to think they are actual. Together the pair locate the real dispute — whether we have reason to believe our sample of goods is representative of all goods.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: Carneades, [The Problem of Evil](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CYEg3SgfEDc) (logical vs evidential forms) → Survey: Howard-Snyder's Introduction to book 027 (the distinction, the map of issues) → Primary: Rowe (ch. 1) and Draper (ch. 2), answered by Swinburne (ch. 3), Alston (ch. 6), Wykstra (ch. 7), Draper (ch. 9) → Full treatment: the whole of book 027, especially the second-round chapters 12–16 where every party replies to replies.

evidential-argument-from-evil.verdict: Exactly where the volume leaves it: unresolved, and unresolved at a well-mapped point. No contributor defends the logical argument (see [The Logical Problem of Evil](logical-problem-of-evil.md)); the evidential argument's fate turns on one inference — from *inscrutable* to *pointless* — and on whether Draper's comparative, explanation-based version avoids needing that inference at all. Rowe concedes his original induction does not by itself make its conclusion more likely than not, and rebuilds it in Bayesian form; Alston concedes his first defence was two projects imperfectly blended, and rebuilds it on unenvisaged reasons alone; Draper concedes the skeptical thesis may be true and argues it does not reach his argument; Plantinga relocates the question to nonpropositional warrant, which by his own account makes the argument's force depend on whether theism is true. The editor's preface already knew the shape of this ending: the problem is "hardly 'old hat'," and the book was built as a stage for dialogue rather than a verdict. Anyone who reports this debate as settled — in either direction — is going beyond these sources.

connections.title: The Logical Problem of Evil
connections.text: [The Logical Problem of Evil](logical-problem-of-evil.md) — the stronger, older claim (strict incompatibility) whose failure is this argument's starting concession; the free-will defence belongs there, and its limits (natural evil) push the debate here.

connections.title: The Cosmological Argument
connections.text: [The Cosmological Argument](cosmological-argument.md) — Bhāviveka's complaint in book 020, ch. 13 is an early version of this problem from inside a creation debate: a Lord who "causes pleasure for some and pain for others, like a cowherd" — Draupadī's charge that the virtuous are ruined by a capricious Lord — is the theodicy problem in epic dress, and Bhāviveka's karma is offered precisely as the non-capricious alternative.

connections.title: Faith, Acceptance, and Hope
connections.text: [Faith, Acceptance, and Hope](faith-acceptance-and-hope.md) — Rowe's friendly atheism and Plantinga's nonpropositional warrant both raise the question that entry takes up: what attitudes toward religious propositions are rational, and on what grounds, when the arguments do not settle the matter.
Dystheism — the exit the lectures note this argument does not take: keep God's existence and drop his perfect goodness (Carneades, [What is Dystheism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NCpPaJQyS6g)).

sources: Howard-Snyder (ed.), *The Evidential Argument from Evil* (book 027): Preface and Introduction — read in full; ch. 1 (Rowe), ch. 2 (Draper), ch. 14 (Rowe) — read in full; ch. 3 (Swinburne), ch. 4 (Stump), ch. 5 (Plantinga), ch. 6 (Alston), ch. 7 (Wykstra), ch. 8 (van Inwagen), ch. 9 (Draper), ch. 10 (Russell), ch. 11 (Gale), ch. 13 (Plantinga), ch. 15 (Howard-Snyder), ch. 16 (Alston) — openings, argumentative structure, and key sections read; ch. 12 (van Inwagen) — opening and plan read.
Eckel, "Who or What Created the World? Bhāviveka's Arguments Against the Hindu Concept of God" (book 020, ch. 13) — read in full, for the Connections.
Lectures (Carneades.org): "The Problem of Evil"; "The Free Will Defense" (for the boundary with the logical problem); "What is Dystheism (Philosophy of Religion)".

faith-acceptance-and-hope.title: Faith, Acceptance, and Hope
faith-acceptance-and-hope.aka: faith and reason; the attitudes of religious commitment
faith-acceptance-and-hope.note: Chignell's Ladder of Liturgical Sincerity; Lamberth on James; Pascal's wager
faith-acceptance-and-hope.question: Philosophy of religion's default picture of religious commitment is *belief*: a person assents to the truth of propositions ("God exists," "the dead are raised") and the philosophical question is whether that belief is justified. But is belief the attitude religious people actually have toward most of their doctrines — and is it the only attitude that matters? The sources in this corpus converge, from very different directions, on a more complicated inventory: belief itself splits from *faith*; faith splits into several rival models; *acceptance* and *hope* emerge as distinct, voluntary, practically grounded attitudes that can structure a religious life without belief; and two decision-procedures — Pascal's wager and James's pragmatism — propose that where evidence runs out, practical reason may legitimately take over. The prior question underneath all of them: who bears the burden of proof in the first place?
faith-acceptance-and-hope.ninety: Start with the difference between *believing* something and *having faith* in it. Belief is plain: you take a proposition to be true. Faith, on one common model, is belief that outruns its evidence — a venture. But watch what people in a liturgy are actually doing. Many of them are reciting doctrines they would not say, flatly, that they *believe* — and they are not simply pretending, either. They are *accepting* the doctrines for the purposes of the practice: taking them on board voluntarily, letting them guide what they say and do, in order to be part of the community and — perhaps — to grow toward belief. Others are *hoping*: Kant thought the minimum of religion might be just the hope that God exists, plus the admission that God is genuinely possible. Add Pascal's famous bet — believing costs you little if you're wrong and gains you everything if you're right — and James's idea that when the evidence genuinely cannot decide, our passional nature lawfully may. The old question "is religious belief rational?" turns out to be several questions wearing one coat. (Distilled from the Carneades lectures [Belief vs Faith](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o8QKkHWUSu0) and [Pascal's Wager](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p3ScupIbdkU), and Chignell's chapter in book 020.)

positions.name: Belief, and the rival models of faith (the lecture taxonomy)

blocks.text: The lecture [Belief vs Faith](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o8QKkHWUSu0) fixes the baseline: belief is a *propositional attitude* — S believes P iff S assents to the truth of P, S thinks P is true — one attitude among others (desire, wonder) that a person can take toward a proposition. Faith has no agreed definition; the lecture surveys the models:

items: **Doxastic venture**: faith is a *kind* of belief — belief without justification or beyond the evidence ("Petro has faith his team will come back": no evidence, believes anyway). Contrasted with knowledge (true justified belief), faith is belief that may be true but is not (yet) justified. Some Christians, especially fideists, hold this for religious faith precisely: the truths of religion are not subject to rational justification and must be taken on faith.

**Aquinas's model**: faith is belief specifically in religious doctrines; some articles of faith can be demonstrated by reason, others are only revealed and must be believed without proof; revealed faith ranks in certainty between demonstrable proof and mere opinion.
**Faith as belief in specific propositions**: faith is simply belief whose objects are a special set (that God exists; the revealed propositions) — no distinctive epistemic gap required.

blocks.text: To these the lecture *Why Science Rests On Faith* ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V-g7Glyxi98)) adds a deliberately provocative levelling model: define faith as *belief based on assumptions* and knowledge as belief with *no* assumptions, and even "Earth's gravity is 9.8 m/s²" fails the knowledge bar — it rests on chains of trust in teachers, experimenters, senses, memory, induction, logic, and on not being systematically deceived. "Science is not the only one. Things like mathematics, religion, logic, and statistics are also based on certain assumptions. You can judge them by the number of assumptions they make, but they all make them." The lecture presents this as a high-bar skeptical exercise, not as a verdict that all faiths are equal.

positions.name: The presumption of atheism: who goes first? (Antony Flew)

blocks.text: Before asking what justifies theistic belief, Flew asks where the debate *starts*. His paper, as the lecture [The Presumption of Atheism (Antony Flew)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pKo7FBUBhKQ) presents it, distinguishes positive atheism (believing God does not exist), *negative* atheism (lacking belief in God — the wider class, including positive atheists), agnosticism, and theism, and argues our default position should be negative atheism: the burden of proof rests with the theist, who must produce a coherent concept of God and evidence for it before disbelief needs any defence. The lecture notes the biographical coda it finds methodologically important: Flew held the presumption as an atheist and kept it after his late move to deism — he claimed to have been *convinced from* the default, not to have abandoned it. The positions this entry's other sections take can be read as so many negotiations with that default: the wager and James try to justify *moving* from it on practical grounds; Chignell's acceptance sidesteps it by changing the attitude in question; Rowe's friendly atheism (book 027, ch. 1) complicates it from the atheist side by granting that theists may be rationally justified in not moving at all.

positions.name: Pascal's wager: belief as a bet

blocks.text: Pascal's argument is openly pragmatic: "we cannot know whether or not God exists," so we should choose the belief "whatever would be the most profitable." The lecture presents a strengthened version of the wager and works it as a decision matrix.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [Pascal's Wager](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p3ScupIbdkU
blocks.text: — a formalization of the lecture's decision-theoretic presentation, labelled as such):

steps.text: Reason cannot settle whether God exists; we must choose whether to believe (the choice is forced — not choosing is itself a choice against).
If we believe and God exists, the gain is infinite (heaven, "all these wonderful things"); if we believe and God does not exist, the loss is finite (some finite bad).
If we do not believe and God exists, we forgo the infinite gain; if we do not believe and God does not exist, we break even or gain finitely.
For any nonzero probability that God exists, believing has infinite expected value and dominates; so we ought to believe.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.source: [Objections to Pascal's Wager](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ACeOPJPsHd8

items: **The many-gods problem** — the lecture calls it the compelling one. The matrix's two columns are not exhaustive: an evil god who rewards *non*-theists infinitely, a skeptical god who rewards only rational nonbelievers, a demon who rewards only cultists — each candidate column plants an infinity of its own, the infinities cancel, and the decision falls back to the finite payoffs the wager was built to avoid. Unlikelihood is no rescue: an infinite payoff "will eclipse any improbability."

**Doxastic involuntarism** — Pascal assumes we can take up belief at will because it profits us; but "we don't always believe in what is good for us, even if we want to." The wager offers a *practical* reason where a *rational* (evidential) reason was wanted.

blocks.text: Note where the wager reappears below: Chignell's Ladder names Pascal as the patron of the *initiate* rung — accepting and practising one's way toward belief ("fake it to make it") is precisely the wager's psychology, redescribed as liturgy.

positions.name: Acceptance, not belief: the liturgical stance (Andrew Chignell, book 020, ch. 6)

blocks.text: Chignell's manifesto begins from an empirical suspicion: "many religious people do not often have the attitude of full *belief* with respect to many doctrines that characterize the traditions of which they are a part," may lack a clear sense of what they are supposed to believe, and rarely believe in an internalistically justified way even when they do. A philosophy of religion fixated on justifying *theistic belief* therefore studies a "regulative (and possibly western) ideal" — the "epistemological saint" — rather than religious life as lived. His alternative object of study is the **liturgical stance**: the complex of attitudes taken toward doctrines in communal practice (kneeling and praying toward Mecca, the Passover seder, taking the wafer), which involves what he calls *teleological insincerity* — "insincerity upwards" — in degrees, his **Ladder of Liturgical Sincerity**: the *inquirer* (performing to understand what membership is like), the *discerner* (trying to decide whether to join), the *conditional seeker* (acting on "if God exists, this is fitting"), the *initiate* (accepting in order to grow into belief — Pascal's posture), and, rarely attained and not always desirable, the *utterly convinced*. The Ladder is explicitly not a ranking of virtue: Chignell argues it is morally preferable that some confessional contents *not* be believed with full sincerity.
Against belief — construed, following Hume, as an involuntary disposition to *feel* a proposition true, with its characteristic "yes-phenomenology" — Chignell sets **acceptance**:

blocks.label: The acceptance model
blocks.source: Chignell, book 020, ch. 6, §6.2.2 — stated as a position, in his terms

items: Acceptance is a *voluntary* attitude toward p, adopted in certain contexts for broadly practical reasons; it can motivate asserting p, deliberating on the basis of p, and acting as if p, while typically lacking belief's phenomenology.

It is more robust than mere assumption-for-the-sake-of-argument, and can be partly justified by something other than evidence — which is why it may be compatible with Clifford-style evidentialism about *belief itself*.
On Chignell's reading, acceptance — not belief — is what James, and Kant before him, actually took to be involved in religious faith and liturgical practice.

blocks.text: **Hope** completes the trio (§6.2.3). Kant's "minimum of theology": the *hope* that God exists together with the belief/faith (*Glaube*) that God is really possible — a standard even agnostics and atheists could meet, read by some as appealingly low and by others as appallingly low. Chignell's reconciliation: rational hope in this "practico-dogmatic" sense requires only one commitment — *acceptance that God's existence is really possible* — while a life-structuring hope may carry a sophisticated train of desires, virtues, and *trust in* (God, nature, history, karma) that needs separate analysis. His summary challenge to the field: it is "clearly consistent with hope that p, and may be consistent with faith that p, that one fails to believe p or even believes that not-p" ('I believe, help Thou my unbelief' becomes 'I hope and sometimes even accept, help Thou my unbelief'). Philosophers of religion should be *pistologists* and *elpistologists* — students of *pistis* and *elpis* — not only of knowledge.

positions.name: James: the pragmatic orientation of faith (via David C. Lamberth, book 020, ch. 16)

blocks.text: Lamberth's James supplies the historical root of Chignell's reading (Chignell cites James as construing religious faith as acceptance). Three elements of Lamberth's account matter here. (i) *Thought exists for action*: in "Reflex Action and Theism" (1881) James sets aside whether God exists and asks what the *concept* of God does — it is "an important, concrete practical idea" that orients action toward our greater welfare and toward our more inclusive, long-run "ideal interests"; "anything short of God is not rational; anything more than God is not possible." To demand that subjective interests stay passive until truth arrives from the environment "is to bid the sculptor's chisel be passive till the statue expresses itself from out of the stone." *The Will to Believe* (1896) belongs to this line of thought. (ii) *Experience as data*: the *Varieties* (1902) treats transformative religious experience psychologically, individually and socially — the corpus's own studied version of the experience that other entries meet as an argument ([The Ontological Argument](ontological-argument.md)). (iii) *Meliorism*: in *Pragmatism* (1907) salvation is treated "neither as necessary, nor as impossible," but as "a possibility, which becomes more and more of a probability the more numerous the actual conditions of salvation become" — faith's object as a live possibility that human effort helps actualize, a structure strikingly parallel to Kant's minimum (hope + real possibility) as Chignell presents it. Lamberth's framing conclusion is about religion's future, not its proof: the twenty-first century is unlikely to see humankind evolve "beyond" religion in any meaningful sense.

thought.name: Petro's team
thought.text: (Belief vs Faith lecture). Petro has faith his team will come back from its deficit — no evidence, belief anyway. The trivial case isolates the doxastic-venture model: if faith is just that, religious faith differs from sports faith only in stakes; the lecture's other models exist because many accounts of faith deny exactly this.

thought.name: The wager's matrix
thought.text: (Pascal's Wager lecture). A toy game first — win $3 or lose $1 at even odds, expected value +$0.50, so play — then the same machinery with an infinite payoff in one cell. The toy case shows the machinery is ordinary decision theory; the objections lecture shows the infinity cell is where all the trouble (rival infinities; forced choices) concentrates.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: [Belief vs Faith](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o8QKkHWUSu0) → [Pascal's Wager](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p3ScupIbdkU) and its objections lecture; [The Presumption of Atheism](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pKo7FBUBhKQ). → Survey: Chignell, book 020, ch. 6 (the liturgical stance, acceptance, hope — the volume's own manifesto). → Primary: James via Lamberth (book 020, ch. 16); Pascal and Kant as presented by the lecture and by Chignell respectively (neither text is in the corpus directly).

faith-acceptance-and-hope.verdict: The sources agree on the diagnosis more than the cure. All of them complicate the picture "religious commitment = justified belief": the lecture by multiplying models of faith; Flew by relocating the argument to burden-of-proof; the wager and James by licensing practical grounds where evidence runs out (with the wager's licence revoked, in the objections lecture, by rival infinities and the involuntariness of belief); Chignell by arguing the field has been studying an idealization and proposing acceptance and hope as the operative attitudes; Lamberth's James by exhibiting a major philosopher for whom the practical orientation was the philosophy. What no source here does is settle the normative question the complication leaves behind: Chignell raises the justification-and-defeat conditions for acceptance and hope as a *programme* ("we will need an account of hope"), explicitly declines to answer his own deepest questions in the chapter, and the lectures present models rather than crown one. It is also worth marking the limit of the levelling move in *Why Science Rests On Faith*: its "faith" (any belief resting on assumptions) is a third sense, neither the venture model nor acceptance — the corpus uses one word for at least three ideas, and this entry keeps them separate.

connections.title: The Evidential Argument from Evil
connections.text: [The Evidential Argument from Evil](evidential-argument-from-evil.md) — when the evidential argument ends in a standoff, the questions here take over: Rowe's friendly atheism is a thesis about the rationality of *belief* across the standoff; Plantinga's nonpropositional warrant is a claim about grounds other than argument.

connections.title: The Future of Philosophy of Religion
connections.text: [The Future of Philosophy of Religion](the-future-of-philosophy-of-religion.md) — Chignell's chapter is that entry's "liturgical turn": the proposal that the field's centre of gravity move from belief to practice.
The presumption of atheism connects backward to the burden-of-proof framing of both evil entries: who must produce the argument, and who may rest on a default?

sources: Chignell, "Liturgical Philosophy of Religion" (book 020, ch. 6) — read in full.
Lamberth, "William James Revisited" (book 020, ch. 16) — read in full.
Rowe, ch. 1 of book 027 — read in full (friendly atheism; cited here for the belief-rationality bridge).

Lectures (Carneades.org) — read in full: "Belief vs Faith (Philosophical Distinction)"; "The Presumption of Atheism (Antony Flew)"; "Why Science Rests On Faith"; "Pascal's Wager"; "Objections to Pascal's Wager".

logical-problem-of-evil.title: The Logical Problem of Evil
logical-problem-of-evil.aka: the deductive / a priori argument from evil; Mackie's logical problem
logical-problem-of-evil.note: Mackie's collapse, the free will defense
logical-problem-of-evil.question: Can the existence of evil and the existence of the God of classical theism both be true — or do the two claims contradict each other, so that believing both is not merely improbable but *positively irrational*? The logical problem of evil is the strongest form the argument from evil can take: a purported disproof, showing theism inconsistent with a fact nobody denies, that evil exists. Its history in our sources is mostly the history of its failure — and of what that failure does and does not settle.
logical-problem-of-evil.ninety: Line up four claims: God is all-knowing; God is all-good; God is all-powerful; and evil exists. If God knows about the evil, wants to stop it, and can stop it, why is it still there? The logical problem says the four cannot all be true — something has to go. You can give up God's knowledge, or his goodness, or his power; you can deny that evil is real; or you can take the fifth exit and argue the four were never inconsistent in the first place. The most famous version of that fifth exit is the free-will defence: a world where creatures genuinely choose, and sometimes choose evil, may be a greater good than a world of guaranteed good behaviour — and not even an all-powerful God can *force* a free choice to come out right, because a forced free choice is a contradiction, and omnipotence was never supposed to include doing contradictions. The lecture's verdict is the consensus one: the defence does not prove God exists; it defends the *possibility* of God against the charge of impossibility, and leaves the question open — with natural evil (earthquakes, hurricanes) and the weaker, evidential form of the problem still on the table. (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [The Problem of Evil](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CYEg3SgfEDc) and [The Free Will Defense](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F1Kd_l-XzUU).)

positions.name: Mackie's incompatibility claim (J. L. Mackie, as book 027 presents him)

blocks.text: Mackie's aim, in the words Howard-Snyder's Introduction quotes, was to show that religious beliefs "are positively irrational, that the several parts of the essential theological doctrine are inconsistent with one another." The three beliefs: "God is omnipotent; God is wholly good; and yet evil exists."

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Howard-Snyder, Introduction to book 027, §2, reporting Mackie, "Evil and Omnipotence" (1955

steps.text: G: God is omnipotent and God is wholly good.
E: Evil exists.
MP1: A good thing always eliminates evil as far as it can.
L: There are no limits to what an omnipotent thing can do.
G and E are incompatible: a good omnipotent thing eliminates evil completely, so if such a being existed, evil would not.

blocks.text: Mackie himself saw that the bare trio is not inconsistent on its face; the argument runs entirely through the "additional premises, or perhaps some quasi-logical rules" MP1 and L.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: Howard-Snyder's diagnosis, which the volume treats as decisive: G, MP1, and L rule out E only if MP1 and L are *necessary truths*. Properly understood, L is one. MP1 is not, because a wholly good being might have a morally justifying reason to permit an evil it could prevent. Substitute the plausible MP2 — a wholly good thing eliminates evil as far as it can, *unless it has a morally justifying reason not to* — and the argument then needs it to be a necessary truth that there is no such reason for God. Nothing we know rules that out: the proposition J (there is a morally justifying reason for God to permit evil, one we could not know of, and he permits evil for that reason) is, for all we know, possible — and G and J together are compatible with E. "Like logical positivism, Mackie's argument has found its way to the dustbin of philosophical fashions."

Howard-Snyder adds a *definitional* residue worth keeping, because it organizes the whole subfield: call an argument from evil **logical** when it has a premise saying theism is incompatible with some *known* fact about evil (Mackie's E is known with certainty), and **evidential** when it lacks such a premise — its key fact about evil being at most probable or reasonable to believe. Even Rowe's evidential argument has an incompatibility premise (its P2), but the fact it is incompatible with — that pointless intense suffering exists — is not *known*, only rationally believed. On that test the names, though "badly named," sort the debate correctly.

positions.name: The free-will defence (Alvin Plantinga, as the lectures and book 027 present him)

blocks.text: A *defence* is weaker than a theodicy: it does not claim to state God's actual reasons, only to describe a possible state of affairs in which God and evil coexist — which is all that defeating a *logical* incompatibility claim requires. Rowe's own note in ch. 1 concedes the point from the other side: "No one, I think, has succeeded in establishing such an extravagant claim [of logical inconsistency]. Indeed … there is a fairly compelling argument for the view that the existence of evil is logically consistent with the existence of the theistic God," citing Plantinga's *God, Freedom, and Evil*.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [The Free Will Defense](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F1Kd_l-XzUU
blocks.text: , presenting Plantinga's response to Mackie — a formalization of the lecture's account, labelled as such):

steps.text: Omnipotence does not include the power to do contradictions (the lecture's warm-up case: a rock so heavy God cannot lift it is a limit on our conception of omnipotence, not on God).

A creature's choice is free only if no one — God included — determines which way it goes; a world in which God forces free creatures always to choose the good is a contradiction ("Leibniz's lapse": Leibniz wrongly supposed an omnipotent being could actualize just any possible world).

Significant free will is a great good, and God may choose the best feasible world containing it even though some evil necessarily remains in such a world, because the evil is created by the creatures, not by God.

The four propositions (God omniscient, omnibenevolent, omnipotent; evil exists) are consistent: the evil that exists is the price-structure of the greater good of free choice, not a contradiction in theism.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the lecture itself raises the two standing limits. First, *natural evil*: earthquakes, hurricanes, and tornadoes kill many people but "don't seem to really be a product of human choice or human free will," and it seems God could have made a world without them that still allowed free will. Second, *scope*: the defence does not touch the evidential problem, which is "more the job for a theodicy." The lecture's summary of the general consensus: Plantinga "has defended theism against the problem of evil but he's done so at a cost — this is not a proof of God's existence; this is a defense of God's possibility."

A Carneades-original counter presses the defence's picture of freedom itself. The **partial free will argument** ([The Partial Free Will Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=znh8-N6QYXE)) arrays figures in a hospital room — Amy in a coma (no choices at all), paralyzed Bob (choices only in thought), Cam with sixty seconds of agency, chained Don, ordinary Ed, the angel Fae, and God — to argue that free will lies on a *spectrum*: partial free will, the ability to choose some things freely but not others, is a coherent and familiar condition. If freedom comes in degrees, the defence's all-or-nothing framing (full freedom with its evil, or none) needs further defence: why could God not grant the degree of freedom that excludes the worst choices? The lecture presents this as a challenge to Plantinga's framing, not as a refutation of the consistency claim strictly understood.

Within book 027, Gale (ch. 11) records the majority verdict and his dissent from it in the same breath: "Almost everyone now believes that adequate defenses have been devised to neutralize this challenge … In particular, it is claimed that the free-will defense, in at least one of its many versions, succeeds in reconciling God's existence with moral evil," while noting his own book argues no version works and "the logical problem posed by moral evil is still with us." That dissent is flagged as *not* the chapter's concern, and the chapter does not argue it — so within this corpus the dissent is registered, not established.

Draper's ch. 9 gives the structural reason the logical form died, in terms of the proposition M (an omnipotent, omniscient being would have a morally sufficient reason for allowing E): to disprove theism one would have to prove M false or necessarily false, but "our knowledge of goods and evils and the logical relations they bear to each other is much too limited to prove that this could not be the case" — an omnipotent being could produce goods that logically entail the existence (or possibility) of E only by allowing E.

positions.name: The exits (the lecture's taxonomy)

blocks.text: The Problem of Evil lecture lays out the logical space the incompatibility claim creates — five "escape routes," four of which save consistency by surrendering part of the classical picture:
1. **Deny omniscience** — God does the best he can but does not know about all the evil ("it doesn't give us the God we're looking for").

2. **Deny omnibenevolence** — God knows and can prevent evil but does not care to, or is vengeful. (The dystheist/maltheist development of this exit — God exists but is not wholly good — is treated in the lectures [What is Dystheism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NCpPaJQyS6g) and [Is God Evil? (Four Arguments)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xxccnitqT_Y), the latter arguing from scriptural acts, from the evidentiary pattern of religious people's suffering, from the "evil God challenge" (the evidence is symmetric between a good and an evil God), and from a trickster-duplication argument.)
3. **Deny omnipotence** — God knows and cares but cannot stop evil.
4. **Deny that evil exists** — the lecture calls this route "a little sketchy": it sits badly with taking God to be all-*good*, a notion that needs evil to contrast with.
5. **Deny the inconsistency** — hold all four propositions together, via a defence (free will) or, for the evidential residue, a theodicy.

thought.name: The murder and the hand of God
thought.text: (The Problem of Evil lecture). A murderer raises a knife over a victim: exactly the sort of evil an all-knowing, all-good, all-powerful God would stop — the hand of God comes down and the evil doesn't happen. But it does happen, daily. The vignette is the incompatibility intuition in its purest form, before the additional premises MP1/L are made explicit — and therefore also a demonstration of why the argument needs them.

thought.name: The bookcase of possible worlds
thought.text: (The Free Will Defense lecture). God at the beginning, browsing a vast bookcase in which each book describes a complete possible world, narrowed to two finalists: the best world with free will (in which some evil necessarily remains, because people are free) and a world with no free will in which everyone always does good. Plantinga's choice, on the lecture's telling, is clear — and the story's work is to make P2 vivid: the second book is not a *freer* world minus evil, it is a different kind of world altogether.

thought.name: The hospital room
thought.text: (The Partial Free Will Argument). Amy, Bob, Cam, Don, Ed, Fae, God — a ladder of agents with strictly increasing ranges of choice. Its point is taxonomic: if each figure plainly has *more* free will than the last without any of them being omnipotent, "free will" does not name an on/off property, and defences built on the binary inherit the burden of saying why the relevant degree could not have been set differently.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: Carneades, [The Problem of Evil](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CYEg3SgfEDc) → [The Free Will Defense](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F1Kd_l-XzUU) → Survey: Howard-Snyder's Introduction to book 027, §2 (Mackie, MP1/MP2, and the logical/evidential test) → Primary (as this corpus has them): the exchanges *about* Mackie and Plantinga inside book 027 (Rowe ch. 1 n.1; Draper ch. 9; Gale ch. 11; Plantinga ch. 5). Mackie's 1955 paper and Plantinga's *God, Freedom, and Evil* themselves are cited in the corpus but are not among its extracted texts.

logical-problem-of-evil.verdict: In these sources, the logical problem is the closest thing the problem of evil has to a closed file — closed by the defence strategy, not by agreement that evil is explained. Howard-Snyder: Mackie's argument is in "the dustbin of philosophical fashions." Alston (ch. 6): "It is now acknowledged on (almost) all sides that the logical argument is bankrupt." Rowe, the evidential argument's own author, calls the inconsistency claim "extravagant" and unestablished. The "(almost)" is doing real work: Gale registers a dissent he does not argue in this volume, and the lecture tradition keeps pressing at the defence's edges (natural evil; degrees of freedom). What the failure of the logical problem settles is only the modality: evil does not *contradict* theism. Whether it *disconfirms* it is the separate, live question of [The Evidential Argument from Evil](evidential-argument-from-evil.md) — the lecture's own closing verdict on the combined problems is deliberately modest: suspend judgment, since the evidential problem "hasn't given us an argument against all gods," only against a specific kind of God.

connections.title: The Evidential Argument from Evil
connections.text: [The Evidential Argument from Evil](evidential-argument-from-evil.md) — the successor problem: same premises, weaker claim (evidence, not contradiction), still open at the end of book 027.

connections.title: The Ontological Argument
connections.text: [The Ontological Argument](ontological-argument.md) and [The Cosmological Argument](cosmological-argument.md) — the lecture in this entry notes the dialectical asymmetry the problem creates: "God exists? We haven't really had an argument for God's existence." The arguments *for* existence are separate entries; Rowe (ch. 1) lists them — ontological, cosmological, teleological, moral — plus religious experience as the grounds a theist might offer in the Moorean shift.

External-world skepticism (epistemology entries) — Rowe's chosen instrument for the theist, the G. E. Moore shift, is borrowed directly from Moore's reply to the skeptics, and Rowe presents it in those terms.

sources: Howard-Snyder (ed.), *The Evidential Argument from Evil* (book 027): Introduction (§§1–2) — read in full; ch. 1 (Rowe, incl. n.1), ch. 9 (Draper, on M and the death of logical arguments), ch. 11 (Gale, opening) — read; ch. 5 (Plantinga) and ch. 6 (Alston) — openings read, for the consensus verdicts.

Lectures (Carneades.org): "The Problem of Evil"; "The Free Will Defense"; "The Partial Free Will Argument (Response to the Free Will Defense)"; "What is Dystheism (Philosophy of Religion)"; "Is God Evil (Four Arguments)" — all read in full.

ontological-argument.title: The Ontological Argument
ontological-argument.aka: ontological arguments (a family, not a single argument)
ontological-argument.note: lecture family (seven arguments + objections); the books barely stage it, and the entry says so
ontological-argument.question: Can the existence of God be proved by reason alone — not from anything observed in the world, but from the concept of God itself? That is the defining ambition of the ontological argument, and the first correction the sources insist on is that there is no single such argument: "a common misconception that there is only one ontological argument for the existence of God. In fact, an ontological argument is just a category of arguments," unified by the method — "an attempt to prove the existence of God solely through pure reason," in contrast to the cosmological argument's appeal to experience. The Carneades series, following the Stanford Encyclopedia's taxonomy, works through seven members of the family. This entry follows the lectures, because in this corpus the ontological argument lives in the lecture layer: the two books touch it only in passing (see "Where the debate stands").
ontological-argument.ninety: Try to think of the greatest being you can possibly conceive. Now ask: would that being be greater if it existed in reality, and not only in your mind? Obviously yes — a real cake beats an imagined cake. So if the greatest conceivable being existed only in your mind, you could conceive a greater one — the same being, existing — which contradicts the idea that it was the greatest conceivable. Conclusion: the greatest conceivable being, God, exists. That is the family's most famous member, and every other member runs the same basic play with different machinery: define God so that existence is built into the definition (and existence is a perfection, so a perfect being has it); or note that God, if he is possible at all, cannot be a *contingent* being — he would have to exist necessarily, in every possible world, including this one. The objections press exactly where the play is run: can you really *conceive* this being, as opposed to listing its properties? Is "it is possible that God exists" doing all the work, so the argument merely unpacks its first premise — begs the question? And does being *truly describable* as existing amount to existing? (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [Seven Ontological Arguments (for the Existence of God)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQybvNQxbMo), [Conceptual Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UXu--moRCoI), [Modal Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m_edcGIK9dw).)

videos.title: Seven Ontological Arguments (for the Existence of God)

positions.name: The definitional argument

blocks.text: The simplest member of the family, and the template the others refine.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [Ontological Argument From Definition](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GcIVSduNz64
blocks.text: ; the lecture's own formulation):

steps.text: God is, by definition, a being who possesses every perfection.
Existence is a perfection. (A cake that exists is better than a cake that doesn't; something with all perfections but no existence would be worse than something that exists and has them.)
God exists.

blocks.text: The lecture is frank that the argument's charm is its parallel with trivial definitional truths ("ice cream is by definition cold, therefore ice cream is cold") — which is also its exposure: everything turns on whether existence can be loaded into a definition this way and then read back out as a fact about the world. Its paired objections lecture ([Objections to the Definitional Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hHnBvYO_F5g)) takes up that pressure point; this entry reports the argument as its source presents it.

positions.name: The conceptual argument (Anselm and Descartes, in the lecture's telling)

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [Conceptual Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UXu--moRCoI
blocks.text: ; attributed there to both Saint Anselm and René Descartes):

steps.text: I can think of a being higher than which it is impossible to imagine.
If such a being does not exist, then I can imagine a being higher than it — one that does exist (an existing perfect being is higher than a merely conceived one).
I cannot conceive of a being higher than that than which no higher can be conceived. (A taller building than the tallest building would simply *be* the tallest.)
Such a being — God — exists.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.source: [Objections to the Conceptual Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AvF8GCofoSQ
blocks.text: ) — the flagship objection attacks P1's picture of conceiving. To conceive a thing, the lecturer argues, is to be able to form some picture of it: the invented creature in the lecture's example (six feet tall, scarf, pea coat, crime-solving) can be pictured; but a being that is "everywhere, all-powerful, all-good, all-knowing" is given only as a *list of properties*, with no answer to "what does it look like — what do I do in my head to imagine such a thing?" Listing properties is not conceiving, and even many theists, the objection continues, speak of wanting to understand God more deeply rather than claiming to conceive him. The objections lecture ranges over P2 and the inference as well; the conceivability objection is its lead and most developed line.

positions.name: The modal argument (Plantinga's version, in the lecture's telling)

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [Modal Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m_edcGIK9dw
blocks.text: — a formalization of the lecture's disjunctive-syllogism presentation, labelled as such):

steps.text: It is possible that God exists (God exists in some possible world).
God is not contingent: either it is impossible for him to exist, or he exists necessarily — necessary existence being one of his attributes, like omniscience and omnipotence.
God exists — necessarily, in all possible worlds, and "since our world is a possible world, God must exist in our world as well."

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: this member draws the series' heaviest fire: the lecturer announces the modal argument is "one of the worst" and devotes a week of videos (36 objections, in the series' own count) to its versions. The deepest objection is that the argument **begs the question** ([Why the Modal Ontological Argument Begs the Question](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O135PuFm08c)): the argument's whole labour falls on its single substantive premise, and that premise "is actually equivalent to your conclusion" — every later step merely unpacks definitions (of possibility, of necessity, of actuality), so "when I say that it is possible that God, the greatest being possible, exists, I really only mean that God does exist." Accepting P1 is already granting the conclusion. The family of replies includes an **anti-modal ontological argument** ([Anti-Modal Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r92bK_S72zI)), constructed to run the same modal machinery to the opposite conclusion and thereby indict the form itself; further dedicated objections treat the modal perfection argument that underlies it ([Modal Perfection Argument (Objections)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VzBPN-gIGKg)) and popular restatements ([Debunking the Modal Ontological Argument Six Ways from Sunday](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kplijirg7ws); [Objections to Inspiring Philosophy's Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZZkx7yZrtRY)).

positions.name: Gödel's argument

blocks.text: The family's most technically elaborate member: three definitions (of a godlike object, of an *essential* property — a property that conditions all and only an object's necessary properties — and of necessary existence) and six axioms built on the undefined intuitive notion of a *positive property*. If the definitions and axioms are accepted, a theorem-chain yields that the property of being godlike is realized: something godlike necessarily exists. The lecture ([Godel's Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2iZzK_opOkg)) is explicit about its own division of labour — it reviews the axioms and definitions, deferring the logical derivation and the objections ([Objections to Godel's Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XfXAs66GW70)) — and remarks that the argument "is probably more interesting from a logical point of view than as an argument for the existence of God." Faithfulness requires the same restraint here: this corpus's lecture states the framework, not the proof.

positions.name: The Meinongian argument

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [Meinongian Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iAz0rXxHMQM
blocks.text: ; presupposing Alexius Meinong's theory of objects):

steps.text: All instances of the statement-form "the *F G* is *F*" are true (Meinong's characterization principle) — indeed analytically true.
"The existent perfect being is existent" is such an instance (F = existent, G = perfect being), so it is true.
The existent perfect being exists; and a perfect being is what we call God, so God exists.

blocks.text: The lecture warns the argument cannot even be assessed without Meinong's theory of objects, and that its objections ([Objections to the Meinongian Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lD2eZ6iVGqU)) are equally steeped in that theory — the crux being the slide from "the statement is true" to "the being exists," which the lecture itself flags in the parallel: "'the sky is blue' is true, therefore the sky is blue."

positions.name: The mereological argument

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [Mereological Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EmE1COo4q5c

steps.text: I exist.
Therefore something exists (existential generalization).
Wherever something exists, the mereological sum of all things exists (mereology's composition principle: there is always a sum of any parts).
God — *defined as* the sum of all things — exists.

blocks.text: The lecture presents the conclusion as resting on that identification: "God is just what we refer to as the sum of all things." The pressure point is correspondingly visible in the argument itself: everything depends on whether naming the totality "God" earns the theological conclusion, and the paired objections lecture ([Objections to the Mereological Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2VZOrsLNj0Y)) pursues it.

positions.name: The religious-experience argument

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [Religious Experience Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MFvimAuI8MI

steps.text: The word "God" has a meaning that is only revealed in religious experience.
The word "God" only has meaning if God exists (unlike "Santa Claus," a term we use precisely for something that doesn't exist).
God exists.

blocks.text: The lecture supports P1/P2 with a thought experiment (see below) and is candid that on first encounter the argument "was not very intuitive and not very persuasive" — the thought experiment is offered as making it "a bit more persuasive, if not fully convincing." Its objections are treated in [Objections to the Religious Experience Ontological Argument](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uZeieIVY54s).

positions.name: A framing objection from the books: what does "exists" even mean for God? (Marion)

blocks.text: Book 020's closing chapter does not present an ontological argument; it questions the terms in which any of them is posed. Before deciding whether God is to be thought of with or without Being, Marion argues, one must ask what "Being" means: as *metaphysica* understands it, Being is perseverance in the present — beings existing according to *causa sui* — a sense that collapses into "the aporia of the present moment" and forgets manifestation, past, and future; but Being can also be understood by "the logic of the *gift* and the *event*," in which beings *are* by surrendering their claim to perseverance. The question "does not consist in the application of the predicate of Being to God, as if it were simply a matter of discussing his existence … without questioning for a moment that the verb, *to exist*, … could legitimately be applied in one way or another to God." Read against the lecture family, Marion's point is not a refutation of any member but a standing challenge to the shared presupposition that "existence" is a single, unproblematic predicate ready to be distributed by definition, conception, or modal logic.

thought.name: The cake
thought.text: (recurring across the definitional and conceptual lectures). A cake that exists is better than a cake that doesn't — you can eat it. The homely case is meant to make "existence is a perfection / an existing being is greater" feel obvious before the same move is made for God; the objections' work begins by asking whether what is obvious for cakes survives the transfer.

thought.name: George in the cave
thought.text: (Religious Experience Ontological Argument). A dark, narrow cave at the village edge admits one visitor at a time. Amy returns reporting a nice man named George who gave her tea; Bob confirms him (weather talk, tea); Karl confirms him again, down to the yellow flannel shirt and the Earl Grey. At some point, the lecture suggests, the villagers are entitled to think the word "George" has a *referent* — something all these experiences are of — and the argument asks why repeated, mutually confirming religious experience should not earn the word "God" the same standing. It is meant to move the argument from semantics to testimony: meaning anchored in convergent experience.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: [Seven Ontological Arguments](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQybvNQxbMo) (the family's map), then the paired argument/objections lectures per member. → Survey: none in this corpus's books — the books do not survey the ontological argument (see below). → Primary: Anselm and Descartes are named as the conceptual argument's authors by its lecture, but their texts are not in the corpus; Gödel's argument is presented only in its axioms/definitions layer by its lecture. → Framing: Marion, "God and the Ambivalence of Being" (book 020, ch. 17).

ontological-argument.verdict: Within this corpus the debate is one-sided in an instructive way: the lecture series presents each argument sympathetically and then subjects it to objections — most heavily the modal argument, which the lecturer judges question-begging in structure — and no corpus source offers a considered *defence* of any member against those objections. The books mention the family only in transit: Rowe (book 027, ch. 1) lists "Ontological, Cosmological, Teleological, Moral, etc." among the traditional arguments a theist might offer as grounds in the Moorean shift, without assessing them; Kant's objection to the *cosmological* argument (see [The Cosmological Argument](cosmological-argument.md)) holds that the cosmological argument covertly depends on this one — God would be logically necessary only if the ontological argument already worked — so the family's fortunes propagate. The honest summary is the lectures' own: seven distinct attempts to get existence out of the concept of God alone, each with a live, identified pressure point (definition-loading, conceivability, question-begging, truth-to-existence slides, totality-naming), and the whole family additionally shadowed by Marion's question whether "Being" means one thing when it is a question of God. Nothing here shows an ontological argument succeeding; nothing here shows the family refuted once for all, either — objections are argued, not conceded by the other side, because the other side is not in the room.

connections.title: The Cosmological Argument
connections.text: [The Cosmological Argument](cosmological-argument.md) — the complementary family (from experience and causation rather than pure reason), and, on Kant's objection as the lectures present it, a dependent one: its "necessary being" conclusion borrows necessity from the ontological argument.

connections.title: The Evidential Argument from Evil
connections.text: [The Evidential Argument from Evil](evidential-argument-from-evil.md) / [The Logical Problem of Evil](logical-problem-of-evil.md) — the arguments *against* God's existence that give these arguments *for* it their dialectical role in book 027: a theist's grounds for the Moorean shift.

connections.title: Faith, Acceptance, and Hope
connections.text: [Faith, Acceptance, and Hope](faith-acceptance-and-hope.md) — if existence cannot be extracted from the concept, the remaining question is what attitude toward "God exists" is rational without such a proof.

The desire argument (Carneades, [The Desire Argument for the Existence of God](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bsbo3Ah2Qew)) — a neighbouring, *abductive* existence argument (C. S. Lewis's form: a desire for perfect happiness unsatisfiable in this world is best explained by another world, and that by God) — not ontological, since it starts from an experienced desire rather than the concept of God; the lecturer counts it among the least convincing arguments precisely because abduction is run twice.

sources: Lectures (Carneades.org) — read in full: "Seven Ontological Arguments (for the Existence of God)"; "Ontological Argument From Definition"; "Conceptual Ontological Argument"; "Objections to the Conceptual Ontological Argument"; "Modal Ontological Argument"; "Why the Modal Ontological Argument Begs the Question"; "Godel's Ontological Argument"; "Meinongian Ontological Argument"; "Mereological Ontological Argument"; "Religious Experience Ontological Argument"; "The Desire Argument for the Existence of God" (for Connections).
Marion, "God and the Ambivalence of Being" (book 020, ch. 17): abstract and framing sections read.
Rowe, ch. 1 of book 027 (read in full for the evidential entry), for the "traditional arguments" list.
Inspected but unusable: "Teleological Arguments From Analogy" — the transcript file records "No English captions available"; it is therefore not used anywhere in this subfield's entries.

religious-diversity-and-salvation.title: Religious Diversity and Salvation
religious-diversity-and-salvation.aka: exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism (views about the afterlife)
religious-diversity-and-salvation.note: exclusivism / inclusivism / pluralism and their formal objections
religious-diversity-and-salvation.question: There are many religions, and they cannot all be right about everything. Leave aside for a moment which of them is true, and ask the question the Carneades "afterlife" mini-series asks: *who gets into the good place?* — heaven, Valhalla, the Elysium fields, whatever a given religion promises. Does reaching it require *believing* the (allegedly) true religion, or only *living* by its standards, or only living well by the standards of one's *own* religion? The three answers — exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism — are positions any adherent can hold without settling the truth question first, and each faces a characteristic dilemma.
