Book 020 supplies the wider frame: a field that has historically studied one tradition's beliefs is being pressed, by its own contributors, to take religious diversity as its starting condition rather than its afterthought.
religious-diversity-and-salvation.ninety: Imagine the door to the good place, and three different door policies. The exclusivist's door checks two things: did you live well *by our standards*, and did you *believe our religion*? Fail either check and you don't get in — which is why exclusivist religions tend to evangelize: your eternal fate may depend on hearing about them. The inclusivist's door checks conduct only: live by our standards — even without ever hearing of us, even while believing something else entirely — and you're in. The pluralist removes the house standards altogether: be a good member of *whatever* religion you belong to, and the good place (perhaps a different one for each) awaits. Each policy buys its kindness at a price. Exclusivism makes your fate turn on the accident of where you were born, and — the sharpest objection — has God *discriminate* on the basis of belief. Inclusivism, if it quietly requires its own rituals, collapses back into exclusivism; if it doesn't require them, it owes its own adherents a reason to perform them. Pluralism must say that followers of a religion commanding objectively wicked acts still arrive — if the acts are really wicked and they really followed their religion. (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [What is Exclusivism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CnXzBnhBlBk), [What is Inclusivism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l3fPYfpR8Hk), [What is Pluralism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qFUcb3F51aM).)

positions.name: Exclusivism

blocks.label: Thesis
blocks.source: Carneades, [What is Exclusivism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CnXzBnhBlBk
blocks.text: ): to reach the positive afterlife you must be a good person by the standards of that specific religion *and* believe in that specific religion. The position is typically defended from holy texts ("only through faith" may one achieve the promised reward) and it motivates evangelism: someone who does only good in the world "will still be punished in the afterlife if they do not believe in that particular religion," so others must be converted for their own sakes. It comes in grades — moderate versions give good nonbelievers a better reward than bad ones while reserving the highest salvation for believing good-doers; broader versions require belief in the right *religion* (Christianity generally) rather than the right sect; strict versions require the specific church or set of beliefs.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the lecture's own structural worry: on any version, most of the world's people are excluded "no matter how good they are just based on the accident of where they were born" — even the largest religion does not form a majority of humanity. The developed argument is the discrimination argument below.

blocks.label: The discrimination argument
blocks.source: Carneades, [The Discrimination Argument Against Religious Exclusivism](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5hNe2_8agj8
blocks.text: — the lecture's own three-statement inconsistency):

steps.text: Discrimination on the basis of religion or belief is morally wrong. (The premise is avowedly intuitive — written into many laws and constitutions; the lecturer concedes the argument will not move anyone who rejects it.)
God (or the religion) discriminates against individuals on the basis of religion or belief in the afterlife — that is the exclusivist tenet: outcomes are assigned by belief.
God (or the religion) is moral, all-good — God could not do something bad.

The three cannot all be held. Run it each way: P1 + P3 entail God does not discriminate (against P2); P1 + P2 entail God is not all-good (against P3); P2 + P3 entail discrimination is not wrong (against P1). The exclusivist must surrender one leg — and the argument's sting is that it makes discrimination not merely present in the system but *moral, indeed morally obligatory*, within it.

positions.name: Inclusivism

blocks.label: Thesis
blocks.source: Carneades, [What is Inclusivism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l3fPYfpR8Hk
blocks.text: ): you must act in accordance with the ethics of the (true) religion to reach the good place, but you need not believe in that religion. If a religion's only commandment were "do not eat pork," a lifelong vegetarian who never heard of the religion qualifies — the act, not the belief or even the reason, is what counts. Shades: some inclusivists excuse only those who never had access to the religion, excluding active rejecters; others count conduct regardless of what the person heard or believed. The position plainly defuses the birthplace objection that presses exclusivism.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: two, both noted by the lecture. First, *feasibility*: excusing the uninstructed is easy for a one-commandment religion, but real religions carry many expectations (rituals on set days, food laws); a standard of pure conduct that starts at "be kind" begins to look "more like a moral philosophy than a religion." Second, the developed dilemma:

blocks.label: The ritual dilemma
blocks.source: Carneades, [The Ritual Dilemma for Inclusivist Religions](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KZmYcYQfvyA
blocks.text: ): divide a religion's requirements into *belief* (a deity exists), *rituals* (pray facing Mecca five times daily), and *moral actions* (do not kill). Then:

steps.text: Either inclusivists require observance of their religion's rituals for the good place, or they do not.

If they do require the rituals, inclusivism is functionally exclusivism — the outsider who never heard of the rituals fails exactly as the unbeliever failed — and inherits exclusivism's objections, the discrimination argument included.
If they do not require the rituals, then *no one* should perform them: there is no justification even for the inclusivist's own adherents to practise them, and the religion as practised dissolves.

Inclusivism is unstable: most believers, pressed, must either appear as exclusivists or abandon their religion's ritual life. (The lecture presents this as an exclusivist's best reply and rates it weaker than the arguments against the other two positions — it depends less on the specifics of a particular religion than the "cherry-picking" charge it sets aside, but it is not decisive either.)

positions.name: Pluralism

blocks.label: Thesis
blocks.source: Carneades, [What is Pluralism?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qFUcb3F51aM
blocks.text: ): to reach the afterlife you simply need to be a good member of *your* religion. Unlike the other two positions there is no house reference point — no sense that one religion is right and the others wrong; the live religions may each be "in some way right, getting at some element of the truth" (some pluralists hold one religion is true but its good place admits good members of others; others posit separate afterlives). It is the most tolerant of the three views: no reason to convert anyone, or even to criticize outsiders' conduct.

blocks.label: Objections
blocks.text: the lecture flags the seams: converts (many religions punish apostasy — is the sincere convert damned by the first religion, saved by the second?); the person raised with *no* religion or moral code (automatically in, or automatically out — "either one seems quite concerning"); and immoral religious practices that should not be condoned. The developed form is:

blocks.label: The cognitivist objection
blocks.source: Carneades, [The Cognitivist Objection to Religious Pluralism](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vyOYFbTcux4
blocks.text: — the lecture's inconsistent triad):

steps.text: People who do things that are objectively wrong should not go to the good place.

Some religions require that people do things that are objectively wrong. (The premise leans on ethical cognitivism — there is a fact of the matter about right and wrong — and on the existence, at least at the margins, of religions requiring human sacrifice, genocide, or cannibalism.)
People who do what their religion requires of them will go to the good place. (Pluralism's core claim.)

The three cannot all be true. The pluralist's exits are unattractive in characteristic ways: deny P3 and pluralism is abandoned; deny P2 by denying objective right and wrong — but most religions themselves preach a moral code, so non-cognitivism sits badly with taking religions seriously.

positions.name: The field-level backdrop (book 020)

blocks.text: The lectures stage diversity as a problem about *salvation*; book 020 stages it as a problem about the *field*. Wildman's "global transformation" (ch. 2) diagnoses a philosophy of religion "typically focus[ed] narrowly on worldview beliefs, often limited to a particular religious tradition (usually Christianity) or set of religious traditions (usually theisms)" — the exclusivism of the syllabus, one might say — and counts the field's response to global religious plurality among its survival tests. Knepper (ch. 5) records progress with a caveat: "the philosophy of religion is finally on its way to becoming religiously diversified," but diversification across creeds leaves class untouched — hence philosophy of *lived* religion, attending to all acts of religious reason-giving, ordinary and spoken as well as elite and written. Eckel's Introduction concedes the volume's own limits (more needed on gender; non-Western perspectives "need to be drawn more fully into discussion"), even as its contents — Jewish philosophy at the margins (chs. 11–12), a Buddhist critique of the Hindu creator (ch. 13), Marion's French phenomenology of God (ch. 17) — enact some of the widening. Chignell (ch. 6) adds a relevant nuance for the salvation debate: his "bare theism" complaint — that the field strips doctrines to the thinnest shared monotheistic core for ease of justification — notes that despite John Hick's influence on the pluralism debate, no community has produced *The Book of Hickean Prayer*: pluralism as philosophers formulate it is not a liturgy anyone actually performs.

thought.name: The vegetarian and the pork commandment
thought.text: (What is Inclusivism?). A religion whose sole commandment is "do not eat pork," and a vegetarian who has never heard of it and abstains for entirely separate reasons. Inclusivism says: qualified. The case isolates the position's core — outcomes track *acts*, not beliefs or motives — and its edge: add real religions' dozens of ritual and dietary requirements, and ask whether the uninstructed can still plausibly qualify.

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: the three definition lectures (Exclusivism → Inclusivism → Pluralism), then the three objection lectures (Discrimination Argument; Ritual Dilemma; Cognitivist Objection). → Survey: Wildman, book 020, ch. 2 (the global transformation) and Knepper, ch. 5 (diversification and its limits). → Primary: none in this corpus states a historical philosopher's diversity theory directly — Hick figures as an influence inside Chignell's ch. 6, not as a text; the entry's positions are therefore the lectures' taxonomies and book 020's field diagnosis, and are labelled as such.

religious-diversity-and-salvation.verdict: As the corpus leaves it, each position stands with its dilemma named and none dissolved: exclusivism with the birthplace accident and the discrimination triad; inclusivism with the ritual dilemma (the weakest of the three objections, on its own lecture's rating); pluralism with the cognitivist triad and the apostasy/no-religion edge cases. The lectures are taxonomy-and-pressure exercises, not verdicts — their method is to show what each door policy costs. Book 020 shifts the question's level without answering it: whether any of these positions is *true* is there displaced by whether the discipline that studies them can itself become as plural as its subject matter — a transformation Wildman treats as still pending. One caution belongs to the record: the corpus frames diversity through *salvation* (the lectures) and *scholarship* (the book); the better-known epistemic framing (what should awareness of disagreement do to one's confidence?) is not developed in these sources and is not supplied here.

connections.title: Faith, Acceptance, and Hope
connections.text: [Faith, Acceptance, and Hope](faith-acceptance-and-hope.md) — exclusivism's belief-requirement is the sharpest case of the belief-centrism Chignell questions: the door policy checks an attitude (belief) that his Ladder suggests many insiders themselves only intermittently have.

connections.title: The Future of Philosophy of Religion
connections.text: [The Future of Philosophy of Religion](the-future-of-philosophy-of-religion.md) — Wildman's global transformation and Knepper's lived-religion proposal are that entry's material; diversity is the test case where the old field and the proposed field diverge most visibly.

connections.title: The Cosmological Argument
connections.text: [The Cosmological Argument](cosmological-argument.md) — Bhāviveka's debate with Hindu theism (book 020, ch. 13) is the corpus's one worked example of inter-religious philosophical argument conducted from inside a tradition, predating the taxonomy above by well over a millennium.

sources: Lectures (Carneades.org) — read in full: "What is Exclusivism (Philosophy of Religion)"; "What is Inclusivism (Philosophy of Religion)"; "What is Pluralism (Philosophy of Religion)"; "The Discrimination Argument Against Religious Exclusivism"; "The Ritual Dilemma for Inclusivist Religions"; "The Cognitivist Objection to Religious Pluralism".

Book 020: Introduction (Eckel) — read in full; ch. 2 (Wildman) — abstract and framing sections read; ch. 5 (Knepper) — abstract and definitional sections read; ch. 6 (Chignell) — read in full (Hick remark in §6.3).

the-future-of-philosophy-of-religion.title: The Future of Philosophy of Religion
the-future-of-philosophy-of-religion.aka: the scope and method of the field; philosophy of religion vs. religious studies
the-future-of-philosophy-of-religion.question: What should philosophy of religion be *about*? The traditional answer — at least in its analytic form — is a small set of questions about a small set of doctrines: does God exist, is belief in God justified, how is evil compatible with God, studied as propositions to be assessed, usually drawn from one tradition (Christianity) or one family (theisms). Book 020 — a whole volume of practitioners reflecting on their field's future — argues, from several directions at once, that this answer is too narrow in its object (beliefs rather than practices), its population (literate elites rather than ordinary practitioners), its map (the North Atlantic theisms rather than the world's religions), and its self-awareness (a discipline that does not examine its own categories, including "religion" and "belief" themselves). This entry states the critique and the main redesign proposals as the volume presents them; it is the subfield's one *meta* entry — a problem about the field, included because book 020 is one of this slice's two source books and this is its central, bottom-up theme.
the-future-of-philosophy-of-religion.ninety: First, separate two things that share a name. *Religion* makes claims about the world — about gods, life, how we should live. *Philosophy of religion* does something else: it translates the wildly varying claims of religions into a common logical language, assesses their justifications, and puts them into dialogue with each other and with science and secular ethics — neutrally, the way it would assess any other claims. Now ask how well the field has been doing that job. One contributor's diagnosis: universities are being reshaped by four transformations — going *global*, going *critical*, going *multidisciplinary*, and going *practical* — and philosophy of religion, huddled around the beliefs of one tradition, has responded to all four slowly, while the jobs named for it disappear. The redesigns on offer share a direction of travel: from texts to *practices* (rituals, disciplines, the ways practices form the people who perform them), from elite writings to *lived* religion (the reasons ordinary people actually give, out loud, today), from justification-of-belief to the attitudes people really bring to worship — acceptance, hope, trust — and from "religion" and "race" as separate filing cabinets to *belief* understood as something material, embodied, and consequential in the world, including in America's history of anti-Black racism. (Distilled from the Carneades lecture [Religion vs Philosophy of Religion](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=onex7xDHQ6k) and book 020, especially Wildman's and Eckel's framing chapters.)

positions.name: The traditional field, as its critics describe it

blocks.text: The critics inside the volume describe a common target. Wildman's opening questions (book 020, ch. 2): "Why is philosophy of religion so rarely about *religion in all its complexity* … but rather typically focuses narrowly on worldview beliefs, often limited to a particular religious tradition (usually Christianity) or set of religious traditions (usually theisms)?" Why is it so distant from critical theory, so unresponsive to other disciplines (physics to cognitive neuroscience to political economy), and so absent from public discourse — and why, meanwhile, are "university positions specializing in and named for philosophy of religion *disappearing* in North Atlantic cultures"? Chignell (ch. 6) gives the internal version of the same portrait: forty years of flourishing analytic work narrowed the field twice over — to *belief* as the attitude that matters, and to *bare theism* as the content that matters — producing "scholastic stasis in which familiar problems are hashed out in ever finer detail, but genuinely new directions are difficult to find." Eckel's Introduction concedes the frame from the editor's chair: the classic questions "seemed parochial," and new work grounds religious studies "more closely in the lives of actual practitioners."

positions.name: The four transformations (Wesley Wildman)

blocks.label: Thesis
blocks.source: Wildman, book 020, ch. 2 — stated as a diagnosis, in his terms

items: Four transformations are impacting all universities in North Atlantic cultures and beyond: the **global** transformation (the study of religion can no longer be one tradition's self-study), the **critical** transformation (critical theories of power, race, gender, and suspicion are ascendant across the academy), the **multidisciplinary** transformation (relevant knowledge now lives in many disciplines), and the **practical** transformation (attention to religious practices and the solution of real-world problems).

Philosophy of religion "has been slow to respond to the associated challenges," even though both its departmental homes — philosophy and academic religious studies — have proved more agile in some respects.

The transformations supply *criteria* for estimating the field's future; recent field-wide empirical studies add specificity; and reversing "the trend of rapid contraction of academic positions in philosophy of religion" requires imagining — and doing — what those criteria demand.

blocks.text: The rest of the volume can be read as a set of responses to this exam, and Eckel's Introduction reads it that way: grouping the essays under the global perspective (the Jewish-philosophy chapters; Bhāviveka), the challenge of critical theory (Pritchard; Dole; Larrimore; Decosimo), multiple disciplinary perspectives (Speight; Reinhard), and religious practice (Schilbrack; Knepper; Chignell).

positions.name: From texts to practices: subjects are formed, not just informed (Kevin Schilbrack)

blocks.label: Thesis
blocks.source: Schilbrack, book 020, ch. 4
blocks.text: the academic study of religion shifted over the past century "from the study of religious texts to a broader vision that includes social practices," and philosophy of religion "ought to expand its traditional object of study to follow suit." The live theoretical question is what practices *do* to people — the *formation of subjects*. Three anthropological approaches are usually read as rivals: Clifford Geertz's hermeneutic approach (inspired by Ricoeur), Talal Asad's disciplinary approach (inspired by Foucault), and Thomas Csordas's embodiment approach (inspired by Merleau-Ponty). Schilbrack argues the disagreement among them about subjectivity is at bottom a *philosophical* one — hence an opportunity for philosophers of religion to contribute to the theorizing rather than merely consume it — and that, properly understood, the three approaches complement one another and can be integrated.

positions.name: Philosophy of lived religion (Timothy D. Knepper)

blocks.label: Thesis
blocks.source: Knepper, book 020, ch. 5
blocks.text: even a field succeeding at Wildman's global test has a second injustice outstanding. Religious *diversification* "is only half the battle: injustices of creed have been addressed while injustices of class remain." Philosophy of lived religion is "the philosophical study of all acts of religious reason-giving, privileging contemporary, ordinary, and spoken acts of religious reason-giving over past, elite, and written ones" — the philosophy "not only of all religious traditions but also of all religious subjectivities (insofar as possible)." Its organizing questions are the basic ones humans ask of anything — what, who, when, where, how, why — now addressed to religion as it is reasoned about in lived discourse and practice. Knepper is careful to distinguish his proposal from the nearest advance, Schilbrack's 2014 manifesto (which widens the field's object to religion's affective and conative dimensions — the ethical, political, ritual — alongside the cognitive): lived religion's unit is the *act of reason-giving* itself, wherever it occurs.

positions.name: The liturgical turn (Andrew Chignell)

blocks.text: Cross-reference: [Faith, Acceptance, and Hope](faith-acceptance-and-hope.md) states this position in full. In this entry's terms it is the redesign of the field's *centre*: set aside the debates over knowledge and justified belief, as an earlier generation set aside the debates over religious language, and study the attitudes actual practice involves — the liturgical stance, acceptance, hope, trust — and the thick, embodied doctrinal objects of liturgy rather than bare theism. Chignell's closing coinage for the redesigned practitioner: *pistologists* and *elpistologists*, students of faith (*pistis*) and hope (*elpis*).

positions.name: Material belief (Elizabeth Pritchard)

blocks.label: Thesis
blocks.source: Pritchard, book 020, ch. 7
blocks.text: the field's master category is itself part of the problem. Scholars who repudiate "belief" as an exclusively cognitive category — a reductionist distortion of religions — "take for granted that belief is nonmaterial." Pritchard argues that presumption does political work: it contributes to "the disaggregation of 'religion' and 'race,' the obfuscation of Christianity's relationship to racism and the perpetuation of American anti-black racism." Her positive case is for the *materiality* of belief — belief as embodied in practices, institutions, and their consequences — supported by recent work that portrays American anti-Black racism itself as a religion and by materialist interpretations of belief from a range of disciplines. For this entry the implication is methodological: a category the field treated as a neutral piece of philosophical psychology (a mental state of affirmation) turns out, on her account, to have a history and interests behind its dematerialization — the sort of reflexive finding the volume's critical transformation demands.

positions.name: Reflexivity about the categories themselves (Arnold; Hammerschlag; Speight; Dole)

blocks.text: A second redesign thread widens the *questions* rather than the object. **Arnold (ch. 3)**: against the descriptivist rule that scholars of religion must not judge, normativity is ineliminable from humanistic inquiry — intentionality itself is irreducibly normative, and freedom is our attunement to normative considerations, which cannot coherently be explained away; philosophy of religion's distinctive work is identifying and clarifying the normative considerations that "inexorably distinguish human activity as such." **Hammerschlag (ch. 12)**: answering Schilbrack's charge (quoted in her chapter) that philosophy of religion is "the least reflexive discipline in religious studies," she proposes — through modern Jewish thought's encounters with philosophy — that the field be reconceived "less as a discipline focused on the validity of concepts and more as one that investigates their historical emergence and evaluates their subsequent usage and dissemination." **Speight (ch. 14)** runs the same historicizing move on the master concept itself: "religion," like "art," may be an essentially modern concept with no ancient counterpart — which changes how the humanities should approach the long pre-histories of both. **Dole (ch. 8)** applies reflexivity to the critical tools themselves: academic *critique* (genealogy, the hermeneutics of suspicion) shares formal features with conspiracy theories — both are "suspicious explanation" — developing Latour's worry about "gullible critique." The remaining chapters extend the volume's range rather than its thesis: Larrimore (ch. 9) on philosophy of religion in the Anthropocene; Decosimo (ch. 10) against Dreyfus and Kelly's religious naturalism; Zank (ch. 11) on Jewish philosophy's fruitful marginality; Reinhard (ch. 15) on psychoanalysis and the monotheistic origins of modern science; Marion (ch. 17) as evidence, for Eckel, that "the tradition is alive and well" (see [The Ontological Argument](ontological-argument.md)).

ladder.label: Start
ladder.text: Carneades, [Religion vs Philosophy of Religion](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=onex7xDHQ6k) (the field defined against its object). → Survey: Eckel's Introduction to book 020 (the volume's own map) and Wildman's ch. 2 (the four transformations). → Primary: the redesign chapters themselves — Schilbrack (ch. 4), Knepper (ch. 5), Chignell (ch. 6), Pritchard (ch. 7) — with Arnold (ch. 3) and Hammerschlag (ch. 12) for the reflexivity thread. → Full treatment: the whole of book 020, whose remaining chapters (chs. 8–11, 13–15, 17) are mapped in the book map for 020.

the-future-of-philosophy-of-religion.verdict: The volume is a symposium, not a settlement, and presents itself as one: the editors' hope is that the essays' "variety, the imagination, and the intellectual seriousness … speak well for the future of philosophy in the study of religion," alongside the admission that "important perspectives have been left out" (gender studies; fuller non-Western coverage). The contributors agree on the diagnosis (the traditional object is too narrow) more than on any single redesign: practice-formation, lived religion, the liturgical turn, and material belief are complementary directions, not rival manifestos, but no chapter argues for their unification, and two standing tensions are visible in the corpus itself. First, Chignell's business-as-usual panelists are not straw men *within* the volume's world: the classical questions retain distinguished defenders, and Marion's closing chapter is offered by the editor precisely as proof the traditional metaphysical tradition continues. Second, the field-level critique never shows that the classical problems are *bad* problems — Wildman's charge is unresponsiveness and contraction, not error. A reader should therefore not take this entry as reporting the death of the arguments treated elsewhere in this subfield; it reports a well-documented dispute about what *else* the field should be, staged entirely from inside the profession.

connections.text: [Faith, Acceptance, and Hope](faith-acceptance-and-hope.md) — Chignell's chapter does double duty: an entry-level theory of religious attitudes there, a field-redesign manifesto here.

connections.text: [Religious Diversity and Salvation](religious-diversity-and-salvation.md) — the global transformation and Knepper's class critique supply that entry's scholarly backdrop: diversity as the field's test, not only the believer's problem.

connections.text: [The Evidential Argument from Evil](evidential-argument-from-evil.md) and [The Cosmological Argument](cosmological-argument.md) — the classical content whose centrality Wildman and Chignell question; note that Bhāviveka (book 020, ch. 13) already shows the classical content was never as exclusively Western as the critique's target.

historical-explanation-and-narrative.title: Historical Explanation and Narrative
historical-explanation-and-narrative.note: built from 011 chs. 7–9 (book 010 is not Day — see DATA_QUALITY)
historical-explanation-and-narrative.question: What kind of explanation is a historical explanation? On one model, to explain an event is to subsume it under a law: given the law and the initial conditions, the event had to follow, and the explanation therefore also tells you what *would* have happened under other conditions. Much historical explanation looks nothing like that. It tells you a story — a chain of particular causes, each plausible, none an instance of any known law connecting the kinds of things the story is about. Is that a defect, a second-class kind of explanation waiting to be replaced by laws? Or are some domains simply historical, so that narrative is not their failed theory but their correct form? This corpus's fullest treatment of the question comes from an unexpected direction: Fodor and Piattelli-Palmarini's *What Darwin Got Wrong* (book 011) concludes that the adaptationist explanations which actually persuade are historical narratives rather than law-subsumptions — and generalises the point to history itself. The dedicated textbook for this subfield, Mark Day's *The Philosophy of History: An Introduction* (book 010), is **absent from the corpus** — its extraction folder contains a different book entirely (see "Sources read") — so Day's own treatment of historical explanation, narrative, and objectivity cannot be stated here, and this entry is built only from what was actually read.
historical-explanation-and-narrative.ninety: The Carneades lecture [Philosophy of History vs History of Philosophy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TGkdxsz2Gek) frames the field this entry belongs to — distilled here, not quoted. *History of philosophy* documents what past philosophers argued; *philosophy of history* asks questions about history itself: what does history consist of — periods, individual actions, civilisations? Does it have a direction or an end, and by what measure would we judge progress? And, most pressingly for this entry, how can we *know* about the past at all: what counts as justification for facts in the distant past, and are we allowed weaker justification for temporally distant events than for present ones? The lecturer is candid that the channel — steeped in the analytic tradition, where the subject is less common than in the Continental one — has barely covered philosophy of history, and names Hegel as its central, and famously difficult, figure. The detailed treatment in this entry — historical explanation as narrative rather than law — is then distilled not from the lecture but from book 011, chs. 7–9, and is marked as textbook material wherever it appears below.

videos.title: Philosophy of History vs History of Philosophy

positions.name: The nomological model (as book 011 characterises it)

blocks.text: On the covering-law picture, an explanation subsumes an event under a natural law: it cites a property of the event in virtue of which a law applies to it, and because laws support counterfactuals, the explanation also settles what would have happened otherwise. "Nothing has a nomological explanation unless it belongs to a natural kind." The authors take the model's virtues to be truisms: prediction and counterfactual support are what such explanation *is*. Their question is not whether the model is coherent but whether the explanations we actually accept, in evolutionary biology and in history, are instances of it.

positions.name: The narrative model: plausible causal chains, post hoc

blocks.text: Historical explanations "offer (not laws but) plausible narratives; narratives that purport to articulate the causal chain of events leading to the event that is to be explained".

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 7, closing sections — a formalization of the authors' stated contrast

steps.text: Nomological explanations rest on relations among *properties* and therefore support counterfactuals; historical narratives rest on causal relations among *events* and therefore do not.

The explanations that persuade in the contested domains have the second form: "Napoleon lost at Waterloo because it had been raining for days, and the ground was too muddy for cavalry to charge" — yet "it doesn't… follow that there are laws that connect the amount of mud on the ground with the outcomes of battles".

Such explanations are inherently post hoc: given the known outcome, a plausible chain can be told — but "there would have been a plausible story to explain what happened whoever had won", so prediction and retrodiction are asymmetric, and several reasonable accounts of the same event can coexist with "nothing to choose between them".

blocks.label: The authors' concession, stated with the argument
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 7
blocks.text: none of this impugns narratives. "Historical narratives are, as far as we know, perfectly OK; certainly they are often thoroughly persuasive." Nor do they deny that the events narrated fall under *some* laws: Waterloo "must have been subsumed by some covering laws or other… laws of the mechanics of middle-sized objects" — the claim is only that there are no laws *about mud so described, or about battles so described*, still less laws connecting them, which is what law-subsumption *of the explanation as given* would require.

positions.name: The application: adaptationist explanation is natural history

blocks.text: The distinction is load-bearing in the book because it is offered as the rescue — and the demotion — of adaptationism. (The argument that adaptationism *needs* rescuing is the subject of the companion entry; here it is the rescue that matters.)

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 7, "Then what kind of theory is the theory of natural selection?"

steps.text: Some textbook adaptationist explanations plainly do give reasons why phenotypes are as they are — why there are many t1s and few t2s.

What they provide, on inspection, are historical narratives: plausible post-hoc causal chains, not laws — exactly as with Waterloo's mud, or with case-by-case stories of why this man got rich (heredity, acuity, luck, highway robbery), where "it is most unlikely that there are generalizations that are lawful… that specify the various situations in which it is possible to get rich".

"If adaptationist explanations are species of historical narratives, everything can be saved from the wreckage except the notion of selection-for." The mechanism of evolution is then not a theory's subject matter but "the vignettes that natural history retails case by case. Evolution is a kind of history, and both are just one damned thing after another."

blocks.text: Natural history, so conceived, has two marks, both drawn from ch. 8: it is **invariably post hoc** ("lacking observations of spiders, nothing… could have predicted that there are creatures that have the spider's kind of adaptation" — somebody watched how spiders make a living and worked backwards) and it **differs wildly from case to case** (the spider's web story and the oak's seed story "have little or nothing in common; there aren't… laws — or even reliable empirical generalizations — about their mechanisms of adaptation"). It also collapses across levels: what fixes a phenotype may be weather, salinity, a prey species' biochemistry, the anatomy of a birth canal, or cosmic radiation, "or all of these acting at once" (ch. 9).

positions.name: The generalisation: there is no level of historical explanation

blocks.text: Ch. 9 states the entry's most sweeping claim, and states it as a comparison. Psychology *has* a level of explanation — the intentional level, whose generalisations (about belief, perception, memory) plausibly support counterfactuals. Historical phenomena, the authors claim, do not constitute such a level at all.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 9 — a formalization of the chapter's closing movement

steps.text: A theoretical domain requires generalisations at its own level that support counterfactuals (as intentional psychology's plausibly do, and as putative "laws of selection" — traits per se vs fitness — plausibly do not, because everything depends on the whole phenotype and the whole ecology).

Historical explanation chains wildly heterogeneous causes — "for want of a nail, the shoe was lost; for want of the shoe, the horse was lost…" — in a vocabulary belonging to no science, under no laws or reliable generalisations that any science articulates.

"Marx and many other nineteenth-century luminaries notwithstanding, there is no level of historical explanation; a fortiori, there is no theory of history." Darwin's mistake is paired with Marx's: each "imagined that history is a theoretical domain; but what there is, in fact, is only a heterogeneity of causes and effects."

blocks.text: **Scope note (the authors' own).** The claim is not that historical processes are uncaused, indeterministic, or unlawful *tout court*: "this is not in the least to suggest that the fixation of phenotypes is other than a deterministic, causal and lawful process through and through." What is denied is a *unitary theory at the historical level* — not causation, but a level. Their preferred replacement image is contagion, not selection: organisms "catch" their phenotypes from their ecologies as they catch colds, by processes that run simultaneously at many levels of organisation and differ from case to case. "Well, actually there are lots" is their answer to "what is the mechanism of the fixation of phenotypes?" — and, by extension, their answer about mechanisms of historical change generally.

thought.name: Waterloo
thought.text: (book 011, ch. 7). Napoleon lost, we're told, because days of rain left the ground too muddy for cavalry. Persuasive — but no law connects mud to battle outcomes, Wellington might equally be explained by the Prussians' arrival or Napoleon's decline, and a story would have been available whoever won. Meant to isolate the narrative form: sufficient-cause chains without counterfactual support. (The same example appears in the book's prospectus, where Napoleon's defeat is explained by "his age, his upbringing, his social class and his personality type… the weather and how much caffeine there was in his morning coffee" — historical explanation as "egregiously 'multilevel'".)

thought.name: The banana peel
thought.text: (book 011, ch. 7). "She fell because she slipped on a banana peel." Very likely true; but "there's no law — there's not even a statistical law — that has 'banana peel' in its antecedent and 'slipped and fell' in its consequent." The minimal case of explanation-without-subsumption.

thought.name: For want of a nail
thought.text: (book 011, ch. 9). The nursery-rhyme chain — nail, shoe, horse, rider, message, battle — "may well explain the loss of the battle", but its transitions instance no science's laws. Meant to show that a narrative can be a complete explanation while belonging to no theoretical level.

thought.name: The extinction of the dinosaurs
thought.text: (book 011, ch. 7). Small mammals outlasted large dinosaurs — because of their smallness (egg-snatching), or because of their temperature tolerance (which mattered only given the meteor)? Both stories are plausible; the narratives on offer support neither counterfactual against the other. Pressures any claim that a narrative explanation settles what *mattered*.

thought.name: Getting rich
thought.text: (book 011, ch. 7). For every rich person there is some explanation — inheritance, cupidity, luck, robbery — irreducibly context-dependent across eras (no one can now get rich as Genghis Khan did). "Adaptationist explanations of the evolution of heritable traits are really a lot like that": convincing stories, case by case, without a theory of getting rich — or of adaptation — behind them.

ladder.text: book 011, ch. 7's closing sections ("Then what kind of theory is the theory of natural selection?" and the rhetorical conclusion) — the narrative/nomological contrast worked out on adaptationist examples.

ladder.text: book 011, ch. 9 (Summary and Postlude) — the generalisation to history itself, the Marx comparison, and the contagion metaphor; supported by ch. 8 on natural history as post hoc and case-specific, and by the multilevel-explanation discussion previewed in the Terms of Engagement.

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: **missing from the corpus.** The intended full treatment for this subfield is Mark Day, *The Philosophy of History: An Introduction* (book 010) — but book 010's extraction folder contains Glenn Dolphin's *Teaching Geology Using the History and Philosophy of Science* (Springer, 2024) instead, and no text of Day exists anywhere in the extracted corpus. Day's positions on historical explanation, narrative, and historical objectivity therefore cannot be placed on this ladder yet.

historical-explanation-and-narrative.verdict: Within this corpus, one-sidedly — and the entry says so rather than smoothing it over. The only sustained treatment read is Fodor & Piattelli-Palmarini's, and their verdict is stated at full strength: historical (including adaptationist) explanation is narrative, narratives do not support counterfactuals, and there is no theoretical level — hence no theory — of history. Two qualifications travel with that verdict in their own text: narratives are legitimate, often rationally compelling explanations, not failed science; and the events they recount remain fully causal and law-governed at *other* levels (physics, mechanics), so nothing supernatural or indeterministic follows. What the corpus cannot supply is the other side: no covering-law theorist (Hempel is mentioned in book 011 only for the heart/function puzzle, not for his model of historical explanation), no narrative theorist, and no Day — so questions the subfield standardly treats as central (whether narratives can be objectively better or worse; whether historical knowledge of a singular past is knowledge at all; whether history has direction) are raised by the framing lecture but answered by no text read for this entry. They stay open here, pending a genuine extraction of book 010.

connections.title: Selection-For and the Critique of Adaptationism
connections.text: [Selection-For and the Critique of Adaptationism](selection-for-and-the-critique-of-adaptationism.md) — the parent argument: it is because adaptationist explanations are narratives, supporting no counterfactuals, that the selection-for/free-rider distinction cannot be drawn inside them. The two entries are the negative and the positive halves of one book's conclusion.

connections.title: The Problem of Induction
connections.text: [The Problem of Induction](../epistemology/problem-of-induction.md) — a neighbouring limits-of-law problem: Hume's gap is between past instances and unobserved cases; the gap here is between a true causal story and the counterfactuals a law would have underwritten.

selection-for-and-the-critique-of-adapta.title: Selection-For and the Critique of Adaptationism
selection-for-and-the-critique-of-adapta.aka: the free-rider problem; the intensionality of selection-for; Fodor & Piattelli-Palmarini's critique of natural selection
selection-for-and-the-critique-of-adapta.note: Fodor & Piattelli-Palmarini at stated strength; no adaptationist-side text exists in the corpus
selection-for-and-the-critique-of-adapta.question: Evolutionary theory says that creatures with adaptive traits are *selected*. Adaptationism says more: that creatures are *selected for* their adaptive traits — that the trait is why they flourished. Are these the same claim? Fodor and Piattelli-Palmarini's *What Darwin Got Wrong* (2010) argues that they are not, that inferring the second from the first is a fallacy, and that no mindless process could ever be sensitive to the difference. On their account, this is not a repairable gap in the theory of natural selection but a crack in its foundations. This entry presents their argument at the strength at which they state it — together with the concessions and counter-considerations the book itself enters — and does not present the argument as settled: the book is a polemic by two authors, and the standing of its conclusion is part of what the entry records.
selection-for-and-the-critique-of-adapta.ninety: *No Carneades lecture covers natural selection, Darwin, or adaptationism (the lecture folder was searched by title and by full text), so this version is distilled from the textbook itself — book 011, Terms of Engagement and chs. 1 and 6 — and is marked accordingly.* A trait can spread through a population in two very different ways: because it helps its bearers survive and reproduce, or because it is glued — genetically, developmentally, geometrically — to another trait that does. Gould and Lewontin made this vivid with the spandrels of St Mark's: domed churches have arches because arches hold the dome up, and the little triangles between the arches, the spandrels, are simply what geometry gives you for free — they are there *because of* the arches, not *for* anything. To say which of two always-together traits is the real adaptation and which is the free-rider, you have to answer a counterfactual: *if the two came apart, which would selection keep?* Breeders and architects can answer such questions because they have minds — they can think about what didn't happen. Natural selection, the argument runs, cannot: it is a purely local process that responds only to actual causes in the actual world, and merely possible predators, merely possible environments, and merely possible separations of traits exert no pressure at all. Yet the vocabulary of adaptationism — *selected-for*, *function*, *ecological niche*, *problem of adaptation* — is built entirely out of such distinctions. Strip out the phantom breeder ("Mother Nature") who alone could make them, and, the authors claim, the theory of natural selection does not become false the way Skinner's learning theory became false; it becomes *empty*.

positions.name: The target: adaptationism, as the authors characterise it

blocks.text: Adaptationism is the thesis that natural selection is the mechanism of evolution: that the distribution of phenotypic traits in populations is explained, in the main, by exogenous (ecological) selection filtering randomly generated heritable variation. The book is careful about what it is *not* attacking. Evolutionary theory has two parts — a **genealogy of species** (GS: species are related by descent, plausibly from a common ancestor) and the **theory of natural selection** (NS). "We have no quarrel to pick with the genealogy of species; it is perfectly possible — in fact, entirely likely — that GS is true even if NS is not." Both authors are atheists and naturalists, seeking mechanical explanations without final causes; the book is explicitly not about God, intelligent design, or creationism. Its contention is only that NS cannot be the causal mechanism that generates the taxonomy of species.

blocks.label: The confusion at the core
blocks.source: book 011, Terms of Engagement

steps.text: Adaptationist theories trade on two claims: (1) evolution is a process in which creatures *with* adaptive traits are selected; (2) evolution is a process in which creatures are selected *for* their adaptive traits.
Darwinism is committed to inferring (2) from (1).

That inference is where the theory breaks: it is invalid — "in fact it's what philosophers call an 'intensional fallacy'" — and, the authors argue across chs. 6–7, there is no way to repair it consistent with naturalism.

positions.name: The Skinner parallel: one architecture, two theories

blocks.text: Before the selection-for argument proper, the book argues that the theory of natural selection and B. F. Skinner's theory of operant conditioning are "identical in all but name": both are black boxes mapping a distribution of traits in a population (phenotypes; stimulus–response repertoires) onto a successor distribution as a function of environmental variables, and both endorse the same six proprietary constraints — iterativity, environmentalism, gradualism, monotonicity, locality, mindlessness. Inside the boxes, both are *generate-and-test* theories: a random generator (mutation; random operants) plus an exogenous filter (selection; reinforcement), "and that is all".

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 1 — a formalization of the chapter's closing move

steps.text: Skinner's learning theory, built on this architecture, is dead beyond resuscitation, and the reasons are principled (the Chomsky critique and its successors): learning is not the exogenous filtering of randomly emitted behaviour.
Darwin's theory of evolution proposes "essentially the same mechanisms to compute essentially similar functions under essentially identical constraints."

"The position that retains the second but not the first is not stable." With a caveat the authors insist on: Skinner's theory is *false* (associationism is a story about filtering, just a wrong one), whereas Darwin's, they will claim, is *empty* — it has no account of the filtering at all.

positions.name: The biological argument: the generator is not random, and the filter is not in charge

blocks.text: Part One of the book argues empirically — from the biology literature as the authors read it — that the generate-and-test picture misdescribes the machinery. Phenotypes are not offered to selection as random, independent variants: between genotype and phenotype stand layers of internal filters (developmental processes and conserved master genes in evo-devo; gene regulatory networks, entrenchment, robustness and pleiotropy; chaperones that bank hidden variation; alternative splicing), and fixation can proceed without selection at all (molecular drive, biased gene conversion). "We think of natural selection as tuning the piano, not as composing the melodies."

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 2 — a formalization of the chapter's conclusion

steps.text: Before any phenotype can be "offered" to selection, "a host of internal constraints have to be satisfied"; mutations, even if random at source, do not produce random phenotypes.

Traits are not independently selectable units ("beanbag genetics" is false: genes are jointly regulated, master genes move many traits at once, developmental modules and coordination bind traits into complexes).

"There is… no single 'arrow' connecting a random generator of genetic diversity to the phenotypes on which exogenous selection acts" — so the more the internalist story is true, "the less work is left for appeals to natural selection to do."

blocks.label: The authors' own caveat, entered in the same Part
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 3, conclusion
blocks.text: the biologists whose work Part One surveys — including the discoverers of these mechanisms — mostly "still today endorse natural selection as the determinant par excellence of the course of evolution", and determined defenders treat the same results as *supporting* selection. The authors "confess to not understanding that", and at this stage "are prepared to settle for a stand-off": the empirical case shows adaptationism is "less than apodictic", no more. The book's claim to a *fatal* flaw rests on Part Two, not on Part One.

blocks.label: A second empirical strand: the laws of form
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 5
blocks.text: . Some biological structures are optimal or near-optimal (quarter-power scaling laws, wiring-minimised nervous systems, optimal foraging ratios), and the spaces of candidate solutions are often astronomically large.

steps.text: By neo-Darwinism's own account, selection only *satisfices* — it finds locally satisfactory solutions and cannot optimise — and blind search of those spaces by random generation plus filtering is intractable.
Optimal and near-optimal solutions nevertheless exist, across unrelated lineages.

"If natural selection cannot optimize, then something else must be involved" — plausibly physico-chemical law and self-organisation. The authors are frank that this is a dilemma, not an explanation: of the parade cases "nobody today really has a clue to a solution", and they claim no rival mechanism.

positions.name: The conceptual argument: selection cannot tell arches from spandrels

blocks.text: Part Two's argument turns on *free-riders*: traits that spread because they are linked to traits that affect fitness (spandrels on arches; heart noises on blood-pumping; in the book's laboratory case, a bacterium's capacity to digest a second sugar, which rode along with selection on the first and silently blocked a third). Distinguishing the selected-for trait from its free-rider always requires a counterfactual — what would happen if the coextensive traits came apart. And that, the authors argue, is a resource natural selection does not have.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 6 — the authors' own numbered argument, lightly compressed

steps.text: Selection-for is a causal process.
Actual causal relations aren't sensitive to counterfactual states of affairs: if it wasn't the case that A, then the fact that A's being the case *would have* caused B does not explain B.
But the distinction between traits that are selected-for and their free-riders turns on the truth (or falsity) of relevant counterfactuals.
So if T and T′ are coextensive, selection cannot distinguish the case in which T free-rides on T′ from the case in which T′ free-rides on T.

"So the claim that selection is the mechanism of evolution cannot be true" — a theory of evolution must explain the distribution of traits by their connection to fitness, and selection cannot perform the individuation that requires.

blocks.label: Why minds are the exception, and why that doesn't save Darwin
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 6
blocks.text: . Architects *can* select for arches rather than spandrels, and breeders *can* select for market value rather than root systems, because minds represent counterfactuals: an architect can think "if I took the spandrels out, the dome would fall", and let a merely possible state of affairs govern actual behaviour. Gould and Lewontin's paradigm case of selection-for, and Darwin's own model of natural selection, are both cases of *mental* causation with the minds then abstracted away. "But that… is what we are saying can't be done." Natural selection is mindless — Darwin was right about that — and what is mindless cannot register the counterfactuals on which trait-individuation depends.

positions.name: The four exits, and why the authors close them

blocks.text: Ch. 7 considers the replies available to adaptationism — in effect, the objections to the argument above — and answers each. They are recorded here as the authors present them; the book engages no named living respondent at length, and Sober (1993) is noted by the authors themselves as the honourable exception who took the counterfactual question seriously.

**Objection 1 — Mother Nature.** Take the breeder analogy literally: what selection selects-for is what it "has in mind". → **Reply:** then the counterfactuals are grounded, but in a fiction. "Natural selection doesn't have a mind. A fortiori, it has nothing in mind when it selects among frogs." Mother Nature, the Blind Watchmaker, and the Selfish Gene are intentional systems only as metaphors, and "fictions can't select things, however hard they try."

**Objection 2 — Laws of selection.** Laws support counterfactuals without minds; perhaps there are laws of the form "all else equal, t1s beat t2s in ecology E with probability p". → **Reply:** fitness is massively context-sensitive. Whether a trait helps depends on the whole phenotype it is embedded in (phenotypes are "fusions of traits", not Swiss apples that fall apart into discrete constituents) and on the whole ecology; outcomes of competitions are interaction effects. So there are no nomological generalisations about which *traits* win — no underlying relation obscured by noise, as with genuine ceteris paribus laws, but "just nothing to choose between" rival generalisations. And where coextensive traits are *nomologically* coextensive, there may be no nearby world in which one is altered and the other left intact, so even laws could not underwrite the trait-level counterfactuals adaptationism needs.

**Objection 3 — Sober's sieve.** A sieve that passes only small red marbles sorts *for size*, not colour — so the select/select-for distinction can be drawn mechanically. → **Reply:** we know what the sieve sorts for only because we know its endogenous mechanism, which is exactly what adaptationist explanations typically lack; and the intuition is unstable — sift flour and the good stuff falls through, pan for gold and the good stuff stays behind, so even for the sieve, what counts as "selected" waits on a sorter's purposes. "Extensions don't determine intensions."

**Objection 4 — A theory schema.** Adaptationism claims only that for each adaptation there *is* some trait that was selected-for and some ecological problem it solved, without saying which. → **Reply:** that is an empirical claim only if "adaptation", "selection-for" and "ecological problem" are independently defined; in practice they are interdefined, so "adaptations are always solutions to ecological problems" collapses into a truism — "like 'bachelors always turn out to be unmarried'".

positions.name: The exquisite-fit argument, and the niche dilemma

blocks.text: Ch. 8 addresses what the authors call perhaps the strongest argument *for* adaptationism: organisms fit their environments too well for it to be luck, and only selection by those environments seems to explain the fit naturalistically.

blocks.label: Canonical argument
blocks.source: book 011, ch. 8 — a formalization of the chapter's dilemma

steps.text: A creature's *environment* is the world, common to all; its *ecology* (or niche) is, by contrast, "whatever-it-is-about-the-world that makes its phenotype viable" — so "ecology" and "phenotype" are interdefined, as are "niche", "adaptation", "problem of adaptation", "good for", and "selection-for".

A claim explained by interdefined terms is tautological, not contingent: if a species fails to fit a supposed niche exactly, it follows only that that wasn't exactly its niche. "If seagulls didn't have wings, their ecology wouldn't be airy."

The exquisite fit is "either true but tautological or irrelevant": fit to the *world* needs no selection theory (anything alive is ipso facto adapted to it), and fit to a *niche* is guaranteed by the individuation of niches. What genuinely needs explaining — in virtue of what a phenotype can make a living, and by what historical process it came to — is the business of natural history, not of a theory of selection.

thought.name: The spandrels of San Marco
thought.text: (Gould & Lewontin 1979, via book 011, ch. 6). Churches with domes need arches; spandrels come free with the geometry. Adaptationist storytelling that asks what spandrels are *for* invents functions for by-products. Meant to show: coextensive traits divide into selected-for and free-rider, and surface fit cannot tell you which is which. In the book's hands it also turns against its inventors: Gould & Lewontin's own case is an architect's — a mind's — selection.

thought.name: The frog and the ambient black nuisance
thought.text: (book 011, ch. 6). Frogs snap at flies; suppose flies are locally coextensive with "ambient black nuisances" (ABNs). Every actual snap is both a fly-snap and an ABN-snap. Which disposition did the frog evolve? Only a counterfactual world — ABNs that aren't flies — could decide, and natural selection, confined to the actual world, cannot consult it. Pressures: any causal theory that fixes a trait (or a content) by actual causes alone.

thought.name: The three sugars
thought.text: (Hall's *E. coli* experiments, book 011, ch. 4). Selecting bacteria for digesting sugar 1 yields, as a free-rider, digestion of sugar 2 — which turns out to block, permanently, digestion of sugar 3; the order of selective steps is irreversible and, in nature, unreconstructible. Experimenters could detect the free-rider because they could run the splitting experiments; "natural selection doesn't perform experiments." Meant to show free-riding is not a marginal exception but undetectable-in-principle wherever traits are coextensive in the selective environment.

thought.name: Sober's sieve
thought.text: (Sober 1993, via book 011, ch. 7). Marbles differing in size and colour pass a sieve; all and only the small ones are red. Intuition: it sorts for size. The authors use it as a test of whether the select/select-for distinction can be grounded without intentions or laws — and argue it cannot (see Objection 3).

thought.name: Pigs with wings
thought.text: (book 011, chs. 8–9). No winged pigs exist, or ever did — not because winged pigs lost competitions, but because "there is no place on pigs to put them": the phenotype is endogenously impossible. Meant to show that the *absences* in the space of forms, which a theory of evolution should explain, are explained by internal constraints, about which selection has nothing to say.

ladder.text: no Carneades lecture exists for this problem (searched by title and full text) — begin with book 011's *Terms of Engagement*, which states the thesis and the selected/selected-for confusion in the authors' own summary form.

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: book 011, ch. 1 (the Skinner parallel and the six constraints) and ch. 6 (the selection-for argument).

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: book 011, chs. 2–5 (the biological argument and laws of form), ch. 7 (the four exits), ch. 8 (the niche dilemma), ch. 9 (summary and postlude).

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: book 011 entire, including the Appendix dossier on adaptationism's export markets. Counter-literature (Sober 1993; Gould & Lewontin's 1979 paper; the responses of the biologists cited in Part One) is *discussed* in the book but is not itself in this corpus; the corpus contains no text that answers Fodor & Piattelli-Palmarini from the adaptationist side.

selection-for-and-the-critique-of-adapta.verdict: As far as this corpus can show: unresolved, and presented by its only source as unresolved in a specific way. Fodor & Piattelli-Palmarini claim the *conceptual* argument of Part Two is fatal — selection-for is intensional, counterfactuals decide trait-individuation, and a mindless local process cannot be sensitive to counterfactuals — while conceding that the *empirical* argument of Part One reaches only a stand-off: the biologists they cite largely still endorse natural selection, read the same evo-devo and epigenetic results as compatible with or supportive of it, and the authors offer no alternative mechanism ("we don't know what the mechanism of evolution is… nobody knows"). Their residual positive claim is deflationary: where adaptationist explanations work, they work as *historical narratives*, case by case (see the companion entry). Nothing in the corpus states the adaptationist rejoinder in its own voice, so this entry's "positions" are the critique and the replies the critics themselves chose to answer. The critique must therefore be cited as *Fodor & Piattelli-Palmarini's argument*, not as a result about natural selection.

connections.title: Historical Explanation and Narrative
connections.text: [Historical Explanation and Narrative](historical-explanation-and-narrative.md) — the book's other major claim: that the adaptationist explanations which succeed are plausible historical narratives rather than law-subsumptions, with everything that follows for prediction, retrodiction, and the very idea of a theory of evolution (or of history).

The problem of induction (epistemology slice) — a structural cousin: there, no law and no experience justifies the step to the unobserved; here, the authors argue there are no laws of selection to justify the step from "selected" to "selected-for".

arrows-theorem-and-the-possibility-of-so.title: Arrow's Theorem and the Possibility of Social Choice
arrows-theorem-and-the-possibility-of-so.aka: Arrow's impossibility theorem; the General Possibility Theorem; the problem of preference aggregation
arrows-theorem-and-the-possibility-of-so.note: both condition-bookkeepings kept distinct; Sen and Maskin replies
arrows-theorem-and-the-possibility-of-so.question: Democracy promises to turn many individual preferences into one collective decision. But what exactly should the conversion rule be — and can any rule be *fair*? Kenneth Arrow asked the question with unusual precision (1951): define a rule that takes any set of individual preference rankings over social alternatives and returns a single social ranking, and require of it only conditions that each look like common sense. His theorem is that, once there are three or more alternatives, no such rule exists: every rule meeting the other conditions is either imposed on the voters or is one person's dictatorship. This entry states the theorem only as precisely as its sources state it, and tracks the three escape routes the literature in this corpus actually pursues.
arrows-theorem-and-the-possibility-of-so.ninety: Kenneth Arrow's impossibility theorem claims there is no voting system that can choose between more than two candidates and satisfy all of our desirability criteria. The lecture proves a simpler single-winner version first: take three voters whose rankings form a cycle — each candidate beats one rival and loses to the other, so there is no Condorcet winner. Now require a system to respect the Condorcet-win criterion (a candidate who beats every other head-to-head must win) and independence of irrelevant alternatives (switching how a voter ranks two candidates must not change the outcome between other pairs). By sliding each voter, one at a time, into profiles where exactly one candidate is the Condorcet winner, the proof shows each candidate in turn *cannot* win the cyclic profile — so the system sometimes produces no winner at all. Arrow's own theorem is then stated, not proved: for systems outputting a full social ranking, no system satisfies unrestricted domain, unrestricted range, the Pareto condition, non-dictatorship, and independence of irrelevant alternatives. The stakes the lecture draws: either fair systems are confined to two choices, or one of the "obvious" criteria has to go. (Distilled from the Carneades lectures: [Arrow's Impossibility Theorem (The Problem of the Third Party)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GCX7gafg0xI), series introduction [Do Third Parties Destroy Democracy?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b_khUtnvhoY).)

videos.title: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem (The Problem of the Third Party)

positions.name: The problem as Arrow poses it (Arrow, *Social Choice and Individual Values*, chs. I–III)

blocks.text: "In a capitalist democracy there are essentially two methods by which social choices can be made: voting… and the market mechanism." Arrow studies the first. Two ground rules shape everything: preferences are *ordinal* rankings only, and — ch. II's foundational exclusion — interpersonal comparisons of utility are not available, so no rule may use intensities or add utilities across persons (the Benthamite sum of utilities is examined in ch. III and set aside for exactly this reason).

blocks.label: Definitions and conditions
blocks.source: Arrow, ch. III — a formalization, labelled as such
blocks.text: A *social welfare function* is "a process or rule which, for each set of individual orderings R₁…Rₙ for alternative social states (one ordering for each individual), states a corresponding social ordering of alternative social states, R," where the social ordering must itself be a genuine ordering (connected and transitive). Arrow imposes five conditions, "of course value judgments," taken together to express "citizens' sovereignty and rationality":

1. **Free triple / range of orderings** — there is a set of three alternatives that individuals are free to order in any way, and the function must still deliver a social ordering (the germ of *unrestricted domain*).
2. **Positive association** — if an alternative rises, or stays, in every individual's ordering and nothing else changes, it does not fall in the social ordering.

3. **Independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA)** — the social choice from any set of alternatives depends only on individual orderings *within* that set (Arrow's illustration: a candidate's death mid-election should change the outcome only by deleting his name from every ballot).
4. **Non-imposition** — the function is not *imposed*: no pair of alternatives has its social ranking fixed in advance, whatever all individuals prefer.
5. **Non-dictatorship** — there is no individual whose strict preference between any pair is always society's, regardless of everyone else's orderings.

positions.name: The theorem (Arrow, ch. V — stated as printed, with its companion interpretation)

blocks.label: Theorem
blocks.source: Arrow, ch. V, Theorem 2, "General Possibility Theorem"
blocks.text: "If there are at least three alternatives which the members of the society are free to order in any way, then every social welfare function satisfying Conditions 2 and 3 and yielding a social ordering [satisfying the consistency axioms] must be either imposed or dictatorial." (The extraction's statement prints "Conditions 2 and 8"; the chapter's own proof summary confirms the content: given positive association, IIA, and freedom to order three alternatives, "either Condition 4 or Condition 5 must be violated.") Arrow's own gloss, ch. V: "If we exclude the possibility of interpersonal comparisons of utility, then the only methods of passing from individual tastes to social preferences which will be satisfactory and which will be defined for a wide range of sets of individual orderings are either imposed or dictatorial."

blocks.label: The contrast case
blocks.source: Arrow, ch. V, Theorem 1
blocks.text: with exactly **two** alternatives, majority decision satisfies the conditions and always yields a social ordering. Impossibility begins at three — the formal root of the lecture series' question whether third parties destroy democracy.

blocks.label: The modern four-condition form
blocks.source: Pattanaik's Introduction to book 036
blocks.text: with at least three distinct social states and finitely many individuals, *no social welfare function simultaneously satisfies unrestricted domain, the Pareto principle, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and nondictatorship.* Pattanaik notes why the result unsettles: the qualifications "are not particularly restrictive, and… each of the four conditions seems to have some prima facie plausibility," giving the theorem "the flavor of a paradox." (The Pareto principle — if everybody strictly prefers x to y, society ranks x above y — is the welfare form of Arrow's positive-association/citizens'-sovereignty conditions; the formulations differ in bookkeeping, and this entry does not merge them.)

positions.name: Escape route 1: restrict the domain (Arrow, chs. V–VII; the lecture on avoiding Arrow)

blocks.text: Arrow himself indicates the first exit at the end of ch. V: give up the demand that the rule work for *every* profile of orderings — suppose individual orderings are known in advance to satisfy restrictions, and find rules satisfactory on that restricted range. Chs. VI–VII develop this (conditions on preference scales; similarity/near-unanimity of orderings as a basis for social judgment). The Carneades lecture [Avoiding Arrow's Impossibility](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WCoNvN9MDDQ) walks the same ground from the third-party advocate's side: each criterion — unrestricted domain, unrestricted range, always-a-winner, Pareto, non-dictatorship, IIA — is one the advocate must argue is worth less than having more than two choices; attempts to *strengthen* domain/range instead (demanding that off-ballot candidates be choosable) only make impossibility worse, since they tighten the requirements.

positions.name: Escape route 2: enrich the information (Sen)

blocks.label: Position
blocks.source: Sen, "The Informational Basis of Social Choice," book 036, ch. 15 in extraction
blocks.text: "Any procedure of social choice makes use of some types of information and ignores others" — majority decision uses votes but ignores intensities of preference, social standing, "prosperity or penury." Impossibility is relative to an informational basis: Arrow's construction *defines away* cardinal and interpersonally comparable information before the proof begins. A procedure permitted richer information is not bound by the result in the same way. Sen's lecture in the same volume adds the political edge: Arrow's axioms also do not accommodate *liberty* — the rights of minorities against majorities — recalling Mill on "busybodies": "The importance of liberty may demand going against the objections of numerous 'busybodies.' … It is not accommodated in Arrow's axioms either."

positions.name: Escape route 3: majority rule is better than the theorem suggests (Maskin; Dasgupta & Maskin)

blocks.label: Position
blocks.source: Maskin lecture, book 036; Dasgupta & Maskin, "On the Robustness of Majority Rule," book 036
blocks.text: the pessimistic reading — no good election method — is "too strong a conclusion." Define majority rule in Condorcet's sense: the winner beats every other candidate head-to-head. Majority rule satisfies the Pareto property, anonymity ("one person–one vote"), neutrality, and IIA — indeed Dasgupta and Maskin's abstract states it satisfies those axioms plus (generic) decisiveness "over a larger class of preference domains than (essentially) any other voting rule. Hence, in this sense, it is the most robust voting rule." Maskin's conclusion: "using the criteria [Arrow] laid out, there is a sense in which we can't do better than majority rule after all." The honest caveat travels with the claim, in Maskin's own footnote: when Condorcet-paradox rankings do arise, majority rule delivers no winner, and practice needs a tie-breaking rule (he suggests plurality) — frequency and cost of the cyclic case are where the argument moves next.

thought.name: The Condorcet cycle
thought.text: (lecture [Arrow's Impossibility Theorem](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GCX7gafg0xI)). Three voters rank three candidates in rotation (the lecture's instance uses Trump, Clinton, Johnson): majority prefers the first to the second, the second to the third, and the third to the first. Every candidate both beats and loses to another; there is no Condorcet winner. Meant to show the failure is not in any particular rule but in the profile itself: pairwise majority — the most natural aggregation of all — is intransitive here, and Arrow's theorem generalizes the embarrassment to *every* rule meeting mild conditions. Pressures: unrestricted domain (exclude such profiles?) and IIA (the lecture's proof turns on it).

thought.name: The candidate who dies
thought.text: (Arrow, ch. III). An election is held; before the count, a candidate dies. Intuition says: delete his name from every ballot and recount. A rule whose winner changes for any other reason violates IIA. Meant to make IIA look undeniable — which is what makes its role in the impossibility worth scrutinizing (Sen and the Borda count, which violates IIA and is still widely used, are the counterweights in our sources: Arrow's own ch. III shows the rank-order method's IIA failure by example).

ladder.text: the Carneades third-party series — [Do Third Parties Destroy Democracy?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b_khUtnvhoY) (roadmap: preference profiles, majority vs plurality, desirability criteria), then [Arrow's Impossibility Theorem](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GCX7gafg0xI) and [Avoiding Arrow's Impossibility](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WCoNvN9MDDQ).

ladder.label: Survey
ladder.text: Pattanaik's Introduction and the Sen and Maskin lectures in Maskin & Sen, *The Arrow Impossibility Theorem* (book 036) — the four-condition statement and the two main replies.

ladder.label: Primary
ladder.text: Arrow, *Social Choice and Individual Values* (book 037), ch. III (the five conditions) and ch. V (Theorems 1 and 2 and Arrow's interpretation).

ladder.label: Full treatment
ladder.text: book 037 entire (compensation principle, ch. IV; domain restrictions, chs. VI–VII; the 1963 literature survey, ch. VIII) and book 036's supplemental papers (Sen on informational bases; Dasgupta & Maskin on majority rule).

arrows-theorem-and-the-possibility-of-so.verdict: The theorem itself is a proof and is not in dispute in these sources; everything live is in the response. Arrow's own response was domain restriction — possibility returns when profiles are constrained (chs. VI–VII) — and the two-alternative case was never impossible (majority decision works). Sen reframes the result as a theorem about a deliberately impoverished informational basis and points social choice toward richer inputs (and toward liberty, which the axioms omit). Maskin argues the practical moral is nearly optimistic: majority rule is the most robust rule available, with cyclic profiles as a tie-breaking problem rather than a refutation. The lecture series leaves the third-party question at the criterion level: a defender of multi-candidate elections must say *which* desirability criterion to surrender — that, and not a counterexample (Arrow proved none can exist), is the honest shape of the remaining argument.

connections.title: Democracy and the Voting Paradoxes
