prose: # Book map — 005: Gary L. Hardcastle & George A. Reisch (eds.), *Bullshit and Philosophy: Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time* (Open Court, 2006)

chapters.title: On Bullshitmania
chapters.note: — George A. Reisch & Gary L. Hardcastle [file ch05]. Why a tiny 1986 essay became a 2005 bestseller: an Iraq-war-era culture of spin, fabricated memoirs (Frey, "J.T. Leroy"), blurred advertising, and scientific fraud made Frankfurt's warning — bullshit as indifference to truth, corrosive of the true/false distinction itself — feel prophetic. Philosophy's own anti-bullshit lineage: Socrates, Descartes, and Hume's "commit it then to the flames" as earlier purges of sophistry and illusion.

groups.heading: Part I — To Shoot the Bull? (Rethinking and Responding to Bullshit)

chapters.title: 1. Scott Kimbrough — On Letting It Slide
chapters.note: [file ch07, "Bullshit and Truth"] ★. Frankfurt's puzzle — why are we *more* tolerant of bullshit than of lying, if bullshit is the greater enemy of truth? — answered socially: politeness and the faked apology (via William Ian Miller's *Faking It*) sacrifice truth for peace, so on Frankfurt's definition "bullshit constitutes the greater part of civility"; entertainment value; and respect for the ends bullshitters serve (selling, recruiting, fund-raising), with contempt reserved for the "suckers" who fall for it. Intolerable bullshit: bad reasons given for decisions that affect us (the passed-over promotion; Orwell on political language). **Bullshit and self-deception**: bullshit can be produced *unintentionally* — the self-deceived talk-radio fan — contra Frankfurt's intentionalism. **Blameless bullshit**: Newton's alchemy is bullshit now, though Newton is no bullshitter; the charge's function is to license dismissal, and its real target is *method* — bullshit results from "lame methods of justification," adopted intentionally, self-deceptively, or blamelessly. Conclusion: bullshit cannot be eradicated, only recognised and "restricted to truly justifiable uses"; wholesale indifference to truth is never justifiable, since even effective bullshitting presupposes a lively concern for truth.

chapters.title: 2. Consuelo Preti — A Defense of Common Sense
chapters.note: [file ch08] ★ (supporting). Both Frankfurt and Cohen omit the third element: the *audience*. Bullshit needs our compliance — it sells us significance and flatters our desire to feel important; academic bullshit (including bullshit in academic decision-making) works the same way. Resistance is therefore partly ours to supply: G. E. Moore as the model "resolute carer" about truth — the method of "What *exactly* do you mean?" Bullshit's paradox: it must make itself matter to us, so if what matters to us is the true/false distinction, bullshit is put "on a short leash."

chapters.title: 3. George A. Reisch — The Pragmatics of Bullshit, Intelligently Designed
chapters.note: [file ch09] ★. A rival definition. Frankfurt's puzzle is an artefact of *semantics*: bullshitters do not sin against truth at all — they sin against *pragmatics*, cloaking one engagement inside another. The case study is Intelligent Design: its advocates are not indifferent to truth (they care intensely about their own truths, about culture and "modernism"); what they conceal is an *agenda* — an evangelical programme inside a science-education programme. Bullshit = the orchestration of two concerns, one used as cover for the other; hence we tolerate it (lies thwart needs we already have; bullshit tries to *create* needs, and fails without a gullible audience; its dupes are often sincere). **Purism**: properly defined, there is much less bullshit than casual usage suggests — bad news and false claims are not bullshit unless the two-engagement structure is present.

chapters.title: 4. Kenneth A. Taylor — Bullshit and the Foibles of the Human Mind, or: What the Masters of the Dark Arts Know
chapters.note: [file ch10]. Public discourse is debased by bullshit, propaganda, spin, and lies — but purveyors "cannot sell what we do not buy": the fault lies partly in enduring cognitive foibles (framing effects and their kin), now expertly exploited, with vastly greater reach. Remedies on two fronts: education (distaste for dogma, re-framing skills, appetite for disquieting evidence) and reconfiguring privileged access to the means of persuasion.

chapters.title: 5. Sara Bernal — Bullshit and Personality
chapters.note: [file ch11] ★. Against Frankfurt: the typical bullshitter is *not* indifferent to truth but is strongly connected to it "via a desire to obscure a specific part of it" — her **target**, which she may know clearly, dimly, or not at all (unconscious motives; split-brain confabulation as evidence such motives operate). Two modes: (a) *indirect implication of falsehood* (Newport's "alive with pleasure") and (b) *distraction* (the Niger yellowcake story). Unlike the liar she never denies the target directly; conscious bullshitting differs from lying only in method, unconscious bullshitting in more. Applied to the DSM-IV personality disorders, whose distorted social perception supplies easy targets and whose bullshitting helps ruin their relationships. The threat: because bullshitting can be unconscious, it provokes less conscience than lying and is therefore easier to make a habit of.

chapters.title: 6. Alan Richardson — Performing Bullshit and the Post-Sincere Condition
chapters.note: [file ch12]. Opens with a parody mission statement, its subject. Frankfurt's Pascal/Wittgenstein anecdote turned back on his account ("shitty attitudes"); bullshit as performance and as a standing condition of institutional life (the corporate mission statement) once sincerity is drained out — "the world as will to bullshit." Remedies are thin: the Jon Stewart gambit (openly made-up news that reveals truth better than "serious" sources — humour as "the sincerest form of unconcern for the truth"), or the hard work of writing institutional statements one actually means.

chapters.title: 7. Cornelis de Waal — The Importance of Being Earnest: A Pragmatic Approach to Bullshitting
chapters.note: [file ch13] ★ (supporting). Names the volume's two schools: Cohen's *structuralist* (bullshit as product) vs Frankfurt's *intentionalist* (bullshit as process). De Waal's own frame: bullshitting as failed or fake *inquiry* — passing claims off as the product of inquiry that was never honestly undertaken — governed by an **epistemic imperative**. Hence some bullshitting is permissible: where a competing purpose (easing an interaction — "It's nice to see you!") rightly overrules the imperative, or where conclusions don't matter and the enjoyment of the game does.

groups.heading: Part II — The Bull by the Horns (Defining Bullshit)

chapters.title: 8. G. A. Cohen — Deeper into Bullshit
chapters.note: [file ch15] ★. The volume's philosophical centre of gravity. The OED already distinguishes two senses: bullshit as *insincere talk* (Frankfurt's — the "bull" wears the trousers: bullshit is whatever a bullshitter produces) and bullshit as *nonsense/rubbish* (Cohen's — the "shit" wears the trousers: a property of the output, whatever the producer's state of mind). Frankfurt's "essence" claim overreaches: he characterises one kind only. Even for that kind, his lying/bullshitting contrast is malconstructed — he identifies the liar by his *goal* (misleading about reality) but the bullshitter by his *tactic* (asserting without caring), so paradigm bullshitters (advertisers) turn out, on his account, to be lying whenever they mislead. Cohen's own kind: **unclarifiable unclarity** — discourse that cannot be rendered clear in anything recognisable as a version of what was said (test: adding or subtracting a negation changes nothing about its plausibility), minus the saving virtue of suggestiveness that acquits good poetry. Bullshit as *product*, not process: polemic should target the visible product, not the invisible process — an honest person can utter bullshit; a Frankfurt-bullshitter can accidentally talk sense.

chapters.title: 9. Gary L. Hardcastle — The Unity of Bullshit
chapters.note: [file ch16]. Is there one phenomenon here? Via Carnap and the Vienna Circle (bullshit as what logical analysis eliminates) and Laura Penny: bullshit is one part *tool* (language amenable to misuse) and one part *intention* (to put something over by means of it). Since intentions cannot be eradicated, control the tool: the language is held in common, and each speaker bears responsibility for its misuse "in our presence."

chapters.title: 10. Andrew Aberdein — Raising the Tone: Definition, Bullshit, and the Definition of Bullshit
chapters.note: [file ch17] ★ (supporting). Frankfurt's innovation recast as naming a linguistic misbehaviour, **semantic negligence** (against the liar's semantic *deception*). Through Frege on sense and reference to *persuasive definition* (PD) — redefining a loaded term while trading on its tone. Verdict: Frankfurt's definition *is* PD (it changes the sense, hence the reference, of 'bullshit' — kindly "help is on its way" cases fall inside it; Cohen's cases fall outside), but PD is malign only when semantically negligent; Frankfurt argues explicitly for his departures from usage, so the definition is PD but diligent — though Cohen's omissions remain "harder to defend."

chapters.title: 11. Hans Maes & Katrien Schaubroeck — Different Kinds and Aspects of Bullshit
chapters.note: [file ch18] ★. The volume's best single survey of Frankfurt: two essential ingredients — indifference to truth *and* pretence (the bullshitter misrepresents his *enterprise*, not the facts; hence bull sessions, which lack pretence, are excluded by Frankfurt) — and the conclusion that bullshit is "a greater enemy of the truth than lies are." Two revisions: (i) **pretence is not essential** — Fania Pascal's "I feel just like a dog that has been run over" is bullshit (for Wittgenstein) with no deceit in sight, and an openly truth-indifferent politician would still be bullshitting; Frankfurt's bullshit/bull-session distinction is artificial. (ii) **bullshit is not always bad** — banter, wit, and polite formulae (Nagel: "How nice to see you" deceives no one, because the convention is common knowledge) are benign and socially load-bearing; this, not a mystery, explains our benign attitude to much bullshit. Then a **third kind** that neither Frankfurt nor Cohen covers: *pseudoscience* — its producers are typically sincere truth-seekers (not Frankfurt-indifferent) whose claims are often perfectly clear (not Cohen-unclarifiable); its marks are insensitivity to evidence and fallacious reasoning.

groups.heading: Part III — It's All Around Us (Bullshit in Politics, Science, Education, and the Law)

chapters.title: 12. Mark Evans — The Republic of Bullshit: On the Dumbing-Up of Democracy
chapters.note: [file ch20]. The **Frankfurt thesis**: democracy itself *requires* citizens to hold and voice opinions on everything, hence structurally encourages bullshitting ("unavoidable whenever circumstances require someone to talk without knowing what he is talking about"). Weighed against a "cynicism thesis"; both partly right. Citizens' own bullshit (not only politicians') degrades political perception; philosophy can inoculate only if it is the truth-aiming kind — fashionable truth-disparaging philosophy is itself part of the clog.

chapters.title: 13. Vanessa Neumann — Political Bullshit and the Stoic Story of Self
chapters.note: [file ch21]. A third context beyond Frankfurt's utterances and Cohen's texts: the *mechanism* of bullshit. Political bullshit works by supplying **stories** that shape feelings and confer identity ("spreading democracy"), bypassing the faculties of reason and debate; its pull is that it makes audiences players in a narrative. Counter-strategy borrowed from Cohen: identify the content in order to eradicate the process.

chapters.title: 14. Heather Douglas — Bullshit at the Interface of Science and Policy
chapters.note: [file ch22]. Two kinds at the science–policy interface: bullshit of the **isolated fact** (cherry-picking one fact or study — climate records — while ignoring the body of evidence) and bullshit of **universal standards** (dismissing good science for failing an impossible standard of proof). The second can be permanently undermined by dropping the fiction of universal standards and arguing instead about strength of evidence and risks of error; the first persists wherever dishonest operators find an audience.

chapters.title: 15. David J. Tietge — Rhetoric Is Not Bullshit
chapters.note: [file ch23]. 'Rhetoric' has been unfairly collapsed into 'bullshit.' Rhetoric *utens* vs rhetoric as methods for analysing texts; postmodernism's bad reputation examined. The vast grey area between Truth and bullshit is rhetoric's domain; rhetorical education (real rhetorical situations, commonplace books) is the citizen's navigation skill for it.

chapters.title: 16. Steve Fuller — Just Bullshit
chapters.note: [file ch24]. The dissenting chapter. The bullshit-detector's stance converts an epistemic attitude into a moral virtue ("reality can be known only by the right sort of person"); bullshit, charitably read, is sophistry — an acknowledgement that truth alone may not defeat an artfully presented claim; its closest theological kin is hypocrisy, which makes bullshitters cognitive *equals* of liars, not truth-indifferents. Bullshit as a call to open-mindedness and as "deferred epistemic gratification"; Wittgenstein as detector-or-bullshitter; closing on science in the courtroom (*McLean v. Arkansas* praised for a neutral standard; *Kitzmiller* criticised for a "customized" one) — justice as cutting through the bullshit on *both* sides.

prose: # Book map — 006: Bertrand Russell, *The Problems of Philosophy* (1912)

chapters.title: Preface
chapters.note: [file ch04]. Russell confines himself to problems where something positive and constructive can be said; accordingly the theory of knowledge takes more space than metaphysics. He acknowledges G. E. Moore (sense-data and physical objects) and J. M. Keynes (probability and induction).

chapters.title: I. Appearance and Reality
chapters.note: [stub ch05, text ch06] ★ → *External-World Skepticism*. The table: its colour, shape, and texture vary with viewpoint, light, and instrument, so no appearance is the table as it is in itself; introduces *sense-data* vs the *physical object* and poses the chapter's two questions — is there a real table at all, and if so, what is it like? Berkeley's idealism is introduced as the first serious answer.

chapters.title: II. The Existence of Matter
chapters.note: [stub ch07, text ch08] ★ → *External-World Skepticism*. Descartes' method of systematic doubt, the deceitful demon, and the cogito — with Russell's caveat that only particular experiences, not a permanent Self, are certain. Argues we cannot prove objects exist independently, but instinctive belief plus the simplicity of the realist hypothesis (the cat that grows hungry while unobserved) justify accepting the external world.

chapters.title: III. The Nature of Matter
chapters.note: [stub ch09, text ch10]. Granting that matter exists, what is it? Works through the physicist's picture (space, time, motion, atoms and their fields) and the gap between that inferred structure and anything we experience.

chapters.title: IV. Idealism
chapters.note: [stub ch11, text ch12]. Idealism defined as the doctrine that whatever exists, or can be known to exist, is in some sense mental; examines Berkeley's grounds for it and where Russell thinks they fail. Supports the skepticism entry's idealism section.

chapters.title: V. Knowledge by Acquaintance and Knowledge by Description
chapters.note: [stub ch13, text ch14] ★ → *Gettier and the Analysis of Knowledge*. Two kinds of knowledge of things: acquaintance (sense-data, memory, introspection, probably the Self, and universals) versus knowledge by description ("the physical object which causes such-and-such sense-data"); ends with the principle that every proposition we understand is composed wholly of constituents with which we are acquainted.

chapters.title: VI. On Induction
chapters.note: [stub ch15, text ch16] ★ → *The Problem of Induction*. The sunrise and the chicken; the uniformity of nature; the two-part inductive principle stated for single cases and for general laws; the verdict that experience can neither prove nor disprove the principle.

chapters.title: VII. On Our Knowledge of General Principles
chapters.note: [stub ch17, text ch18] ★ → *The Problem of Induction*. Self-evident logical principles (the laws of thought; "whatever follows from a true proposition is true"); the empiricist–rationalist controversy settled in favour of a priori knowledge that experience elicits but does not prove; the inductive principle placed among the probability-yielding principles of inference.

chapters.title: VIII. How A Priori Knowledge Is Possible
chapters.note: [stub ch19, text ch20]. Kant's critical philosophy and the synthetic a priori, with Russell's account of why Kant thought such knowledge possible and where the explanation needs supplementing. Feeds the future a-priori-knowledge problem entry.

chapters.title: IX. The World of Universals
chapters.note: [stub ch21, text ch22]. Plato's theory of ideas; relations shown to be universals with a kind of being distinct from physical objects, minds, and sense-data. Feeds the universals problem (metaphysics).

chapters.title: X. On Our Knowledge of Universals
chapters.note: [stub ch23, text ch24]. Universals, like particulars, divide into those known by acquaintance (qualities given in sense-data), those known by description, and those unknown; how a priori truths about universals are known.

chapters.title: XI. On Intuitive Knowledge
chapters.note: [stub ch25, text ch26]. Whether beliefs need proof or probability; intuitive knowledge as the un-inferred base, and self-evidence as its mark — the topic ch. XIII develops into two kinds of self-evidence. Feeds the analysis-of-knowledge cluster.

chapters.title: XII. Truth and Falsehood
chapters.note: [stub ch27, text ch28] ★ → *Gettier and the Analysis of Knowledge* (background: the "true" in justified true belief). Three requisites for a theory of truth; coherence rejected as a *definition* (though retained as a test); truth defined as correspondence, via the multiple-relation theory of judgement (Othello, Desdemona, loving, Cassio).

chapters.title: XIII. Knowledge, Error, and Probable Opinion
chapters.note: [stub ch29, text ch30] ★ → *Gettier and the Analysis of Knowledge*. True belief is not knowledge when deduced from a false belief (the Balfour/Campbell-Bannerman case) or by fallacy; derivative vs intuitive knowledge; degrees of self-evidence; knowledge shading into probable opinion, with coherence as a criterion that raises probability but never yields certainty.

chapters.title: XIV. The Limits of Philosophical Knowledge
chapters.note: [stub ch31, text ch32] ★ → *External-World Skepticism* (closing stance). Against Hegel's a priori metaphysics of the Whole and against complete scepticism alike: no argument can compel someone who stands wholly outside knowledge, but scepticism of that kind is unreasonable; philosophy is the criticism, not the destruction, of knowledge.

chapters.title: XV. The Value of Philosophy
chapters.note: [stub ch33, text ch34]. Philosophy's value is not in definite answers but in the questions: it enlarges our conception of what is possible, diminishes dogmatic confidence, and keeps alive speculative interest in the universe.

prose: # Book map — 008: Douglas R. Hofstadter, *Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid* (1979)

chapters.title: Introduction: A Musico-Logical Offering
chapters.note: [in ch17 stratum / Overview, O]. Bach's *Musical Offering* as the book's theme: self-reference and interplay of levels in Bach, Escher, and Gödel; a brief history of logic and paradox; mechanical reasoning and the AI question.

chapters.title: Ch. I: The MU-puzzle
chapters.note: ★ [ch18, R] → *Gödelian Self-Reference and the Limits of Formal Systems*; *Arguments, Validity, and Soundness* (background). The MIU-system (Post production system): strings, the four rules, the **Requirement of Formality**; **theorems** as strings *produced* by rules (vs Theorems, statements *proved*); axioms, rules of production/inference, derivations; working **inside vs outside the system** (M-mode / I-mode / U-mode); **decision procedures** — a test for theoremhood guaranteed to terminate; axioms, unlike theorems, must have one. The chapter file ends with Carroll's *Two-Part Invention* ("What the Tortoise Said to Achilles"): the infinite regress of having to add each rule of inference as a further premise.

chapters.title: Ch. II: Meaning and Form in Mathematics
chapters.note: ★ [ch19, R in key sections] → *Gödelian Self-Reference…*; *Semantic Analysis and the Clarity of Meaning* (connection). The pq-system: apparently meaningless symbols acquire meaning when an **isomorphism** (information-preserving mapping) between theorems and true additions is perceived; meaning in a formal system is *passive* — it licenses reading strings, never creating new theorems beyond the rules (the Requirement of Formality again). *Sonata for Unaccompanied Achilles* (figure/ground).

chapters.title: Ch. III: Figure and Ground
chapters.note: [ch20, O]. Figure/ground in art vs theorems/nontheorems; recursively enumerable vs recursive sets. *Contracrostipunctus* — the dialogue carrying paraphrases of Gödel's construction ("for each record player, a record it cannot play").

chapters.title: Ch. IV: Consistency, Completeness, and Geometry
chapters.note: [ch21, O + opening]. How symbols acquire meaning; Euclidean vs non-Euclidean geometry and "undefined terms"; consistency of rival geometries. *Little Harmonic Labyrinth* (nested stories).

chapters.title: Ch. V: Recursive Structures and Processes
chapters.note: [inside ch21, O]. Recursion across music, language, geometry, mathematics, programs. *Canon by Intervallic Augmentation*.

chapters.title: Ch. VI: The Location of Meaning
chapters.note: [ch22, O]. Meaning divided among coded message, decoder, receiver: DNA, undeciphered inscriptions, records in space; is meaning inherent or manufactured by the interpreting mechanism?

chapters.title: Ch. VII: The Propositional Calculus
chapters.note: ★ [ch23, R in key sections] → *Arguments, Validity, and Soundness*. A formal system for "and," negation, implication: formation rules for well-formed strings; Rule of Joining, Rule of Separation, Double-Tilde Rule; the **Fantasy Rule** (assume x, derive y, conclude <x⊃y>) and the Carry-Over Rule — the system's machinery doing what Achilles could not make the word "and" do for the Tortoise. Examples are Zen sentences ("Zentences").

chapters.title: Ch. VIII: Typographical Number Theory (TNT)
chapters.note: [ch24, O + opening]. The Propositional Calculus extended to number theory: rigid symbol manipulation for arithmetical reasoning; Gödel-numbering prepared; indirect self-reference in the *Crab Canon*.

chapters.title: Ch. IX: Mumon and Gödel
chapters.note: [ch25, O]. Zen and the philosophy of mathematics; **Gödel-numbering** introduced and a first pass through the Incompleteness Theorem.

chapters.title: Ch. X: Levels of Description, and Computer Systems
chapters.note: [ch26, O]. Gödel's string G and a Bach fugue as things understandable on several levels; hardware/software, ants and ant colonies. *Ant Fugue* (holism vs reductionism).

chapters.title: Ch. XI: Brains and Thoughts
chapters.note: [inside ch27, O]. Brains as symbol systems; active subsystems ("symbols") as the level at which minds might be mapped. *English French German Suite*.

chapters.title: Ch. XII: Minds and Thoughts
chapters.note: [ch28, O]. Isomorphism (or partial isomorphism) between two brains at the symbol level.

chapters.title: Ch. XIII: BlooP and FlooP and GlooP
chapters.note: [ch29, O]. Three toy computer languages for primitive vs general recursivity — the machinery that will make "proof-pair" a testable property in Ch. XIV. *Air on G's String* (quining: how a sentence can reproduce itself).

chapters.title: Ch. XIV: On Formally Undecidable Propositions of TNT and Related Systems
chapters.note: ★ [ch30, R] → *Gödelian Self-Reference and the Limits of Formal Systems*. The proof in intuitive form, built from two ideas: **Gödel-numbering** (TNT strings can speak about TNT strings — introspection via proof-pairs, a primitive recursive and hence TNT-representable property) and the **diagonal focusing trick** ("arithmoquining": substituting a formula's own Gödel number into itself). Result: the string G whose interpretation is "G is not a theorem of TNT"; neither G nor ~G is a theorem (if TNT is consistent); **Gödel's Second Theorem** — "TNT is consistent" is expressible in TNT but provable there only if TNT is inconsistent; TNT is ω-incomplete; the two extensions (add G, or add ~G with its "supernatural numbers") and non-standard number theory; Hilbert's Tenth Problem.

chapters.title: Ch. XV: Jumping out of the System
chapters.note: ★ [ch31, R in main sections] → *Gödelian Self-Reference…*. The construction reapplied to every extension (TNT+G, axiom schemas): **essential incompleteness**; the three conditions under which any consistent system is vulnerable (expressiveness, proof-pair representability, self-reference capacity — the "critical mass" passage); **Lucas's argument** that Gödel's theorem refutes mechanism and Hofstadter's rebuttal begun (the "Gödelizing operator," Escher's *Dragon*, the limits of intelligent systems — we too cannot Gödelize arbitrarily complex systems on demand).

chapters.title: Ch. XVI: Self-Ref and Self-Rep
chapters.note: [ch32, O]. Mechanisms of self-reference in sentences, and of self-reproduction in DNA and machines, compared.

chapters.title: Ch. XVII: Church, Turing, Tarski, and Others
chapters.note: [ch33, O]. The book's thesis stated: every aspect of thinking as a high-level description of a system governed at low level by simple, even formal, rules; computability and the limits of formalisation.

chapters.title: Ch. XVIII: Artificial Intelligence: Retrospects
chapters.note: [ch34, O]. Turing's 1950 article and the first decades of AI.

chapters.title: Ch. XIX: Artificial Intelligence: Prospects
chapters.note: [ch35, duplicated at ch44; O]. Counterfactuals and "almost" situations; how thought lets some features "slip" — the flexibility formal systems lack.

chapters.title: Ch. XX: Strange Loops, or Tangled Hierarchies
chapters.note: [ch36, O]. The closing chapter: Strange Loops, tangled hierarchies, and whether machines can possess originality.

prose: # Book map — 010: catalogued as Mark Day, *The Philosophy of History: An Introduction* — extraction contains a different book

**State of the extraction itself.** Ironically good: 12 files, ~124,000 words, no stubs, no truncated chapters, no corrupted files. Front matter and back matter (an index) are present. Chapter titles in the file names match the book's own chapter titles. What follows is a map of Dolphin's book on its own terms — it is a work of geoscience *education research* that uses history and philosophy of science as teaching material, which is the only sense in which it belongs anywhere near this slice.

chapters.title: Front Matter
chapters.note: [file ch01]. Series page for *Science: Philosophy, History and Education* (a series devoted to leveraging history and philosophy of science to improve science education), title page, and the book's opening apparatus. Author: Glenn Dolphin.

chapters.title: Part I — Designing the Course with Teaching the Nature of Science in Mind
chapters.note: [divider + introduction, file ch02]. Frames the book's project: an introductory geology course for non-science majors (200–300 students) redesigned as an exercise in instructional "design engineering" — understand the problem, delineate constraints, implement strategies, measure outcomes, iterate — with geoscience literacy as the public-facing rationale.

chapters.title: 1. Earth Science Education: Rationales and Current State
chapters.note: [file ch03]. Why geoscience matters (the earth system, natural hazards, resources, soils, water) and why it is neglected in science literacy. The sections nearest to this KB's concerns are §1.3, on the role of history and the nature of science (NOS) in geoscience education — characterising NOS for science education, the "family resemblance" approach, "questions rather than tenets" — and §1.4, on using *history* to teach NOS and on helping students "think like a geologist", with case studies as the vehicle. §1.5 lays out the book's structure. This is philosophy of science at one remove: NOS scholarship summarised for course design, not argued.

chapters.title: 2. Transformative Teaching: From Educator to Design Engineer
chapters.note: [file ch04]. The design-engineering model of teaching: surveying the educational landscape and its constraints, interactivity and interpretation, ideation and prototyping of strategies, classroom experiments. Education theory and course logistics; no philosophy-of-history content.

chapters.title: 3. Biographies of Three Different Concepts
chapters.note: [file ch05]. The book's substantive core, and the only chapter with extended history-of-science narrative. Dolphin teaches the course as three braided *historical narratives* ("biographies" of concepts), each framed by an essential question: (I) *the earth's biography* — "How can we understand the historical nature of the earth?" (§3.2: Steno reading the "signs" in the rocks — superposition, original horizontality, lateral continuity, cross-cutting — and reasoning out an earth history; Hutton's eternal, cyclical earth and uniformitarianism, "the present is the key to the past"; fossils given historical meaning through Anning, Cuvier's fixity of kinds against Lamarck, and Darwin's 1859 synthesis; fossil-based mapping; ice ages — the earth emerges as *historical and contingent*, against Hutton's eternalism); (II) *the age of the earth* (§3.3: bottom-up empiricism, Kelvin-era thermodynamics as a "top-down" approach, and radioactivity transforming the dating game — the discovery of deep time); (III) *developing a theory of the earth* — "Why are there still mountains?" (§3.4: contractionism and permanentism, drifters vs fixists, and the geophysics — seismology, seafloor exploration, geomagnetism — that assembled plate tectonics). §3.1 explains the narrative pedagogy: historical interludes present observations *and competing interpretations* so students decide without hindsight, then inquiry and model-based learning iterate toward the current consensus. This chapter is a competent *retelling* of the history of geology; it advances no philosophical theses of its own about historical explanation, narrative, or objectivity, and cites the history through secondary sources (Rudwick, Repcheck, Cutler).

chapters.title: 4. Transformative Teaching Strategies
chapters.note: [file ch06]. The course's methods in detail: team-based learning as foundation, case/problem-based learning, inquiry activities (visible geology, seismic, seafloor data, age of the earth, earth dynamics), model-based learning, a Wikipedia project highlighting women of geology, and explicit reflective NOS instruction. Of peripheral note for this KB: §4.8.2, "Geology as a Historical and Hermeneutic Science", §4.8.3 on resolving controversy in geology, §4.8.5 on serendipity, and §4.8.6 on prematurity in geologic discovery — the book's closest approach to philosophy of a historical science, in a few pages of teaching commentary.

chapters.title: Part II — Measuring Shifts in Students' Content Knowledge and Nature of Science Understandings
chapters.note: [divider + introduction, file ch07]. Introduces the assessment programme: click-on-diagram questions via a classroom response system, the Geoscience Concept Inventory (GCI), and the VOSTS survey, administered pre/post.

chapters.title: 5. Measuring Student Learning
chapters.note: [file ch08]. Methods and results for the three instruments of Part II, with discussion. Empirical education research.

chapters.title: 6. Students' Understandings of Science and Scientists
chapters.note: [file ch09]. Qualitative study of how students' views shifted over the course: from "science is situational" to doing science; from routine to creative; scientific knowledge "from an always changing truth to grades of reliability"; scientists "from an idealized to humanized" picture. The chapter in which the extracted book comes closest to epistemological *findings*, though its subject is students' beliefs, not the justification of historical knowledge itself.

chapters.title: 7. Students' Metaphors for Science
chapters.note: [file ch10]. Conceptual-metaphor analysis of student language: science knowledge as moving along a path, as an edifice, as a landscape, as liquid/ocean, as a plant; scientific theory as a puzzle; ideas as objects. Discussion of how such metaphors frame science processes and products.

chapters.title: 8. Concluding Remarks
chapters.note: [file ch11]. Recapitulation: the importance of geoscience education; design engineering and reflective practice; the three narratives; the strategies; the learning measurements; final words on results and on process.

chapters.title: Back Matter
chapters.note: [file ch12]. The book's index only (case studies → Wikipedia). 158 words of index entries; no bibliography file is present in the extraction.

011-what-darwin-got-wrong.title: 011: Jerry Fodor & Massimo Piattelli-Palmarini, *What Darwin Got Wrong* (2010)
011-what-darwin-got-wrong.layer: Book layer · source textbook for the philosophy-of-science-and-history slice. ★ = chapter feeds one of this slice's problem entries.
011-what-darwin-got-wrong.extraction: **Extraction note.** The extracted folder (`data/philosophy_readings/markdown/011 - What Darwin Got Wrong/`) holds 24 files and the text is essentially complete — but the file titles are misleading: most content files are named after a *section heading inside* the chapter they contain ("Conclusion to this chapter", "Rhetorical conclusion", "Environment versus ecological niche") rather than after the chapter itself. The book's own chapter titles and numbering are recoverable in full from the table of contents [files ch04–ch05, two TOC files of 482 words each, not byte-identical]. The map below uses the book's numbering, with extraction file numbers in brackets. Two files are part-divider stubs only (ch09, ch14; 21 words each). The back matter is real: Appendix [ch20], Notes [ch21, ~13,500 words], References [ch22], Index [ch23]. Nothing in the main text is a citation stub, partial, or corrupted. One caution that governs every use of this book in the KB: it is a *polemic* — a two-author critique of adaptationism — not a survey text, and its empirical claims are its authors' selection and construal of the biology literature. Entries built on it present its arguments as its authors' arguments, at their stated strength, together with the caveats the book itself enters.

prose: # Book map — 011: Jerry Fodor & Massimo Piattelli-Palmarini, *What Darwin Got Wrong* (2010)

chapters.title: Epigraph
chapters.note: [file ch03]. Two quotations that set the book's tone: Chomsky (1972) — attributing a development to "natural selection" is safe only so long as we realise "there is no substance to this assertion" — and Darwin's own concession that facts can be adduced for conclusions opposite to his.

chapters.title: Acknowledgements
chapters.note: [file ch06].

chapters.title: Terms of Engagement
chapters.note: [preface; file ch07] ★ → both entries. The book's self-description and its ground rules. Not about God, intelligent design, or creationism: both authors are "outright, card-carrying… atheists" seeking thoroughly naturalistic — mechanical, non-teleological — explanations of evolution. The main contention: "there is something wrong — quite possibly fatally wrong — with the theory of natural selection." The central confusion they allege, stated here in advance: adaptationism infers (2) creatures are *selected for* their adaptive traits from (1) creatures *with* adaptive traits are selected — an invalid inference, "what philosophers call an 'intensional fallacy'". Also announced: the Darwin/Skinner analogy (the objections that killed Skinner's learning theory apply, *mutatis mutandis*, to Darwin's), and the disciplinary complaint that neo-Darwinism is taken as axiomatic in philosophy of mind, semantics, psychology and other export markets of the theory (see Appendix). The authors concede up front that the book is "mostly a work of criticism" and that they do not know how evolution works.

chapters.title: 1. What Kind of Theory Is the Theory of Natural Selection?
chapters.note: [file ch08; its closing pages are the chapter's own summary] ★ → *Selection-For and the Critique of Adaptationism*; *Historical Explanation and Narrative*. Distinguishes the genealogy of species (GS — common descent; accepted without quarrel) from the theory of natural selection (NS — the purported *causal mechanism* of speciation; the book's target). Both NS and Skinner's operant conditioning theory (OT) are presented as black boxes mapping trait distributions in a population onto successor distributions, and shown to share six "proprietary constraints": iterativity, environmentalism, gradualism, monotonicity, locality, and mindlessness. Inside the boxes, both are "generate and test" theories — a random generator of traits plus an exogenous filter — "and that is all". The chapter's verdict, to be argued in Part Two: Skinner's theory of conditioning is *false* (associationism is not true), but Darwin's theory of selection is *empty*, because ET offers no remotely plausible account of how filtering by natural selection could work.

chapters.title: PART ONE — THE BIOLOGICAL ARGUMENT
chapters.note: [divider, file ch09]. The empirical half of the book: recent biology as the authors read it, marshalled against the random-generator/exogenous-filter picture.

chapters.title: 2. Internal Constraints: What the New Biology Tells Us
chapters.note: [file ch10] ★ → *Selection-For and the Critique of Adaptationism*. Opens with a concession and a slogan: shifting equilibria in trait distributions are real and ubiquitous, but they are phenomena to be explained, not explanations; natural selection is "tuning the piano, not… composing the melodies". Against the "unidimensional" neo-Darwinian picture (ecology explains phenotype; internal structure abstracted away — Mayr's "many roads lead to Rome" quoted against it) and against "beanbag genetics" (traits as independently selectable units; Mayr himself, and Dover, quoted against it). The evo-devo revolution: conserved master genes (Pax6 and kin) across distant phyla, development as an internal *filter* on the phenotypes selection ever sees — "evolution is the evolution of ontogenies". Further internal filters: mutation hotspots and DNA repair, RNA editing, micro-RNAs, chaperones (HSP90 as an "evolutionary capacitor" that banks hidden variation), alternative splicing (one gene, many proteins), molecular drive and biased gene conversion (fixation of variants — even deleterious ones — independently of selection). Conclusion: even if mutations were random at source, the phenotypes are not; "there is… no single 'arrow'" from random variation to selectable phenotype.

chapters.title: 3. Whole Genomes, Networks, Modules and Other Complexities
chapters.note: [file ch11] ★ (supporting) → *Selection-For and the Critique of Adaptationism*. Gene regulatory networks (Davidson: microevolutionary processes cannot explain body-plan differences; network change has "inhomogeneous and discontinuous effects"); entrenchment; robustness (which lets hidden genetic variation accumulate, and whose buffering mechanisms cannot readily be disentangled into selected vs unselected); pleiotropy — "master genes are 'masters'", one viable mutation moving many traits at once (the tentative Otx/brain case: cortex features as possible *spandrels* of selection on kidneys, larynx, etc.); developmental modules; Schmalhausen's coordination (selection cannot select isolated traits, only coordinated complexes); morphogenetic explosions (Ediacara, Cambrian, white-eye radiation) against gradualism; plasticity and the *non-transitivity* of fitness (A beats B, B beats C, C beats A when all compete; criss-crossing norms of reaction). Closing caveat — the book's own, and load-bearing for honest use of it: "the majority of biologists whom we have cited here… still today endorse natural selection as the determinant par excellence of the course of evolution"; the authors settle, at this stage, for a stand-off — the empirical case makes adaptationism "less than apodictic", no more.

chapters.title: 4. Many Constraints, Many Environments
chapters.note: [file ch12] ★ (supporting) → both entries. Selection at many levels, and phenomena that strain the canonical picture: Waddington's genetic assimilation (ether-shocked fruit flies, a second pair of wings, stabilised with *no adaptive relation* to the selecting environment — "selection without adaptation"); the *E. coli* sugar case (Hall's experiments: strains that gain sugar-2 digestion become dead ends for sugar-3; the order of selective steps is crucial and cannot be reconstructed in nature; free-riders detectable only because experimenters could dissociate coextensive traits — "natural selection doesn't perform experiments"); drift, frequency- and density-dependence, "ascent of the abundant"; West-Eberhard on environmentally initiated novelty and genetic accommodation ("genes are probably more often followers than leaders"); epigenetics and imprinting (Dutch famine and Swedish harvest records as transgenerational cases; heritability of epigenetic marks flagged as still open — "the jury is still out"); horizontal gene transfer and transposons (the "tree of descent" becoming a bush/network); interchangeability of internal and external perturbations (bearded-dragon sex determination as a GSD/TSD transition case).

chapters.title: 5. The Return of the Laws of Form
chapters.note: [file ch13] ★ → *Selection-For and the Critique of Adaptationism*. Constraints "from above": physico-chemical and mathematical invariants (Fibonacci phyllotaxis, quarter-power scaling laws and the fractal "fourth dimension" of vascular networks, wiring-minimisation in nervous systems — Cherniak's "non-genomic nativism", grey/white-matter segregation, locomotion invariants, birdsong, leaf design, optimal foraging ratios, the invariant bird wing-stroke, the zombifying wasp's rigid behavioural programme). The recurring form of the argument: the search space is too large for blind trial-and-error plus filtering to have found these near-optimal solutions, and neo-Darwinism itself insists selection only *satisfices* — so if optima exist, "something else must be involved" (physics, chemistry, self-organisation). History of the idea: D'Arcy Thompson, Lotka–Volterra, Turing, Prigogine, Thom, Waddington, Kauffman, Gould & Lewontin. The authors concede these cases are unexplained at present — "we have no such explanation at present" — and rest on the dilemma, not on a rival mechanism.

chapters.title: PART TWO — THE CONCEPTUAL SITUATION
chapters.note: [divider, file ch14]. The a priori half of the book: the intensionality argument.

chapters.title: 6. Many Are Called but Few Are Chosen: The Problem of 'Selection-For'
chapters.note: [file ch15] ★ → both entries. The core chapter. Free-riding after Gould & Lewontin: spandrels of San Marco (architects select *for* arches; spandrels come along willy-nilly) — but Fodor & Piattelli-Palmarini argue Gould & Lewontin's own remedy stays inside adaptationism, and that the rot is deeper. Avatars of one problem: Hempel's heart (pumping blood vs making noises — which is the *function*?); learning theory's "what is learned?" (split-stimulus and split-response experiments settle post hoc which coextensive property was the effective one); the naturalisation of content (the frog snaps at *flies* or at *ambient black nuisances* — cause alone cannot fix content). Diagnosis: selection-for problems arise wherever an explanation must distinguish the causal roles of *coextensive* properties; the distinction is decided by counterfactuals; but selection is a *local* process, sensitive only to actual causal transactions, and "merely possible predators do not affect the evolution of a population". The chapter's numbered conclusion: (1) selection-for is a causal process; (2) actual causal relations aren't sensitive to counterfactual states of affairs; (3) the selected-for/free-rider distinction turns on counterfactuals; (4) so, for coextensive T and T′, selection cannot distinguish which free-rides on which; (5) "so the claim that selection is the mechanism of evolution cannot be true." The escape available to architects and breeders — minds, which *can* represent counterfactuals — is exactly what natural selection lacks; Darwin's breeder analogy "abstracts the minds away", and that, the authors say, cannot be done.

chapters.title: 7. No Exit? Some Responses to the Problem of 'Selection-For'
chapters.note: [file ch16] ★ → both entries. Four candidate rescues for adaptationism, each examined and rejected by the authors: (i) *Give Mother Nature a chance* — take the breeder analogy literally (fails: natural selection "doesn't have a mind"; Mother Nature, selfish genes etc. are fictions, and "fictions can't select things"); (ii) *Laws of selection* — laws support counterfactuals (fails, in the authors' view: fitness is massively context-sensitive — the "fallacy of the Swiss apple", phenotypes are fusions not bundles of independent traits, competition outcomes are interaction effects — so there are no nomological generalisations about which traits win); (iii) *Sober's sieve* — the marble-sorting example (fails twice over: the intuition works only because we know the sieve's endogenous mechanism, which adaptationist explanation typically lacks; and which marbles count as "selected" flips between sifting flour and panning for gold, i.e. with the sorter's intentions); (iv) *Adaptationism as theory schema* (fails: "adaptation" and "ecological problem" are interdefined, so "adaptations are solutions to ecological problems" is a truism, not an empirical claim). The chapter then re-describes the adaptationist explanations that *do* work: they are **historical explanations** — plausible narratives articulating causal chains (Waterloo and the mud; a banana peel), not subsumptions under laws; hence post hoc, non-predictive, and unable to support the counterfactuals trait-individuation needs. Closing analogy: explanations of why this man got rich, case by case, without any theory of getting rich.

chapters.title: 8. Did the Dodo Lose Its Ecological Niche? Or Was It the Other Way Around?
chapters.note: [file ch17] ★ → *Selection-For and the Critique of Adaptationism*. Replies to what the authors call perhaps the strongest argument for adaptationism: the "exquisite fit" of organisms to their environments (Sober, Mayr quoted). Their reply is a dilemma. *Environment* (the world, common to all) must not be confused with *ecology/niche* (whatever-it-is-about-the-world in virtue of which this phenotype can make a living): "ecology" and "phenotype" are *interdefined*, so fit to one's niche is true but tautological, while fit to the *environment* simpliciter needs no selection theory — anything alive is ipso facto adapted to the world. Mayr's Platonic niches ("open niches… virtually calling" for woodpeckers in New Guinea) are mocked; Dawkins's "making a living" rejoinder is argued to belong to the same circle of interdefinition (niche ↔ adaptation ↔ good-for ↔ selection-for). The extinction of the dodo *was* the extinction of the dodo's way of making a living, so neither explains the other. What does explain adaptivity is natural history, synchronic (how does it make a living?) and diachronic (by what actual process did it come to?) — and the absence of phenotypes (no winged pigs: "there is no place on pigs to put them") is explained by endogenous constraints, not by selection against them.

chapters.title: 9. Summary and Postlude
chapters.note: [file ch18] ★ → both entries. The short answer to "so what is the mechanism of evolution?": "we don't know… nobody knows exactly how phenotypes evolve"; possibly there is no unitary mechanism. Recapitulates the two complaints (the free-rider/intensionality argument; the underestimation of endogenous factors) and draws the philosophy-of-science moral: adaptationism falsely claims there is a *level* of evolutionary explanation. Psychology has such a level (the intentional), evolution does not; natural history "collapses across ontological levels" and is "just one damned thing after another" — as is history tout court. Darwin's mistake is paired with Marx's: imagining that history is a theoretical domain. Preferred replacement metaphor: organisms "catch" their phenotypes from their ecologies as they catch colds — multilevel, endogenous-structure-dependent contagion rather than selection. The closing claim is negative and naturalistic: no ghost in their machine — no God, Mother Nature, Selfish Genes, World Spirit, or phantom breeders.

chapters.title: Appendix
chapters.note: [file ch20]. " 'That' kind of Darwinian in psychology and the philosophy of mind": a dossier of quotations (Boltzmann, James, Peirce, Dewey, Quine, and evolutionary psychology/epistemology up to 2009) meant to show that hard-line adaptationism thrives in the theory's export markets even if wet biologists have abandoned it. Documentation, not argument.

chapters.title: Notes
chapters.note: [file ch21], **References** [file ch22], **Index** [file ch23], **Copyright page** [file ch24]. The notes carry substantive asides (including the authors' footnote-level qualifications) and were treated as apparatus, not as chapter text, for this slice's entries.

chapters.title: Preface
chapters.note: [ch06]. The essays are "canonical texts in contemporary political philosophy" but only a sample; the collection is a companion to the editors' *Companion to Contemporary Political Philosophy*, designed to show political philosophy "as a set of ongoing conversations and disputations, arguments, and debates."

chapters.title: 1. Realism and Moralism in Political Theory
chapters.note: — Bernard Williams [ch08]. Enactment vs political-realist models of theory; the first political question and the Basic Legitimation Demand.

chapters.title: 2. What Do We Want from a Theory of Justice?
chapters.note: — Amartya Sen [ch09]. Transcendental institutionalism vs the comparative approach to justice.

chapters.title: 3. Utopophobia
chapters.note: — David Estlund (per TOC sections; file ch10). Defends aspirational/ideal theory against feasibility objections.

chapters.title: 4. *Political* Political Theory
chapters.note: — Jeremy Waldron [ch11]. Hume on persons vs institutions; realism vs moralism; the dominance of justice as a topic.

chapters.title: 5. The State
chapters.note: — Quentin Skinner [text begins ch13]. The modern concept of the state, from Hobbes onward.

chapters.title: 6. State Simplification
chapters.note: — James C. Scott [ch14]. Legibility: how states simplify social facts (the scientific-forestry parable) to govern.

chapters.title: 7. The Liberal State
chapters.note: [ch15]. (Author not verified from the extraction head.)

chapters.title: 8. The Market and the Forum
chapters.note: — Jon Elster [ch16]. Three views of politics; social choice theory treated as an instrumental, aggregative model — background to the Arrow entry.

chapters.title: 9. Invoking Civil Society
chapters.note: — Charles Taylor [ch17]. The revived concept of civil society against the state.

chapters.title: 10. The Public Sphere
chapters.note: — Jürgen Habermas [ch19]. Concept and history of the public sphere; its form in mass welfare-state democracies.

chapters.title: 11. Procedural Democracy
chapters.note: — Robert A. Dahl [ch20] ★ → *Democracy and the Voting Paradoxes*. Criteria a procedure must meet to be fully democratic, derived from minimal assumptions about an association; closes on the problem of inclusion — who counts as a citizen entitled to participate.

chapters.title: 12. Deliberation and Democratic Legitimacy
chapters.note: — Joshua Cohen [ch21]. Deliberative democracy as a fundamental, not derivative, ideal.

chapters.title: 13. Dealing with Difference
chapters.note: — Anne Phillips [ch22]. Politics of ideas vs politics of presence.

chapters.title: 14. A "Selection Model" of Political Representation
chapters.note: [ch23]. Sanctions vs selection models of the representative relation.

chapters.title: 15. Justice as Fairness
chapters.note: — John Rawls [ch25] ★ → *Distributive Justice*. The 1958 paper (not *A Theory of Justice*): justice as a virtue of practices; two principles — equal right to the most extensive liberty compatible with a like liberty for all, and inequalities arbitrary unless reasonably expected to work out for everyone's advantage and attached to positions open to all.

chapters.title: 16. Nozick's Entitlements
chapters.note: — Onora O'Neill [ch26] ★ → *Distributive Justice*. A critical staging of Nozick: patterned vs end-result vs entitlement theories; argues the Wilt Chamberlain argument presupposes the full capitalist property rights it is meant to establish; presses the missing principle of just acquisition.

chapters.title: 17. Justice Engendered
chapters.note: — Martha Minow [ch27]. The dilemma of difference in law and policy.

chapters.title: 18. Political Responsibility and Structural Injustice
chapters.note: — Iris Marion Young [ch28]. Structural injustice and forward-looking political responsibility (the Sandy housing case).

chapters.title: 19. Superseding Historic Injustice
chapters.note: — Jeremy Waldron [ch29]. Reparation, counterfactual approaches, and when changed circumstances supersede historic claims.

chapters.title: 20. Are There Any Natural Rights?
chapters.note: — H. L. A. Hart [ch31]. Argues that if there are any moral rights there is at least one natural right: the equal right of all men to be free.

chapters.title: 21. Taking Rights Seriously
chapters.note: — Ronald Dworkin [ch32]. Rights as trumps; rights of citizens, controversial rights, and why take rights seriously.

chapters.title: 22. Basic Rights
chapters.note: — Henry Shue [ch33]. Subsistence and security rights; the tripartite duties (avoid, protect, aid) and their interdependence.

chapters.title: 23. The Dark Side of Human Rights
chapters.note: [ch34]. Norms, aspirations, cynicism; state obligations, control and blame.

chapters.title: 24. A Defense of Abortion
chapters.note: — Judith Jarvis Thomson [ch35]. Grants the fetus personhood for argument's sake and denies the conclusion follows. (Same paper is the one full-text item besides Berlin in the 2nd-edition reconstruction folder.)

chapters.title: 25. Justice and Minority Rights
chapters.note: — Will Kymlicka [ch36]. Three forms of group-differentiated rights; the equality argument; historical agreements; cultural diversity.

chapters.title: 26. Two Concepts of Liberty
chapters.note: — Isaiah Berlin [ch38]. Negative vs positive freedom; the retreat to the inner citadel; the one and the many. (Full text also in the 2nd-edition reconstruction folder, ch24 there.)

chapters.title: 27. What's Wrong with Negative Liberty?
chapters.note: — Charles Taylor [ch39]. Exercise vs opportunity concepts of freedom.

chapters.title: 28. A Third Concept of Liberty
chapters.note: — Quentin Skinner [ch40]. Freedom as non-dependence, against the MacCallum one-formula view.

chapters.title: 29. Libertarian Paternalism
chapters.note: — Thaler & Sunstein [ch41]. Choice architecture; whether paternalism is inevitable.

chapters.title: 30. Political Liberalism and Religion
chapters.note: — Cécile Laborde [ch42]. Public reason, separation and establishment.

chapters.title: 31. Complex Equality
chapters.note: — Michael Walzer [ch44]. Spheres of goods; dominance and monopoly; simple vs complex equality.

chapters.title: 32. Equality of What?
chapters.note: — Amartya Sen [ch45]. Utilitarian, total-utility, and Rawlsian equality all found limited; basic capability equality proposed.

chapters.title: 33. Equality and Priority
chapters.note: [ch46]. Egalitarianism vs the priority view (Nagel's two-children case appears in the extracted text).

chapters.title: 34. Chance, Choice, and Justice

013-metaphysics.title: 013: Helen Beebee & Nigel Sabbarton-Leary (eds.), *The Semantics and Metaphysics of Natural Kinds* (Routledge, 2010)
013-metaphysics.layer: Book layer · Metaphysics slice. ★ = chapter feeds one of this slice's problem entries. Status tags describe the corpus file, not the reading itself.
013-metaphysics.extraction: **Extraction note — read this first: this is not the book the catalogue says it is.** The folder (`data/philosophy_readings/markdown/013 - Metaphysics/`) was commissioned and described — in PLAN.md and in this slice's brief — as Richard Taylor, *Metaphysics*, and every one of its 21 files carries the H1 / filename title "The Semantics and Metaphysics of Natural Kinds". On inspection the files are **not mis-titled chapters of Taylor**: they are a complete, correctly titled extraction of a different book altogether — the Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary edited volume *The Semantics and Metaphysics of Natural Kinds* (Routledge Studies in Metaphysics, first published 2010; copyright and title pages in files ch03–ch05 say so). There is **no Taylor text anywhere in the folder**: no chapter on fate, free will, causation in Taylor's sense, time, personal identity, or the self exists here, and none of those problem entries could be built from this book. The real "chapter titles" were therefore recovered not from Taylor but from this volume's own apparatus: the **Contents page (file ch06)** lists all twelve papers with authors, and each paper file carries its own real heading inside the text (e.g. file ch09 opens "2 Rigidity, Natural Kind Terms, and Metasemantics"). The map below uses the book's own paper numbering, with extraction file numbers in brackets.

prose: # Book map — 013: Helen Beebee & Nigel Sabbarton-Leary (eds.), *The Semantics and Metaphysics of Natural Kinds* (Routledge, 2010)

**Quantification of the discrepancy.** 21 files; **all 21 (100%) share the identical filename/H1**, which is the *book's* title, not any chapter's. Of the 21: 7 are front matter (ch01–ch07), 12 are the papers themselves (ch08–ch19, each ~5,800–11,600 words, full text), and 2 are back matter (ch20 contributors, ch21 index). No paper text is missing, stubbed, or corrupt — this is the cleanest extraction in the pilot's experience; the defect is purely one of **cataloguing/attribution** (wrong author, wrong book, generic folder label "Metaphysics"), not of extraction. PLAN.md's data-quality note ("Taylor, *Metaphysics* (013) — every chapter file is titled…") should be corrected accordingly: the remedy is to re-catalogue 013 as Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary (2010), not to recover Taylor titles that were never here.

groups.heading: Front matter [files ch01–ch07 — stubs/fragments, no philosophical text]

chapters.title: ch01
chapters.note: [14 words]. Cover/title stub only.

chapters.title: ch02
chapters.note: [21 words]. Title stub only.

chapters.title: ch03
chapters.note: [34 words]. Routledge Studies in Metaphysics series page; names the volume and its editors.

chapters.title: ch04
chapters.note: [31 words]. Title page: edited by Helen Beebee and Nigel Sabbarton-Leary; New York / London.

chapters.title: ch05
chapters.note: [230 words]. Copyright page: first published 2010 by Routledge; Taylor & Francis e-Library edition 2010; Library of Congress cataloguing data begins.

chapters.title: ch06 — Contents
chapters.note: [167 words]. The volume's table of contents — the authoritative source used to recover every paper title and author below. Lists papers 1–12 (see below).

chapters.title: ch07 — Acknowledgments
chapters.note: [98 words]. Editors thank the AHRC (project *Metaphysics of Science*, AH/D503833/1) and the Leverhulme Trust.

chapters.title: 1. Introduction — Helen Beebee & Nigel Sabbarton-Leary
chapters.note: [file ch08; full text, ~11,600 words] ★ → *all six entries (survey chapter for the whole slice)*. §1, Classifying nature: the metaphysics perspective — what makes a kind *natural* (Quine on similarity and theoretical standards; "nargs"; Ellis's six a priori criteria; Boyd's homeostatic property clusters). §2, Natural kind semantics — Kripke on proper names against Frege–Russell (the modal, epistemological, and semantical arguments; baptism and direct reference), then the extension to natural kind terms. §3, Kripke, a posteriori necessity, and the metaphysics of natural kinds — theoretical identities, essence after Locke and Hume. §4, Putnam, incommensurability, and natural kinds. Also the volume's own summaries of every later paper, used here to cross-check each paper's thesis.
unresolved: all six entries (survey chapter for the whole slice)

chapters.title: 2. Rigidity, Natural Kind Terms, and Metasemantics — Corine Besson
chapters.note: [file ch09; full text, ~10,000 words] ★ → *Rigidity and Natural Kind Terms*. Rigidity trivializes for general terms on Kripke's definition; Besson's remedy is *de jure* obstinate rigidity grounded in the metasemantics of "dubbing": natural kind terms are introduced by name-acquiring transactions that other general terms cannot undergo.

chapters.title: 3. General Terms as Designators: A Defence of The View — Genoveva Martí & José Martínez-Fernández
chapters.note: [file ch10; full text, ~9,100 words] ★ → *Rigidity and Natural Kind Terms*. General terms designate universals/kinds ("The View"); answers the trivialization problem, the overgeneralization problem (biting the bullet: all simple general terms behave alike semantically), and the necessity of theoretical identifications (kind vs exemplifier semantics).

chapters.title: 4. Are Natural Kind Terms Special? — Åsa Wikforss
chapters.note: [file ch11; full text, ~9,700 words] ★ → *Rigidity and Natural Kind Terms*. No: neither rigidity nor non-descriptionality marks natural kind terms off semantically, and externalism does not rescue a special metasemantics either; a version of descriptivism is preferable, and any specialness these terms have comes from their role in scientific explanation.

chapters.title: 5. The Commonalities between Proper Names and Natural Kind Terms: A Fregean Perspective — Harold Noonan
chapters.note: [file ch12; full text, ~10,400 words] ★ → *Rigidity and Natural Kind Terms*; supports *The Necessary A Posteriori*. Explains the Kripkean commonalities of names and kind terms within a Frege–Russell framework (the modal argument, propositional attitudes and deferential intentions, Twin Earth); rejects the necessary a posteriori for kind terms as a conflation of essence with contingent a posteriori thought.

chapters.title: 6. Theoretical Identity Statements, Their Truth, and Their Discovery — Joseph LaPorte
chapters.note: [file ch13; full text, ~10,700 words] ★ → *Essences and Theoretical Identities*. Mixed verdict on the Kripke–Putnam tradition: theoretical identities can be *true* (clades such as Mammalia and Chordata have specifiable essences), but they are not *discovered* to be true — scientists stipulatively decide how to use traditional terms when inquiry is disrupted (whales/fish, birds/dinosaurs; conflicting delimitations of taxa; stipulation needed even given one agreed characterization).

chapters.title: 7. Discovering the Essences of Natural Kinds — Alexander Bird
chapters.note: [file ch14; full text, ~6,100 words] ★ → *Essences and Theoretical Identities*. Reply to LaPorte: vernacular kind concepts leave far less room for precisifying decision than open texture suggests (the division of linguistic labour; D₂O and "water = H₂O"); many essential truths are not identities at all; and identities between scientific (non-vernacular) terms — e.g. nineteenth-century elements named before atomic structure was known — are discovered, not stipulated.

chapters.title: 8. The Elements and Conceptual Change — Robin Findlay Hendry
chapters.note: [file ch15; full text, ~10,600 words] ★ → *Essences and Theoretical Identities*. Chemical kinds as the test case: what chemical kinds have to do, Lavoisier on the elements, elements before and after Lavoisier, whether element identity across theory change is discovery, and (§5) necessity and essence — sceptical that essence can be *deduced* from necessity (Fine's singleton case), but argues nuclear charge earns its individuating role through its explanatory, counternomic use in chemistry.

chapters.title: 9. On the Abuse of the Necessary *A Posteriori* — Helen Beebee & Nigel Sabbarton-Leary
chapters.note: [file ch16; full text, ~9,800 words] ★ → *The Necessary A Posteriori*. Even granting Kripke on names and kind terms, extending the category needs argument case by case: a claim needs both a *Necessity* component (a Twin Earth–style judgement that the underlying nature is the essence) and an *A Posteriority* component (the term not introduced by stipulative definition). Brian Ellis's scientific essentialism — laws of nature as metaphysically necessary but a posteriori — is the worked example of the abuse: his extended kinds (substance kinds, process kinds) fail the model, undermining his de re necessity.

chapters.title: 10. Crosscutting Natural Kinds and the Hierarchy Thesis — Emma Tobin
chapters.note: [file ch17; full text, ~5,900 words] ★ → *Classification and the Hierarchy Thesis*; supports *Natural Kinds*. The hierarchy thesis (overlapping kinds must nest as genus/species; Kuhn's no-overlap principle) fails in biology (mammals/quadrupeds) and even in paradigmatic chemistry (proteins/enzymes — albumin, renin, the hairpin ribozyme). With Khalidi and Dupré: reject the hierarchy thesis, but — *pace* Hacking — rejecting it does not entail conventionalism about kinds.

chapters.title: 11. From Constitutional Necessities to Causal Necessities — Jessica Wilson
chapters.note: [file ch18; full text, ~9,100 words] ★ → *Causal Necessity and Hume's Dictum*. Humeans accept necessary connections between entities that are not wholly distinct (sets/members, fusions/parts, determinates/determinables, kind members/intrinsic properties) while denying, per Hume's Dictum, necessary *causal* connections between wholly distinct entities. Wilson's conditional — *Constitutional → Causal*: if one accepts certain constitutional necessities, one should accept certain causal necessities — argues the differential treatment is unprincipled: Schaffer's "compelling proof" criterion warrants necessities of identity but not the other constitutional necessities Humeans already accept, whose warrant is the same non-compelling, systematizing kind available in the causal case. The non-Humean framework faces no such tension.

chapters.title: 12. Realism, Natural Kinds, and Philosophical Methods — Richard N. Boyd
chapters.note: [file ch19; full text, ~9,900 words] ★ → *Natural Kinds*. Scientific realism developed as thoroughgoing naturalism: the accommodation theory of reference, homeostatic property cluster (HPC) kinds (no precise membership conditions; species as paradigm), the discipline-relativity of naturalness, anti-foundationalist epistemology, natural kinds as in part social constructions without loss of mind-independence, and the consequences for philosophical method itself (against a priori conceptual analysis as a foundation).

chapters.title: ch20 — Contributors
chapters.note: [597 words]. Author biographies (Beebee, Besson, Bird, Boyd, and the rest).

chapters.title: ch21 — Index
chapters.note: [~2,700 words]. The volume's index (partially garbled diacritics in places; usable as a finding aid only).

The single defect is the catalogue-level misattribution documented above: **013 is Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary (2010) on natural kinds, not Taylor's *Metaphysics*** — so the Taylor-derived candidate problems in the original brief (free will & determinism, personal identity, time, fate/fatalism, mind/body, the nature of metaphysics in Taylor's sense) have *no* textual support in this folder and no entries were written for them. The six entries built instead are exactly the problems this book stages: natural kinds; rigidity and natural kind terms; essences and theoretical identities; the necessary a posteriori; classification and the hierarchy thesis; and causal necessity and Hume's Dictum.

018-existentialism.title: 018: Walter Kaufmann (ed.), *Existentialism from Dostoevsky to Sartre* (1956; Pickle Partners Publishing reprint)
018-existentialism.layer: Book layer · primary-text anthology. ★ = chapter feeds one of this subfield's problem entries.
018-existentialism.extraction: **Extraction note — AUTHORSHIP CORRECTION.** This folder is catalogued in the corpus simply as "018 - Existentialism." It is **not** a book by Robert C. Solomon: the title page (file ch02) reads *Existentialism: From Dostoevsky to Sartre*, "Edited, with an introduction, prefaces, and new translations by **Walter Kaufmann**," and file ch04 is Kaufmann's author page. The extracted folder holds 18 files: publisher front matter (ch01), title page (ch02), Contents (ch03), About the Author (ch04), Preface (ch05), the ten anthology chapters (ch06–ch15), Sources and Acknowledgments (ch16), a publisher's review-request page (ch17, not book content), and endnotes (ch18). Chapter text is full where it matters most (Kaufmann's introduction, Jaspers, Sartre) but the finale is partial — see ch15 below. Kaufmann's editorial choices matter for citation: in the Sartre chapter he changes Hazel Barnes' rendering of *mauvaise foi* from "bad faith" to "self-deception" throughout, so quotations from this corpus say *self-deception* where most of the literature says *bad faith*.

prose: # Book map — 018: Walter Kaufmann (ed.), *Existentialism from Dostoevsky to Sartre* (1956; Pickle Partners Publishing reprint)

chapters.title: Preface
chapters.note: [file ch05]. Kaufmann against anthologies as "a cultural supermarket": the book is an argument in selection and arrangement, not a sampler.

chapters.title: ONE — Kaufmann, "Existentialism from Dostoevsky to Sartre"
chapters.note: [file ch06, ~16,300 words] ★ → both existentialism entries (framing). The editor's introduction, in sections on Dostoevsky, Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Jaspers, Heidegger, Sartre, and "A Story with a Moral." Opening thesis: "Existentialism is not a philosophy but a label for several widely different revolts against traditional philosophy"; the figures share "perfervid individualism," refusal of systems, and dissatisfaction with academic philosophy — not tenets. Also carries Kaufmann's caution against the slogan: it "has become a commonplace that existentialism is the doctrine that existence precedes essence, and this phrase obstructs the understanding of this complex movement as well as of Sartre's philosophy."

chapters.title: TWO — Dostoevsky, *Notes from Underground*, Part One
chapters.note: [file ch07, ~13,400 words]. The Underground Man's spiteful monologue against rational egoism and the crystal palace; only Part One is reprinted (per Sources, ch16). Kaufmann's preface calls the *Notes* (1864) "one of the most revolutionary and original works of world literature" and man's inner life — "his moods, anxieties, and his decisions" — moved to the centre. Feeds the absurdity entry's background (the revolt against a world that will not make sense on demand).

chapters.title: THREE — Kierkegaard, "On Himself"
chapters.note: [file ch08, ~6,900 words]. Selections from the *Concluding Unscientific Postscript* ("On his Mission," published over a pseudonym with Kierkegaard named as editor) and *The Point of View for My Work as an Author*: the individual against the theoretical system; Kierkegaard's own account of his authorship and his protest against institutional Christianity.

chapters.title: FOUR — Nietzsche, "Live Dangerously"
chapters.note: [file ch09, ~5,100 words]. Selections (from *Schopenhauer as Educator*, *The Gay Science*, *Zarathustra*, and others, per Sources) chosen "to bring out that aspect of his thought which makes his inclusion in the story of existentialism imperative" — self-overcoming and living dangerously rather than the moral critique, which this KB takes from book 019 itself. Kaufmann's preface also handles the Nazi misappropriation: Nietzsche's books as wholes were of no use to them.

chapters.title: FIVE — Rilke, *The Notes of Malte Laurids Brigge
chapters.note: * [file ch10, ~3,100 words]. Excerpts (newly translated by Kaufmann) from Rilke's prose work of urban dread and seen death; included partly because *Malte* influenced Sartre's *La Nausée*.

chapters.title: SIX — Kafka, "Three Parables"
chapters.note: [file ch11, ~4,100 words]. "The Imperial Message," "Couriers," and the parable from *The Trial* (pp. 268–278 of the Muir translation, per Sources) — Kaufmann calls the three "among the most important documents for the interpretation of *The Castle*." Parables of unreachable authority and endlessly deferred arrival; background to the absurd.

chapters.title: SEVEN — Jaspers, *Existenzphilosophie
chapters.note: * [file ch12, ~28,600 words]. The largest selection after Sartre: "On My Philosophy" (autobiographical essay), the first two lectures of *Reason and Existenz* (1935) — on Kierkegaard and Nietzsche, and on "The Encompassing" — and the postscript material. Jaspers' own route into *Existenz* philosophy and his reading of the two "exceptions," Kierkegaard and Nietzsche, as the indispensable precursors.

chapters.title: EIGHT — Heidegger, "The Way Back into the Ground of Metaphysics"
chapters.note: [file ch13, ~6,400 words]. Heidegger's 1949 introduction to the fifth printing of *What is Metaphysics?* (1929), translated for this volume with Heidegger's own answers to the translator's questions on key terms (*Sein* as Being). A self-contained late essay on the ground of metaphysics, not an excerpt from *Being and Time*.

chapters.title: NINE — Sartre, "Existentialism"
chapters.note: [file ch14, ~39,000 words] ★ → *Existence Precedes Essence: Sartre on Freedom and Self-Deception*. Four selections: (1) "The Wall" (the short story); (2) "Self-Deception" — the *mauvaise foi* chapter of *Being and Nothingness*, unabridged in Barnes' translation as Kaufmann amended it (the lie-to-oneself puzzle; the woman on the first date; the café waiter who plays at being a waiter); (3) "Portrait of the Anti-Semite" (slightly abridged); (4) "Existentialism is a Humanism" — the 1946 lecture, unabridged in Mairet's translation (existence precedes essence; the paper-knife; anguish, abandonment, despair; "condemned to be free"; the pupil torn between his mother and the Free French).

chapters.title: TEN — Camus, "The Myth of Sisyphus"
chapters.note: [file ch15, ~1,500 words] ★ → *The Absurd and Sisyphus*. **Partial:** only the concluding chapter of Camus' book of that name is reprinted — the Sisyphus essay itself, complete as an essay ("One must imagine Sisyphus happy"), but the book's earlier chapters, where the absurd is defined and the argument about suicide is made, are **not in the corpus**. Kaufmann's preface adds the standing caution: Camus "is often called an existentialist, though many critics insist that this is an invidious error."

chapters.title: Sources and Acknowledgments
chapters.note: [file ch16]; **notes** [file ch18] — the anthology's endnotes (Dostoevsky's author's note, Kierkegaard pseudonymity notes, etc.).
