019-beyond-good-and-evil.title: 019: Friedrich Nietzsche, *Beyond Good and Evil: Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future* (1886), translated with commentary by Walter Kaufmann (Vintage Books edition, 1989; translation first published 1966)
019-beyond-good-and-evil.layer: Book layer · primary text. ★ = part feeds one of this subfield's problem entries.
019-beyond-good-and-evil.extraction: **Extraction note.** The extracted folder (`data/philosophy_readings/markdown/019 - Beyond Good and Evil - Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future/`) holds 33 files, all carrying the same generic title. The layout is regular and recoverable: front matter (ch01–ch08, including the Translator's Preface at ch05, ~3,300 words, and Bibliographical Note at ch07), Nietzsche's Preface (ch09), a contents file (ch10), then for each of the nine Parts a one-page part-title stub followed by the part's full text (ch11–ch28), then the Aftersong "From High Mountains" in German and in Kaufmann's translation (ch29–ch31), and the edition's back matter (ch32–ch33). Section (§) numbers below are Nietzsche's own, as printed; the aphoristic text is complete — all 296 sections are accounted for by the part ranges, which follow the part openings in the extraction.

prose: # Book map — 019: Friedrich Nietzsche, *Beyond Good and Evil: Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future* (1886), translated with commentary by Walter Kaufmann (Vintage Books edition, 1989; translation first published 1966)

chapters.title: Nietzsche's Preface
chapters.note: [file ch09]. "Supposing truth is a woman" — dogmatism as a noble childishness built on "any old popular superstition"; Plato's "invention of the pure spirit and the good as such" named "the worst, most durable, and most dangerous of all errors so far," with Christianity as "Platonism for 'the people'"; the fight against it has bred Europe's "magnificent tension of the spirit."

chapters.title: Part One: On the Prejudices of Philosophers
chapters.note: (§§1–23) [stub ch11, text ch12] ★ → *Master Morality, Slave Morality, and the Problem of Morality Itself* (framing). §1 asks not what truth is but what the *will to truth* is worth: "Suppose we want truth: why not rather untruth? and uncertainty? even ignorance?" §2 names the metaphysicians' "faith in opposite values"; §4 argues the falseness of a judgement is no objection to it — the question is whether it is life-promoting, and renouncing false judgements "would mean renouncing life"; §5 charges philosophers with defending, with reasons found afterwards, "a desire of the heart that has been filtered and made abstract."

chapters.title: Part Two: The Free Spirit
chapters.note: (§§24–44) [stub ch13, text ch14]. Opens (§24) on the "strange simplification and falsification" in which man lives: knowledge itself rose on "a far more powerful will: the will to ignorance, to the uncertain, to the untrue! Not as its opposite, but — as its refinement!" The free spirit as the one who can live with that.

chapters.title: Part Three: What Is Religious
chapters.note: (§§45–62) [stub ch15, text ch16]. §45 sets the psychologist's "great hunt" through "the whole history of the soul so far"; the part works through the religious neurosis, sacrifice, and the ascetic ideal's prehistory in the soul's economy.

chapters.title: Part Four: Epigrams and Interludes
chapters.note: (§§63–185) [stub ch17, text ch18]. Short aphorisms ("'I have done that,' says my memory. 'I cannot have done that,' says my pride, and remains inexorable. Eventually — memory yields," §68; "'Knowledge for its own sake' — that is the last snare of morality," §64).

chapters.title: Part Five: Natural History of Morals
chapters.note: (§§186–203) [stub ch19, text ch20] ★ → *Master Morality, Slave Morality, and the Problem of Morality Itself*. §186: the "science of morals" has so far tried to supply a *rational foundation* for a morality it simply accepted as given, so "the problem of morality itself" was never seen — the real problems "emerge only when we compare *many* moralities"; what is needed first is a *typology* of morals, and moralities are "merely a sign language of the affects" (§187). §188: every morality is "a bit of tyranny against 'nature'" whose long compulsion is what has educated the spirit. The part continues through herd morality, the morality of timidity, and the English moralists.

chapters.title: Part Six: We Scholars
chapters.note: (§§204–213) [stub ch21, text ch22]. §204 opens against the "unharmful shift in the respective ranks of science and philosophy": the scholar's emancipation from philosophy as an effect of the democratic order; the scholar as instrument, the philosopher as commander and legislator.

chapters.title: Part Seven: Our Virtues
chapters.note: (§§214–239) [stub ch23, text ch24]. §214: "we Europeans of the day after tomorrow, we firstborn of the twentieth century" — if we still have virtues they will not be our grandfathers' "simpleminded and four-square" ones; the part tests honesty, pity, and the virtue of the free spirit against that standard.

chapters.title: Part Eight: Peoples and Fatherlands
chapters.note: (§§240–256) [stub ch25, text ch26]. §240 opens on Wagner's *Meistersinger* overture as an emblem of Germanness; the part ranges over the English, French, Jews, and Germans, against nationalism and for the "good European."

chapters.title: Part Nine: What Is Noble
chapters.note: (§§257–296) [stub ch27, text ch28] ★ → *Master Morality, Slave Morality, and the Problem of Morality Itself*. §257: every enhancement of the type "man" has been the work of an aristocratic society that "needs slavery in some sense or other," and of the *pathos of distance*. §259: mutual non-exploitation universalized as society's principle would be "a will to the *denial* of life," since life "simply *is* will to power." §260 (the entry's core): the two basic types — **master morality** (good/bad = noble/contemptible; value-creating self-glorification) and **slave morality** (good/evil; pity, patience, humility honoured as the useful virtues of the suffering) — with the caveats that mixed cultures mediate and interpenetrate both, "even in the same human being, within a *single* soul." §262 closes the historical arc: when the old discipline relaxes, "the 'individual' appears, obliged to give himself laws."

chapters.title: From High Mountains: Aftersong
chapters.note: [files ch29–ch31]. The closing poem, given with Kaufmann's translator's note, the German text, and his English version.

prose: # Book map — 020: M. David Eckel, C. Allen Speight & Troy DuJardin (eds.), *The Future of the Philosophy of Religion* (2021)

**Identification note.** The corpus folder is labelled only "020 - Philosophy of Religion," and this volume is sometimes misdescribed as a classical anthology of the field. It is not one: it is a 2021 symposium volume — essays by a reconvened group of philosophers of religion (first gathered at Boston University's Institute for Philosophy and Religion in the early 2000s, reconvened spring 2017) on *the future of their field*. It contains no classical arguments-for-God's-existence survey and no problem-of-evil chapter; its primary-paper chapters are contemporary essays, plus two historical studies (Bhāviveka; William James) and a closing metaphysical essay (Marion). Entries in this subfield are therefore built bottom-up from what these chapters actually argue.

chapters.title: Front matter
chapters.note: [file ch01]. Series information (Boston Studies in Philosophy, Religion and Public Life, series editor C. Allen Speight), title page, and the volume's contents — the source for the author attributions used throughout this map.

chapters.title: 1. Introduction
chapters.note: — M. David Eckel [file ch02] ★ → *The Future of Philosophy of Religion*. The volume's frame: the classic questions of the field "seemed parochial," new theoretical orientations bypassed them for the lives of actual practitioners, and the diversification of Religious Studies no longer permits easy assumptions about philosophy's relevance to it. Summarizes each essay under Wildman's four challenges — a global perspective, critical theory, multiple disciplinary perspectives, and religious practices and real-world problems — and notes candidly what is missing (gender studies; fuller non-Western coverage).

chapters.title: 2. Reading Tea Leaves, Drinking Tea: Four Transformations in Philosophy of Religion
chapters.note: — Wesley Wildman [file ch03] ★ → *The Future of Philosophy of Religion*; *Religious Diversity and Salvation* (background). Four transformations are reshaping North Atlantic universities — the *global*, the *critical*, the *multidisciplinary*, and the *practical* — while philosophy of religion, typically narrowed to worldview beliefs in one (usually Christian, usually theistic) tradition, has been slow to respond; academic positions in the field are contracting rapidly. Drawing on field-wide empirical studies, Wildman uses the transformations as criteria for estimating the field's future and what reversing the contraction would require.

chapters.title: 3. What Religious Studies Can Teach the Humanities: A Philosophical Perspective
chapters.note: — Dan Arnold [file ch04]. Against the idea that scholars of religion should only describe and never judge: following Tyler Roberts, humanistic inquiry ineliminably involves first-personal questions, and intentionality is irreducibly *normative*; in Kantian terms, freedom just is our attunement to normative considerations, which cannot coherently be explained away. Philosophy of religion's role is to identify and clarify these normative considerations; illustrated through controversies over religion in American constitutional law, with Franklin Gamwell's claim that religion is an essential dimension of human being considered as the stronger, specifically religious conclusion.

chapters.title: 4. Religious Practices and the Formation of Subjects
chapters.note: — Kevin Schilbrack [file ch05] ★ → *The Future of Philosophy of Religion*. The study of religion has shifted from texts to social practices; philosophy of religion should expand its object of study to follow. Three anthropological approaches — Geertz's Ricoeur-inspired hermeneutics, Asad's Foucault-inspired account of discipline, Csordas's Merleau-Ponty-inspired embodiment — are usually taken to conflict over whether practices *form* the subjectivities of participants; Schilbrack argues the disagreement is a philosophical one, that the approaches properly understood complement each other, and that an integrated account is available for philosophers of religion to contribute to.

chapters.title: 5. Philosophy of Lived Religion: The Next Revolution?
chapters.note: — Timothy D. Knepper [file ch06] ★ → *The Future of Philosophy of Religion*; *Religious Diversity and Salvation* (background). Diversifying *which religions* the field studies addresses injustices of creed but not of class. Philosophy of *lived* religion is proposed as the next step: the philosophical study of *all* acts of religious reason-giving — privileging contemporary, ordinary, and spoken acts over past, elite, and written ones — organized around the basic questions humans ask (what, who, when, where, how, why). If philosophy of religion is to be the philosophy of *all* religion, not of theism or literate elites, this is what it must attend to.

chapters.title: 6. Liturgical Philosophy of Religion: An Untimely Manifesto about Sincerity, Acceptance, and Hope
chapters.note: — Andrew Chignell [file ch07] ★ → *Faith, Acceptance, and Hope*; *The Future of Philosophy of Religion*. A manifesto for a "liturgical turn": set aside the field's fixation on the justification of theistic *belief* (a regulative, largely academic ideal — many practitioners do not fully believe many of their tradition's doctrines, and utter them in liturgy in a mode of "insincerity upwards," mapped on a Ladder of Liturgical Sincerity from inquirer through discerner, conditional seeker, and initiate to the utterly convinced). The attitudes that actually structure religious practice are *acceptance* (a voluntary, practically motivated taking-to-be-true, distinct from belief's involuntary felt conviction), *hope*, and *trust* — Kant's "minimum of theology" is hope that God exists plus acceptance that God is really possible. Philosophers of religion should become "pistologists" and "elpistologists" — students of *pistis* (faith) and *elpis* (hope) — and attend to the thick, "vested" doctrinal objects as they are embodied in liturgy rather than to bare theism.

chapters.title: 7. Belief that Matters: Religion, Anti-Black Racism and the Future of the Philosophy of Religion
chapters.note: — Elizabeth Pritchard [file ch08] ★ → *The Future of Philosophy of Religion*. Scholars who repudiate the category of "belief" as exclusively cognitive presume belief is *nonmaterial* — a purely mental affirmation. Pritchard argues that presumption helps disaggregate "religion" from "race," obscures Christianity's relationship to racism, and perpetuates American anti-Black racism. She makes the case for the *materiality* of belief — belief as embodied, practised, and consequential — drawing on work portraying American anti-Black racism as itself a religion and on materialist theories of belief from several disciplines.

chapters.title: 8. Critical Theory, Conspiracy, and "Gullible Critique"
chapters.note: — Andrew Dole [file ch09]. Develops Bruno Latour's 2004 worry about the resemblance between academic "critique" (critical theory, genealogy, the hermeneutics of suspicion) and conspiracy theories: both are forms of *suspicious explanation* sharing formal features — hidden agents, debunking surface appearances, self-sealing responses to counterevidence. A critique of critique, ending with an account of what Latour meant by "gullible critique."

chapters.title: 9. Learning to Do Philosophy of Religion in the Anthropocene
chapters.note: — Mark Larrimore [file ch10]. Philosophy of religion and Anthropocene discourse have barely noticed each other. Engaging Roy Scranton, Amitav Ghosh, Bronisław Szerszynski, and Deborah Bird Rose: in a world of "vertiginous loss of long-taken-for-granted futures," the field's grasp of histories and traditions of interpretation could free the humanities from "paleological" thinking — but only by relinquishing the secular "immanent frame," learning to discern the spectres of a post-secular present, and conversing with speculative fiction and the environmental humanities' practices of mourning and kin-making with the more-than-human world.

chapters.title: 10. Skills Without Values, Rallies Without Virtues: Beyond Hipster Heideggerianism and Shining Things
chapters.note: — David Decosimo [file ch11]. A critique of Hubert Dreyfus and Sean Dorrance Kelly's *All Things Shining*, an influential religious naturalism proposing a non-supernatural polytheism — "luring the gods back" by cultivating skills and communal ecstasy — as an antidote to nihilism. Decosimo argues the vision fails in each dimension: its account of attunement to value (the athlete "playing out of his mind"), its confusion of mere skill (*poiesis*) with virtue, and its handling of the ethical dangers of "whooshing up" (*physis*).

chapters.title: 11. A Peripheral Field. Meditations on the Status of Jewish Philosophy
chapters.note: — Michael Zank [file ch12]. Through the law of gleanings (Lev 23:22) — leave the edges of the field for those in need — Jewish philosophy is located at the margins of Jewish existence and of mainstream philosophy of religion alike: marginal, but "as it ought to be," marking boundaries and transitions between particular and universal, and directing an otherwise introverted community's attention outward. Traditionally skeptical, in its modern version constructive and apologetic.

chapters.title: 12. Nearly Neighbors: Reflections on Philosophy of Religion and Its Close Encounters with Modern Jewish Thought
chapters.note: — Sarah Hammerschlag [file ch13]. Taking up Schilbrack's charge that philosophy of religion is "the least reflexive discipline in religious studies": through three modern encounters between Judaism and philosophy (Mendelssohn and Levinas among them), Hammerschlag proposes the field be understood less as a discipline adjudicating the validity of concepts and more as one investigating their historical emergence and subsequent usage and dissemination.

chapters.title: 13. Who or What Created the World? Bhāviveka's Arguments Against the Hindu Concept of God
chapters.note: — M. David Eckel [file ch14] ★ → *The Cosmological Argument*; *The Evidential Argument from Evil* (connection). In his commentary on Nāgārjuna's *Mūlamadhyamakakārikāḥ* 1.1, Bhāviveka reads "no-cause" (*ahetu*) as an *implicative* negation — a "bad cause" (*kuhetu*), like a "no-wife" who exists but does not do what a wife does — and counts the Hindu Lord (*īśvara*) among such no-causes: he may exist, but he does not *create*. Conventionally: the Lord cannot cause the world's arising "because he causes pleasure for some and pain for others, like a cowherd" — Draupadī's complaint in the *Mahābhārata* that the virtuous Yudhiṣṭhira's ruin shows the Lord capricious and cruel, which Eckel explicitly reads as the problem of theodicy; and the world, being an object of cognition (*prameya*) like the Lord himself, has no single creator. Ultimately, anything arising from the Lord would have to be himself, different, or both — all already refuted. Conventionally, the world's real "creator" is *karma*, a self-contained cosmos of ethical retribution; the chapter develops the arguments further from Bhāviveka's *Verses on the Heart of the Middle Way* and its commentary *The Flame of Reason*.

chapters.title: 14. On the Past and Future of Religion, Art and Philosophy
chapters.note: — C. Allen Speight [file ch15]. Critics argue "religion" is an essentially modern concept with no ancient counterpart; the same has been argued for "art." Speight compares the two cases: if both concepts have such brief histories, what should change in how the humanities approach the much longer pre-histories of religious and artistic phenomena, and what is the future role of philosophy vis-à-vis both fields under this new historical self-awareness?

chapters.title: 15. Psychoanalysis and the Monotheistic Origins of Modern Science
chapters.note: — Kenneth Reinhard [file ch16]. For Freud, psychoanalysis continued the Enlightenment: on the side of science, allied with philosophy, against religion. Reinhard traces Freud's formation in the Berlin physicalists' synthesis (Helmholtz's and Brücke's indestructible, displaceable energy → libido), his expectation that psychoanalysis would eventually rest on a quantitative foundation, and — via Lacan's reading of Freud — speculates on the monotheistic origins of modern science and the future of religion itself.

chapters.title: 16. William James Revisited: "Pragmatic" Approaches to Religion
chapters.note: — David C. Lamberth [file ch17] ★ → *Faith, Acceptance, and Hope*. How James conceived philosophy of religion, in three movements. (i) The pre-*Varieties* essays: thought exists for the sake of action (the reflex arc), and the concept of God is a concrete practical idea orienting us toward our "ideal interests" — in "Reflex Action and Theism" (1881), "anything short of God is not rational; anything more than God is not possible"; *The Will to Believe* (1896) belongs to this period. (ii) The psychology of religion in *The Varieties of Religious Experience*: transformative experience, individual and social. (iii) The mature pragmatic/radical-empiricist period: *meliorism* — salvation treated "neither as necessary, nor as impossible," but as a possibility that becomes more probable as its conditions are actualized — with transformative religious experience re-read in *A Pluralistic Universe* as data for a collaborative, pluralistic interpretation of reality. Lamberth's conclusion: the twenty-first century is not likely to see humankind evolving "beyond" religion in any meaningful sense.

chapters.title: 17. God and the Ambivalence of Being
chapters.note: — Jean-Luc Marion [file ch18] ★ → *The Ontological Argument* (framing). Before deciding whether God is to be thought *with* or *without* Being, ask what "Being" means. As the metaphysical tradition (*metaphysica*) understands it, Being is perseverance in the present, beings existing according to *causa sui* — a sense that annuls itself in the aporia of the present and forgets manifestation, past, and future. But Being can also be understood by the logic of the *gift* and the *event*, in which beings are precisely by surrendering their claim to perseverance — the mode Marion sees perfectly implemented in Christ as son in relation to the Father (and, in his earlier *God without Being*, God named as *agapē*, radically outside Being). The debate about God and Being is therefore "ambivalent" until this prior question — what do we understand by Being, when it is a question of God? — is settled.

chapters.title: Preface
chapters.note: [file ch08] ★. The book's thesis stated up front: "Individuals have rights, and there are things no person or group may do to them (without violating their rights)." Main conclusions: a minimal state "limited to the narrow functions of protection against force, theft, fraud, enforcement of contracts, and so on, is justified; … any more extensive state will violate persons' rights"; the state may not use coercion "for the purpose of getting some citizens to aid others, or in order to prohibit activities to people for their *own* good or protection."

groups.heading: Part I — State-of-Nature Theory, or How to Back into a State without Really Trying

chapters.title: 1. Why State-of-Nature Theory?
chapters.note: [ch11] ★ → *The Minimal State*. Political philosophy's fundamental question is whether there should be any state at all — "Why not have anarchy?" State-of-nature theory has an explanatory purpose: show how a state could arise without anyone intending it and without rights violations.

chapters.title: 2. The State of Nature
chapters.note: [ch12] ★ → *The Minimal State*. Locke's state of nature and its inconveniences (biased self-judging, feuds, no settled dispute-ending); the remedies available *within* the state of nature — protective associations, then the dominant protective association — and invisible-hand explanations (the money analogy).

chapters.title: 3. Moral Constraints and the State
chapters.note: [ch13] ★ → *The Minimal State*. Minimal vs *ultraminimal* state (monopoly of force, but protection only for purchasers); why the night-watchman state only *appears* redistributive; rights as side constraints rather than goals (against utilitarianism — the innocent man punished to calm a neighbourhood); the individualist anarchist's challenge stated.

chapters.title: 4. Prohibition, Compensation, and Risk
chapters.note: [ch14] ★ → *The Minimal State*. Independents living among a dominant agency's clients; when an unreliable private enforcement procedure may be prohibited, and the principle of compensation owed to those prohibited.

chapters.title: 5. The State
chapters.note: [ch15] ★ → *The Minimal State*. Prohibiting private enforcement of justice; the "principle of fairness" considered and found insufficient; procedural rights; the *de facto* monopoly; the step from ultraminimal to minimal state — the dominant agency is morally required to compensate those it prohibits from self-help, and compensation takes the form of protective services, which is what makes the state minimal rather than ultraminimal. The invisible-hand explanation of the state assessed: it explains the monopoly, not any special rights (the state has none).

chapters.title: 6. Further Considerations on the Argument for the State
chapters.note: [ch16] ★ → *The Minimal State*. Objections: does the self-defence right prove too much (could each side forbid the other from combining)? Preemptive attack, legitimacy, preventive restraint.

groups.heading: Part II — Beyond the Minimal State?

chapters.title: 7. Distributive Justice
chapters.note: [ch18 + ch19] ★ → *Distributive Justice*. §I: the entitlement theory (justice in acquisition, justice in transfer, rectification — a distribution is just if everyone is entitled to their holdings); historical vs end-result (current time-slice) principles; patterning; "How Liberty Upsets Patterns" — the Wilt Chamberlain example; redistribution and property rights ("Taxation of earnings from labor is on a par with forced labor"); Locke's theory of acquisition and the Lockean proviso (the desert water-hole case). §II (continues in file ch19): Rawls's theory — social cooperation, the original position and the difference principle, the argument from the moral arbitrariness of natural assets reconstructed and contested (arguments A–D), collective assets.

chapters.title: 8. Equality, Envy, Exploitation, Etc.
chapters.note: [ch20]. Equality and equality of opportunity; self-esteem and envy; meaningful work and workers' control; Marxian exploitation and voluntary exchange; philanthropy; the non-neutral state.

chapters.title: 9. Demoktesis
chapters.note: [ch21]. A deliberately parallel derivation: an attempt to continue the legitimate-steps story toward a more-than-minimal state ("demoktesis" — ownership of the people by the people), offered to expose what such derivations actually show; hypothetical histories.

chapters.title: 10. A Framework for Utopia
chapters.note: [ch23]. No single best world for everyone; the model of imagined worlds and emigration between them; the framework — a minimal-state meta-utopia within which diverse communities form by voluntary association and exit — as "utopian common ground."

chapters.title: I. Introductory
chapters.note: [file ch03] ★ → *The Harm Principle and Freedom of Expression*. The subject is civil or social liberty: "the nature and limits of the power which can be legitimately exercised by society over the individual." From the old struggle against rulers to the new one: the tyranny of the majority and, deeper, "a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression," exercised through prevailing opinion. The essay's "one very simple principle" is asserted here: "the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant." Scope limits (children; "backward states of society") and the ground: "I regard utility as the ultimate appeal on all ethical questions; but it must be utility in the largest sense, grounded on the permanent interests of man as a progressive being."

chapters.title: II. Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion
chapters.note: [file ch04] ★ → *The Harm Principle and Freedom of Expression*. "If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion… mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind." Silencing robs the human race whether the opinion is true (exchange of error for truth) or false (clearer perception of truth by collision with error). The chapter closes by recapitulating **four grounds**: (1) the silenced opinion may be true — denying this assumes our infallibility; (2) even error commonly contains a portion of truth, supplied only by collision of adverse opinions; (3) an uncontested true doctrine is held as prejudice, without comprehension of its rational grounds; (4) the doctrine's very meaning is lost, becoming "a mere formal profession." Also: social intolerance stifles without fining or imprisoning, at the price of "the entire moral courage of the human mind."

chapters.title: III. Of Individuality, as One of the Elements of Well-Being
chapters.note: [file ch05] ★ → *The Harm Principle and Freedom of Expression*. The same reasons require freedom to act on one's opinions "at their own risk and peril" — with the chapter's limit case, the **corn-dealer example**: "even opinions lose their immunity, when the circumstances in which they are expressed are such as to constitute their expression a positive instigation to some mischievous act"; the opinion that corn-dealers are starvers of the poor "ought to be unmolested when simply circulated through the press, but may justly incur punishment when delivered orally to an excited mob assembled before the house of a corn-dealer." Individuality and spontaneity as components of well-being; the danger of custom and mediocrity.

chapters.title: IV. Of the Limits to the Authority of Society over the Individual
chapters.note: [file ch06] ★ → *The Harm Principle and Freedom of Expression*. Where the harm principle's boundary runs in practice: the individual "is the person most interested in his own well-being"; society's interest in his self-regarding conduct "is fractional, and altogether indirect." Marks the distinction between the loss of consideration rightly incurred by imprudence and the reprobation/punishment due for infringing others' rights.

chapters.title: V. Applications
chapters.note: [file ch07]. The principles applied: trade, poisons, drunkenness and the Maine Law, dealers' interests, gambling houses, polygamy (Mormonism), education, and the state's role — the essay's test of where "harm to others" does and does not license interference in hard cases.

groups.heading: *The Subjection of Women* (same 1879 volume — a separate work)

chapters.title: I
chapters.note: [file ch09]. The thesis: "the principle which regulates the existing social relations between the two sexes — the legal subordination of one sex to the other — is wrong in itself, and now one of the chief hindrances to human improvement," to be replaced by "a principle of perfect equality." The burden of proof lies on the defenders of inequality, since the arrangement rests on force and custom, not on any trial of alternatives.

chapters.title: II
chapters.note: [file ch10]. The laws of marriage as they stand: the wife's legal non-existence, property, custody, and the husband's power — marriage analysed as a relation of legalized dependence.

chapters.title: III
chapters.note: [file ch11]. Women's admissibility to all functions and occupations monopolized by men; the alleged natural incapacities argued to be artifacts of the system that produces them.

chapters.title: IV
chapters.note: [file ch12]. What equality would do: the moral regeneration of mankind, the doubling of available talent, and the effect on marriage itself as a relation between equals.

prose: # Book map — 025: Montague Brown, *The One-Minute Philosopher* (Sophia Institute Press, 2001)

groups.heading: The book's structure (from the reconstructed TOC)
prose: An alphabetically arranged reference of **88 paired entries**, each exactly two facing pages, each distinguishing a genuine good or virtue from its look-alike counterfeit (the publisher's "over 175 fundamental concepts" counts both sides of the 88 pairs). Each entry is designed to be read "in about a minute." Back matter: bibliographical references (pp. 179–198) and an index. The publisher describes the aim as "plain-spoken wisdom" on the concepts that "form the basis of any decent human life," grounded "on common sense rather than on theology," aimed at parents and teachers who must "speak in sound bites." *First Things* (Feb. 2002) reviewed it sceptically: the subtitle "promises much more than any book should promise."

prose: # Book map — 026: Jeremy Harwood, *Philosophy: A Beginner's Guide to the Ideas of 100 Great Thinkers* (2010)

chapters.title: Introduction: What is Philosophy?
chapters.note: [file ch05]. "Philosophy begins in wonder" (Plato, as quoted here); philosophy defined as the quest to comprehend the world through reason. Branches listed: metaphysics, ontology, logic, epistemology, ethics, plus language, politics, art, science, law, religion, mind. Schools sketched in a paragraph each: sceptics, empiricists, idealists, utilitarians, logical positivists, existentialists (Sartre named the school's "founding father" — a popular simplification), analytic philosophers.

chapters.title: The Ancient World
chapters.note: (*c.* 7th century BC–5th century AD) [file ch06, ~9,600 words]. Era frame: Greek reason alongside the Buddha in India and Confucius and Lao-tzu in China. Thinkers: Thales of Miletus (spelled "Melitus" in the Contents), Anaximander, Siddhartha Gautama the Buddha, Confucius, Heraclitus, Parmenides, Lao-tzu, Zeno of Elea, Socrates, Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, Epicurus, Marcus Aurelius, Sextus Empiricus, Tertullian, Origen, Plotinus, St Augustine. → Connections to the epistemology entries (Sextus, scepticism) and to *Sophie's World* chs. 3–15, which cover the same ground as narrative.

chapters.title: The Middle Ages
chapters.note: (AD 500–1400) [file ch07, ~4,900 words]. Era frame: loss of ancient learning in the West, its preservation in the Muslim world, and the medieval project of reconciling philosophy with Christian faith — Aquinas' theology-as-science is the frame's centre. Thinkers: Avicenna, St Anselm of Canterbury, Peter Abelard, Averroes, Moses Maimonides, St Thomas Aquinas, John Duns Scotus, William of Ockham.

chapters.title: The Early Modern Era
chapters.note: (1400–1800) [file ch08, ~10,300 words]. Era frame: the Renaissance and the new science; the rationalists (Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz) against the empiricists (Locke, Berkeley, Hume), whose principle "has influenced most philosophical thinking in the English-speaking world ever since." Thinkers: Niccolò Machiavelli, Michel de Montaigne, Sir Francis Bacon, Thomas Hobbes, René Descartes, Blaise Pascal, Baruch Spinoza, John Locke, Gottfried Leibniz, George Berkeley, Voltaire, David Hume, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Adam Smith, Immanuel Kant, Edmund Burke, Thomas Paine, Jeremy Bentham, Mary Wollstonecraft. → orientation for *External-World Skepticism* and *The Problem of Induction* (epistemology).

chapters.title: The Modern Era
chapters.note: (1800s–1950s) [file ch09, ~13,400 words]. Era frame: the 19th-century German "golden age," British reform and American pragmatism, then the early-20th-century reassessment of knowledge under modern science (Frege on logic, Russell on language, Heidegger on the meaning of life). Thinkers: Johann Gottlieb Fichte, Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, James Mill, Arthur Schopenhauer, Alexis de Tocqueville, John Stuart Mill, Søren Kierkegaard, Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels, Henry Sidgwick, Charles Sanders Peirce (spelled "Pierce" in the Contents), William James, Friedrich Nietzsche, Gottlob Frege, Émile Durkheim, Edmund Husserl, John Dewey, Henri Bergson, Alfred North Whitehead, George Santayana, Max Weber, J. M. E. McTaggart, Bertrand Russell, G. E. Moore, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Martin Heidegger, Rudolf Carnap. → background for the existentialism and Nietzsche entries in this subfield.

chapters.title: The Post-Modern Era
chapters.note: (mid-1950s–present) [file ch10, ~13,000 words]. Era frame: postmodernism's roots pushed back to structuralism and, by some accounts, to Nietzsche and Heidegger; after Einstein, "the only certain thing was uncertainty," with Popper extending conjecture to political and social thought. (The frame dates Lyotard's first use of "post-modernism" to 1978 — a popular-level dating; treat as the book's claim, not a settled fact.) Thinkers: Max Horkheimer, Herbert Marcuse, Gilbert Ryle, Hans-Georg Gadamer, Jacques Lacan, Karl Popper, Jean-Paul Sartre, Ayn Rand, Hannah Arendt, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Simone de Beauvoir, Willard Van Orman Quine, Claude Lévi-Strauss, Simone Weil, A. J. Ayer, Alan Turing, Donald Davidson, Peter Strawson, John Rawls, Thomas Kuhn, Paul Feyerabend, Michel Foucault, Noam Chomsky, Bernard Williams, Jacques Derrida, Robert Nozick, Saul Kripke. → background for *Postmodernism and Its Applied Turn* (this subfield), where Foucault and Derrida reappear as book 003 presents them.

prose: # Book map — 027: Daniel Howard-Snyder (ed.), *The Evidential Argument from Evil* (1996)

chapters.title: Preface
chapters.note: [file ch08]. Howard-Snyder: philosophical study of evil has shifted from compatibility ("logical") questions to "the evidential problem of evil"; the volume mixes a handful of the best previously published essays with new work written for it, each new essay refereed by other contributors, aiming at a dialogue a student can follow.

chapters.title: Introduction: The Evidential Argument from Evil
chapters.note: — Daniel Howard-Snyder [file ch09] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*; *The Logical Problem of Evil*. Argues "the problem of evil" is a misleading name for a family of *arguments*. Draws the book's master distinction by its paradigm members: a *logical* argument (Mackie) has a premise saying theism is incompatible with some *known* fact about evil; an *evidential* argument lacks such a premise — its key fact about evil is at most probable or reasonable to believe. Shows Mackie's version fails because his moral principle needs strengthening (MP2), after which compatibility can no longer be ruled out. Then maps the volume's central issues: total evidence, theodicy, the concept of (epistemic) probability, arguments from inscrutable evil, and explanatory arguments.

chapters.title: 1. The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism
chapters.note: — William L. Rowe [file ch11] ★ → both evil entries. The founding statement of the evidential argument: (1) there exist instances of intense suffering an omnipotent, omniscient being could have prevented without losing a greater good or permitting an equal or worse evil; (2) a wholly good omniscient being would prevent any such suffering it could, on those terms; (3) so no omnipotent, omniscient, wholly good being exists. Premise (2) is common ground; premise (1) cannot be *proved* (the burned fawn's suffering is only *apparently* pointless) but is, Rowe argues, rational to believe given the variety and scale of suffering. The theist's best reply is not a direct attack (naming the goods served — which the theist cannot do case by case) but the indirect "G. E. Moore shift": argue from God's existence plus (2) to the denial of (1). Closes by defending *friendly atheism* — some theists are rationally justified in their belief — against unfriendly and indifferent atheism. A note concedes the *logical* form of the problem fails, citing Plantinga's *God, Freedom, and Evil*.

chapters.title: 2. Pain and Pleasure: An Evidential Problem for Theists
chapters.note: — Paul Draper [file ch12] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. A different, *explanatory* evidential argument that never claims any evil is pointless. Against theism Draper sets the Hypothesis of Indifference (HI): neither the nature nor the condition of sentient beings on earth results from benevolent or malevolent actions by non-human persons. Let O report our observations and testimony about pain and pleasure; Draper's claim C is that O is antecedently (epistemically) much more probable on HI than on theism — Pr(O/HI) >! Pr(O/theism) — because of the *biological utility* of pain and pleasure in goal-directed organisms. §III then evaluates theodicies (free will and moral advancement, responsibility, the "infinite intellect" defence) to defend the assumption that theistic stories do not significantly raise Pr(O/theism). If C holds, we have a prima facie reason to reject theism.

chapters.title: 3. Some Major Strands of Theodicy
chapters.note: — Richard Swinburne [file ch13] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. Theodicy defined as showing that evils of the kind and quantity found on Earth are neither incompatible with nor render improbable God's existence. A perfectly good being may allow an evil only if he has the *right* to do so and some good is brought about by allowing it that could not be brought about in any better (logically possible) way. Swinburne then works through goods that, he argues, logically require the occurrence or possible occurrence of evils: the satisfaction of persisting desire (which requires temporary frustration), compassion and kindred responses to suffering, significant free choice between good and evil (natural evil supplies the knowledge of how to harm that makes such choice possible — a strand he flags but sets aside here), responsibility, and more. He is explicit that showing the goods *outweigh* the evils cannot be done conclusively in one paper.

chapters.title: 4. Aquinas on the Sufferings of Job
chapters.note: — Eleonore Stump [file ch14] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil* (theodicy section). Aquinas's commentary on Job does not treat innocent suffering as evidence against God's existence but as a question about how providence operates: Job's friends wrongly suppose providence rewards virtue and punishes sin *in this life*, whereas for Aquinas earthly goods and evils can be justified only by reference to the afterlife, and suffering functions as medicine for a condition that hinders eternal communion with God. Stump's moral: how suffering looks depends on prior views about human happiness and the goal of human life, and those larger issues must be settled before theodicy's prospects can be assessed.

chapters.title: 5. Epistemic Probability and Evil
chapters.note: — Alvin Plantinga [file ch15] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*; *The Logical Problem of Evil*. Distinguishes the pastoral/existential problem of evil from the epistemic one. Concedes the theist cannot say in detail why God permits particular evils — and calls many theodicies "shallow, tepid, and ultimately frivolous" — but denies that this alone threatens rationality. Examines the deductive (Mackie) and probabilistic atheological arguments, finds the prospects of the probabilistic version bleak on standard accounts of probability, argues those accounts lack the resources for the question anyway, and closes by relocating the issue: what matters is not the *propositional* warrant of theistic belief but its *nonpropositional* warrant.

chapters.title: 6. The Inductive Argument from Evil and the Human Cognitive Condition
chapters.note: — William P. Alston [file ch16] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. Grants that the logical argument "is bankrupt" and attacks Rowe's inductive argument at premise (1): the *agnostic thesis* — our cognitive situation (our grasp of possible goods, their values, and the conditions of their realization) is radically insufficient to justify judging that any particular intense suffering is gratuitous, i.e., that God could have no sufficient reason to permit it. The bulk of the chapter catalogues these cognitive limitations.

chapters.title: 7. Rowe's Noseeum Arguments from Evil
chapters.note: — Stephen John Wykstra [file ch17] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. Rowe's inference — we *see no* outweighing good for sufferings like the fawn's, so probably there *is no* such good — is dubbed a "noseeum" argument. Wykstra's CORNEA (Condition of Reasonable Epistemic Access): an inference from "we see no X" to "there is no X" is licensed only when X has reasonable *seeability* — when, if it existed, we could reasonably expect to see it (a dog in a garage, yes; a flea, no). Given the disparity between a creator's vision and ours, God-purposed goods should not be expected to be seeable, so Rowe's argument fails CORNEA. The chapter then refines CORNEA against Rowe's replies, via a dispute about how defeaters work.

chapters.title: 8. The Problem of Evil, the Problem of Air, and the Problem of Silence
chapters.note: — Peter van Inwagen [file ch18] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. Takes up the strongest evidential argument in Draper-style form (a rival hypothesis on which the observed suffering is far more easily explained) and replies that we are in no position to judge what to expect on theism — we cannot assign the relevant probabilities. The diagnosis is supported by two constructed parallel arguments meant to be obviously faulty in the same way: an "evidential argument from air" addressed to an ancient atomist, and an argument from divine silence.

chapters.title: 9. The Skeptical Theist
chapters.note: — Paul Draper [file ch19] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. Names and examines *skeptical theism*: the thesis (ST1) that humans are in no position to judge directly that God would be unlikely to have a morally sufficient reason to permit the evils we find. Draper's complaint is not ST1 itself but the inference from ST1 to the failure of *all* probabilistic arguments from evil: Draper's own ch. 2 argument, for instance, never needs to judge that God probably lacks a sufficient reason, so it is untouched by ST1. Concludes skeptical theists "have not yet solved the evidential problem of evil."

chapters.title: 10. Defenseless
chapters.note: — Bruce Russell [file ch20] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. Sorts evidential arguments into a matrix (inductive vs abductive routes to "there is gratuitous evil," applied to kinds, instances, amounts, or patterns of suffering) and defends them against the charge that our sample of known goods is unrepresentative: goods "beyond our ken" count against representativeness only if there is reason to believe there are any — just as hypothetical unobservable crows do not undermine the inference from "no blue crows observed" (the zagaloops case marks where suspension of judgment *is* required: when we simply have no idea whether our sample is representative).

chapters.title: 11. Some Difficulties in Theistic Treatments of Evil
chapters.note: — Richard M. Gale [file ch21] ★ → both evil entries. Distinguishes theodicy (a defence plus reason to think its possible world is actual) from the weaker *defensive skepticism*, and presses difficulties for both: against defensive skepticism, that we may reasonably judge it improbable in the extreme that there are justifying goods outside our ken, and that if some good justified God we would very likely know of it; against theodicies, charges of epistemic laxness and axiological laxness. (His own book argues no free-will defence succeeds against the *logical* problem for moral evil, but that is expressly not this chapter's concern.)

chapters.title: 12. Reflections on the Chapters by Draper, Russell, and Gale
chapters.note: — Peter van Inwagen [file ch22]. A technical sequel to ch. 8: epistemic probability is best understood as epistemic judgment about non-epistemic (objective) probability, modelled via an "ideal bookmaker"; Draper's evidential challenge is reconstructed in those terms, ch. 8's reply restated against it, and Draper's conditions on how an evidential challenge must be met rejected as "intolerably restrictive."

chapters.title: 13. On Being Evidentially Challenged
chapters.note: — Alvin Plantinga [file ch23] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. A point-by-point examination of Draper's ch. 2: what O is (person-relative), what C claims, and why Plantinga doubts C is true; then the *total evidence* point — other evidence may outweigh O's disconfirmation — and the closing move of ch. 5: the theist may have nonpropositional grounds for belief better than any propositional grounds an argument from evil supplies against it, so whether an evidential argument renders theistic belief unreasonable depends on whether theism is true.

chapters.title: 14. The Evidential Argument from Evil: A Second Look
chapters.note: — William L. Rowe [file ch24] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. Rowe restates his argument around two cases — E1, the fawn ("Bambi"), and E2, the rape and murder of a five-year-old girl ("Sue"): P (no good *we know of* justifies God in permitting E1 and E2) inductively supports Q (no good *at all* justifies God in permitting them), and Q deductively yields not-G. He catalogues four lines of criticism (P unjustified; the P→Q inference weak; defeaters; Q not entailing not-G), answers the objections to P→Q from Alston and Wykstra, and develops the Bayesian version Howard-Snyder's Introduction describes — one that, in a further variant, bypasses Q and argues from P toward the probable falsity of theism more directly. Notably, Rowe now concedes the bare enumerative induction from P raises Q's probability without, as it stands, making Q more likely than not.

chapters.title: 15. The Argument from Inscrutable Evil
chapters.note: — Daniel Howard-Snyder [file ch25] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. Attacks a presupposition of appeals to particular horrors (Ivan Karamazov's tortured children are the epigraph and test case): that if God exists he *must* have a reason to permit *that* evil — that boy, then and there, by that means. By a series of basketball-coach analogies Howard-Snyder argues God need have no reason at that level of specificity, and that the appeal further presupposes a questionable "threshold" thesis — an exact amount of horrific evil such that slightly less would not serve God's purposes. Distinguishes inscrutable evil (we cannot grasp God's reason) from pointless evil (there is none) and argues the first does not justify belief in the second; closes with a Rowe-style Bayesian argument and the silence of God.

chapters.title: 16. Some (Temporarily) Final Thoughts on Evidential Arguments from Evil
chapters.note: — William P. Alston [file ch26] ★ → *The Evidential Argument from Evil*. Alston's self-critical "clean-up" chapter: his ch. 6 tried to do two things that did not blend — neutralize Rowe/Russell-style arguments from refractory cases, and mine theodicies for unexcludable *possibilities* of divine reasons. He now drops the theodicy rehearsal and rests the case on the live possibility of divine reasons unenvisaged by us, which he thinks can "take up the slack, … including 100 percent if needed"; also engages Rowe's new Bayesian argument, conceding it improves on the bare P→Q induction while denying it succeeds.

chapters.title: Bibliography
chapters.note: [file ch27]. Compiled by Alicia McKissen, Kellie Holzer, and Daniel Howard-Snyder; the volume's working bibliography for the debate.

chapters.title: Contributors

chapters.title: Preface
chapters.note: [chunk ch02]. The book examines the presuppositions of moral theories rather than moral issues themselves. Two families of presupposition: *metaethics* (moral concepts, language, thought — are moral judgments true/false assertions or expressions of attitude? is value objective or dependent on us?) and *moral psychology* (moral agents, motivation, reason/desire/pleasure). Every theory presupposes stands on both, usually without stating them.

chapters.title: 1. Objectivity and Subjectivity
chapters.note: (pp. 1–41) [chunk ch02] ★ → *Moral Objectivity and Realism*; *Moral Relativism and Subjectivism*; *Emotivism and Expressivism* (background). Seven interpretations of objectivity: Plato (the Form of the Good — value as impersonal, absolute, intelligible reality); Moore (good a real, irreducible, non-natural property known by intuition, though not a standalone reality); Kant (objectivity as universal rational necessity — the categorical imperative — not a mind-independent realm); Rawls's Kantian constructivism (moral facts constructed by a procedure of reasoning); Nagel's normative realism (objective *reasons*, no occult value-entities needed); Mill (naturalistic objectivity — value grounded in the empirical fact of what is desired for its own sake, i.e. pleasure); Aristotle (objective goods fixed by human nature and its proper function; the practically wise agent). Then monism vs pluralism about value (Kant/Mill monists; Moore and Nagel pluralists). Then the turn to subjectivism: Mackie's queerness argument (objective values would be metaphysically and epistemologically "queer"; the unexplained "because" linking natural features to wrongness; the inertness/motivation objection, with Hume — reason alone "has no hold of the affections"); Mackie's **error theory** (ordinary judgments claim objectivity and are all false). Subjectivity and sentiment: Hume and Adam Smith ground morality in a *common* human sentiment (the general point of view; the impartial spectator) — subjectivist but not "anything goes," and not relativist. Ayer's expressivism stated (moral sentences "do not say anything"; pure expressions of feeling). Blackburn's quasi-realist expressivism (truth *within* the moral point of view). **Relativism**: correctness relative to a culture's norms; no neutral standpoint; the argument from persistent diversity (Mackie: variations are better explained by ways of life than by distorted perceptions of objective values); relativism does *not* entail tolerance. Objectivist replies: disagreement doesn't disprove facts; explanations of diversity are compatible with objective values; the group-specification problem (which group? why not the individual? were the abolitionists wrong?); objectivity is compatible with context-sensitive application.

chapters.title: 2. Moral Theory and Moral Psychology
chapters.note: (pp. 42–73) [chunks ch02 + ch03] ★ → *Moral Motivation: Can Reason Alone Move Us?*; *Self-Interest and Egoism*; *Moral Luck*; *Are Moral Considerations Overriding?* **Moral Motivation**: the stranded-motorist case (ten possible motives); Kant — reason alone can motivate, and action has moral worth only when done because it is right; Hume — "reason of itself is utterly impotent," morals cannot be derived from reason since morals move us and reason doesn't; Korsgaard's Kantian reply (practical identity; reflective endorsement as the source of normativity); Mackie's middle position (universalizability gives no intrinsic authority; opting out of morality is not itself irrational). **Virtue and Motivation**: Aristotle's third way — in the virtuous agent reason and desire are *aligned*; the virtuous enjoy acting well; neither Kantian nor Humean, and not a mixture of them. **Self-interest and Morality**: psychological egoism is neither a definitional truth nor supported by the "every motive is someone's motive" inference; Hobbes's strategy (morality recommended by rational self-interest; the social contract); Hume/Smith/Mill replies (benevolence and the social feelings are real, natural motives; "it pleases me to help" does not make helping self-interested); Plato/Aristotle (justice profits the just by ordering the soul — not narrow egoism); the egoist plays the skeptic's role — that egoist reinterpretations are *possible* does not show they are *true*, any more than global skepticism must be refuted before knowledge claims stand. **What about Luck?** (see the moral-luck entry): Kant's attempt to make moral worth luck-immune (worth lies in rational volition alone; Williams: Kantianism's allure is "an ultimate form of justice… solace to a sense of the world's unfairness"); Mill's indifference (motive bears on the agent's worth, intention on the act's morality — yet intentions and outcomes are both luck-exposed; Nagel: what one *did* often depends on outcome); objective vs subjective rightness as the consequentialist's way of registering luck; luck in character-formation against the virtue approach (Aristotle: upbringing is "all-important," yet virtuous activity, not fortune, controls happiness — though happiness needs external goods). **Are Moral Considerations Overriding?**: impartialist readings of Kantianism and utilitarianism (Williams: the utilitarian agent as "representative of the satisfaction system"); whether equal moral status requires blanket impartiality in attention and care; Hume and Smith on why private connexions properly prevail; Susan Wolf's "moral saints" — a life in which non-moral excellences survive only as happy accidents.

chapters.title: 3. Forms of Moral Theory
chapters.note: (pp. 74–109) [chunk ch03] ★ → *Forms of Moral Theory: Where Is Moral Value Located?* The organising question: what is the *locus* of moral value — consequences, the act itself, character, agreement? **Consequentialism**: rightness fixed by the state of affairs brought about; Mill's principle of utility as the single criterion; secondary principles; no act-type intrinsically right (even deception can be right); the assisted-suicide case used to separate consequentialist from intrinsic-wrongness reasoning; monist (Mill) and pluralist (Moore) variants. **Kantian non-consequentialism**: moral worth "does not lie in the effect"; persons as ends in themselves, of unconditional worth; the categorical imperative as the one criterion; conditional vs unconditional value. **Intuitionist non-consequentialism**: Ross's plurality of self-evident *prima facie* duties (justice, beneficence, gratitude…), known by reason without a special faculty; actual duty all-things-considered is *not* self-evident; Rawls's "unconnected heap of duties" objection and the intuitionist's fidelity-to-complexity reply; Reid on first principles. **The virtue-centred approach**: Aristotle seeks no criterion of right action; the practically wise person as "a sort of standard and measure"; virtue basic, principle derivative (the reverse of Kant and Mill); Hursthouse on the "what ought I to do?" objection; Williams's worry that the view depended on a collapsed teleological picture of nature — virtue with or without "essentialist perfectionism." **Contractarianism**: moral facts (if any) are fixed by rational agreement — Hobbes and Locke (state of nature), Rawls (original position, veil of ignorance), Gauthier (bargaining without the veil), Scanlon (principles no one could reasonably reject); everything turns on how the contracting parties are described. Closing section: all five forms share the idiom of duty while explaining it differently; a theory need not be purely of one type (Mill's struggle to domesticate virtue and justice to utility).

chapters.title: 4. Naturalism and Non-naturalism
chapters.note: (pp. 110–152) [chunks ch03 + ch04] ★ → *Naturalism, Non-naturalism, and the Open Question*; *Emotivism and Expressivism*; *God and Morality*. Naturalism characterised (nothing beyond nature; anti-rationalist epistemology); seven possible relations between moral and natural properties (definition, constitution, dependence, identity-without-definability, full independence, expressive understanding, supernatural grounding). **Moore**: the naturalistic fallacy and the **open question argument** — for any natural candidate D, "Is what is D good?" remains an open question, so good is simple and indefinable. **Reconstructed naturalism**: supervenience by constitution (wetness/H₂O) and the stronger identity thesis (water = H₂O) — necessary connections discoverable by theory, not by meaning, so the open question loses its bite; why Moore himself is not such a naturalist. **Non-cognitivist alternatives**: Ayer's emotivism ("mere pseudo-concepts"; ethical symbols add nothing to factual content) and Hare's prescriptivism (moral judgments as *universalizable* prescriptions); expressivism's consistency constraint (no two exactly alike cases judged differently — Hare's gallery pictures); *subjective* supervenience (uncomfortable loudness) vs objective supervenience. **Hume and naturalism**: "skeptical naturalism" — only natural materials (sentiment, propensity), no value-detection; Blackburn: the expressivist "affirms *all that could ever properly be meant* by saying that there are real obligations." **Reconnecting Facts and Values**: Foot's attack on the fact/value split (evaluative meaning cannot be detached from its object — can one understand *fairness* without understanding it as good?); McDowell's secondary-quality analogy (redness as a disposition to look red, yet genuinely possessed), the "no-priority" view, and judgments being *merited* by their objects. **Aristotle and naturalism**: normative nature and flourishing; the modern Aristotelian retrieval (Foot, McDowell) keeps character and the reason–desire alignment while dropping the teleological metaphysics — contested. **Moral Facts and Explanation**: Harman's challenge (moral facts are explanatorily idle — psychology + non-moral facts explain every moral judgment) vs Sturgeon (Hitler's depravity explains his actions) and Railton (ought-facts as a special kind of is-fact; trial by ordeal). **What about God?** (see the God-and-morality entry): divine command as the guarantor of unconditional obligation; the *Euthyphro* dilemma stated; the theist's three-part reply (commands largely rationally intelligible; a perfect being could only command what is right; some commands' rationale may be beyond us); Aquinas's natural law (morality knowable without revelation — so the atheist can have moral knowledge, differently interpreted); grace, cosmic justice and redemption as what naturalism allegedly cannot supply; the motivation question (is the non-believer *disabled* for moral motivation, or is that a psychological fact about some agents?); faith-based morality is not thereby relativism.

chapters.title: Conclusion
chapters.note: (pp. 153–155) [chunk ch04]. Metaethics and moral psychology raise the "resolution" of concrete problems; analogies with free will, perception, and laws of nature; positions are not finished products to be selected but conclusions to be reached by reasoning.

chapters.title: Glossary
chapters.note: (pp. 156–161), **Bibliography** (pp. 162–165), **Index** (pp. 166–175) [all chunk ch04]. The glossary is substantive (antirealism, cognitivism, constructivism, egoism in its psychological and ethical forms, emotivism, etc.) and was used to check terminology in this slice's entries.
