prose: # Book map — 031: Bill VanPatten & James F. Lee (eds.), *Second Language Acquisition / Foreign Language Learning* (1990)

**⚠ Folder mislabel — read this first.** The extraction folder is named `031 - Language Matters`, and the commissioning brief identified the book as *Language Matters* by Bauer, Holmes & Warren. **The extracted text is not that book.** The cover file (ch01) gives the title as *Second Language Acquisition / Foreign Language Learning*, editors Bill VanPatten and James F. Lee, Multilingual Matters 58 (Clevedon / Philadelphia, 1990), ISBN 1-85359-053-3 (pbk); the title page (p. iii) and the Library of Congress data (p. iv) agree. No text by Bauer, Holmes or Warren appears anywhere in the folder. The volume is the proceedings of a conference held at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, 3–4 April 1987, on the relationship between second language acquisition (SLA) research and foreign language learning (FLL). The map below maps the book that is actually in the corpus; the philosophy-of-language entries built from it follow the book where it actually goes (applied linguistics and sociolinguistics), not the sociolinguistic textbook the folder name promises.

chapters.title: Preface
chapters.note: [pp. ix–xii]. SLA and FLL have been treated as largely unrelated fields; FL professionals filter SLA research through pedagogy and react mainly to Krashen's Monitor / Input Hypothesis, while SLA research has ignored non-Western contexts and indigenized varieties of English (Sridhar & Sridhar; Kachru). Poses the volume's three conference questions: do classroom learners follow different acquisition paths, are the internalization processes fundamentally different, and what is the theoretical relationship?

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.note: [pp. 1–2] ★ → *Second or Foreign?* Summarizes Berns (ch. 1): the foreign/second dichotomy fades from the learner's point of view. The editors' own test case: Spanish in the United States is "foreign" in Alaska (like English in Japan), "second" in Los Angeles and Dade County (like English in India), and in between in Chicago, New York and Dallas (like English in West Germany) — yet learners in the same community can differ in purpose and in whether they seek outside input at all. Berns's chapter, couched in a sociolinguistic framework, is flagged as unique in the volume.

chapters.title: 1. 'Second' and 'Foreign' in Second Language Acquisition / Foreign Language Learning: A Sociolinguistic Perspective
chapters.note: — Margie Berns [pp. 3–11] ★ → *Second or Foreign?*; *Language as a Resource*. Following Stern (1983), a language is "foreign" if learned with reference to a speech community outside the country, "second" if inside it. Sociolinguistic profiles of English in Japan (school subject and "uplifting" pastime; business necessity for the *kokusaijin*), West Germany (school subject, media presence, *lingua franca* across Europe) and India (medium of instruction, law, administration and national literature for 18 million English-using bilinguals) show Japan fits "foreign" and India fits "second," but West Germany fits neither. Berns proposes a **cline** (continuum) of language status with Japan near the foreign pole, India near the second pole and West Germany near the midpoint, plus a third term, **"international,"** for English used between non-native speakers. Closes from the learner's perspective: speech communities need not be native-speaking, and the competence a learner needs depends on the role (tour guide, manager, tourist, opera singer, grandchild) they aim to fill.

chapters.title: Part I introduction: Some Perspectives on SLA/FLL
chapters.note: [pp. 13–16]. Behind the SLA/FLL question "lurks a sociology of each discipline": SLA aims to describe and explain, FL research to influence the classroom. Perspectives are coloured by researchers' language backgrounds (the ESL researcher's syntax-heavy English vs the Spanish researcher's morphology-heavy Spanish — they may not be exploring "the same thing"). VanPatten and Kramsch both want partnership, from opposite directions; Gass and Andersen offer frameworks.

chapters.title: 2. Theory and Research in SLA and FLL: On Producers and Consumers
chapters.note: — Bill VanPatten [pp. 17–26] ★ → *Second or Foreign?* The received relationship is unidirectional: SLA produces theory, FL teaching consumes it, with FLL subsumed as a subset of SLA. VanPatten attacks its three assumptions — that SLA has answers (on input alone, eleven open questions and counting), that SLA is cross-linguistic (of 25 papers in Gass & Madden 1985, only three study learners of languages other than English; the Larsen-Freeman frequency account of morpheme order fails on Spanish *ser/estar*, where communicative value outranks frequency), and that acquisition is not FL's research domain (a historical accident of FL's turn to education schools). Proposes the reverse flow: the FL classroom, where outside variables are already controlled, is the best testing ground for SLA hypotheses, and a theory of SLA should be the overlap of FLL, ESL and untutored acquisition — a product of research in all contexts, not a precursor to it.

chapters.title: 3. What is Foreign Language Learning Research?
chapters.note: — Claire J. Kramsch [pp. 27–33] ★ → *Communicative Competence*; *Second or Foreign?* FLL is the immediate concern of neither SLA (learner as biological/psychological entity; quantitative, ESL-based) nor FL education (teacher- and procedure-centred). Defines FLL by its setting (schooling variables: error correction, turn-allocation, encouraged vs discouraged voice), its object (understanding classroom conditions, not controlling acquisition), its methods (interpretive and ethnographic as well as quantitative) and its **concept of language**: language must not be split into separate skills; it is "quintessentially indeterminate and culturally relative," and cross-cultural communication is "the negotiation of meanings intended and interpreted within an interactional context" (quoting Buber via Cook: meaning is "between us and things"). Learning is a social construct, mediated by Bruner's Language Acquisition Support System rather than Chomsky's LAD alone; Bourdieu: social acceptability "cannot be reduced to grammaticality alone." Ends with an eight-question research agenda, including how learners pass "from one-to-one equivalence to multifunctionality within the L2 system of semantic relations" (Q1) and what "political, economic, ideological and societal forces" govern teaching regardless of research (Q8).

chapters.title: 4. Second and Foreign Language Learning: Same, Different or None of the Above?
chapters.note: — Susan M. Gass [pp. 34–44] ★ → *Second or Foreign?*; *Names, Descriptions and Reference* (anchor only). Internal variables: the fundamental learning processes do not plausibly depend on context (all learners generalize and misinterpret; Stenson's classroom-induced *any*-errors differ in instantiation, not process); Krashen's learning/acquisition distinction cuts across contexts. **Completeness**: native-like mastery may be unattainable by *any* L2 learner — Coppieters (1987) found even "fluent" non-natives' French intuitions diverge from natives'; Swain's immersion children lack *comprehensible output* opportunities. External variables: negative evidence (information that an utterance is deviant) is frequent in conversation and typically direct in classrooms, indirect outside them; input is controlled in both settings (foreigner talk; teacher talk), but some information — e.g. the sentence-interpretation strategies Italian requires (agreement, semantic and pragmatic cues vs English word order) — may be available only from ambient speech, not textbooks. Verdict: quantitative *and* qualitative differences exist; the research question is not same-or-different ("the answer is 'yes'") but the extent and nature of each.

chapters.title: 5. Models, Processes, Principles and Strategies: SLA Inside and Outside the Classroom
chapters.note: — Roger W. Andersen [pp. 45–68] ★ → *Names, Descriptions and Reference* (anchor only). A cognitive-interactionist **Nativization Model**: learners create an autonomous interlanguage system (nativization) that new input must assimilate to, countered by restructuring toward the input (denativization). Cognitive operating principles include **One-to-One** (one intended meaning, one clear invariant surface form — the learner's first entry into a language), **Multifunctionality** (pressure toward forms doing many jobs, driven by Slobin's charges to be expressive, quick and easy), Formal Determinism, Distributional Bias, Relevance (aspect before tense before agreement), Transfer to Somewhere, and Relexification (fall back on L1 structure with L2 words when the target pattern cannot be perceived — the pidgin case). Communication strategies and repair ("learning to say 'Huh?'") complete the model. Andersen assumes the same processes operate across settings, and casts the classroom as the better laboratory for testing them.

chapters.title: Part II introduction: Frameworks and Approaches to Research Issues
chapters.note: [pp. 69–71]. The interlanguage papers (chs. 6–8) all reconcile L2 and FL data at the level of theory, differently: Eubank dissolves context into universal principles × input; Odlin makes metalinguistic awareness itself context-defining; VanPatten distinguishes deep (process) from superficial (output) differences. The language-use papers (chs. 9–11) answer Kramsch's call for classroom-specific research: discourse worlds (Wildner-Bassett — noting her English learners are the FL group and her German learners the L2 group), classroom social roles (Brooks), and topic choice in testing (Bacon).

chapters.title: 6. Linguistic Theory and the Acquisition of German Negation
chapters.note: — Lynn Eubank [pp. 73–94]. Tests acquisition theories against Pinker's **learnability** and **extendibility** conditions (how a transitional rule system could be learned from the input, and how it could then be converted — or unlearned — without negative evidence). Clahsen's processing strategies fail both conditions on German negation data from L2 and FL learners; supplementing the theory with Government-Binding principles and parameters is proposed. Implies a unified theory of acquisition in which contextual output differences trace to universal principles interacting with different input, not to different processes. (Read: opening, framing and editors' summary in full; the negation data analysis sampled.)

chapters.title: 7. Word-Order Transfer, Metalinguistic Awareness and Constraints on Foreign Language Learning
chapters.note: — Terence Odlin [pp. 95–117]. Against universalist claims (Rutherford; Zobl) that basic word order cannot transfer: attested counter-cases (Hawaiian Pidgin English, Bamboo English, Andean Spanish, Pidgin Fijian, Cairo Nubian, Mauritian Bhojpuri, Young People's Dyirbal) show SOV order transferred into SVO contact languages. The scarcity of such transfer is explained instead by observational problems, universal constraints, and above all **metalinguistic awareness**: transfer is likeliest where awareness is low and the language system *unfocused* (Le Page & Tabouret-Keller); FLL, as instruction-focused behaviour, is focused by definition, while SLA may be either. (Read in full.)

chapters.title: 8. The Acquisition of Clitic Pronouns in Spanish: Two Case Studies
chapters.note: — Bill VanPatten [pp. 118–139]. Compares Anthony (14, naturalistic learner in Puerto Rico; Andersen's data) with David (US classroom learner) on Spanish clitic pronouns. Orders of difficulty are broadly shared (*me* early and easy; third-person clitics hard for both); formal instruction isolates forms (David's pre-verbal *se*) without reordering acquisition, and the study cannot speak to rate. Generates eight hypotheses on instruction's impact and the deep/superficial distinction the Conclusion takes up. (Read: introduction, framing and discussion in full; quantitative tables sampled.)

chapters.title: 9. Coexisting Discourse Worlds: The Development of Pragmatic Competence Inside and Outside the Classroom
chapters.note: — Mary E. Wildner-Bassett [pp. 140–152] ★ → *Communicative Competence*. Learners face sociocultural conventions for managing conversation that may conflict with their L1 culture (contrastive / interlanguage pragmatics; Thomas's distinction between **sociopragmatic** and **pragmalinguistic** failure). Using Coulmas's **situational frame** (participants, setting, purpose, contextual restrictions, concomitant activity) and Edmondson's **coexisting discourse worlds** — a unit of talk gets its negotiated communicative value, including its intended speaker meaning or *illocutionary value*, within a world, and several worlds (role-play, real life, native-speaker–learner, teacher–student) operate at once, with one dominantly operant — she reanalyses role-enactment data: the hotel-booking correction that only makes sense as a classroom-world switch; the bicycle-fall correction that negotiates content, not accuracy, where the asymmetry is a knowledge gap, not a power gap; and the learner whose curse "this bloody England" is cancelled by his own smile — pragmatic failure by concomitant activity, and an instance of Harder's **"reduced personality"** of the foreign-language learner, who is not permitted the full repertoire and may not take his own utterance seriously. Classroom learners can risk more under self-parody's suspension of evaluation; learners in the target culture risk negative personal judgements from sociopragmatic failure. Prescription: teach routine formulas explicitly and add metapragmatic instruction.

chapters.title: 10. Foreign Language Learning: A Social Interaction Perspective
chapters.note: — Frank B. Brooks [pp. 153–169] ★ → *Communicative Competence*. Ethnographic study of one university elementary Spanish lesson. Two students doing a paired "communicative" activity in fact reproduce the teacher's interactional patterns — repeat-the-error correction and *muy bien* topic-shift / evaluation signals (the initiation–response–feedback pattern) — turning the simulation into quiz preparation. They had learned these norms by imitation and inference, not instruction (Student A, interviewed later, had not known he did it until he saw the video). Framework (Green & Weade): classrooms are communicative environments with asymmetrical teacher–student relations; contexts are constructed in interaction; **meaning is context-specific**; "communicative competence is reflected in appropriate behaviour"; communication is rule-governed but its rules are implicit and built over time. Students are always learning two things at once: the language, and how to be competent members of the classroom.

chapters.title: 11. On Topic Choice in Oral Proficiency Assessment
chapters.note: — Susan Cameron Bacon [pp. 170–180] ★ → *Communicative Competence* (assessment case). 187 Spanish students, 10-minute oral interviews, free choice among structured topics (guiding questions supplied), unstructured topics and their own. Quality of speech correlated positively with quantity, with choosing unstructured/original topics, and with developing them at length; the top-rated 8% developed unstructured topics far more than structured ones, the bottom 8% the reverse — the able treated the interview as communication (circumlocuting around missing words, e.g. the 24-hours-as-a-cat answer), the weak as a test to escape ("darn! Next card"). Against the ACTFL Guidelines' suggestion that proficiency is not context-bound: context — previous knowledge, experience, interest — is "of prime importance in effective communication." Hymes (1972), quoted at the chapter's head, defines the target as knowing "when to speak, when not, and … what to talk about with whom, when, where, [and] in what manner" — decisions the classroom normally predetermines.

chapters.title: Part III introduction: From Research and Theory to Practice
chapters.note: [pp. 181–183]. Part III's papers seek principles and philosophies, not Monday-morning techniques. Savignon: ignorance of research breeds simple solutions to complex problems. Nattinger and Kiraly each build a curriculum on one research finding (routines and patterns; communicative competence for translators, the translator as "co-creator" of the target text). Schinke-Llano's definitions are product-oriented and her bias explicit (SLA qualitatively superior). Campbell & Lindholm reverse the direction: a curriculum (bilingual immersion) as a challenge *to* SLA research, closing the circle back to Berns — a US population that, allowed full bilingual development, would itself be a foreign-language resource. "What, then, is a foreign language in the United States?"

chapters.title: 12. In SLA/FLL, Nothing is More Practical than a Good Theory
chapters.note: — Sandra J. Savignon [pp. 185–197] ★ → *Communicative Competence*. Keynote defence of theory against the FL profession's impatience with it. Two targets: the **ACTFL Proficiency Guidelines** (1986), promoted as a universally valid, theory-free hierarchy of performance levels — Savignon: the claim to be "not based on a particular linguistic theory" is misleading, and Kramsch's verdict is quoted (behavioural functions over notional development; static content; accuracy over discourse aptitude); and **Higgs & Clifford (1982)**, whose claim that communicative teaching without early error correction produces irreversible fossilization — the "terminal 2" profile — rests, on the seminar audit Savignon reports, on anecdote and "experiential data" rather than rigorous evidence, yet underwrites accuracy-first policy. Positive programme: communicative competence in the broad sense — grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic competence (Lapkin & Swain, 1984) — as the framework in which immersion results make sense; Savignon's own 1971 Illinois study, in which adults given the chance to communicate in French from the start outperformed on communicative measures, as the model of research-led practice; and the rule that recommendations be resisted "in the absence of compelling evidence."

chapters.title: 13. Prefabricated Speech for Language Learning
chapters.note: — James R. Nattinger [pp. 198–206] ★ → *Communicative Competence*; *Names, Descriptions and Reference* (anchor only). Teachers should take their grammar from theories of language *use* (performance), not competence: conventional grammars offer word-lists, correctness prescriptions, or the abstract system of an idealized speaker-hearer, and "the precise relationship between the theoretical competence of an idealized speaker-hearer and the actual language performance of a specific human being is a highly tenuous matter." Acquisition research (Peters; Hakuta; Wong-Fillmore) shows learners begin with **prefabricated** chunks — unvarying *routines* and *patterns* with a movable slot ("wanna + VP") — which are not peripheral to the creative system but its raw material: chunks are stored whole, then segmented ("the words almost audibly cracked," Brown 1973, on *korewa* splitting into *kore* + *wa*) into words and rules; item-learning precedes system-learning at every level. Proposes a curriculum of chunks grouped by function — Social Interactions, Necessary Topics, Discourse Devices — revisited cyclically with widening variation, introduced after automatic control but before fossilization (the optimum segmentation point is an open research question).

chapters.title: 14. A Role for Communicative Competence and the Acquisition-Learning Distinction in Translator Training
chapters.note: — Don Kiraly [pp. 207–215] ★ → *Communicative Competence*. Traditional European translator training rests on Catford's (1965) **equivalence paradigm** — translation as "the replacement of textual material in one language by equivalent material in another language," a search-and-replace for formal equivalents — and produces the silent, product-obsessed classroom Röhl (1984) describes. Against it, a communicative model built on Firth: language behaviour as "a network of relations between people, things, and events," every utterance embedded in a **context of situation** (participants' personalities and persons, verbal and non-verbal action, relevant objects and events, effects of the verbal action). Mapped onto Krashen's distinction: the *learner* consciously identifies elements and equivalence relations inside linguistic subsystems, while the *acquirer* uses language for self-expression inside real contexts of situation. The translator is receiver of the source text and co-creator of the target text, so **translation competence is a special type of communicative competence** — trainees must acquire, not only learn. Closing question: should translators "translate texts or words, messages or linguistic signs"?

chapters.title: 15. Can Foreign Language Learning Be Like Second Language Acquisition? The Curious Case of Immersion
chapters.note: — Linda Schinke-Llano [pp. 216–225] ★ → *Second or Foreign?* Redefines the pair by product: SLA *results in* native-like use, FLL does not. Compares FLEX (exposure only), FLES (some proficiency) and immersion (target language as medium of instruction) for majority-language elementary children. Immersion best matches the facilitative-SLA environment assembled from Krashen (acquisition over learning; comprehensible input at *i*+1; low affective filter), Long (negotiated interaction as the necessary-and-sufficient condition), Swain (comprehensible output) and the silent period — yet immersion pupils still do not reach native-like speaking and writing, and Genesee (1986) is quoted: no student restricted to the school environment is likely to attain "totally native-like competence," because school offers only a limited functional range. Verdict: facilitative environments *can* be approximated in classrooms, and classroom-interaction research is the tool for closing the remaining gap.

chapters.title: 16. Conservation of Language Resources
chapters.note: — Russell N. Campbell & Kathryn J. Lindholm [pp. 226–239] ★ → *Language as a Resource*. The resource: the proficiency linguistic-minority children bring to school free of charge. A hypothetical Korean-American five-year-old in Los Angeles already commands Korean phonology, most morphology and syntax, discourse rules and sociolinguistic rules (lexicon, honorifics, voice and body language varying by interlocutor) — rated, with stated limits (no literacy, thinner semantic networks), at 3+/4 on the US Government scale, where 1,400 hours of Defense Language Institute instruction yields 2/2+. US practice is nonetheless **subtractive** — "an unspoken national policy" requiring children to surrender the ancestral language "as dues" for majority membership — which the authors call misguided for the children's English and education as well as for the national FL resource base. Three additive counter-models, with first-year evaluations: elementary two-way bilingual immersion in California (112 pupils; gains in *both* languages; content learned in Spanish available when tested in English); secondary bilingual partial immersion at Mount Miguel High School (SNS > ISSL > traditional SPANISH streams on listening, reading, writing); and a UCLA–Seoul National University intensive Korean programme for heritage students (proficiency, self-esteem and ethnolinguistic loyalties monitored; analysis incomplete at writing). Programmes are "in their infancy"; the heritage population itself is under-researched and its tests inadequate.

chapters.title: 17. Contexts, Processes, and Products in SLA and FLL
chapters.note: — Bill VanPatten & James F. Lee [pp. 240–245] ★ → *Second or Foreign?* The editors' synthesis. On terminology there is "quite simply" **no consensus** in the volume. Their own resolution sorts the distinction by research domain: it **matters for context** (social situations shape the quality and quantity of input and output); it is **of varying importance for processes** — irrelevant for psycholinguistic processes (the acquisition faculties do not change with environment), important for psychosocial processes (pragmatic and communicative devices do change with discourse context); and it is **useful for products** (eventual proficiency, degree of L1 influence in the product). Hence overlapping circles, not containment: FLL is neither inside SLA nor vice versa. For teaching, research yields **principles that constrain** rather than methods that dictate (Principle 1: learners need communicatively oriented, comprehensible input — with corollaries on interaction, written input, ease and quality). Final admission: no definitive answer has been given; whether SLA and FLL are "the same or different, overlapping or exclusive … is a function of one's own purpose."

chapters.note: [pp. 246–268]. Collected bibliography for all chapters.

Full text throughout; nothing is a stub. The volume is the printed record of the second
annual Kenneth J. Arrow Lectures: two lectures (Sen, Maskin), Arrow's own commentary,
an introduction, and three supplemental papers.

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.note: — Prasanta K. Pattanaik [file ch08] ★ → *Arrow's Theorem and the Possibility of Social Choice*. The state of welfare economics when Arrow published (1950/51): Bergson–Samuelson social welfare functions, the Pareto principle and its incompleteness, the failed compensation criteria. States the theorem in the clean modern form used by this KB: with at least three distinct social states and finitely many individuals, **no social welfare function simultaneously satisfies unrestricted domain, the Pareto principle, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and nondictatorship** — and notes the result "has the flavor of a paradox" precisely because each condition seems plausible.

chapters.title: Opening Remarks
chapters.note: — Joseph E. Stiglitz [ch10]. Occasion-setting for the Arrow lectures.

chapters.title: Arrow and the Impossibility Theorem
chapters.note: — Amartya Sen [ch11] ★ → *Arrow's Theorem…*. The theorem explained and proved in elementary steps; its democratic sting — a dictatorial outcome is "a major embarrassment for that set of axioms," not an acceptable corollary; the informational presumption behind social choice (social judgments must depend, transparently, on individual preferences). Closes by noting what Arrow's framework does **not** accommodate: liberty and the rights of minorities against majorities — Sen invokes Mill on "busybodies": "The importance of liberty may demand going against the objections of numerous 'busybodies.' … It is not accommodated in Arrow's axioms either." Feeds the entry's "where the debate stands."

chapters.title: The Arrow Impossibility Theorem: Where Do We Go from Here?
chapters.note: — Eric Maskin [ch12] ★ → *Arrow's Theorem…*. Recasts the theorem for elections: plurality rule vs Condorcet's majority rule (the candidate beating each other head-to-head), and how the same rankings elect different winners under different rules. Argues the pessimistic reading ("no good election method") is too strong: using Arrow's own criteria, "there is a sense in which we can't do better than majority rule after all" — while conceding that when Condorcet-paradox rankings arise, a tie-breaking rule is needed in practice.

chapters.title: Commentary
chapters.note: — Kenneth J. Arrow [ch13]. Arrow responds to both lecturers.

chapters.title: The Informational Basis of Social Choice
chapters.note: — Amartya Sen [ch15] ★ → *Arrow's Theorem…*. "Any procedure of social choice makes use of some types of information and ignores others": majority decision uses votes but ignores preference *intensities*, social standing, prosperity or penury. The escape route this opens: impossibility results are relative to an informational basis — Arrow's framework excludes cardinal and interpersonally comparable information by construction — so enriching the information a procedure may use changes what is possible.

chapters.title: On the Robustness of Majority Rule
chapters.note: — Partha Dasgupta and Eric Maskin [ch16] ★ → *Arrow's Theorem…*. Paper with abstract: "simple majority rule satisfies five standard and attractive axioms — the Pareto property, anonymity, neutrality, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and (generic) decisiveness — over a larger class of preference domains than (essentially) any other voting rule. Hence, in this sense, it is the most robust voting rule." Shows concretely how Borda/rank-order and plurality violate IIA while majority rule's x-vs-y choice depends only on x-vs-y preferences.

chapters.title: The Origins of the Impossibility Theorem
chapters.note: — Kenneth J. Arrow [ch17]. Arrow's personal account of the steps by which he arrived at the theorem.

036-the-arrow-impossibility-theorem.coverage: Full text present; read in full for the Introduction and both lectures (files ch08, ch11, ch12), and at abstract/argument level for the supplemental papers (ch15, ch16) and Arrow's commentary and origins piece (ch13, ch17). The only defect is the uniform file titling. Note for citers: this book *discusses* Arrow's theorem — the primary statement and proof are in book 037, which this slice treats as the primary rung.

chapters.title: I. Introduction
chapters.note: [file ch10] ★ → *Arrow's Theorem and the Possibility of Social Choice*. The motivating frame: "In a capitalist democracy there are essentially two methods by which social choices can be made: voting, typically used to make 'political' decisions, and the market mechanism." Poses the question whether a method exists for passing from individual tastes to a social preference satisfying "certain natural conditions."

chapters.title: II. The Nature of Preference and Choice
chapters.note: [ch11]. Ordinal preference orderings; the book's foundational exclusion — "the viewpoint will be taken here that interpersonal comparison of utility" is not available — and choice functions and consistency axioms (the social ordering must be connected and transitive: Axioms I and II).

chapters.title: III. The Social Welfare Function
chapters.note: [ch12] ★ → *Arrow's Theorem…*. The formal problem (after Bergson): a *social welfare function* is "a process or rule which, for each set of individual orderings … states a corresponding social ordering of alternative social states." The five conditions are imposed, each presented as an apparently reasonable value judgment expressing "citizens' sovereignty and rationality": **Condition 1** (a set of three alternatives exists that individuals can order in any way — the germ of unrestricted domain); **Condition 2** (positive association of social and individual values — if an alternative rises in every individual's ordering, it does not fall socially); **Condition 3** (independence of irrelevant alternatives — the choice from a set depends only on orderings within it; the rank-order/Borda method's failure is shown by example); **Condition 4** (the function is not *imposed* — no pair's social ranking is fixed regardless of all individual orderings); **Condition 5** (the function is not *dictatorial* — no individual whose strict preferences are always society's, regardless of everyone else). The Benthamite sum of utilities is considered and set aside as requiring the rejected cardinal, interpersonally comparable utility.

chapters.title: IV. The Compensation Principle
chapters.note: [ch13]. The Kaldor–Hicks–Scitovsky compensation criteria examined as candidate welfare functions — and shown capable of contradiction (a change and its reversal can both pass the test), sharpening the suspicion that no satisfactory construction exists.

chapters.title: V. The General Possibility Theorem for Social Welfare Functions
chapters.note: [ch14] ★ → *Arrow's Theorem…*. The theorem chapter. **Theorem 1 (two alternatives):** majority decision satisfies the conditions and always yields a social ordering — with two alternatives, possibility holds. **Theorem 2 (General Possibility Theorem), as printed:** "*If there are at least three alternatives which the members of the society are free to order in any way, then every social welfare function satisfying Conditions 2 and 3 and yielding a social ordering satisfying Axioms I and II must be either imposed or dictatorial.*" (The extraction prints "Conditions 2 and 8" at this point — an OCR/typographical artifact in the file; the surrounding proof text confirms the operative conditions are the five of ch. III, and the chapter's own summary states the result as: assuming Conditions 2 and 3 and Condition 1's freedom over three alternatives, "either Condition 4 or Condition 5 must be violated.") Arrow's interpretation, verbatim in substance: "If we exclude the possibility of interpersonal comparisons of utility, then the only methods of passing from individual tastes to social preferences which will be satisfactory and which will be defined for a wide range of sets of individual orderings are either imposed or dictatorial." His indicated escape: relax the *range of admissible orderings* — suppose individual orderings are known in advance to satisfy restrictions, and seek functions satisfactory only on that restricted range.

chapters.title: VI. The Individualistic Assumptions
chapters.note: [ch15]. What happens under restrictions on tastes: two conditions on individual preference scales (single-peakedness-type assumptions enter here) and what social welfare functions they permit.

chapters.title: VII. Similarity as the Basis of Social Welfare Judgments
chapters.note: [ch16]. Complete unanimity and near-unanimity as a basis: if individuals' orderings are sufficiently similar, collective judgments become possible — the domain-restriction route developed.

chapters.title: VIII. Notes on the Theory of Social Choice, 1963
chapters.note: [ch17]. Arrow's survey of the literature that grew up around the theorem in the decade after 1951 ("When the first edition of this book was prepared, the relevant literature was summarized in four pages").

What the files actually contain, complete and internally coherent, is a different book: **_Gilles Deleuze and Film Criticism: Philosophy, Theory, and the Individual Film_**, edited by Dominic Lash and Hoi Lun Law (Palgrave Macmillan, Palgrave Film Studies and Philosophy series, 2023; ISBN 978-3-031-33304-0; DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-33305-7, printed in every chapter file). The wrong book was evidently downloaded or extracted under book 039's number, and the extraction pipeline then titled every file from the folder name, so the mislabelling is invisible until the text is opened. The map below therefore maps the book that is actually there (its proper home would be aesthetics / philosophy of film, outside this slice), so the corpus audit can reassign or re-extract it.

039-philosophy-of-law.coverage:
Every file was inspected and its opening read; the identification is not in doubt (editors, series, ISBN, and per-chapter DOIs all agree). Of the book the folder *claims* to hold — Feinberg & Coleman, *Philosophy of Law*, 7th ed. — coverage is **zero**: no chapter, excerpt, or stub of it exists in the corpus. Secondary defects in what is present: the Part III chapter numbers in the extraction titles are scrambled (the *Chimes at Midnight* chapter is titled "3." though its DOI suffix `_7` shows it is chapter 7), and the three part dividers are 23-word stubs.

**Consequence for this KB (the law decision):** because book 039 contains no philosophy of law at all, it supports **no** jurisprudence problem entries, and no `entries/philosophy-of-law/` subfield was created from this slice. The corpus's only genuinely legal-philosophical lecture, Carneades' *What is a Deodand? (Philosophy of Law)*, is a single definitional lecture about a historical forfeiture practice; it stages good questions about responsibility for the harms done by things one owns, but with no textbook or primary text behind it in the corpus there is no faithful way to build positions-and-arguments entries from it (see the slice report). The correct fix is upstream: re-extract the real Feinberg & Coleman, and re-home this Deleuze volume under its own number.

quality.intro:
# Data quality — readings corpus extraction audit

*Compiled 2026-10-18 from the epistemology pilot and the nine subfield build reports. Every problem found while actually reading the corpus for the KB, per book. The builders worked from what genuinely exists; nothing below was papered over.*

sections.heading: Headline: the catalogue itself is wrong about 8 of 26 books
sections.md:
The folder names (and the original textbook list) misidentify these books. In each case the extraction is of a real book — just not the catalogued one. All KB book maps declare the true identity at their head.

| № | Catalogued as | Actually is |
|---|---|---|
| 004 | *On Manners* (etiquette anthology) | Melissa Manners, *The Pannell Witch* (2022) — a self-published historical novel; zero philosophy content |
| 010 | Day, *The Philosophy of History: An Introduction* | Dolphin, *Teaching Geology Using the History and Philosophy of Science* (Springer, 2024), complete |
| 012 (folder 1) | Kymlicka, *Contemporary Political Philosophy: An Introduction* | Goodin & Pettit (eds.), *Contemporary Political Philosophy: An Anthology*, **3rd ed. (2019)**, full text. No Kymlicka *Introduction* exists in the corpus |
| 013 | Taylor, *Metaphysics* | Beebee & Sabbarton-Leary (eds.), *The Semantics and Metaphysics of Natural Kinds* (Routledge, 2010) |
| 018 | Solomon, *Existentialism* | Walter Kaufmann (ed.), *Existentialism from Dostoevsky to Sartre* (authorship correction) |
| 020 | Cahn (ed.), *Philosophy of Religion* anthology | Eckel, Speight & DuJardin (eds.), *The Future of the Philosophy of Religion* (Springer, 2021) |
| 031 | Bauer, Holmes & Warren, *Language Matters* | VanPatten & Lee (eds.), *Second Language Acquisition / Foreign Language Learning* (Multilingual Matters 58, 1990) |
| 039 | Feinberg & Coleman, *Philosophy of Law* | *Gilles Deleuze and Film Criticism* (eds. Lash & Law, Palgrave, 2023) |

Downstream consequences: no philosophy-of-law subfield could be built (039); no Day-based philosophy-of-history entries (010); no Taylor-based free-will / personal-identity / time entries — the matching Carneades lectures stand unassigned in `lectures-index.md`; no manners/etiquette entry (004); the religion slice has no classical anthology (020).

sections.heading: Per-book detail
sections.md:
- **001 — Sophie's World.** No book text at all: only `_meta.json` (provenance "reconstructed", no epub/PDF found) and a 35-chapter TOC compiled from Wikipedia/LitCharts. Orientation/source-ladder use only.
- **002 — 李天命的思考藝術.** Folder interleaved with a different book: 38 of 59 files are *The Simpsons and Philosophy*; only 21 files are Li's Chinese text (~200k chars). Two formulas lost in ch. 10 §IV(B) (angle-bracket fallbacks kept and flagged in the translation); one Robbins formula lost in ch. 9's notes (flagged, not invented). TOC source is the folder's ch04 file; page numbers lost except one (p. 99).
- **003 — Cynical Theories.** Extraction complete and clean. Limitation is stance (advocacy), labelled in map and entry.
- **004 — "On Manners".** See headline table. 51 files, ~72,000 words, all inspected; "philosoph-" occurs 3×, all incidental.
- **005 — Bullshit and Philosophy.** File titles name each chapter's *last* section heading, not the chapter (e.g. file "ch07 — Bullshit and Truth" is Chapter 1). ch01/ch02 are empty stubs; ch28 is collected endnotes; ch29's summary misspells "Frankfort". Frankfurt's *On Bullshit* itself is **not in the corpus** — the bullshit entry uses Frankfurt only as presented by the volume's essayists, and says so.
- **006 — Russell, Problems of Philosophy.** Each chapter split into a near-empty title stub + a content file under a generic "Vook Classics" name; the Preface is counted as chapter 1, shifting all numbers +1 against the book's own numbering. ch36 empty; ch35 publisher credits. Text otherwise complete.
- **007 — Human Knowledge.** A reconstruction, not the book: 12 of 39 readings usable in full/part, 25 citation stubs, editors' General Introduction absent. Specific losses: ch06 (Descartes) is a failed fetch — 4 KB of Wikisource navigation boilerplate, no *Meditations* text; ch18 (Quine, "Two Dogmas") and ch20 (Gettier) have corrupted bodies (header intact, ~2.5 KB binary garbage; both from ditext.com) — the Gettier loss is the corpus's most consequential single gap; ch05 (Aquinas) is prologue/contents only; the whole A Priori section (chs. 23–25) is stubs. Several "selections" are entire works: Locke's *Essay* (ch7), Leibniz's *New Essays* (ch8), James's essay collection (ch13), the Aristotle volume (ch2), and ch14 = the entire *Problems of Philosophy*, duplicating book 006. OCR faults inside usable text: Reid (ch11) VI §24's key credulity sentence is interleaved with unrelated page matter mid-sentence; Kant *Prolegomena* (ch12) §2 has an apparent misprint ("analytical" where the argument requires "synthetical"); Leibniz (ch8) OCR misreadings are scattered but the Preface argument is legible.
- **008 — Gödel, Escher, Bach.** Stratified extraction: ch01–15 files are TOC fragments only; usable text begins at ch18 (= Ch. I); ch21 contains Chs. IV *and* V; ch44 duplicates ch35; ch37–43 are endnotes; heavy OCR noise in formulas.
- **010 — "Philosophy of History".** See headline table (Dolphin, complete, ~124k words, 12 files). Extraction quality of the Dolphin text is good; nothing of Day exists anywhere in the corpus.
- **011 — What Darwin Got Wrong.** Complete (Terms + chs. 1–9). File titles are internal section headings rather than chapter titles (recoverable from the TOC files); two non-identical TOC files; part dividers counted as chapters.
- **012 — Anthology, 3rd ed. (folder "012 - Contemporary Political Philosophy").** Full text, 49 chapters in 9 parts. File titles are epub-spine labels and unreliable — files titled "References" carry the next chapter's body; chapters split across files. Ch. 45 (Luban) suspiciously short (14k chars) — possibly excerpted.
- **012 — Anthology, 2nd ed. (folder "… - An Anthology").** A reconstruction: 46 of 48 readings are citation stubs; only Thomson (ch21) and Berlin (ch24) are full text. `toc.md` is a sourced reconstruction (LOC/IA/Google Books, 2026-10-04); its 1st-edition list is partly inferred.
- **013 — "Metaphysics".** See headline table. Extraction itself excellent: the Contents page (file ch06) lists all 12 papers + authors; 12/12 papers full text (~5,800–11,600 words each); ch01–ch07 are front-matter fragments; ch20 contributors; ch21 index has some garbled diacritics. PLAN.md's earlier note ("every chapter mis-titled") was the same fact seen from the wrong side: the shared title is the volume's real title.
- **018 — "Existentialism".** See headline table (Kaufmann ed.). Camus present only as the concluding chapter of *The Myth of Sisyphus* (the absurd's definition and the suicide argument are absent — the entry declares this); Dostoevsky is Part One only; two files are Pickle Partners publisher matter.
- **019 — Beyond Good and Evil.** Full text, all 296 §§ (Kaufmann tr., Vintage 1989). Only defects: generic identical filenames and part-title stubs.
- **020 — "Philosophy of Religion".** See headline table. Extraction clean: 18 files, titles match the printed contents, all chapters full text.
- **021 — Anarchy, State, and Utopia.** Ch. 7 split across files ch18+ch19; ch19 opens mid-argument with no heading. All 26 files share one title — cite by internal chapter heading.
- **024 — On Liberty.** The folder holds two works from the combined 1879 edition: *On Liberty* (files ch03–ch07) plus *The Subjection of Women* (files ch09–ch12); the *Subjection* files have bare colliding titles ("CHAPTER I", …).
- **025 — The One-Minute Philosopher.** No text at all: only `_meta.json` + a MARC-505-reconstructed TOC (owner instruction 2026-10-04; no obtainable ebook, final verdict 2026-10-13). Title-level coverage only; no entry could be built from it.
- **026 — 100 Great Thinkers.** Clean text but popular level: reports positions, rarely argues them. Contents misspells Thales of "Melitus" and Charles Sanders "Pierce"; its Lyotard-1978 dating is the book's claim, flagged in the map.
- **027 — The Evidential Argument from Evil.** All 29 files carry the identical book title; chapter identity recoverable from in-text author headings + the contents file (ch07), which agree. Files ch01–ch06 and ch10 are front-matter fragments (17–199 words). All 16 papers otherwise full text — no stubs or corruption.
- **028 — Dimensions of Moral Theory.** Text complete (~73,135 words) but chopped into 3 mega-chunks whose file titles name a section near each chunk's *end*; both seams verified continuous, no text lost. ch01 is cover only; ch05 a duplicated TOC stub.
- **031 — "Language Matters".** See headline table. Extraction is page-per-file (284 files); 4 single pages missing — pp. 12, 72, 184 (blank/divider) and front-matter p. viii — no chapter content lost; no stubs or corruption.
- **036 — The Arrow Impossibility Theorem.** Uniform file titles (as with 021/037) — cite by internal chapter heading, never filename alone.
- **037 — Social Choice and Individual Values.** Main text intact (files ch05–ch19), but ~180 files (ch20–ch201) are footnotes shattered into separate fragments. Theorem 2's statement in file ch14 contains a misprint ("Conditions 2 and 8"); entries cross-checked it against the chapter's proof summary and interpretation passage.
- **039 — "Philosophy of Law".** See headline table. Extraction titles were generated from the folder name, hiding the mismatch; Part III chapter numbers are scrambled in the titles.

sections.heading: Lectures (global)
sections.md:
- Auto-captions are unreliable as text throughout: Goodman's "grue" rendered "green"/"gru"/"Grün"; Frege as "Fraga"; Quine as "Quin"; *salva veritate* garbled. All entries distill, never quote.
- Two lectures have **no transcript at all**: `gGO8A9wiI5o` (Teleological Arguments From Analogy) — which blocks any design-argument entry — and `VsmQdpD21iE` (What is Expected Consequentialism, 18 words).
- The Gettier lecture mis-titles Gettier's paper ("Is Knowledge a Grounded True Belief?").
- The "Experience Machine" lecture actually presents Vonnegut's "UFO machine" against hedonism and flags itself as not a skeptical scenario; used only as a series neighbour.
- The Moore's Open Question lecture outruns its source (concludes goodness "is not a property / does not exist" via a Russell spin; Moore and Jacobs hold good is real and indefinable) — flagged in the entry.
- The *Can Theists Be Moral* lecture's title promises 5 arguments; it covers 4 plus a general objection — noted in the entry.

shortfalls:
- **Philosophy of law:** not built (039 is the wrong book).
- **Missing books:** Taylor's *Metaphysics*, Day's *Philosophy of History*, Kymlicka's *Introduction*, Bauer et al.'s *Language Matters*, Cahn's religion anthology, Feinberg & Coleman's *Philosophy of Law* — none exists in the corpus; their problem areas (free will, personal identity, time, historical knowledge, language & identity, linguistic relativity, jurisprudence) have lectures standing by in the index, unassigned.
- **Textless books:** 001 and 025 have no extractable text at all.
- **Book 002 translation remainder:** chs. 11–12 were read in the Chinese and used (fallacies entry) but their translations are still outstanding — the entry, map, and translation README all flag this; chs. 5, 6, 14–21 and the ch. 13 note tail (27–38) are untranslated and unused.
- **Book 007's contemporary sections** are stubs, capping epistemology's modern coverage; Gettier's paper and Quine's "Two Dogmas" are corrupted files.
- **Design argument:** unbuildable for now — its only lecture has no transcript.
